Text-to-image models can produce harmful content, so concept erasure methods suppress unwanted ideas inside the model. Most erasure tools and their attack tests were built for Stable Diffusion, and they transfer poorly to newer rectified flow transformers such as Flux. The authors present ReFlux, the first attack designed specifically for that newer architecture.

Their key observation is that erasure on Flux leans on attention localization, so they attack exactly that property. A reverse-attention optimization reactivates the suppressed signal while keeping attention stable. Velocity guidance and a consistency objective protect the rest of the image layout during the attack. Across extensive experiments, ReFlux reliably revived erased concepts, giving the field a benchmark for judging erasure robustness.
arxiv-2510-00835:
Hegland and Kaya estimate probability densities through optimal control theory in this 2025 arXiv paper on statistics and applied mathematics. Density estimation turns a sample of data points into a smooth curve describing the underlying distribution. Histograms are crude, and kernel methods depend heavily on tuning choices. The authors instead pose the estimation task as a variational problem and then recast it as a multi-stage optimal control problem.

Applying the maximum principle reduces the optimality conditions to a two-point boundary-value problem with interior conditions. They propose a numerical scheme for its discretized form and test it on synthetic and real datasets. The real examples are the eruption intervals of the Old Faithful geyser and the measured speeds of a group of galaxies. Comparisons with the popular statistics package R show the control-based estimates behave sensibly against a standard reference.
arxiv-2510-01235:
Ghosh and Tewari send AI agents into the scientific literature to harvest materials data that humans never tabulated. Materials discovery stalls because experimental results hide inside article prose and tables. Their workflow reads roughly ten thousand full-text papers on thermoelectric materials automatically.

Specialized agents split the work, with dynamic token budgets balancing accuracy against cost. Table parsing handles the numbers that prose-only extraction misses. A hand-checked benchmark of fifty papers showed the strongest model extracting properties with high fidelity. The harvest yielded tens of thousands of normalized property records, ready for machine learning. Thermoelectric properties pair with crystal structure in every record. The cheaper mini model nearly matched the flagship's accuracy. Zero-shot agents avoided task-specific training entirely. Normalized units make the records merge cleanly with existing databases. Literature mining turns archives into fuel for discovery at scale.
arxiv-2510-01335:
Das, Iosue, and Albert build a harder measuring stick for methods that guess the hidden dimension of data. Learning works, the manifold hypothesis says, because real data hugs a low-dimensional surface inside huge spaces. Estimators of that dimension disagree wildly, and existing benchmarks are too easy to referee them.

Their quantum-inspired benchmark embeds topologically tricky spaces with known true dimension. Curvature can be bent and noise added along endless families of test cases. Estimators performed notably worse here than on standard benchmarks at equal effort. A fractal spectrum even let the team probe effective dimension beyond whole numbers. Homogeneous spaces from quantum optics supply the raw manifolds. Six estimator methods faced the new benchmark in this study. Weak correlations with data properties limit easy explanations of failure. Hofstadter's butterfly contributed a genuinely fractal test case of its own.
arxiv-2510-01535:
Yang warns that a popular tool for studying extremes can mislead the very studies that rely on it. Tail index regressions link how heavy an outcome's tail is to other measured factors. Finance and climate work lean on such models to price rare disasters and plan for them.

Conditioning on extreme outcomes quietly distorts the data, he shows. In linear models the usual full-rank requirement can collapse, since tail samples push factors toward constants. The surviving data cluster where the tail index is smallest, and densities elsewhere fade toward zero. Flexible local fits then converge painfully slowly. Practical fixes close the paper for applied users. The estimation sample is not random, which is the root of every symptom. Similar traps may lurk in neighboring methods for extremes. Knowing the failure modes is the first defense for honest risk work.
arxiv-2510-01735:
Ma, Wang, and Alkhalifah tackle seismic velocity model building in this 2025 geophysics paper. Knowing how fast sound travels underground helps explorers map buried structures before drilling. Classic inversion methods refine a model through many slow rounds of computation. The authors instead train a neural operator to jump straight from a rough model to a sharp one.

Their network also reads time-lag migration images, which add fine detail about rock layers. Because neural operators learn mappings between functions, the model works across different grid sizes. On synthetic tests it rebuilt fine structures and complex geology, even salt bodies unlike its training cases. On real survey data collected offshore Australia, its models matched well-log data closely. The method beat standard multi-scale inversion on accuracy and finished each prediction within seconds.
arxiv-2510-02035:
Mihailescu, Alushi, Di Candia, Felicetti, and Gietka teach quantum sensing at critical points in this 2025 tutorial. Quantum sensors can measure more finely than classical tools, but noise and scaling problems stall progress. Near a quantum phase transition, a system grows sharply sensitive and its correlations turn nonclassical. Critical metrology treats that touchiness as a resource rather than a flaw.

The tutorial builds the ideas through examples, step by step. Readers meet the main strategies that exploit critical behavior across physical systems. Special care goes to how the gains scale with the resources spent, the figure of merit that decides usefulness. The authors also face noise and setup hurdles honestly. Worked protocols show where the critical edge survives real-world settings. For researchers entering the field, the article maps both the promise and the fine print. In the end, criticality becomes an engineering dial.
arxiv-2510-02435:
Monnee, Weigand, and Wiesner revisit odd corners of string theory moduli space. Their 2025 physics paper studies type II zero limits. These limits arise in Type IIB compactifications on Calabi-Yau threefolds. Mirror symmetry, the usual guide, cannot describe them. Earlier work tied them to a weakly coupled heterotic string. That dual picture uses a K3 surface times a tiny torus. The new paper asks what extra sectors decouple from gravity there. The authors argue those sectors are spacetime filling NS5-branes. The branes wrap the small heterotic torus in their picture.

A fingerprint supports the claim in the math. At leading order, the prepotential grows exponentially with the dilaton. Applied to K-point limits, the picture fits two famous conjectures. Distance and Emergent String conjectures both hold in this frame. Light towers come from the weakly coupled string itself. String duality gains another checked consistency case.
arxiv-2510-02535:
Qadri and co-authors release a dataset for predicting how people respond to health campaigns. Their 2025 paper introduces PHORECAST for public health outreach research. Communities react to health messages in sharply different ways. Models that guess those reactions could guide better campaigns. No rich dataset existed for testing such guesses. PHORECAST pairs health messages with individual response data. Demographics, personality traits, and context ride along with each case. Both personal reactions and community engagement patterns are tracked. Vision-language models can train and be graded on the resource.

Early results expose limits in current large models. They miss much of the nuance in human responses. Individual level reasoning showed clear promise in the tests. English speaking participants dominate the current data. That skew limits global use until the set grows. Health agencies need tools that respect audience diversity. This dataset gives model builders a fair test bed.
arxiv-2510-02635:
Fang, Sheng, Su, and Zhou solve very high dimensional diffusion equations with a localized random method. Their 2025 numerical analysis paper avoids meshes and derivatives entirely. Such equations model heat flow, pricing, and control problems. Size crushes grid based solvers completely. Their method rewrites the equation as a forward-backward random system. Small particle clouds fit local linear regressions on the fly. A decoupling trick solves the gradient system without matrices. A Newton step handles the curved scalar part. Everything runs pointwise and in parallel.

Tests reached ten thousand dimensions for Burgers' equation. The Allen-Cahn case ran in one hundred dimensions. All experiments ran on a personal laptop. Rigorous error analysis backs the algorithm. Convergence comes with proofs, not just plots. Simple parts, sampling plus regression, carry the weight. High dimensional modeling gains an interpretable workhorse. No neural network training is required anywhere.
arxiv-2510-02735:
Zheng and Lamperski analyze a workhorse method of machine learning. The method is projected stochastic gradient descent. It trains a model by taking small noisy steps downhill. After each step, it projects the result back into an allowed region. The loss surface is non-convex, so it has many bumps and valleys. The authors want hard numbers on how fast the method settles down.

Their key move is a new way to measure progress. They measure how far the gradient sits from a set called the Goldstein subdifferential. This measure matches the standard one when no constraints are present. It also works without variance reduction tricks. The team proves rates for steps in expectation. For well-behaved random data, they prove the first high-probability rates of this kind. The results cover both fresh random data and data with memory.
arxiv-2510-02835:
Bu and co-authors build a health prediction tool that people can actually read. The data are daily lifelogs from phones and wearables. The goals are to predict sleep quality and stress for each person. Big neural networks do this well, but they hide their logic. The team's framework is called SASL. It is a sparse linear model that adapts to each subject.

SASL splits effects into global patterns and person-specific ones. A careful elimination process keeps only features that pass strict tests. Scores that fall into ordered bands get a regression step, then a threshold step. When a case looks hard, a small boosted-tree model helps through a confidence gate. On a data set of about 450 days from ten people, SASL matched black-box rivals. It used far fewer parameters. It also placed in the top one percent of a public contest.
arxiv-2510-02935:
Desbuis and co-authors compare how Hall currents waste energy. In a magnetic bar, a sideways Hall voltage appears across the current. Many assume that sideways flow costs no power. The team wired Hall bars to a side load circuit. They measured current, voltage, and power as the load changed. Three magnetic materials took part in the tests. Each makes its Hall effect by a distinct route.

One bar was an altermagnet with an inborn, topological effect. One was a ferrimagnet with an extrinsic effect. One was a plain ferromagnet showing the planar Hall effect. The power curves for all three overlapped closely. Each followed the same law in load and Hall angle. Dissipation is set by charges piling at the edges, not by the inner mechanism. The result held to leading order in the Hall angle. It reshapes how engineers should model Hall device losses.
arxiv-2510-03235:
Smaldore collects the many disguises of one small, famous strongly regular graph. The graph NO+(6,2) has twenty-eight vertices in its standard form. Each vertex touches fifteen others in a rigid pattern. Adjacent pairs share six neighbors, non-adjacent pairs share ten. Its symmetry group is an orthogonal group over the field of two elements. The note lists constructions that all yield this same graph. Each construction lives in a different ambient setting.

One version starts from points outside a Klein quadric. Another takes points on the quadric minus a generator plane. Lines in a small projective space give two more versions. Point-line antiflags and non-degenerate conics give others still. A symmetric-matrix model over the binary field closes the list. Such catalogs help researchers translate between geometric languages. A problem stated in one setting may crack open in another.
arxiv-2510-03335:
Daigavane and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on training diffusion models that build point clouds, such as molecules and proteins. A point cloud has no fixed facing, so training spins each sample at random. Before scoring a cleaned guess, software rotates it to line up with the true sample. The team asked what that alignment step really does to learning. Their answer ties the best possible denoiser to a distribution over rotations.

The math shows that alignment picks the most likely rotation under that distribution. For low noise, alignment acts as the simplest rough version of the ideal denoiser, which explains why it works so well. The authors then derive sharper versions for the low noise range. Tests confirmed that alignment stays good enough at the noise levels that matter most in training. The result reassures builders of molecule generating models and shows where care could still pay off.
arxiv-2510-03435:
Conte presents a 2025 arXiv paper in mathematical physics on a discrete version of the sixth Painlevé equation. Painlevé equations form a family of nonlinear equations with ties to geometry. The q-discrete variant steps by scaling rather than by smooth change. A Lax pair, linked matrix equations, proves such a system is integrable and exposes its structure. Earlier pairs broke down in a special case where two key values coincide.

Conte builds several matrix Lax pairs whose entries stay rational and behaved even in that special case. Fifteen pairs appear in the count of the study. The pairs rest on the same two by two matrix frame as the case. One open question is whether a change of basis can reveal a symmetry in these pairs. A symmetry would link the equation to discrete Bonnet surfaces, a topic in surface geometry that the author flags for future work.
arxiv-2510-03535:
Anderson, Chung, and Choi present a 2025 arXiv paper on faster stand in models for physics simulations. Reduced order models compress a simulation into a small latent space where equations mimic the real dynamics. The LaSDI framework learns those equations, but forcing them during training degrades how well the model rebuilds the full data. Their multi stage version, mLaSDI, trains extra decoders in sequence. Each new decoder cleans up the leftover errors of the stages before it.

Tested on the Vlasov equation, a model of plasma physics, the staged method beat standard LaSDI across many network shapes. Prediction errors fell, and training time shrank at the same time. Keeping the interpretable latent equations matters, since scientists can read them like ordinary physics. Plasma and fusion teams need fast surrogates they can still trust and inspect. Sequential correction offers a trick for other latent dynamics frameworks facing the same accuracy squeeze.
arxiv-2510-03935:
Javed and Husain present this 2025 arXiv paper on black holes in semiclassical gravity, where matter is quantum but gravity is classical. The usual semiclassical Einstein equation is hard to define cleanly, so the authors use a Hamiltonian version. Their system couples classical gravity to a quantum scalar field, replacing matter terms with averages taken in a fixed quantum state. They look for still, spherically symmetric solutions.

Solving the equations numerically, they find both boson stars and regular black holes with no central singularity. The solutions come in flat, de Sitter, and anti-de Sitter flavors, describing different far-away space behaviors. Two famous nonsingular proposals, the Bardeen and Hayward black holes, turn out not to solve their equations. Parts of the matter averages spill beyond the horizon, which the authors read as a kind of quantum hair. The work tests which imagined regular black holes a concrete semiclassical theory allows.
arxiv-2510-04135:
Gong and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on the energy appetite of AI coding agents and how to trim it. A single agent run on a real software task can consume over one hundred thousand tokens across many model calls. Optimizing code with such an agent can burn more energy than the optimized code ever saves. The authors treat agent configuration itself as a multi-objective optimization problem.

Their framework, GA4GC, searches agent hyperparameters and prompt templates for Pareto-optimal trade-offs. The objectives balance agent runtime against the performance and correctness of the code produced. On the SWE-Perf benchmark, the search improved the trade-off frontier dramatically and cut runtime by over a third while improving correctness. Temperature emerged as the single most influential hyperparameter. As coding agents scale across organizations, configuring them for sustainability becomes an engineering requirement, not a nicety.
arxiv-2510-04235:
Derkachov, Isaev, and Shumilov present this 2025 arXiv paper analyzing a family of Feynman integrals known as conformal four-point ladder diagrams. Such integrals appear in scattering amplitude calculations across quantum field theories and dimensions. The authors use an operator representation from conformal quantum mechanics to expose the family's structure. They study its symmetries together with identities that shift loop order and spacetime dimension.

In even integer dimensions, the shift identities reduce every case to the two-dimensional one, where a striking factorization holds. For a specific choice of propagator powers, that factorization pays off concretely. The integrals become linear combinations of classical polylogarithms with rational-function coefficients. The authors explore the structure of those resulting expressions in detail. Closed forms like these feed precision calculations in conformal field theory and gauge theory amplitudes. Ladder diagrams are a benchmark family: methods that tame them usually generalize to harder integrals.
arxiv-2510-04635:
Emanuele Sobacchi wrote this 2025 paper on how cosmic rays trap themselves near shock fronts. Charged particles gain energy at supernova remnant shocks, but the highest energies demand stronger magnetic turmoil than standard theory gives. Cosmic rays streaming ahead of a shock stir the plasma, and that stirring can scatter them back. Sobacchi studies an acoustic instability fed by the pressure gradient of the rays themselves. Sound like waves grow as they ride toward the shock.

He ran magnetohydrodynamic simulations to test the expected growth rates of the instability. The runs measured the scale and energy of the magnetic wiggles the process creates. For particles whose spiral radius is about a thousandth of the precursor length, diffusion dropped sharply in the results. Stronger trapping near the shock means particles cross it more often and gain more energy per visit. The paper gives the acoustic route a footing it lacked before.
arxiv-2510-04935:
Guoxin Chen and twelve co-authors present MARS, a multi-agent system for deep research tasks, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The system splits work between fast, intuitive processing and slow, careful reasoning, much like the two modes of human thought. It also pulls in outside tools such as web search and a Python interpreter.

The fast side reads and sums up large piles of outside material. The slow side reasons over those short briefs instead of raw text. A shared training scheme tunes both sides together across many rounds of tool use. On Humanity's Last Exam, a very hard benchmark, MARS improved scores by 3.86 percent over its base model. Across seven knowledge-heavy tasks, its average gain reached 8.9 percent. The split keeps reasoning sharp without drowning it in raw search results.
arxiv-2510-05035:
C. Ian Short announces an upgrade to a suite of star-modeling codes in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Chroma+ suite computes stellar atmospheres and the spectra they emit. Earlier versions treated a star's atmosphere as locally flat. Real stars are spheres, and that shortcut distorts predictions near the edge of the visible disk.

The new version solves the radiative transfer equation for a spherical atmosphere directly. It uses the analytic formal solution published by Chapman in 1966. Short shows how the change affects computed observables such as surface brightness profiles. One demo computes the light curve of a planet crossing its host star. All of the codes are freely available through the OpenStars site.
arxiv-2510-05435:
Arango-Restrepo and Rubi study how tiny particles move faster when reactions run on their surfaces. Their 2025 paper looks at catalytic Janus particles, which carry a reactive coating on one side only. The particles sit in liquid with no outside gradient pushing them. Standard theories credit this motion to self-generated flows, yet they fail to match many lab results.

The authors argue that surface reactions create excess energy and lasting surface stress. That energy adds to normal heat motion and pushes diffusion past the thermal limit. Their model tracks how diffusion first rises and then falls as reaction rate grows. It matches data from coated nanoparticles and enzyme-covered vesicles powered by ATP. Two methods, one based on stored energy and one on lost energy, give the same answer. The result offers design rules for building synthetic swimmers with tuned mobility.
arxiv-2510-05535:
Liu and colleagues improve how machines choose which data features to keep. Feature selection strips redundant inputs, which speeds models and clarifies their decisions. Order should not matter in that choice, yet many learning methods quietly depend on feature order. Their 2025 paper builds a selection framework that ignores order by design.

The framework embeds chosen feature sets into a continuous space that treats reorderings alike. A reinforcement learning agent then searches that space for stronger subsets. This journal version adds a federated mode for data split across separate clients. Clients fuse their knowledge without sharing raw records, and uneven sample sizes get fair weights. Partner teams joined from Arizona State and RMIT. Broad experiments confirm gains in accuracy, robustness, and speed across many settings. The team released its code and data openly for other groups to test.
arxiv-2510-05635:
Murphy and colleagues adapt vision models at test time with no optimization at all. Models degrade when deployment data shifts, as with corrupted or stylized images. Existing adaptation methods need backpropagation, many samples, or fussy hyperparameters. Their 2025 method, NEO, fixes shift by re-centering embeddings.

Latent-space geometry shows shifted samples drift away from the source cloud's center. Moving target embeddings back to the origin restores much of the alignment. With one batch of sixty-four samples, ViT-Base accuracy on corrupted ImageNet rose from about fifty-six to fifty-nine percent. At five hundred twelve samples, NEO beat seven rival methods on three benchmarks. Calibration metrics improved alongside raw accuracy in their tests. Adapting from a single class even helped the other nine hundred ninety-nine. It also cut inference time sharply on small edge devices.
arxiv-2510-05835:
Bhuiyan and colleagues automate code smell detection with tuned machine learning. Code smells flag poor design that accumulates technical debt in large systems. Traditional detectors suffer low accuracy and poor generalization across datasets. Their 2025 framework benchmarks eight classifiers on six smell types.

SMOTE oversampling first balances the heavily skewed training data. Pearson correlation then selects features and removes redundancy. Grid, random, and Bayesian searches tune each model's hyperparameters. AdaBoost reaches perfect accuracy on the evaluation. Random Forest and XGBoost follow at about ninety-nine percent each. Two smells sit at class level and four at method level. Accuracy, F-measure, and confusion matrices all support the rankings. Early detection supports proactive maintenance before debt compounds further. The novelty is the integrated pipeline, not any single algorithm.
arxiv-2510-05935:
Bal-Ghaoui and Sabri make feature selection deliberate through a team of language model agents. High-dimensional data hurts both interpretability and efficiency in machine learning pipelines. Single-agent LLM selectors give selections without structured reasoning or justification. Their 2025 LLM-FS-Agent stages a role-based debate among agents instead.

Four roles structure the deliberation: Initiator, Refiner, Challenger, and Judge. Each feature's relevance is argued collectively, producing human-readable rationales. Evaluation targets IoT intrusion detection on a 2024 benchmark dataset. The method matches or beats LLM-Select and PCA baselines across subset sizes. A near-optimal subset emerges at just twenty features. Downstream classifier training time drops by about forty-six percent on average. Transparency and efficiency improve together rather than trading off. Cybersecurity is the test domain, but the architecture is domain-general. Accountability in automated pipeline decisions is the deeper motivation.
arxiv-2510-06035:
Týbl and Neumann build a single search space for neural network designs in a 2025 machine learning paper. Architecture search usually works inside one family, such as convolutional networks or transformers. Their system, called UniNAS, places both families and their hybrids inside one graph-based framework.

Inside UniNAS, each network block is a small directed graph whose wiring can change freely during search. The authors add a search algorithm that walks this space with help from a training-free accuracy estimate. Their search found a new network, UniNAS-A, which beat leading hand-crafted designs under identical training rules. It won across classification, detection, and segmentation tasks. The team also releases a toolkit with a fixed training and scoring protocol, so future search methods can be compared fairly.
arxiv-2510-06235:
Scholz and three co-authors report their Algonauts 2025 Challenge entry predicting brain responses to movies in a 2025 neuroscience paper. The challenge asks models to forecast fMRI activity while people watch films. Good predictions need representations capturing sight, sound, and language together.

The team combined features from language models, video encoders, audio models, and vision–language models. They mixed off-the-shelf networks with fine-tuned variants and enriched text with transcripts and summaries. They explored stimulus tuning and fine-tuning for the language and vision components. A stacked regression merged the individual predictions into one forecast. Competing as team Seinfeld, the submission ranked tenth. All code and resources are public. The entry shows which multimodal ingredients help brain encoding models, a step toward predicting perception rather than classifying stimuli.
arxiv-2510-06335:
Alsubaie and five co-authors reconstruct MRI scans from heavily undersampled data with a conditional diffusion model in a 2025 medical imaging paper. MRI is diagnostically vital but slow, a problem in time-sensitive care. Undersampling speeds acquisition yet adds artifacts reconstruction must remove without inventing anatomy.

Their framework embeds the measurement model into every reverse diffusion step. Iterative data-consistency corrections keep images faithful to the actual measurements. Training uses paired undersampled and ground-truth scans, unlike unsupervised score-based approaches. Earlier diffusion methods applied consistency only as post-processing, if at all. On fastMRI, the framework consistently beat recent deep learning and diffusion methods. It won on structural similarity, signal-to-noise, and perceptual LPIPS scores alike. The perceptual metric tracks what radiologists actually see. Marrying generative flexibility to MRI physics offers a principled route to trustworthy faster scans.
arxiv-2510-07035:
Tengwei Song, Min Wu, and Yuan Fang teach models chemistry from both diagrams and 3D shapes of molecules. Their 2025 paper presents FlexMol, a pre-training framework for molecular representation learning. Representations drive drug discovery and materials design. Earlier methods demanded paired 2D and 3D data for every molecule, which is costly or sometimes impossible to get.

FlexMol handles single-modality and paired inputs in one framework. Separate encoders handle the diagram and the geometry, sharing some parameters for efficiency. A decoder generates features for whichever modality is missing. Training used about three point four million paired examples plus two million single-modality ones. Despite the modest data, FlexMol beat much larger models on benchmarks. Those rivals trained on more than ten million samples. Modality-specific strengths survive the unification, the authors report. The flexible design fits real chemistry datasets, where full records are the exception rather than the rule.
arxiv-2510-07135:
El Khoury and colleagues build the first structured test of quick learning for satellite image models. Their 2025 paper concerns models that link images with text. Such models often do well with no task training at all. How well they adapt from just a few labeled examples was unclear. The team set out to measure that skill in a fair, repeatable way.

The benchmark covers ten sets of satellite scene photos. It tries five common adaptation methods on three leading models. Models with equal no-training scores often behaved very differently once few examples were given. One model, GeoRSCLIP, adapted best across most settings. No single adaptation method won everywhere. The authors share their code so later teams can compare methods on the same footing. The results guide groups that must label land from scarce examples.
arxiv-2510-07335:
Chattopadhyay reconstructs a modified gravity theory from holographic dark energy assumptions. The 2025 paper works with f(G) gravity, where the standard gravity action gains a function of the Gauss-Bonnet invariant. Two dark energy inputs drive the reconstruction. One is a generalized holographic form, the most flexible in its family. The other is Barrow holographic dark energy, which tweaks entropy with a fractal-style exponent. A power-law expansion history is assumed throughout.

The reconstructed gravity function satisfies a key criterion for a realistic model, the author reports. Both reconstruction routes are then checked against the four standard energy conditions. The Barrow case reduces to ordinary holographic dark energy when its deformation vanishes. Reconstruction studies like this translate a desired cosmic history into the gravity law that would produce it. They help screen modified gravity ideas before facing telescope data.
arxiv-2510-07435:
Feng, Afroz, and Sarma model how adopting generative AI tools affects developer burnout. Their 2025 study applies the Job Demands-Resources model, a standard lens in occupational health. Four hundred forty-two developers across organizations and experience levels answered a survey. Statistical modeling linked adoption patterns to demands, resources, and exhaustion, while open-ended answers supplied context. The headline result cuts against the productivity hype: adopting these tools raised burnout, mainly by increasing job demands. Faster output expectations and mandate-driven rollouts piled pressure onto developers.

Two factors softened the blow. Job resources, such as autonomy and support, buffered the added demands. Developers who viewed the tools positively also fared better, reframing adoption as opportunity. The authors warn that hype cycles distribute resources unevenly across teams. One respondent compared the tools to a chisel in a craftsman's belt: valuable when chosen, harmful when forced without training.
arxiv-2510-07535:
Lee and co-authors fix speculative decoding, the trick that lets a small draft model race ahead of a large one, for the long inputs where it currently fails. Their 2025 paper shows that standard methods were benchmarked on short contexts and degrade badly as inputs grow. One leading method actually slows generation below plain decoding at long lengths. The team releases LongSpecBench to measure the real regime. Their model, OWL, rethinks the drafter: a recurrent network conditioned only on the last token's state. Nothing in its design ties it to a particular input length, and it generalizes across scales.

A special token enriches the verifier's representation fed to the drafter. A hybrid algorithm mixes tree and non-tree drafting. The payoff is about five times the accepted draft length of the leading rival on long inputs. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2510-07635:
Kiyohara and four coauthors wrote this 2025 machine learning paper on recommender systems. Streaming and shopping services add new items all the time. Showing those new items helps long-term engagement, but untried items can also perform badly. Standard training from logged data can push a system toward unsafe choices. The authors want exploration of new items with a firm safety guarantee.

They first build a method called Safe OPG, which trains from logged data only. In tests, Safe OPG almost always met the safety requirement while rivals broke it badly. Yet Safe OPG proved too cautious, exposing a tradeoff between safety and exploration. Their second framework, DEPSUE, relaxes the safety margin gradually across a few deployments. That staged approach let the system explore new items while keeping performance safely above the required floor. Music services face this same choice each time new songs appear.
arxiv-2510-07835:
Jiang and Pan wrote this 2025 paper on defending language models against jailbreaks planted through fine-tuning. A few harmful examples in fine-tuning data can undo a model's safety training. Attackers also disguise harmful queries with templates the alignment stage never saw. Existing defenses fail on those unseen disguises. Yet the authors note that models can still tell disguised harmful queries apart inside their embedding space. Their defense, MetaDefense, acts on that signal twice.

Before generation, it screens the incoming query for harmfulness. During generation, it watches the partial reply and can stop output early. Special prompts train the model to make both judgments itself. Across three model architectures, MetaDefense beat current defenses on seen and unseen attack templates. It also kept performance on benign tasks competitive. Guarding both the door and the conversation, the authors argue, closes the window that fine-tuning attacks exploit.
arxiv-2510-08135:
Cheng, Wu, and Wu wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper giving weak-line quasars a physically grounded definition. These quasars show strikingly weak high-ionization emission lines despite normal continua, and earlier definitions were ad hoc. The authors analyzed over three hundred seventy thousand quasars from a major sky survey. They examined outliers in three established relations. Two thresholds in carbon line strength emerged, near nine and nineteen angstroms.

Below the lower threshold, quasars qualify as weak-line objects. They show enhanced blueshifts, defy the usual line-strength relation, and are X-ray weak in nearly half of cases. Between the thresholds sit bridge quasars with transitional behavior. Line attenuation grows with ionization energy, as a shielding gas model predicts: a thick inner disk blocks the photons powering high-ionization lines. The authors map the populations onto slim versus standard disk regimes.
arxiv-2510-08435:
Rui Zhao, Zihan Chen, and Zemin Zheng tackle high-dimensional bandit problems with two kinds of sparsity in a 2025 arXiv paper. Contextual bandits choose actions from context data and learn from rewards, balancing exploration and exploitation. In high dimensions, learning is cursed unless the problem is sparse somewhere. Past methods assumed sparsity either in the model weights or in the context covariance eigenvalues, not both.

The authors introduce a pointwise reward estimator that adapts to either sparsity type automatically. Their algorithm, HOPE, builds on this estimator to choose actions round by round. Theory shows HOPE improves regret bounds in the classic single-sparsity settings studied before. It also handles two new mixed settings where both sparsity types appear together, a first in this literature. Experiments confirmed HOPE beat existing methods across the scenarios tested.
arxiv-2510-09135:
Bacha and George trace a vision model's mistakes back to the exact patches of the exact photos it trained on, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Explanations of AI decisions usually take one of two forms: which pixels in this image mattered, or which training examples mattered. The authors argue the two should be fused. Their notion, training feature attribution, blames or credits a specific region inside a specific training image for a given test prediction.

Experiments on vision datasets show the explanations are fine-grained and specific to each test case. The method surfaced individual harmful training examples that were actively driving misclassifications. It also exposed spurious shortcuts, cases where the model had learned to lean on an irrelevant patch pattern instead of the object itself. Those shortcuts stayed invisible to conventional attribution tools. They offer the technique as a debugging lens for data curation.
arxiv-2510-09335:
Shaoyun Bai and Jae Hee Lee define new operations in algebraic geometry in a 2025 arXiv paper. They work in quasimap K-theory, a framework that counts maps between spaces with a K-theoretic weighting. Adams operations are classic tools of K-theory, and the authors build quantum deformations of them, meaning versions adjusted by the counting data of the theory.

The new operations mirror quantum Steenrod operations, which come from symplectic geometry, on the K-theory side. The authors check that the operations fit with the theory's difference module structures in both the Kähler and equivariant settings. Sample computations use localisation for a cyclic group action. They also identify the operations with curvature operators of certain connections, verify, at roots of unity, a K-theoretic quantum Hikita conjecture, and propose a purely algebraic-geometric definition of quantum Steenrod operations.
arxiv-2510-09435:
Hyunin Lee and eleven co-authors, among them Somayeh Sojoudi, rethink a core mechanism of recommendation models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Cross-domain sequential recommendation predicts what a user will want next by aligning their behaviour across different domains, such as shopping and media. Cross-attention is the standard tool for that alignment, usually read as keeping useful parts of one sequence and dropping redundant parts.

The authors identify a second behaviour they call orthogonal alignment, where cross-attention finds genuinely new information that the input sequence did not contain. Across more than three hundred experiments, models performed better whenever the input and output of cross-attention stood orthogonal, meaning unrelated in direction. The effect emerged on its own, with no constraint forcing it. The team links it to better scaling, since models with cross-attention beat size-matched baselines in accuracy per parameter.
arxiv-2510-10035:
Zhang and co-authors rethink how language model workflows are optimized in this 2025 arXiv paper. The usual approach is a global search: generate candidate workflows, score each with one number, and keep the best. The authors argue this suffers from information collapse.

A single success-or-failure score throws away the rich detail in each multi-step run, so the optimizer cannot see how failures are distributed or where they cluster. The team reconceives the problem as distributional: model the pattern of failures, then refine the workflow against that pattern. Their failure-driven refinement uses the shape of what goes wrong, not just how often. That extra signal should guide fixes that a scalar score would never suggest.
arxiv-2510-10435:
Ming Gong proves a long assumed result about particles drifting through a wavy energy landscape in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Lifson-Jackson formula gives the effective diffusion constant, a measure of how fast particles spread, for periodic landscapes that repeat evenly. Many believed the formula failed for landscapes that almost repeat but never quite do. Gong had earlier claimed that it still holds in that harder setting.

Here he proves the claim exactly, using the mean first passage time, the average time a particle needs to reach an absorbing boundary. He solves the equation for that time exactly with the Jacobi-Anger expansion. The proof shows the diffusion constant follows from the first passage time at the center point. He argues the result extends to other potentials and higher dimensions, and discusses when a well defined diffusion constant exists at all.
arxiv-2510-10635:
Dengke Chen and six co-authors optimize how light gets from an optical fiber into a photonic chip, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Efficient, reliable coupling is arguably the central practical problem in integrated photonics, affecting data links, quantum processors, and more. A common approach pairs an inverse taper on the chip with a lensed fiber. Many taper designs exist, but the lensed fibers themselves have been little optimized. The team fills that gap with a co-optimization strategy.

They refine the shapes of both the taper and the lensed fiber together. Crucially, they put the genuine fiber shape into their simulations, capturing its true emission profile instead of the usual Gaussian approximation. They fabricated and characterized many fibers and silicon nitride tapers. Simulation and experiment agreed well, both reaching coupling efficiencies above 80 percent per facet. They close by summarizing the best choices, ready for deployment in modern CMOS foundries.
arxiv-2510-10835:
Yichen Xu and three co-authors rigorously estimate how much physical noise fault tolerant quantum circuits can tolerate, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The threshold theorem promises that quantum computation can be made reliable if the error rate sits below a critical value. Transversal gates implement logical operations efficiently, but they spread errors and can lower that threshold. The team generalizes a statistical mechanics mapping from quantum memories to circuits with transversal gates.

For two toric code blocks joined by a transversal CNOT gate, they quantify two error spreading mechanisms. With persistent bit flip errors, the gate lowers the optimal threshold to 0.080, a 26 percent drop from the memory threshold of 0.109 in their simulations. Including syndrome errors gives a conservative threshold of at least 0.028, a modest reduction from 0.033. They extend the mapping to all transversal Clifford gates and to arbitrary CSS codes, showing each gate alters the model only locally in time.
arxiv-2510-10935:
James Tian asks when a kernel defined on short words can be extended to all words, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The kernels here are operator valued and positive definite, living on a free semigroup, where words are strings of symbols with no simplifying rules. Only words up to a fixed length are given at first. Tian finds a clean sufficient condition on the given piece: a one step dominance inequality that compares the kernel at neighboring lengths.

When that inequality holds on the interior, a global extension always exists, and it preserves both the interior data and the dominance property. Matching the kernel on the boundary is harder. Tian introduces a shift consistency condition, a compatibility requirement between overlapping pieces of the data. He proves this condition is sufficient to guarantee a global extension that agrees with the original kernel on its entire domain.
arxiv-2510-11035:
Longjie Guo and nine co-authors test whether AI agents fall for the same interface tricks as people, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Computer use agents now click through real websites autonomously, so manipulative design aimed at humans may also steer them. The team built SusBench, a benchmark of dark patterns: interface designs that deceive users into unintended actions. They took nine common dark pattern types from existing taxonomies and injected them into 55 real consumer websites through code changes, creating 313 evaluation tasks.

A study with 29 participants showed the injected patterns looked highly realistic; most people never noticed the tampering. Five state of the art agents then took the benchmark. Both humans and agents proved particularly susceptible to preselection, trick wording, and hidden information, while resisting more overt patterns. The findings feed three audiences: agent builders, regulators, and researchers who might use agents as stand ins for humans when auditing deceptive design.
arxiv-2510-11335:
Take a time series and keep what it tracks, but redraw how it wiggles by copying a second series. That swap is style transfer, a tool long used on pictures and text. Nagda and a large team bring the idea to time series data in this 2025 arXiv paper. This matters most where real records are scarce, such as patient care or power use. Made-up series can then add training cases and let teams test new scenes.

DiffTSST first splits a series with convolutional encoders into two parts, one for content and one for style. A diffusion step, guided by attention and taught without labels, then joins content with style to make a new series. Tests in both words and numbers show the swap works as hoped. Adding such made-up series to training data helped spot odd patterns where real cases were few.
arxiv-2510-11435:
The Bohm-Hiley view of quantum mechanics explains quantum behavior through a quantum potential that guides particles, but extending it to relativistic electrons described by the Dirac equation is not easy. Calum Robson takes up that extension in this 2025 arXiv foundations paper, written in dialogue with the late Basil Hiley's research program. His main tool is Clifford algebra, the geometric algebra Hiley championed as the right language for basic physics.

Robson first discusses the geometry of the Dirac equation as clarified by Clifford algebras. He then rewrites the two-dimensional Clifford form of the Dirac wavefunction in polar form, splitting it into size and phase-like parts. That rewriting shows new behavior arising from nonlocality, effects tied to global winding rather than local values. He closes by discussing how the Dirac equation relates to the nonrelativistic Schrödinger equation within this algebraic Bohmian picture.
arxiv-2510-11735:
M. M. Fedin and A. A. Morozov prove a result about the structure of diagonal operators in quantum theory. Diagonal operators act on the basis states of a system labeled by the U(N) symmetry group. Their 2025 arXiv paper shows that any such operator can be broken into products built from smaller matrices and tensors. The focus falls on the analytic shape of the resulting formulas and on the symmetries it carries.

The authors draw diagrams that make the structure of each decomposition easy to see at a glance. They also examine the symmetries of their construction in detail. The aim reaches well beyond pure mathematics. Factoring big operators into small ones can shrink the cost of quantum computing algorithms, where diagonal operations appear all the time. The authors also point to uses in crystallography, biological analysis, and tuning artificial intelligence models.
arxiv-2510-11835:
Yiming Liu and four colleagues ask why CLIP makes a better vision backbone for vision-language models than DINO. CLIP learns from image-text pairs, a form of language supervision, while DINO learns from images alone. CLIP also trains on far more data, so either factor could explain its edge. Their 2025 arXiv paper separates the two by pretraining both models under identical conditions: same architecture, same dataset, same training setup.

Controlled this way, the two reach similar accuracy on ImageNet classification. Their internal representations differ in character, though. CLIP captures high-level meaning such as object categories and text, while DINO responds more to colors and styles. Plugged into vision-language models and tested on twenty question-answering benchmarks, CLIP wins on text-heavy tasks. DINO edges ahead slightly on purely visual ones.
arxiv-2510-11935:
Eleftherios Tachtsis and Eliza Wajch build exotic topological spaces in a universe without the axiom of choice. Set theorists ask whether a crowded Hausdorff P-space can exist when choice fails. Crowded means no point sits isolated; a P-space is one where countable intersections of open sets stay open, a rare and delicate property. Their 2025 arXiv paper answers the question inside several models of choice-free set theory.

Their construction starts from a set X and a topology woven from its finite and countable subsets. In ZF alone, for uncountable X the space is crowded, zero-dimensional, and Hausdorff. If X is also quasi Dedekind-finite, the space is a P-space. One test case turns on whether the first uncountable ordinal is regular. Sharpest of all, the axiom of countable choice for finite sets proves exactly equivalent to one P-space statement.
arxiv-2510-12035:
Heather M. Russell and Julianna Tymoczko give a sprawling diagram calculus its missing skeleton. Webs are planar labeled graphs encoding invariant vectors for quantum representations of the special linear Lie algebra. The theory grew case by case: classical for rank two, formalized by Kuperberg for ranks two and three, then extended several ways. Their 2025 arXiv paper formalizes Fontaine's version of webs, prized for computation but lacking foundations.

The key structure is strandings, a global decoration of the web's edges. First, the authors give a state-sum formula that builds invariant web vectors directly from stranding orientations. Second, they list a complete set of relations and prove them, tying strandings to binary labelings, the established local data. Third, they show through applications and examples how strandings make computations tractable. Diagram chasers gain both a construction kit and a rulebook.
arxiv-2510-12135:
Peng Wang and Tianshu Wu sort a black hole's ringing tones into the trustworthy and the treacherous. Gravitational-wave detectors read a merged black hole's quasinormal modes to test general relativity, assuming those frequencies are stable under small nudges. Recent work showed a secondary potential barrier, forming a well outside the horizon, can destabilize the spectrum. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks what remains when the well is gone.

Spectral instability, they find, can persist even after the potential well vanishes. A distinct family of unstable modes emerges, separate from the stable modes huddled near the potential peak by the photon sphere. Yet time-domain simulations soothe the worry: early ringdown waveforms stay dominated by the stable modes, with unstable ones contributing only subdominantly. What telescopes actually record is governed by the most stable tones. Black hole spectroscopy remains robust: nature plays the stable notes loudest.
arxiv-2510-12335:
Orfanoudakis and co-authors charge electric vehicles with a reinforcement learning algorithm that respects the physics of the power grid, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Uncoordinated charging by many vehicles can push voltages in distribution networks outside safe limits. Earlier learning based controllers often ignored physical grid constraints or scaled poorly to large fleets.

Their algorithm embeds a differentiable power flow model inside a standard deep reinforcement learning method and shapes rewards around voltage, a design they call physics informed. Vehicles can then supply real time voltage support while still meeting user charging demands. On the IEEE thirty four bus and one hundred twenty three bus test networks, the method beat model free learning and optimization baselines in constraint management, user satisfaction, and economic measures. It converged faster and used samples more efficiently, and it held up under uncertain, overloaded conditions with hundreds of vehicles.
arxiv-2510-12635:
Zhang and co-authors teach language model agents to edit their own working memory as part of doing a task, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Long horizon tasks overwhelm an agent's limited context with distracting or irrelevant material. Existing memory methods are external heuristics, bolted onto the agent rather than learned by it.

Their Memory as Action framework makes memory editing an explicit action inside a unified policy, trained by reinforcement learning to balance curation against long term task success under resource limits. Editing memory breaks the ever growing prefix that standard training assumes, creating what they call trajectory fractures. Their Dynamic Context Policy Optimization algorithm restores stable end to end training by segmenting trajectories at memory actions and assigning advantages at the segment level. Jointly optimizing reasoning and memory management both cut computational consumption and improved task performance, with curation strategies adapted to the model's own capabilities.
arxiv-2510-12935:
Verma and co-authors predict a family of topological materials in this 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum spin Hall insulators conduct spin currents along their edges without loss, but strong spin-orbit coupling usually mixes spins and spoils the perfect quantization of that conduction. The family studied here has a seven-layer square-octagonal structure combining a metal, a silicon-like element, and a pnictogen element.

Their calculations find that versions with phosphorus, arsenic, or antimony are topologically nontrivial with a robust, large energy gap and nearly quantized spin Hall conductivity, while nitrogen versions are ordinary insulators. An emergent approximate symmetry protects the spin conservation behind the clean quantization. Some arsenic and antimony compounds also host quasi-flat electronic bands and multiple high-order van Hove singularities, points where electron density of states spikes, which could amplify correlation effects.
arxiv-2510-13035:
Alhulaymi and co-authors develop a framework for routing waves through complex enclosures in this 2025 arXiv paper. Controlling how linear waves scatter inside irregular multiport geometries, spaces with several entry and exit channels, has long been hard beyond simple symmetric setups. Their idea uses interference itself as the routing mechanism.

They show that perfect steady-state routing is possible at any frequency. It takes tuning geometric parameters until several complex eigenfrequencies coincide on the real axis. The states are constrained scattering processes. In them, destructive interference suppresses a chosen set of outgoing channels. Focusing on electromagnetic waves, simulations showed high-discrimination routing and signal demultiplexing inside a chaotic cavity with a known number of tunable scatterers. The authors note the same approach could serve filtering, power division, directional lasing, and even quantum matter waves.
arxiv-2510-13135:
Nilsson summarizes lessons from perturbation theory for bumblebee gravity in this 2025 arXiv proceedings paper from a Lorentz and CPT symmetry symposium. Bumblebee models are vector-tensor theories of gravity that spontaneously break Lorentz invariance, the principle that physics looks the same to all moving observers. That makes them a testbed for modified gravity.

Working with cosmological perturbation theory on an exact de Sitter background, Nilsson reports a key finding. Non-minimal coupling to gravity introduces a ghost mode, an unstable excitation, unless a degeneracy condition links the coupling and the parameters. A meter-scale deviation from general relativity, missed by earlier work, shows a preferred direction in infinitesimal translations, where earlier studies had suggested none. The metric is displaced by a preferred-frame amount. A generalized linear momentum density can grow huge near the horizon. Nilsson also constrains the bumblebee coupling using gravitational waves and the black hole shadow.
arxiv-2510-13235:
Zhang and colleagues add language prompts that evolve with their targets in this 2025 arXiv paper on multi-object tracking. Tracking must follow many targets through video while keeping identities straight despite occlusion and crowding. Textual descriptions can help, but existing methods take static descriptions from language models, which cannot adapt as targets change state and sometimes hallucinate.

Their framework, EPIPTrack, builds two prompt types. Explicit prompts translate spatial motion information into natural language, giving spatiotemporal guidance. Implicit prompts combine pseudo-words with learnable descriptors to form individualized knowledge representations of each target's appearance. Both are dynamically adjusted through a text encoder as target states change, and a discriminative feature augmentor strengthens visual and cross-modal features. On the MOT17, MOT20, and DanceTrack benchmarks, EPIPTrack outperformed existing trackers across diverse scenarios.
arxiv-2510-13335:
Fomin and co-authors settle open questions about layered crossing minimization, a graph drawing problem. In this 2025 arXiv paper, vertices sit on two or more parallel lines, joined by straight edges. The task is to order the vertices so that edges cross as rarely as possible. A decade-old question asked whether fast algorithms exist when the crossing budget is small. The team works in parameterized complexity, which measures cost against a chosen parameter.

The authors give a subexponential fixed-parameter algorithm for the two-layer case. They extend the result to three layers with a similar fast algorithm. For five or more layers, they prove no such fast algorithm exists, assuming a standard hypothesis about hard problems. They also fully resolve whether small kernels exist for these problems. A kernel is a small compressed version of an input that keeps the answer unchanged.
arxiv-2510-13435:
Zhao, Noheda, and Sarott grow ferroelectric barium titanate films on silicon with clean switching behaviour. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets energy-efficient memory and logic devices. Ferroelectric oxides promise much on silicon, but a structural mismatch degrades the interface. That mismatch also spoils the switching traits that devices depend on. The films are single-crystalline, with atoms ordered across the whole layer.

The films switch with no imprint, low coercivity, and high remanent polarization. Coercivity measures how hard the polarization is to flip. They also show no fatigue after more than ten billion switching cycles. The key is an inserted strontium tin titanate layer on a buffered silicon wafer. This layer eases the thermal strain that silicon imposes on the film. It also adds mild compressive strain that stabilizes polarization pointing out of the plane. The authors see a path to low-power, silicon-compatible non-volatile memory.
arxiv-2510-13635:
Piva and co-authors report evidence for a field-induced Lifshitz transition in the Weyl semimetal CeAlSi. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies a magnetic material whose crystal lacks a centre of symmetry. It orders ferromagnetically below eight kelvin, breaking time-reversal symmetry as well. That rare mix makes it a model system for topology meeting strong electron correlations.

The team measured quantum oscillations in electrical resistivity under fields up to sixty-eight tesla. Near fourteen tesla, the oscillation frequencies change abruptly, the signature of the transition. A Lifshitz transition reshapes the Fermi surface, the boundary between filled and empty electron states. The results also fit a picture where magnetic order pulls the Weyl nodes closer to the Fermi level. They further suggest the RKKY interaction, a coupling between magnetic moments, plays an important role.
arxiv-2510-13835:
Dutta and co-authors build ConDABench, a benchmark for data analysis done through conversation rather than one-shot prompts. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that real analysis tasks arrive vague, with dirty data attached. Users clarify goals over several turns while the assistant works. Existing benchmarks ignore that interactivity entirely, the authors argue.

A multi-agent workflow generates realistic problems from articles describing insights in public datasets. The suite yields 1,420 conversational analysis problems built that way for the benchmark's first release, complete with an evaluation harness for testing tools end to end, the team reports. Leading language models were then run against the generated problems. Newer models solve more instances overall than older ones do. Yet they are not clearly better at tasks needing long, sustained engagement. The gap defines the collaborative frontier the benchmark aims to measure.
arxiv-2510-13935:
Kenan Alkiek, David Jurgens, and Vinod Vydiswaran ask how small language models, the kind that run on phones and edge devices, can handle expert problems, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Small models store fewer facts and struggle with multi-step procedures, while fine-tuning them for every domain is costly and retrieved passages leave the model to find and apply the right fact alone.

Their answer is instruction retrieval. A teacher model writes a reusable instruction for each cluster of similar problems. Each instruction covers background knowledge, a solving procedure, and common mistakes. At question time the small model retrieves the nearest instructions and follows them, with no retraining. On medicine, law, and mathematics tests the method beat zero-shot prompting everywhere, and on MedQA it raised accuracy by over ten points, well beyond retrieved textbook passages.
arxiv-2510-14235:
Kama Svoboda and Tosiron Adegbija survey neural architecture search for spiking neural networks, the brain-inspired models whose neurons communicate by spikes, from a hardware-software co-design perspective, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Spiking networks promise power efficiency and processing for edge and Internet-of-Things devices, but designing architectures by hand is hard because training quirks and hardware constraints interact.

The survey first explains how spiking networks work and how they differ from neural networks, then reviews search methods developed for conventional networks and why they do not transfer. It surveys approaches built for spiking networks, which must respect spike timing, surrogate training methods, and neuromorphic chips. The authors close with directions. They emphasize that co-designing the network and the hardware together is the likeliest route to unlocking the capabilities of spiking systems. They aim the survey at researchers and practitioners entering the field.
arxiv-2510-14435:
Nicola Borri, Yukun Liu, Aleh Tsyvinski, and Xi Wu organize what economists know about cryptocurrencies into seven stylized facts, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They ask whether crypto has matured into an investable asset class. The paper reads cryptocurrencies through the lens of asset pricing, the discipline that explains returns in stocks and bonds, to see which regularities carry over.

They find similarities with traditional markets: risk-adjusted performance so far is comparable, and the cross-section of crypto returns can be captured by a small set of factors, much as with equities. But crypto keeps its own character too: price jumps are frequent and large, and blockchain information helps drive prices. The authors read the common set of facts as evidence that cryptocurrency is emerging as an investable asset class. They also flag data quality issues and possible regulatory changes that could reshape the market's future behavior.
arxiv-2510-14635:
Li and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a training method for the test cases that catch bugs in machine-written code. Language models write code well, but their output often hides subtle faults. Good tests are the bottleneck. Existing test generators learn from fixed datasets, so the difficulty of their practice bugs has a ceiling, and novel faults escape them.

Their framework, ATGen, removes the ceiling with adversarial reinforcement learning. A test generator faces an opposing code generator that keeps crafting harder bugs designed to evade the current tests. This contest creates a curriculum of rising difficulty. The test generator is rewarded for checking program output correctly and for exposing the planted bugs. In experiments, ATGen beat leading baselines by a clear margin. It also proved useful for filtering the best of several candidate programs and as a reward source for training code models.
arxiv-2510-15035:
Sarkar, Moitra, and Sensarma find, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a route from measurements to entanglement entropy, one of quantum theory's slipperiest diagnostics. For interacting scalar fields, computing a subsystem's entanglement is hard. The authors work with Rényi entropies, a family of measures indexed by an order, and focus on the odd orders.

They show each odd-order Rényi entropy equals the free energy of a replicated system. The replicas are copies, joined by quadratic couplings inside the subsystem at the moment of measurement. These couplings replace the boundary matching conditions that complicate replica calculations. The dictionary works in and out of thermal equilibrium, for closed and open systems, and analytic continuation reaches the von Neumann entropy. For non-interacting theories they give a formula in terms of correlation functions; for interacting ones, rules for building every Feynman diagram. Even orders resist the trick, blocked by zero modes.
arxiv-2510-15435:
Luo Long, Coralia Cartis, and Paz Fink Shustin help an expensive search algorithm work in high dimensions by shrinking the problem first. Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns Bayesian optimization, a sample-efficient way to maximize costly black-box functions. Its weakness is scale, since searching a vast space directly wastes precious evaluations.

Their approach runs the search inside a learned latent space of much lower dimension, produced by a variational autoencoder that compresses candidate designs. A deep metric loss shapes that space so similar designs sit close together, and retraining the encoder adapts it to promising regions found along the way. They further narrow the latent search region as evidence accumulates, a step they call sequential domain reduction in latent space. Benchmarks showed better optimization quality than random projections, which the autoencoder clearly outperformed. The study also clarifies which design choices make latent-space search reliable.
arxiv-2510-15635:
Five-dimensional supersymmetric gauge theories flow between a free regime and a strongly coupled one. Amihay Hanany and Elias Van den Driessche compute the Higgs branch chiral ring for such theories. Their 2025 arXiv paper works at strong coupling, where ordinary perturbative tools fail. Turning on an instanton mass deforms the theory and changes the chiral ring structure. A nilpotent operator, the gaugino bilinear, renormalizes the weak-coupling ring along the flow.

Because of this effect, the standard F-term equations no longer determine the vacuum space alone. Perturbative non-renormalization arguments, often used to protect such results, are invalidated here. The work shows how nonperturbative effects reshape protected quantities in five dimensions.
arxiv-2510-15935:
Nikos A. Mitsiou, Ioannis Krikidis, and George K. Karagiannidis bring a quantum algorithm to the beamforming problem in multi-antenna radio. MIMO systems use many antennas at both ends for speed and reliability, a core design for sixth-generation networks. Fully digital versions, though, cost much hardware and power, so low-bit designs with quantised phase shifters are attractive despite their hard combinatorial design problem.

The three authors apply the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm, joined with alternating optimisation, to choose quantised phase shifts at transmitter and receiver together. Beamforming phases map directly onto rotation gates in a quantum circuit, a link they claim is shown first here. They derive the Hamiltonian for the general bit case and study a warm-start variant that cuts computation. Simulations show better quantised beamforming gain than classical benchmarks from the literature.
arxiv-2510-16235:
Vishal Manikanden, Aniketh Bandlamudi, and Daniel Haehn design a neural network to spot mouth cancer early. The target is oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma, the most common head and neck cancer. It grows slowly in deep, hidden spots, so it is often caught late, with deadly results.

Their network sorts mouth images into cancerous, harmless, and clean classes, trained on more than four thousand pictures. They then fed it the same test images at five levels of sharpness to learn how much detail it needs. Accuracy rose with sharpness but with shrinking gains, a curve like a log plot. The team also built a camera rig to capture sharper mouth images and an app that opens the tool to others. The findings guide how good a clinic's camera must be for AI screening to work.
arxiv-2510-16335:
Bo Peng leads a team of four authors in a 2025 study on sorting images with help from words. The task is called language-assisted image clustering. It groups like images when no true class names are given. The hard part is picking nouns that truly fit the images from a wild pool of text.

The team scores each noun by gradient size. A gradient shows how much a small change would shift the model's output. Their method, GradNorm, comes with a proof that it bounds the error. Tests show top scores on standard data sets. The proof also shows older filters are just narrow cases of this one.
arxiv-2510-16435:
Lennart Wachowiak, Andrew Coles, Gerard Canal, and Oya Celiktutan built a 2025 data set of questions people ask home robots. As chat tools spread, robots must answer users well, not just act. The team showed 100 people videos and texts of robots doing home tasks. Each person wrote what they would ask the robot in that scene.

The set holds 1,893 questions in 12 groups and 70 subgroups in all. Most ask about task steps, skills, or how well the robot did. Users rate rare but hard what-if questions as most vital to answer. New users ask more plain fact questions than skilled users do. Builders can use the set to plan what robots should log and say.
arxiv-2510-17135:
Himanshu Gupta and four co-authors study spectra of graphs tied to perfect matchings in this 2025 paper. A perfect matching pairs all points of a full graph with no leftovers. Pairs of matchings form cycles, and cycle shapes sort the matchings. Each sort class acts as a matrix in one shared scheme.

The authors guess where the second largest value of each matrix sits. They claim it sits on the space tied to a near-full split shape. They prove the claim for six key split shapes. They also prove it when the first part of the shape is large. The work narrows how these matching schemes spread their values.
arxiv-2510-17335:
Digging in sand or soil is a hard task to automate, because grains shift in complex ways and each batch of material behaves a little differently. Xintong Yang and three co-authors build a digging robot that learns the material as it goes. Their framework, called DDBot, pairs the robot with a physics simulator that can be adjusted smoothly by gradient methods and runs fast on graphics hardware.

Yang and her co-authors use that simulator to identify unknown material properties and then to polish the digging motion before the real robot moves. In tests, the system settled on material estimates within minutes and carried its fine tuned skills into real world digging with high precision. It also beat leading comparison methods on robustness and speed.
arxiv-2510-17435:
Placing a shared facility so that no one gains by lying about where they live is a classic puzzle in game theory. Ido Farjoun and Reshef Meir study that puzzle on a circle, a setting that fits services arranged around a ring, with exactly five agents. They focus on one known truthful rule, called PCD, which picks an agent reported spot with a chance proportional to the arc of the circle ahead of it.

Farjoun and Meir shrink the space of cases step by step until standard optimisation tools can settle the worst case performance of the rule. They prove that the bound they find is tight, meaning no better guarantee is possible for that rule. They also offer a guess for how the same rule performs with any odd number of agents.
arxiv-2510-17735:
Omer Bahadir Eryilmaz, Cihan Katar, and Max A. Little study signals that repeat over time. Such signals trace loops in state space as they return near earlier states. Analysts need a careful rule for when two states count as close. The team builds that rule from local flow patterns.

Their method gives each point an ellipsoid, a stretched sphere matched to nearby motion. Older methods use round balls that ignore flow direction. When a clear loop appears, its persistence sets a natural scale. Tests show better noise removal and better first-return estimates. The work shows topology tools gain power when they respect motion.
arxiv-2510-17835:
Jithin D. George and eleven co-authors rethink how electrochemical impedance spectra should be interpreted. The technique probes charge transfer and transport in devices without harming them. Analysts usually guess a circuit model first, then fit data to it. That habit leans heavily on personal experience and intuition.

Their approach extracts key features using pure complex analysis instead. The features reveal whether inductors or imperfect capacitors belong in a model. They also test whether a circuit model is uniquely determined by data. For resistor-capacitor models, they can list every possible model family. Real electrochemical systems illustrate the framework in action.
arxiv-2510-18035:
Arindam Bhattacharjee and Muktajyoti Saha follow charged black holes in an expanding universe as they evolve near their coldest limit. Flat-space charged holes drift toward extremality, but with a cosmological horizon present the story changes. These holes instead settle toward thermal balance with that far horizon.

A one-dimensional theory captures the near-horizon physics, joined to the quantum fields of the wider space. Energy flows through light scalar particles at rates that differ from the classic Hawking picture. Hotter holes radiate less than their flat-space twins. Gravity readers get a careful account of how an expanding backdrop rewrites black hole aging.
arxiv-2510-18135:
Jiahan Zhang, with sixteen co-authors, benchmarks world models by whether they help an agent act, not just by how pretty their videos look. Generative world models can simulate scenes with striking realism. Yet open-loop tests say little about decisions in a live loop, and prior benchmarks were fragmented.

Their World-in-World platform puts many world models inside one closed-loop setting with a shared planning method and action interface. Four environments score task success above visual quality. Embodied AI researchers get the first common yardstick for a simple question: does imagining the world help an agent finish the job?
arxiv-2510-18335: In-Jee Jeong and Deokwoo Lim study vorticity growth for spinning fluid flows in high dimensions. Vorticity measures local spinning in a fluid, and the Euler equations describe ideal flow without friction. Under bi-rotational symmetry without swirl, the equations shrink to one scalar equation in a single quadrant. For patch-type starting vorticity, the authors show the patch's support diameter grows without bound over time.
arxiv-2510-18535:
Sarth Dubey, together with Subimal Ghosh and Udit Bhatia, builds a stand-in model for the Global Flood Awareness System that stays trustworthy when data arrive late or go missing. Most rainfall-runoff research grades models only under perfect data, yet real forecasting must cope with delays and outages. Their emulator pairs memory-based neural networks with a relaxed water-balance rule, so its river flows still obey basic physics.

Five versions of the system were tested, spanning full historical and forecast data down to harsh latency and outage cases. Training used lightly managed catchments in the United States, and testing covered more than five thousand basins, including heavily regulated rivers in India. Performance fell smoothly as information quality dropped, and results stayed physically sensible in new climates. The work treats operational toughness as something flood models should be scored on, not assumed.
arxiv-2510-18635:
Paolo Seghetti and his four co-authors present a framework for testing, inside a computer model of the heart, whether a dangerous rhythm can be triggered. Such virtual inducibility studies could one day guide real treatment, but the field suffers from results that others cannot reproduce and from procedures that vary from lab to lab. Their framework, AutoVARP, standardizes the whole study through shareable input files, built on open simulation tools.

A study runs in four stages: preparation pacing, steady-state pacing, induction attempts with extra stimuli, and a check of whether any triggered rhythm sustains itself. The authors demonstrated the framework on a large cohort of virtual subjects, where it exposed numerical artifacts caused by careless setups, and on a detailed two-ventricle heart mesh. Their aim is a shared, repeatable standard for a technique moving toward clinical use.
arxiv-2510-18935:
Nathan Mankovich and five co-authors review feature extraction across the remote sensing data value chain. Earth observation data keeps growing, and it supports work on the environment, cities, and disasters, but its many dimensions bring repeated information and heavy computing costs.

Feature extraction cuts that bulk while keeping the traits that matter, which helps machine learning models work better. The authors offer a practical framework, trace how methods changed along the chain from raw data to final use, and sum up trends. Their guide helps readers choose methods for real remote sensing tasks.
arxiv-2510-19035:
Amirreza Hosseini and Amro M Farid work to connect classic project scheduling with the language of model-based systems engineering, aiming at mega-projects. The resource-constrained scheduling problem sits at the heart of project management, yet it has stayed separate from systems engineering methods used to design complex projects.
