The authors translate an activity-on-node network step by step into hetero-functional graph theory terms, giving schedulers and systems engineers a shared model. That bridge should help huge projects, where many resources and teams interact, be planned and controlled as one system rather than as disconnected charts.
arxiv-2510-19235:
Hongyu Wang and Yizhi Zhang study pure core sets of square matrices over finite fields, asking how the shared structure of a similarity class shapes these sets. The size and purity of core sets depend on the factors of a matrix's minimal polynomial and the degrees those factors carry.

Over fields of prime order, the authors bound how large a non-core set inside one similarity class can be. As the field grows, almost every subset becomes a pure core set, with the proportion tending toward one. Such counting results clarify the hidden order inside the huge space of matrices over a finite field.
arxiv-2510-19435:
Gakusei Sato, Hiroya Nakao, and Riccardo Muolo study timbre with topological data analysis. Timbre lets listeners tell instruments apart. Pitch and loudness may match, yet the sound still differs. Frequency analysis can miss subtle parts of that signature. Machine learning can miss them too. Topology might capture them, if sound is embedded well.

The team tests time delay embeddings on synthetic and real audio. Delays tied to fractions of the fundamental period work best. They let the analysis reveal harmonic structure clearly. A good delay choice turns a vague picture into a practical tool. Instrument and speech research both stand to gain.
arxiv-2510-19935:
Felix B. Christensen, Iñaki García Etxebarria, and Enoch Leung study when a brane partition function must vanish because of anomalies. In quantum field theory, an anomaly can leave a net background charge, and on a closed space that charge forces the partition function to be zero. They extend that idea to anomalous higher-form symmetries.

Working from the phase that the anomaly theory assigns even under rigid transformations, the authors derive vanishing results for several examples, some with and some without a Lagrangian description. Among the outcomes are the counterpart of the Freed-Witten cancellation condition for the M5-brane and a related condition for the D3-brane in S-fold backgrounds.
arxiv-2510-20335:
Zixuan Wu and six co-authors propose Dino-Diffusion Parking, a domain-agnostic pipeline for autonomous parking that joins visual foundation models with diffusion-based planning. End-to-end parking systems perform well in their training domain but often falter when weather or lighting changes. Instead of collecting more data, their design aims at generalized perception and robust motion planning under such shifts.

Trained in the CARLA simulator under regular settings, the pipeline transfers in zero-shot fashion to more adversarial settings. Parking success stays above ninety percent across all tested out-of-distribution scenarios, and ablation studies credit both the architecture and the algorithmic design. A test in a 3D Gaussian splatting reconstruction of a real parking lot shows promising simulation-to-real transfer.
arxiv-2510-20535:
Hippolyte Pilchen, Edouard Grave, and Patrick Pérez explore ARC-Encoder, an encoder that compresses long text contexts into a small set of continuous representations for large language models. Longer contexts from retrieval and chain-of-thought reasoning raise inference costs, and the strongest compression methods fine-tune or alter the target model, which can damage its general abilities. Their encoder instead replaces token embeddings with compressed vectors while leaving the decoder untouched.

A systematic study of training strategies and architecture choices shapes the final design, which typically outputs four or eight times fewer representations than the input token count. Evaluations across in-context learning and context window extension, on instruction-tuned and base decoders, reach leading benchmark performance with better inference efficiency. One encoder can also serve several decoders at once.
arxiv-2510-20835:
Dezhi Luo, Qingying Gao, and Hokin Deng revisit a split in how minds and machines are said to handle space, by inner simulation or by rendered scenes. Borrowed accounts from human cognition are often vague, and the authors use evidence from aphantasia, where people lack voluntary mental images, to sharpen the debate.

Work on the brain basis of visual awareness suggests that simulation and felt perception share structured maps of relations between things. Rich perceptual detail also helps embodied AI systems act better in physical settings, backing the shared map view. The team calls for machine designs that keep structured perceptual records as a core part of spatial thought, rather than treating images as mere decoration.
arxiv-2510-20935:
Vittorio De Falco and one co-author expand a letter on the motion of compact binary systems at second post Newtonian order in general relativity. The earlier work gave coordinate time as a function of eccentric anomaly for eccentric orbits, a key step in timing merging neutron stars and black holes.

Full calculation details are laid out here, and a matching formula for circular orbits is derived as a new result. Two astrophysical applications, binary neutron star and black hole systems, show the formulas at work. Precise timing expressions feed waveform models that gravitational wave detectors use to read masses and spins from chirps.
arxiv-2510-21935:
Samuel Bright-Thonney leads a nine-author team building a pipeline that hunts for genuinely new phenomena in scientific data without crying wolf. Experiments produce noisy, high-dimensional data, and most anomaly hunters flag oddities without the statistical backing a discovery claim demands.

Their system, AutoSciDACT, first compresses data into compact representations using contrastive training, leaning on the plentiful simulations many fields already have and on smart transformations guided by expert knowledge. A sensitive two-sample test, built on machine learning, then judges whether real data departs from the expected pattern strongly enough to matter. The authors present the pipeline as a first step toward novelty detection whose outputs can support quantified discovery statements rather than hunches, across scientific domains.
arxiv-2510-22235:
Yixiao Nie, Yang Zhang, Yingjie Jin, Zhepeng Wang, Xiu Li, and Xiang Li design a team-up between self-driving vehicles and service robots. Two autonomous cars ferry service robots around an office park. The robots carry out a series of tasks there. A large language model helps coordinate the work.

Their inference mechanism is called CGoT. An agent carries its reasoning as composable graphs of thoughts. These are structured diagrams of partial conclusions. They can be assembled, shared, and extended, rather than forming one chain of words. The study tests whether weaving language models into the loop raises efficiency. It also tests the cooperative machinery between the machines. The work is offered as an architecture for embodied multi-agent systems. Cars and robots must divide labor in the physical world there.
arxiv-2510-22335:
Xu Zhang, Ruijie Quan, Wenguan Wang, and Yi Yang rebuild viewed images from brain activity without leaning on diffusion models. Reading a picture out of fMRI signals usually routes the brain data through one fixed neural embedding that steers a diffusion generator from start to finish. A single static hint throws away the layered structure of vision and mismatches what each generation stage actually needs.

Their framework, MindHier, goes coarse to fine in the autoregressive style instead. A hierarchical encoder pulls multi-level embeddings out of the fMRI signal, an alignment scheme ties each level to the matching level of a vision model's features. A scale-aware guidance strategy feeds each embedding in at the matching scale of reconstruction. The authors present the design as both more efficient and closer to how the brain itself builds a scene, layer upon layer.
arxiv-2510-22635:
Paul Alexander Bilokon, writing alone in 2025, constructs a sieve that lists rational imbalances built from two integers. Each imbalance takes a difference over a sum, is reduced to lowest terms, and the order follows the two starting integers in dictionary style.

Bilokon records each new denominator the first time it appears. He shows every positive integer appears exactly once as such a denominator, and its first appearance matches a simple unit fraction. The sieve lists every rational number between negative one and one without repetition, then extends to all rationals. Connections to hyperbolic geometry and rational enumeration theory are discussed.
arxiv-2510-22735:
Solitary waves can lose stability when they bend across a channel. Christian Klein and Christof Sparber study that question in 2025. Their model is a nonlinear wave equation. It has cubic and quintic terms that compete. The domain is a line crossed with a ring.

The model is well posed in the global sense. It admits line shaped solitary waves. The pair test two kinds of disturbance. One is localized in space. The other repeats in a periodic way. Both tests point to a critical ring length. Above that length, the wave becomes unstable. Below it, the wave stays stable.
arxiv-2510-23135:
Ning Sun, Lei Feng, and Pengfei Zhang show that universal relations, a powerful idea from ultracold gases, also appear in long-range quantum spin chains. In gases, one quantity called the contact ties together many measurable properties. Finding the same pattern in spin chains would link few-body traits to many-body behavior in a new setting.

The authors demonstrate those relations for chains where spins interact over long distances. Their result extends the few-to-many philosophy to a distinct class of systems. Physicists can use the relations to predict or cross-check properties of spin materials and simulators from a single measured quantity.
arxiv-2510-23235:
Anton Savostianov, Michael T. Schaub, and Benjamin Stamm tackle a cost problem in signal processing on graphs in their 2025 paper. Low-pass graph filters keep the slow, smooth part of a signal on a network and are basic tools. For graph families that change with a parameter, each new graph forces a fresh eigenvalue problem to find its low frequency subspaces.

They interpolate between known subspaces instead of solving each problem from scratch. The method moves on the Grassmann manifold, the space of subspaces of a fixed size, using normal coordinates. They prove an error bound and test two uses. One use ties changes in node features over time to changes in graph shape. A correction adjusts how alike linked nodes are.The other builds a dot product family from one fixed graph, yielding better message passing for node classification.
arxiv-2510-23335:
Dhairya Kantawala studies near-optimal policies for average-cost Markov decision processes whose structure is almost separable. For a fully separable baseline, with no perturbation, he derives an explicit stationary rule that is exactly optimal for average reward. Real systems, though, are only nearly separable.

Kantawala shows that under a small epsilon perturbation of the separable structure, the same policy stays epsilon-optimal: the loss in average reward is on the order of epsilon. Decision makers can therefore use a simple closed-form rule with a guaranteed small penalty when their system is close to separable.
arxiv-2510-23435:
K Huynh, V Bajaj, J Mack, and A Calamida improve aperture corrections for the Hubble Space Telescope UVIS camera using focus-diverse point spread function maps. In crowded fields, small apertures reduce contamination from neighbors. But the fraction of light inside a small aperture varies with detector position and with focus changes over an orbit.

Using empirical point spread functions by Anderson, they compute two-dimensional maps of the correction between five and ten pixel apertures. The maximum change is about one hundredth of a magnitude across focus levels at a fixed position. Precise maps keep crowded-field photometry honest.
arxiv-2510-23835: Enrico Lampetti constructs good moduli spaces starting from moduli of objects in the sense of Toën and Vaquié. A good moduli space is a well-behaved quotient whose points classify a family of objects, making an abstract moduli problem concrete and usable. Toën and Vaquié's framework describes moduli of objects in broad categorical terms, and Lampetti's construction supplies good spaces in that generality. As an application, he obtains good moduli spaces for perverse sheaves, objects central to modern geometry and representation theory.
arxiv-2510-24035:
Xinqi Li and eight co-authors release GraphNet, a large set of real deep-learning computation graphs meant to sharpen tensor compiler research. Compilers such as TorchInductor decide how a network actually runs on hardware, but judging them takes realistic workloads. GraphNet provides 2,700 graphs with rich metadata, spanning six task types across several frameworks.

To score compilers on the corpus, the authors define a Speedup Score that weighs runtime gains and correct execution together, under adjustable tolerance. An error-aware extension folds in numerical error, helping developers spot where bottlenecks hide. As a demo, they benchmark the default compilers of PaddlePaddle and PyTorch on vision and language samples. The full pipeline — graph extraction plus scoring tools — is public. The authors intend GraphNet as shared infrastructure: one realistic testbed, so compiler gains can be compared honestly instead of on cherry-picked models.
arxiv-2510-24335:
Mingyu Jeong and three co-authors present NVSim, a framework that builds large navigable indoor simulators from ordinary image sequences alone. Traditional simulators rely on costly 3D scanning, which limits their scale. Their method adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting, a technique that renders scenes from many small soft blobs, to robot traversal data.

Sparse views of floors often cause visual artifacts, so they add a floor aware version of the method to keep a clean, walkable ground plane. A mesh free check then builds a topological navigation graph by analyzing rendered views directly. Tests on real world data show the system generates valid large scale navigation graphs for robot planning.
arxiv-2510-24435:
Benjamin Grando Moreira compares the logical and abstract reasoning of many large language models against human performance, working alone. Judging reasoning matters because it shows whether models truly understand information and draw valid conclusions, beyond fluent language performance. He tests models including GPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok, Llama, Mistral, Perplexity, and Sabiá on eight custom reasoning questions.

The same questions were given to human participants as a benchmark. Results reveal significant differences between models and humans, with models struggling on deduction tasks that require strict logical steps. The study highlights where current models fall short of human level reasoning despite strong language skills.
arxiv-2510-24735:
Daria Fedyaeva, Georgy Lukyanov, and Hannah Tollie model school as a cure for wrong views formed by group learning. In their model, some agents read past acts wrong, as if each act were a fresh sign on its own. Schooled agents use the right odds and may also get sharper own signs.

They set a cut point: agents learn when the cost of school falls low enough, and acts then track a single score. A closed form stat weighs how much a schooled call beats an un schooled one. When a wrong rush of acts takes hold, school can break it in finite time. The work also weighs gains in group good from wider school reach.
arxiv-2510-25135:
Junyi Guo, Pan Du, Xiantao Fan, Yahui Li, and Jian-Xun Wang test neural fields that shrink thick flow data to a small hid code, with no grid tied in. Such fields map a point in space to flow facts, steered by that code. The team match them with two classic shrink tools in one shared test frame.

Three ways to steer the field are checked: by acts, by low rank shifts of weights, and by last layer ties. A split zone form that keeps hard parts local is also new. Tests split in range reads from strict out of range ones. The low rank form had the least error in training and in range tests, across flow sets.
arxiv-2510-25535:
Christopher R Schwarze led four co-authors reviewing interferometry. Anthony D Manni, David S Simon, and Abdoulaye Ndao helped. Alexander V Sergienko closes the five-author team. Their 2025 review covers next-gen optical reading technology. Interference phenomena like fringe patterns enable precise reading. Systems have evolved for over a century now. Major parts themselves hardly change, they note.

Most interferometers use conventional beam separation parts. Plate optics and beam-splitters dominate current designs. That limits design scope and likely results. Novel higher-dimensional linear-optical splitters may improve designs. The review covers theory of such optical scatterers. Basic optical interference and phase sensing principles appear. Familiar and unfamiliar scatterers are treated jointly. The Grover multiport is one highlighted example. Its action stays unchanged under gauge transformations. Gauge-invariant multiports form a new building block class. They can tailor interference for metrology unconventionally.
arxiv-2510-26335:
Julian M. Bopp, Lucca Valerius, and Tim Schroder introduce a corrugated photonic crystal cavity design, nicknamed Dinosaur, for coupling color centers to triangular waveguides. Color centers are atomic defects in a crystal that can emit single photons, and coupling them to flying photonic qubits, photons that carry quantum information, is key for quantum networks. Triangular nanostructures made by angled etching need fewer fabrication steps than undercut designs, but standard hole based cavities fit them poorly.

Bopp and the team develop a tapered interface between cavity and waveguide that converts Bloch modes to waveguide modes with almost no loss. Optimizing the interface minimizes photon losses, and adjusting it tunes the light matter interaction strength precisely, which suits embedded color center applications.
arxiv-2510-26435:
Lin Long, with ten co-authors, tracks how four quasars change in brightness across many colours of light. Quasars are the bright cores of far galaxies, and multi-colour records over time are still rare. The four were picked for strong change in near-infrared light in the VISTA survey of the Milky Way region.

Long and the team add optical records from Pan-STARRS1 and the Zwicky Transient Facility, plus mid-infrared records from the WISE satellite. They compare the curves to find time lags between bands, which can reveal the size of the dust ring around the core. For two quasars they measure both lags after cleaning the infrared light of disk glow and time stretch. The dust sizes fit the known link between size and brightness, and one grain measure compares graphite with silicate dust.
arxiv-2510-26535:
Mustafa Mullahasanoglu reviews recent work that turns dualities in gauge theories into new spin models. Gauge theories describe forces, and some come in dual pairs that say the same physics in two languages. A link between those dualities and the Yang-Baxter equation, a key test for exact solvability, lets researchers build lattice spin models, grids of tiny magnets used in statistical mechanics.

The review surveys how dual gauge theories have been used to construct fresh spin models that are dual to Ising-like models, the classic grid magnet systems. Mullahasanoglu presents the gauge and Yang-Baxter link as a strong tool for finding such models. The piece is short and aimed at readers who want a map of this fast-moving corner of theory.
arxiv-2510-26735:
Narendra N Hegade, with eleven co-authors, proposes a hybrid quantum-classical method for sampling from energy-based models. Sampling from a Boltzmann distribution, which favours low-energy states, is central to physics and machine learning, but classical methods slow down badly at low temperatures. Their method, digitized counterdiabatic quantum sampling, uses shortcuts that suppress unwanted transitions during a quantum evolution.

Hegade and the team steer sampling toward low-energy regions step by step with a bias field, then reweight the gathered samples classically to rebuild the target distribution. They test it on one-dimensional Ising models with up to one hundred twenty-four qubits, where exact answers exist. A harder spin-glass case with one hundred fifty-six qubits ran on IBM quantum processors. Classical rivals needed up to a thousand times more samples to match its quality.
arxiv-2510-27135:
Tong Shen, Jingai Yu, Dong Zhou, Dong Li, and Emad Barsoum design a leaner diffusion model for text-to-image generation. Diffusion models make high-quality images but often need huge training data, heavy structures, and slow inference. Their model, E-MMDiT, holds only about three hundred million parameters and trains on modest public data in about a day and a half on a single eight-chip node.

Savings center on token reduction, since cost grows steeply with token count. A highly compressive visual tokenizer plus a multi-path compression module shrink the token stream, while position reinforcement and subregion attention preserve spatial coherence cheaply. A light modulation module tunes each block efficiently. Scores on a standard generation benchmark are competitive, with code released as a practical baseline.
arxiv-2510-27235:
Tianyang Chu, Xiaoying Dai, Jing Wu, and Aihui Zhou analyze a gradient flow model for the Gross-Pitaevskii eigenvalue problem. That problem computes the ground state of a Bose-Einstein condensate, a cloud of atoms in one quantum state, and normalized gradient flow is a widely used route to numerical schemes for it. The paper supplies the missing mathematical and numerical backing.

The authors prove well-posedness and describe the solution long-time behavior for the flow model. They then propose a normalized implicit-explicit fully discrete scheme and prove its well-posedness plus optimal convergence of the approximation. Numerical experiments validate the theory. The results give practitioners firmer ground for trusting a popular condensate solver and guidance on how its accuracy scales.
arxiv-2510-27635:
X. Dumusque leads a team with fifty-five co-authors who present ten years of solar data from HARPS-N in 2025. The tool watches the Sun to measure tiny shifts in its light, a method called radial velocity that can reveal planets around other stars. Sharp data need careful fixes for tool drift and sky flaws over a long span.

Checks over thirteen years expose tool shifts near one meter per second. After fixes, the scale holds steady to better than three quarters of that unit. The team drops thirty percent of shots hurt by clouds or known faults. The cleaned set holds more than one hundred thousand spectra. Typical noise sits well below one meter per second.
arxiv-2511-00135:
Kanka Ghosh and Andreas Menzel ask whether a hole in an elastic material can be mechanically concealed by surrounding it with a stiff shell. A bare hole normally lowers overall stiffness, but a shell of adjusted thickness can compensate. They examine the question from macroscopic continuum theory down to atomistic scales, focusing on an isotropic, homogeneous, linear elastic material under compressive plane strain with few holes.

A mathematical condition gives the shell thickness that maintains the overall stiffness of the system. Materials science readers get a design principle for invisible defects. Concealed holes could allow lightweight porous materials that behave, mechanically, as if solid.
arxiv-2511-00335:
Weidong Zhang, Pak Lun Kevin Ding, and Huan Liu test small vision models where it counts: outside the dataset they are usually judged on. Lightweight classifiers such as MobileNet, ShuffleNet, and EfficientNet run on phones and embedded chips, yet most rankings rest on ImageNet alone. The team trains eleven such models under one fixed schedule and tests them across seven varied datasets.

They introduce xScore, a single metric for how steady a model stays across domains, estimable from just four datasets. ImageNet rank, they find, fails to predict skill on fine-grained or medical images. Design choices matter: isotropic convolutions at higher resolution and channel-wise attention helped models generalize, while transformer blocks added cost with little gain.
arxiv-2511-00435:
Yaoting Gui, Yuqiao Li, and Jun Sun study geometric flows that move surfaces while preserving volume or area, inside a Schwarzschild space, the spacetime around a non-rotating black hole. Mean curvature flow normally shrinks surfaces toward rounder shapes, and the preserving versions add a constraint that keeps size fixed. The question is stability: do surfaces near a coordinate sphere settle down smoothly?

If the starting surface is close enough to a coordinate sphere, both flows exist for all time and converge smoothly to one: a constant mean curvature surface. For spaces that are only asymptotically Schwarzschild, with pinched curvature far out, center manifold analysis gives the same conclusion with exponential speed. A side benefit is an existence result for such special surfaces in asymptotically flat space.
arxiv-2511-00935:
Akhil Rao, in a working paper, examines how public money should be spent to grow markets for advanced space systems. Such systems carry high fixed costs, face thin private demand, and are often driven by motives beyond profit, which makes ordinary market building tools unreliable.

Rao offers a graphical framework showing how many competitors a market can sustain. The count depends on cost structure, on the split of government support among direct purchases, direct investment, and shared infrastructure, and on the size of private demand. Drawing on public goods theory, shared infrastructure can support more competitors per dollar. A stylized case based on NASA's commercial space station program turns industry wide losses into profits when core infrastructure is shared.
arxiv-2511-01235:
Shruthi Kannappan, Ashwina Kumar, and Rupesh Nasre accelerate the maximum flow problem on graphics processors, including graphs that change over time. Max flow, the largest throughput from a source to a sink under edge capacities, underlies networking, transport, and image segmentation. The push relabel algorithm suits parallel hardware because its operations are local to each vertex.

They present a GPU algorithm that incrementally recomputes max flow after a batch of edge updates, rather than starting over, plus a high performance static GPU algorithm for the initial computation. A series of CUDA specific optimizations targets performance, scalability, and memory efficiency. Dynamic graphs, from live networks to evolving road systems, are the motivating use case.
arxiv-2511-01335:
Nishith Mohan and Christina Surulescu prove that a model of tissue regeneration always has solutions. The model tracks human mesenchymal stem cells and chondrocytes, the cartilage producing cells, interacting in a medium with a differentiation factor. That factor attracts the chondrocytes and steers both cell types toward or away from differentiation.

Stem cells move by haptotaxis toward extracellular matrix. The chondrocytes produce that matrix, the stem cells degrade it, and cartilage forms as part of it. The growth factor is supplied periodically to sustain the dynamics. For a simplified version of a more complex model, the authors prove global existence of weak solutions. That is the mathematical guarantee that the model stays well posed for all time rather than breaking down.
arxiv-2511-01535:
Marco Cayuela, Vincent Le Chenadec, Peter Schmid, and Taraneh Sayadi try to open the black box of Fourier neural operators. These models predict fluid flows well but hide their reasoning. Their design, HFNO, is built to be read. It handles different wavenumber bands, meaning different scales of motion, in separate parallel channels.

Inputs are lifted to a larger space and Fourier-transformed. They are then split into wavenumber bins. Each bin is processed by its own small network. The outputs are recombined, returned to physical space, and polished by a correction model, either a convolutional network or an echo state network. The design is tested on problems of rising difficulty: the one-dimensional Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow, and predicting wall shear stress in turbulent channel flow.
arxiv-2511-01635:
Asma Shirin T, Brian Reville, Nils Schween, Florian Schulze, and John Kirk revisit a famous prediction of shock acceleration theory. Particles bouncing across a shock front should emerge with a power-law energy spectrum. In diffusive shock acceleration this clean result is usually taken for granted; the authors show it is fragile when the shock's magnetic field is oblique rather than aligned.

Power laws survive only if the particles' scattering rate grows in direct proportion to their gyro radius, the Bohm scaling, and stays uniform in space. Other scalings curve the spectrum, and an abrupt change in scattering upstream breaks it. Using the Sapphire++ code, the team maps how big these effects are. They are strongest at fast shocks. Such shocks occur in active galactic nuclei, microquasar jets, and young supernova remnants.
arxiv-2511-01835:
Rafał Kalinowski, Monika Pilśniak, Elżbieta Sidorowicz, and Elżbieta Turowska color the edges of graphs so that the sums around each vertex identify it. In a neighbor sum distinguishing coloring, each vertex adds up the colors of its incident edges, and neighbors must receive different sums. The authors add a fairness constraint: at every vertex, no single color may cover more than half, rounded up, of its incident edges.

This quasi-majority version has its own index, the fewest colors that suffice. For nice graphs, those without a component that is a single edge, they prove 12 colors always enough. Bipartite graphs need only 6, and graphs whose maximum degree is at most four need only 7, giving concrete universal bounds for a constrained labeling used in network identification problems.
arxiv-2511-02135:
Joseph Suh, Suhong Moon, and Serina Chang question a fashionable assumption: that simulating people requires a large language model. They study close-ended simulation tasks, where a person's behaviour is a choice among fixed options, with uses from predicting survey answers to modelling test-taking. Their alternative, GEMS, treats the task as link prediction on a graph connecting individuals to the choices they might make, and learns with a graph neural network.

Across three datasets and three evaluation settings, GEMS matched or beat the strongest language-model-based methods while using about a thousand times fewer parameters. The authors argue graph-based modelling can complement language models as a cheaper and more transparent route to human simulation, and they release their code.
arxiv-2511-02435:
Virgile Dine, Teddy Furon, and Charly Faure improve machine unlearning, the process of making a trained model forget specific data. They first reframe the whole problem as a constrained optimisation task, a formulation that unifies the existing family of first-order approximate unlearning methods. Within that frame they define feasible updates: directions for changing the model's parameters that advance forgetting without damaging the model's general usefulness.

Feasible updates are found by masking, carefully choosing which parameters are worth touching at all. The method also accounts for the noise in gradient estimates from each data batch, yielding a statistical guarantee that the chosen updates are locally feasible. Because the technique is an add-on, it can wrap around any first-order approximate unlearning method. Experiments with image classifiers confirmed that the plug-in improves the forgetting-versus-utility balance.
arxiv-2511-02535:
Lucas Palazzolo, Mickaël Binois, and Laetitia Giraldi study a microscopic swimmer steered by magnets: a spherical magnetic head dragging an elastic, non-magnetic tail. At that scale water behaves like syrup, in the low-Reynolds-number Stokes regime, so ordinary swimming intuition fails and motion must come from the tail's deformation. The swimmer is modelled with resistive force theory, and the question is whether magnetic steering can drive it anywhere nearby, the property called small-time local controllability.

The answer is a clean negative: under planar motion the system is provably not locally controllable, and the authors map numerically which configurations remain unreachable. Yet the swimmer is not useless: simulations show its trajectory can still be made to track a desired path using Bayesian optimisation, although only by allowing large sideways deformations of the tail. The contrast between uncontrollable and trackable is the paper's pointed lesson for microrobot design.
arxiv-2511-02635:
Avijit Pal and Bhaskar Paul work in operator theory, on Hilbert spaces and the contractions that act on them. Their 2025 paper studies two special families of seven-operator tuples named with the letter Gamma and a set-like symbol E. The central objects are fundamental operators, smaller operators that encode how a tuple fails to be unitary.

The authors show that swapping the roles of a tuple and its adjoint swaps their fundamental operators in a precise way, under stated commuting and bound conditions. They then build a unitary tuple directly from a contraction, and develop functional models of Douglas, Sz.-Nagy-Foias, and Schaffer types for these families. Such models let hard operator tuples be studied through concrete function spaces, a standard payoff in this field.
arxiv-2511-03035:
Oscar Chavez Ortiz and twenty colleagues examine GHZ2, one of the most distant galaxies known, seen at redshift 12.34. Its spectrum shows very strong ultraviolet and optical emission lines, including carbon emission far stronger than stars alone seem able to power. Their 2025 paper asks how much of that light comes from an accreting black hole rather than young stars.

Fitting spectrum and photometry together with the BEAGLE-AGN tool, models with a black hole component won clearly over star-only models. The black hole supplied about 54 percent of the key carbon line's strength. Its inferred mass is about ten million suns, roughly five percent of the galaxy's stellar mass, in line with other early systems. If confirmed, GHZ2 hosts the most distant black hole yet identified.
arxiv-2511-03135:
Eli Berger and Daniel McGinnis prove a common strengthening of several rainbow matching results. The setting joins two matroids, abstract structures that capture independence, on one shared ground set. Given a long list of sets, each independent in both matroids and growing in size up to a cap, their 2025 theorem gives a guarantee. There is a partial rainbow set of a set size that stays independent in both matroids at once.

A rainbow set picks its elements from distinct lists, so the result says two independence systems can be satisfied together while respecting the rainbow rule. The theorem unifies earlier results on bipartite graphs by Aharoni and co-workers and on two-matroid intersections by Kotlar and Ziv. Unifications like this often reveal which assumptions in each older proof were truly essential.
arxiv-2511-03235:
Yi-Fei Liu, Yi-Long Lu, Di He, and Hang Zhang test whether large language models can guess a person's wider traits from a short personality survey. They gave models Big Five answers from more than eight hundred people and asked them to role-play answers on nine other scales. The models had no training on that data set.

Model answers matched human patterns very closely, far better than word likeness alone would predict. Their skill nearly matched computer methods trained directly on the data. Reading the models' reasoning showed a two-step habit: first boil the survey down to a short portrait in plain words, then answer from that portrait. Those portraits added useful signal beyond the raw scores. The work suggests models build compact summaries that capture how traits hang together.
arxiv-2511-03335:
Guillaume Aubian and co-authors open a new line on coloring signed graphs, where edges carry plus or minus signs. A balanced coloring groups vertices so each group stays free of sign conflict, and the aim is to use few groups. The classic Gyarfas-Sumner question asks which banned patterns force a bounded coloring number in plain graphs.

For signed graphs, the authors ask which pairs of banned patterns do the same job. They prove any working pair must start with one of two small signed cliques. The second member must be a linear forest, a loose chain-like shape. With the smaller clique banned, any linear forest works as partner. The result charts the first ground for coloring hereditary classes in the signed world.
arxiv-2511-03535:
Kazuki Okamura proves sharp large-sample results for estimating the center of a heavy-tailed Pearson Type Seven distribution. That family includes the Cauchy distribution, whose wild tails break many standard statistical habits. The maximum likelihood estimator is the focus, with scale treated as known.

Multiple roots of the likelihood equation are the main obstacle, since a solver might land on the wrong one. Despite that risk, Okamura establishes strong consistency, a normal limit law, and exact asymptotic variance, plus a strong efficiency ranking. Heavy tails show up in finance and physics data, so knowing the best estimator still works there is reassuring. The proofs give a template for other stubborn likelihood problems.
arxiv-2511-03635:
Apoorva Upadhyaya, Wolfgang Nejdl, and Marco Fisichella build IRIS, a stance detector that must explain itself on topics it has never seen. Stance detection judges whether a post favors or opposes a target, and zero-shot versions face unseen targets cold. Rival methods lean on blunt explicit reasoning and give coarse explanations that hide the real basis of a call.

IRIS blends implicit signals with explicit reasoning steps that are modeled openly. Attitude toward the target is built up in stages a reader can inspect. The aim is trust: moderators and analysts need to know why a post was flagged as opposed, not just that it was. Transparent zero-shot stance tools could serve election and brand monitoring alike.
arxiv-2511-03935:
Vahid Salari is the lead author among ten authors reviewing quantum optical methods for biomedical imaging. Techniques that use entanglement, squeezing, and quantum correlations aim to beat classical limits, promising sharper resolution, better signal relative to noise, stronger phase sensitivity, and lower radiation dose for delicate samples.

Coverage includes quantum optical coherence tomography, quantum microscopy, ghost imaging, multi-parameter quantum imaging, and imaging with quantum-grade cameras. For each method the review explains how it works, where it could help in biomedicine, and what blocks translation into real practice. The survey is meant as a guide for moving quantum imaging from laboratory demonstrations toward tools that affect care.
arxiv-2511-04035:
Dongji Gao is the lead author among eight authors on WST, a weakly supervised transducer for speech recognition. Transducer models perform well but depend on large, high-quality labelled speech, which is costly to collect, so training must survive transcripts that contain many errors.

A flexible training graph lets the model handle transcript errors well without confidence scores or extra pretrained models. On synthetic and industry datasets, performance held up even when transcript error rates reached seventy percent in the tests described. The method steadily beat connectionist temporal classification based weakly supervised rivals. Code was promised for public release, aiming at real settings where perfect transcripts never arrive.
arxiv-2511-04235:
Zhengru Fang is the lead author among six authors building shared spatial memory for multi-agent systems through predictive coding. Partial views and tight bandwidth often wreck coordination, so the framework treats coordination itself as minimizing mutual uncertainty among agents, with an information bottleneck deciding who says what, and when.

A grid-cell-like internal code for self-location emerges from self-supervised motion prediction. On top of it, agents develop bandwidth-efficient communication and specialised populations encoding partners' locations, likened to social place cells. A hierarchical policy explores to cut joint uncertainty. On a maze benchmark, success fell only gently as bandwidth shrank drastically, while a comparison method degraded far more sharply.
arxiv-2511-04335:
Srimoy Bhattacharya, Mukesh Kumar, Rachid Mazini, and Bruce Mellado report a growing excess consistent with a new scalar resonance near one hundred fifty-two gigaelectronvolts in Large Hadron Collider data. The authors present the signal as an emerging hint, not a discovery, and multi-lepton anomalies in collider data motivate the search for added scalars beyond the Higgs boson.

Excesses appear across photon-pair, Z-plus-photon, and W-pair channels, and their combined significance is described as pointing toward a real resonance. A simplified model, where a heavy scalar decays into two lighter scalars, fits the multi-lepton pattern consistently. Upcoming high-luminosity data and precision studies, the team stress, must confirm or kill the idea.
arxiv-2511-04435:
Hyeonyong Kim leads twenty-five authors comparing galaxy simulations at the edge of cosmic dawn. Telescopes with JWST found early galaxies brighter and heavier than models predicted. The AGORA project runs the same young galaxies through six major simulation codes to test agreement.

The codes are Enzo, Ramses, Changa, Gadget-3, Gadget-4, and Gizmo. All use the shared AGORA physics setup tuned at lower redshift, with no extra high-redshift fixes. Target halos hold ten billion to one hundred billion solar masses at redshift ten. Comparing outputs shows where codes agree on early galaxy growth and where their methods pull apart.
arxiv-2511-04735:
Peter B. Denton and his co-author release NuFast-Earth, a code for neutrino travel through Earth. Oscillation probabilities in sharply varying matter are getting costlier to compute. Next-generation detectors like DUNE, HyperK, and KM3NeT will need them at scale.

Their algorithm extends a long-baseline method to atmospheric, night-time solar, and supernova neutrinos. It handles arbitrary Earth models with two schemes for layered density profiles. Speed, flexibility, and accuracy are the stated design goals. A C++ release with a full user manual accompanies the method, so experiment teams can drop it straight into their pipelines.
arxiv-2511-04835:
Shubham Natraj and two colleagues bias robot motion planning toward certified regions using conformal prediction. Sampling planners usually scatter points uniformly, which wastes effort in complex spaces. A heuristic first guess, from a classic search or a vision model, can point the way.

Conformal prediction wraps that guess in a set with a stated coverage guarantee. With a user-chosen probability, the set must contain the optimal path. Sampling then concentrates inside the certified region while keeping the guarantee. The authors present it as the first such conformalized strategy, speeding feasible planning without giving up probabilistic honesty.
arxiv-2511-05135:
Robin Armingaud and a co-author present ManufactuBERT, a language model tuned for factory and plant work. Broad models read plain text well, but their skill drops in fields like manufacturing, where terms and senses are their own.

The team built a large text set for the field from web data, with a filter step and a multi-stage clean-up that strips repeats. More training of a RoBERTa model on that set yields ManufactuBERT. In tests it sets a new best score on the manufacturing tests used, which shows the value of domain text.
arxiv-2511-05235:
Dominika Popelová and co-authors report eye-safe lasers made from calcium fluoride crystals doped with thulium, plus inert buffer ions such as yttrium, lanthanum, gadolinium, or lutetium. The crystals are pumped by diodes inside their own band.

One mix, with yttrium as buffer, reached a slope efficiency near half of the absorbed pump power in free-running mode. With a birefringent plate, its output tuned smoothly across a wide span in the near infrared. The team also maps the light traits of thulium in each host, which guides picks for broad, fast laser designs.
arxiv-2511-05435:
Adrián González Casanova and co-authors study chains of particles where types can switch, through the lens of partial exchangeability. They look at consistent Markov chains on a finite state space whose rates must fit a swap symmetry that holds only in part.

The authors sort all valid rates by a split into solo motion and joint motion of particles. That sort yields a full account of multitype Lambda-coalescents with many switches, models of how family lines merge. They add convergence and duality results for the limit of type shares, a process they call the de Finetti measure process.
arxiv-2511-05535:
Trivikram Satharasi and S Sitharama Iyengar examine model collapse, the decay that can hit AI models trained on AI-made content. As synthetic text and images fill the web, new models may learn from that output instead of fresh human work. The authors warn this loop can shrink the range and quality of language over time.

To track the risk, they measured how alike English Wikipedia texts grew from 2013 to 2025. They used transformer embeddings and a similarity score across years. Similarity rose steadily, and the rise sped up after public chatbots spread. The study frames collapse as a forecast problem, not just a past event.
arxiv-2511-06035:
Vincenzo Mottola and co-authors use dimensional analysis to make eddy current testing measure what matters while ignoring what wobbles. This nondestructive method probes metal plates with magnetic fields. Engineers may want a plate's thickness and conductivity, but the probe's lift-off distance is uncertain and pollutes the reading.

Fewer parameters govern the data once they are grouped into dimensionless combinations, a classic result called Buckingham's theorem. The authors give a systematic way to build invariant transformations: remappings of the signal that cancel one or more nuisance parameters. One can then estimate thickness and conductivity regardless of lift-off, or other pairs in turn. The method suits real-time use and aims to make nondestructive testing more accurate and reliable.
arxiv-2511-06635:
Lulu Yu and colleagues ask whether labels written by language models can replace real user clicks when training search ranking. Click logs are cheap but noisy, human labels are dear, and model-written relevance judgments sit between the two. A head-to-head comparison across many dimensions had been missing.

On a public dataset and an industrial one, click-trained models won on frequent queries while model-label training won on medium and rare queries. Clicks captured document quality signals better, while model labels captured semantic matching better. Two combined training schemes, data scheduling and frequency-aware multi-objective learning, lifted ranking at every query frequency, with the frequency-aware version stronger.
arxiv-2511-06935:
Nienke van der Marel and six co-authors compare infrared emission from planet-forming disks with high-resolution images of their dust. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, carbon-rich molecules known as PAHs, glow at characteristic wavelengths in many disks, but their brightness varies widely for unknown reasons. The team assembled twenty-six disks within 300 parsecs with measured PAH intensity and ALMA continuum images.

A strong correlation emerged between the 3.3 micron PAH intensity and the mass of warm dust, with a Pearson coefficient near 0.88, far stronger than links to radiation field or total dust mass. The pattern fits a picture where PAHs sit frozen on pebbles until the pebbles drift into warm dust traps inside the thirty-kelvin radius and loft upward, releasing the molecules into the gas.
arxiv-2511-07035:
Keyao Zhang and five co-authors speed up the checkpointing that protects large language model training from crashes. Periodically saving a model lets training resume after failures, but standard saving pauses or slows GPU computation while data moves to the CPU and storage. Their system, GoCkpt, spreads one checkpoint transfer across multiple training steps so saving overlaps with useful work.

Each step transfers part of the checkpoint state plus some gradient data. Once the transfer finishes, the partial states are updated on the CPU into one consistent version, avoiding the inconsistency that multi-step transfer would otherwise cause. A transfer strategy maximizes both GPU-to-CPU bandwidth and SSD throughput. In tests GoCkpt raised training throughput by up to about thirty-eight percent over standard asynchronous checkpointing, and cut interruption time sharply.
arxiv-2511-07835:
Yiqiao Bao, Anindya De, Shivam Nadimpalli, Rocco Servedio, and Nathan White ask how to test a polynomial for sparsity using noisy values. The unknown polynomial has low degree in many variables. A tester sees random points with noise added and must tell sparse cases from ones far from sparse.

The team gives an exact boundary for when a constant number of samples, independent of dimension, can suffice. Above that boundary they supply a matching constant sample algorithm. Below it, even noise free testing needs samples growing with dimension. Their Fourier tail tools may also help beyond this problem.
arxiv-2511-07935:
Seyedehanita Madani, Rama Chellappa, and Vishal Patel detect change between satellite views that refuse to line up. Change detection supports disaster response and city monitoring, but real image pairs suffer parallax, viewpoint shifts, and long time gaps. Pipelines that register first and compare later still crack under large displacement.

DiffRegCD fuses dense registration and change detection in one model, using diffusion features to anchor correspondence. Joint handling beats sequential patching when scenes move substantially. Reliable change maps from messy archives could speed damage assessment after floods and earthquakes, where the first available images are rarely the tidy ones algorithms prefer.
arxiv-2511-08635:
Fei Yang and Dong Liu challenge a basic belief about the quantum Hall effect: that frozen disorder in the material is what creates its flat plateaus. They show that pure dephasing, the loss of quantum phase coherence, can produce the same critical behavior on its own.

Starting from a Keldysh formulation, they derive an open-system sigma model with a topological term and no Cooperon sector, then show that instantons still drive the two-parameter flow of conductances. In a quantum anomalous Hall setting the theory predicts a critical point at half-integer Hall conductance with finite longitudinal conductance. Boundary-driven simulations of a standard lattice model with local dephasing match the prediction. The authors propose reading conductances from Hall potential maps as an experimental check.
arxiv-2511-08835:
Yejin Yoon and seven co-authors build conversational agents that can slide between doing tasks and making small talk, the way people actually chat. Assistants are usually trained for one mode or the other, yet real conversations switch modes constantly, driven by either side.

Their dataset, TACT, packs structurally varied dialogues where task talk and chitchat interweave and transitions flow both ways. Two new metrics, Switch and Recovery, grade how well an agent starts a mode change and how gracefully it returns. Models trained on TACT beat baselines at intent detection and transition handling. A round of preference optimization pushes joint mode-intent accuracy to about seventy-six percent, and human judges preferred the tuned model over GPT-4o seventy percent of the time.
arxiv-2511-08935:
Ningnan Wang and six co-authors give exploring robots a sense of which unknown territory is worth entering. Their zero-shot navigation system, SCOPE, scores the frontiers between seen and unseen space with a vision-language model, turning raw edges into scores of exploration potential.

Those scores are grouped into a spatio-temporal potential graph that tracks how those edges evolve, supporting plans that look many steps ahead. A second-look step then revisits earlier decisions and corrects overconfident ones before they compound. On two embodied robot tasks the system beats state-of-the-art baselines by four point six percent in accuracy. Ablations credit the main parts with better calibration, stronger reach into new settings, and higher decision quality overall.
arxiv-2511-09135:
Jieun Han and seven co-authors rewrite English reading tests around each student's interests, on the theory that engaged readers comprehend more and stay motivated longer. Their transcreation pipeline starts from the RACE-C comprehension dataset and rebuilds texts and questions on topics each learner cares about.

Four stages do the work: pulling out topics, question sorting by Bloom's taxonomy, language feature analysis, and the transcreation itself, performed with GPT-4o. The new texts then read at the same level while carrying new content. A controlled experiment with English learners in South Korea then compares custom against standard materials. Students with interest-aligned texts comprehend more and stay motivated longer. The authors frame this rewriting, long used in media localization, as a practical engine for custom learning materials.
arxiv-2511-09335:
E. Abasov and six co-authors lay out a method for training foundation transformer models for collider physics. Particle collision data come with many kinematic signatures, and analysts usually build separate tools for each. Their universal model instead pre-trains on combined simulated data sets spanning many processes at once.

The focus is simultaneous analysis of events producing one to four top quarks, along with their background processes. Multi-task pre-training lets the model learn universal patterns before task-specific fine-tuning, while adaptive attention keeps each process's distinctive traits. The authors plan to show the architecture stays sensitive to rare three- and four-top events without sacrificing standard channels. One unified approach would replace many separate analysis pipelines.
arxiv-2511-09435:
Francesco Morri and three co-authors study how a coordinator can steer a noncooperative game. The steering tool is the design of players' conjectures. In dynamic games, each player guesses how others will react before choosing a move. Equilibria can be multiple and bad, problems usually handled one by one through opponent modeling or incentives.

Their approach first computes a good equilibrium by optimizing a chosen goal, then sends it to players as a target. In central settings the coordinator also tunes the conjectures; in spread-out ones, players compute conjectures on their own toward their own targets. An equilibrium is guaranteed to exist in both cases. Because conjectures split the game into separate subproblems, the work parallelizes well in large settings.
arxiv-2511-09735:
Ahmed Alia, Mohcine Chraibi, and Armin Seyfried upgrade the Social LSTM pedestrian predictor so it respects the physical space each person occupies. Most path models treat pedestrians as points, letting predicted paths overlap unrealistically in crowds. Their new loss function penalizes collisions while accounting for crowd density and individual body size.

The dynamic occupied space loss combines ordinary displacement error with a density-sensitive collision penalty. Training and testing used five data sets built from real paths. They were recorded at Lyon's 2022 Festival of Lights, spanning low to very high densities. The model cuts collision rates by up to about 31 percent, the authors report. It also improves displacement errors modestly, beating several leading predictors on most test sets.
arxiv-2511-09935:
Canwen Wang, Jionghao Lin, and Kenneth R. Koedinger explore whether large language models can identify knowledge components, the named skills behind test questions that adaptive learning systems depend on. Experts normally build these labels by hand, which is slow, and earlier automated attempts used tiny datasets and produced redundant labels. The team scaled a simulated textbook prompting strategy to 646 multiple-choice questions.

The raw model output performed worse than an expert-designed model and invented 569 components where experts used 101. The fix was merging labels whose meanings were highly similar: at the best threshold, the count fell to 428 and prediction error improved clearly. Generation alone is not enough, they conclude, but generation plus semantic merging is a viable path.
arxiv-2511-10135:
Kwing Hei Li, Alejandro Aguirre, Joseph Tassarotti, and Lars Birkedal present Foxtrot, a separation logic for proving that one probabilistic concurrent program safely refines another. The programs are higher-order, manipulate higher-order local state, and interleave threads while drawing random values, a combination no earlier logic could handle for contextual refinement. Foxtrot adapts invariants and ghost resources from concurrent separation logic to this richer setting.

It adds probabilistic tools such as tape presampling and induction by error amplification for reasoning about distributions created by racing threads. Soundness relies on a form of the axiom of choice inside the Iris framework, a first for Iris-based logics. Examples range from an adversarial von Neumann coin to a random-bytes function from the Sodium cryptography library, all mechanized in Rocq.
arxiv-2511-10235:
Nobuhisa Tateno and ten co-authors built a full-field coherence microscope that keeps cell-level detail sharp through a long depth range. Stock coherence microscopes see cells well from the side but blur fast with depth, and point scanning loses signal when software tries to refocus. Their system lights the whole field at once, refocuses by computer, and repeats scans on a set cycle so it can also film motion inside tissue.

Side detail came out near one and a half micrometers, with depth detail of a few micrometers. On spheres of human breast cancer cells, the system showed both the 3D form and live inner motion at cell scale, through the full depth of each sphere. That pairing of form and motion is the step past stock coherence imaging.
arxiv-2511-10335:
Oscar Damanik, Giacomo Bastianel, Dirk Van Hertem, and Hakan Ergun optimize power flow on high-voltage direct current grids that must stay secure even when one converter pole fails. Bipolar converter stations can run asymmetrically, injecting different currents at their two poles, which adds flexibility after an outage. Their security-constrained model chooses how many stations may operate asymmetrically while minimizing operating cost under post-contingency conditions.

More asymmetric operation lowered costs in their results, and the analysis maps how sensitive costs are to the allowed degree of asymmetry. The trade-off is voltage: asymmetry raises direct current neutral voltage offsets, sometimes to unwanted levels, and capping them raises costs again. A neutral line switching strategy for the post-contingency state is proposed to soften that tension.
arxiv-2511-10735:
David Trestini works out exact links for pairs of dense dead stars, such as black holes, that move on oval paths and do not spin. He connects the pair's stored energy and spin-like motion to how fast they swing around and move in and out. The math is carried to the fourth level in a step-by-step scheme past Newton.

To get there, he rewrites the motion in angle form and treats the delayed tail effect as a small shift. He also finds a mean redshift value for oval paths that matches self-force results. At the end he restates known energy loss rates in terms of the two basic rates.
arxiv-2511-10935:
Yifan Zhuang, Calvin Huang, and their colleagues built CAT-Net to read Mandarin tones from brain and muscle signals. Tone matters in Mandarin because the same sound with a different tone can mean a different thing. Their system is meant to help people who cannot speak, by reading intent from the head and face.

CAT-Net joins brain waves and muscle signals with a cross-attention step and trains to work across new users. It used few sensors, with twenty brain and five muscle channels, on trials from ten people. It beat prior methods for both voiced and silent speech and stayed strong when tested on fresh users.
arxiv-2511-11135:
Hussam Al Daas and Nicholas Gould present TREK and NREK, methods for trust-region and norm-regularization subproblems that recur inside larger optimization routines. Those subproblems limit each step or penalize step size, and they are usually solved with repeated matrix factorizations, which cost time. The authors show the solutions, as the control setting varies, effectively live in a very low-dimensional subspace.

They build a basis for that subspace with one factorization through an extended Krylov iteration. Inside the small subspace, high-order root finding solves the problem cheaply. Numerical results show the approach is effective, offering an alternative to multi-factorization and standard Krylov routes.
arxiv-2511-11435:
Maria-Teresa De Rosa Palmini and Eva Cetinic study text-to-image diffusion models. Their topic is multimodal iconicity. That is the pull by which a prompt naming a shared cultural reference evokes a familiar artwork or film scene. In such cases, memorization of one image and generalization from culture are tangled together, which defeats standard tests for copying. The authors propose an evaluation frame to separate the two.

Their Cultural Reference Transformation metric splits behavior into recognition, whether a model evokes the reference, and realization, how it renders it, by copying or by fresh interpretation. Five diffusion models were tested on hundreds of Wikidata-derived references spanning still and moving imagery, with clear differences in recognition strength and copying habits.
arxiv-2511-11535:
Kadin Worthen and seven co-authors report millimeter telescope observations of HD 166191, a young star whose dust disk was recently thought to show a giant collision between rocky bodies. Data come from the ALMA telescope in band 7 and from the Submillimeter Array, taken years apart.

Both instruments detect dust emission, and ALMA also picks up a carbon monoxide gas line from the disk. No silicon monoxide, a expected sign of a violent impact, is found, and the team sets an upper limit on its mass. The dust brightness shows no change between 2014 and 2024, and modeling places gas and dust within twenty astronomical units of the star.
arxiv-2511-11735:
Yonatan Sverdlov, Eitan Rosen, and Nadav Dym examine whether point cloud neural networks preserve the natural distances between shapes. Such networks are built to ignore permutations and rigid motions, but ignoring symmetry is not the same as respecting the geometry that symmetry defines.

Two symmetry-aware distances are compared: the Procrustes matching metric and hard Gromov-Wasserstein distances. The two turn out not to be bi-Lipschitz equivalent, so no network can preserve both at once. As a corollary, popular invariant architectures fail to be bi-Lipschitz under the Procrustes metric. The negative result is useful guidance: designers must choose which geometry their models will faithfully keep.
arxiv-2511-11935:
Munib Mesinovic and Tingting Zhu tackle a quiet problem in medical AI. Survival models on health record data cannot be fairly compared across papers. The preprocessing that shapes the data is usually undocumented. It differs from paper to paper. A gap in reported concordance may reflect cohort choices, not modeling skill.

Their pipeline, SurvBench, is open source. It converts raw PhysioNet exports into model-ready tensors. Four critical-care databases are covered: MIMIC-IV, eICU, MC-MED, and HiRID. Four input types are handled, from time-series vitals to diagnosis codes. Standard preparation would let the field argue about models. Invisible plumbing would stop deciding the results.
arxiv-2511-12035:
Wenxuan Miao and nine co-authors speed up video diffusion models through the data's own structure. Nearby frames and patches are strongly linked in latent space. These models generate high-quality video, but self-attention at inference is very costly. Earlier sparsity tricks were borrowed from language models. They ignore that space-time structure.

Attention patterns are traced to dominant links across space and time. Timeripple prunes work along exactly those lines. Principled sparsity, derived from the data's overlap, beats imported rules of thumb. Cheaper video generation decides the technology's reach. It could stay a studio tool, or become an everyday medium.
arxiv-2511-12135:
Letian Chen, Runhan Shi, Gufeng Yu and Yang Yang rethink how molecules and text about molecules are aligned. Linking a molecule, often written as a SMILES string, to a plain description matters for drug search, materials design and reading chemical literature. Captioning a molecule and designing one from text are usually trained as separate tasks.

Their system, RTMol, joins both directions in a round trip: text to molecule and back, or the reverse. That loop gives new measures of success and lets captioning be trained without paired examples. Tests show large gains in both directions across several language models, and a more consistent two-way link.
arxiv-2511-12235:
Josef Simbrunner, Clemens Krenn, Martin Zach and Andreas Habring propose a cleaner way to build the system matrix for cone-beam CT scans. That matrix is the math core that links a scanned object to its detector readings. Accurate matrices matter for sharp reconstructions, and common line-based methods approximate the geometry.

Their method splits the overlap between the cone beam and each voxel into subvolumes that feed distinct detector elements. Each piece has an exact formula, so no costly iterative substeps are needed. Tests on synthetic and real scans show reconstructions that beat line-based approaches. The team also provides a graphics-processor implementation for two- and three-dimensional cases.
arxiv-2511-12735:
Ankita Raj and Chetan Arora carry out the first study of backdoor attacks on open-vocabulary object detectors. Such detectors find objects named by free text prompts, which makes them flexible and popular for robotics, driving, and surveillance. The authors show that prompt tuning, a light way to adapt these models, opens a new attack surface. Their attack, TrAP, jointly tunes image and text prompt tokens together with a visual trigger, planting hidden behavior without retraining the base model.

Training shrinks the trigger patch step by step, so that even a small patch activates the backdoor at test time. Across several datasets, TrAP achieved high success rates for making objects be misclassified or disappear entirely, while clean-image performance on downstream data actually improved over the zero-shot baseline. The study is a warning: a cheap adaptation method can quietly compromise a detector that otherwise looks healthy.
arxiv-2511-13335:
Maram Alharbi and 5 co-authors report AHaSIS, a shared task on sentiment analysis for Arabic dialects in hotel reviews. Arab hospitality firms rely on guest feedback, yet tools that read feeling across dialects are still weak. The task centers on spotting positive, neutral, and negative feeling in dialect text.

The dataset holds five hundred thirty-eight balanced reviews, first written in Modern Standard Arabic and then rendered into Saudi and Moroccan dialect by checked translation. Native speakers validated the versions for dialect accuracy and preserved feeling. Over forty teams registered and twelve sent systems; the best reached an F1 score near point eight one, showing both promise and remaining difficulty.
arxiv-2511-13935:
Federico Battini turns weather maps into tokens for a transformer model that forecasts renewable power. Good forecasts help grids cut fossil fuel use, but older methods merge the spatial pattern of weather with its movement over time only weakly. Battini encodes each hourly weather map with a small convolutional network, then lets a transformer read the sequence.

The system predicts wind and solar output across a 45-hour horizon. Judged against the operational forecasts of the European grid body ENTSO-E, it cut wind forecast error by about sixty percent and solar error by about twenty percent. A live dashboard publishes the model's daily forecasts for Sardinia.
arxiv-2511-14135:
Promise Ekpo, Saesha Agarwal, Felix Grimm, and two co-authors enforce fairness as a hard constraint when robot or agent teams share work. Uneven workloads in heterogeneous multi-agent systems are usually handled with fixed penalties, which cause inefficiency, unstable training, and clashing incentives, and never guarantee the fairness target is actually met. Their framework, AdaFair-MARL, states fairness as an explicit constraint instead.

A primal-dual update adjusts Lagrange multipliers automatically to hold the constraint while the team optimizes performance. The fairness rule is derived from the geometry of Jain's fairness index, giving the feasible set a second-order cone form that supports principled updates without hand-tuned penalties. Simulation experiments test the approach.
arxiv-2511-14235:
Pradosh Keshav MV, NS Kavya, and Kenath Arun give dark energy a switch that flips late in cosmic history. Measurements of the expansion rate and of matter clustering sit uneasily with the standard model, motivating new physics that slows structure growth without rewriting the early universe. Their scalar dark energy field has a symmetric quartic potential and couples to dark matter.

Once matter thins past a critical density, spontaneous symmetry breaking gives the field a growing value and turns the coupling on. Energy then flows from dark matter to dark energy, suppressing growth while early times stay identical to the standard model. Fits to redshift-space, distance, supernova, and microwave background data show noticeably different clustering predictions.
arxiv-2511-14335:
Jeryes Danial, Yosi Ben Asher, and Itzik Klein give micro drones a lightweight way to map rooms in three dimensions. A single camera keeps drones cheap and small, but monocular mapping faces a scale ambiguity and a choice between sparse, detail-poor maps and heavy learning-based dense ones. Their system pairs sparse keypoint pose tracking with dense edge reconstruction.

Learned depth prediction and edge detection feed an optimization that keeps keypoints and edges geometrically consistent, without global loop closure or heavy neural computation. An extended Kalman filter fuses inertial data to fix scale and sharpen accuracy. The system ran in real time on a DJI Tello and navigated indoor corridors autonomously.
arxiv-2511-14435:
Angelo Ferrando argues, in a vision paper, that runtime verification and large language models should guard each other. Autonomous systems with learned components in open environments strain formal methods, which need complete models, while language models are flexible but error-prone and guarantee nothing. Runtime verification monitors live executions and, in predictive form, can anticipate violations before they happen.

The pairing runs both ways: monitors act as guardrails on model-driven autonomy, and models help write specifications, reason ahead about risks, and handle uncertainty for the monitors. Ferrando contrasts this symbiosis with existing surveys, and discusses what it means for certification and for research toward dependable autonomy.
arxiv-2511-14635:
Geneviève Bélanger, Aoife Bharucha, and three co-authors explore a dark matter model in which the dark sector heats up on its own, apart from the rest of the early universe. A mediator particle that mixes scalar and pseudoscalar traits links dark matter to normal matter only weakly. After reheating, almost no dark particles exist at first.

If the dark coupling is strong enough, the dark sector reaches its own balance at its own temperature, then freezes out on its own schedule. The team solves coupled equations to find the leftover density. This decoupled path can dodge strict cosmic microwave background limits while still giving signals that detectors might see.
arxiv-2511-14835:
M. A. Arroyo-Ureña, O. Félix-Beltrán, and three co-authors ask whether the High-Luminosity LHC could reveal charged lepton flavor violation, a process the Standard Model almost forbids. They study photon collisions that produce an electron and a muon together, a clear sign that flavor rules have broken.

Working within an effective field theory that respects strict bounds from rare decays, the team runs full Monte Carlo simulations with advanced selection methods. They find a clear discovery could be reached with enough data under favorable conditions. The results argue that photon fusion deserves dedicated searches by the LHC experiments.
arxiv-2511-14935:
Peter Benner, Volker Mehrmann, and two co-authors compute safety margins for a class of energy-based dynamical models. Dissipative-Hamiltonian systems are built so that energy bookkeeping guarantees stability from the start. The natural question is how large a structured change to the model would push it to the edge of stability.

That smallest destabilizing change is the structured stability radius, and the authors derive formulas that can actually be computed for it. The search is recast as minimizing Rayleigh quotients of Hermitian matrices, sometimes singly and sometimes as a sum of two. Engineers modeling physical systems gain a direct way to certify how much modeling error their design can absorb.
arxiv-2511-15635:
Maleeha Khawaja and Samir Siksek study new algebraic points on curves, in a number theory paper about which number fields can first give a curve new points. A curve here is a smooth projective shape of genus at least two defined over the rational numbers. A point is new for a field when it appears over that field but over no smaller field inside it.

They conjecture that, for fields of any fixed degree at least two ordered by size, the new point set is empty for almost all fields. For degrees two and three they give checkable criteria tied to an explicit model of the curve. They verify cases for several modular curves and prove a matching result for the unit equation.
arxiv-2511-15735:
Levente Fekésházy and Oliver Schnetz present LinApart2, a major update of a program for partial fraction decomposition. That algebraic task rewrites a rational function, a ratio of polynomials, as a sum of simpler fractions, a step needed in many symbolic calculations. The earlier version struggled with denominators that are high-degree polynomials unless they were factored first.

The new version handles denominators of arbitrary degree without explicit factorization, while keeping the speed and parallel structure of its Laurent series method. Series expansions around chosen points carry the needed information. Benchmarks show major gains in run time and memory over a leading commercial routine and over the classic Euclidean algorithm, enabling computations that were previously out of reach.
arxiv-2511-16035:
Kieron Kretschmar, Walter Laurito, Sharan Maiya, and Samuel Marks introduce Liars Bench, a testbed for evaluating detectors that claim to catch language models lying. A lie here means generating a statement the model itself believes is false. Prior detection techniques were validated in narrow settings that miss the diversity of lies models can produce, varying by motive and by what belief is targeted.

The bench holds tens of thousands of lies and honest responses from four open-weight models across seven data sets. Settings capture qualitatively different lie types along those two dimensions. Evaluating three black-box and white-box detection techniques, the authors find systematic failures on certain lie types, especially where the transcript alone cannot reveal the lie, setting a practical guide for progress.
arxiv-2511-16235:
Robin Wroblowski and Rodolphe Sepulchre revisit two classical tools for analyzing rhythmic and excitable systems. The describing function approximates how a nonlinear system responds to rhythmic input, and the phase response curve measures how a stimulus shifts the timing of the next spike or cycle. Both tools are widely used in control engineering, biology, and neuroscience, but they have known limits for relaxation oscillators and excitable systems.

Their new approach is tailored to excitable systems and centers on a discrete-event operator that maps trains of input events to trains of output events. The Hodgkin-Huxley excitability model illustrates the method. The framework supports design and analysis of central pattern generators, the rhythmic circuits in networks of excitable neurons, relevant to neuromorphic control and neurophysiology.
arxiv-2511-16535:
Haytham Ziani analyzes optical flow computation from local methods to a multiresolution global implementation. Optical flow figures motion between video frames. Local methods like Lucas-Kanade use small windows, while global methods like Horn-Schunck enforce smoothness across the image. Ziani explores theoretical and useful sides of both families in an applied study.

A multiresolution Horn-Schunck version is implemented with bilinear interpolation and prolongation between scales. Coarse to fine processing should improve exactness and convergence on large motions. Effectiveness is investigated under varying image settings. The combined strategies are judged on motion estimation quality. The work serves practitioners choosing flow algorithms for tracking, robotics, and video analysis where speed and robustness trade off.
arxiv-2511-16735:
An Le and Christopher L. Baldwin revisit adiabatic reverse annealing, a quantum annealing variant that starts from a guessed solution to dodge bad phase transitions, after computer studies suggested decoherence kills its advantage. Their treatment is analytical, using the exactly solvable p-spin model and the master equation for the environment.

In that limit the system tracks its instantaneous equilibrium state unless the protocol crosses a finite-temperature phase transition. Reverse annealing then fails at high temperature for one of two reasons: no path avoids transitions, or that state itself is disordered. At low enough temperature neither occurs and the method succeeds. Some regimes have no safe path at zero temperature yet gain one at nonzero temperature, so the environment can actually help.
arxiv-2511-17435:
Zengyu Zou and three co-authors design a learning system for fleets of vehicles handling pickup and delivery requests that arrive on the fly.
