The problem generalizes vehicle routing: several vehicles cooperate while new stochastic requests appear, and classical optimization methods buckle under the scale and pace. Earlier reinforcement learning approaches decoded each vehicle's actions on their own, missing how the choices interact, and struggled with the huge joint action space.

Their framework, the Multi-Agent Pointer Transformer, reads the scene with a transformer encoder, then generates the fleet's joint actions one step at a time with a decoder joined to a pointer network. A relation-aware attention module captures interactions between entities, and informative priors guide exploration. Across eight datasets, the system clearly outperformed existing learning baselines and answered far faster than classical operations research methods.
arxiv-2511-17735:
Jacob Beattie, Samuel Stevens, Neil Rosser, Yu Su, and Tanya Berger-Wolf test whether large vision models can help scientists find new patterns, not just confirm known ones. They use sparse autoencoders, tools that split a model's inner features into clearer parts, plus simple ranking rules to surface promising features.

Trials cover scene images, fish images, and butterflies. The method rediscovers known concepts, recovers fine fish body features without labels, and picks out traits that separate look alike butterfly groups. The authors frame the work as a needed first step, with finding truly new phenomena still ahead.
arxiv-2511-17835:
Sebastián V Romero, Xi Chen, and Yue Ban study a quantum battery, a tiny device that stores energy in quantum states, charged through a kicked Ising chain. Entanglement has been cast as a key resource for fast charging, and the authors examine a special point of the model where the dynamics can be described exactly. At that point, the fastest entanglement growth lines up with the largest energy input.

Using exact methods in momentum space, they characterise the charging process and find its performance stable while reaching the top rate. A fixed-window protocol speeds charging toward the steadily driven limit. Analysis of spin links shows that scrambling and the spread of influence govern how well the battery charges. The schemes are presented as workable across several hardware platforms.
arxiv-2511-17935:
Govind Rajendran, Kushagra Sharma, Vijayalakshmi Chetlapalli, and Jatin Parekh compare two Wi-Fi timing protocols used to measure distance between devices. Fine Time Measurement ranging promises metre-level location indoors, where satellite signals fail, and two standards versions are now in use. The team runs real-world tests to see how each performs and which factors most affect accuracy.

Channel width, interference, the radio setting, and calibration offsets all matter. In clear line of sight on wide channels, metre-level accuracy is reached steadily by both, while blocked paths give errors near five metres. The newer protocol holds an edge in heavy multipath settings, where signals bounce along many routes. The findings give network planners practical guidance on what accuracy to expect.
arxiv-2511-18135:
Huaidian Hou, Arpan Kusari, and Brian Lin evaluate five classic car following models, which predict how a driver responds to the vehicle ahead, using naturalistic data recorded in real congestion. Earlier comparisons rarely used rich real world congestion data in a unified way.

When all models are tuned on the same error measure, they perform similarly overall. Where they disagree with drivers, cabin and road video points to distraction and driving with momentum. Drivers also coast and creep at idle in ways the models cannot capture. Clustering of time series supports those findings and motivates adding coasting behavior to future models.
arxiv-2511-18435:
Tieguang Zi, Peng-Cheng Li, Bao-Min Gu, and Fu-Wen Shu test if a space antenna can bound the mass of a hypothetical field. The field is a massive vector, or Proca, field. In an extreme mass ratio inspiral, a small object with charge like hair from this field spirals into a huge black hole.

The hair sheds extra dipole waves, which drain energy and shift the orbit over time. That drift leaves a phase gap in the wave form next to pure general relativity. Wave form mismatch checks show the LISA antenna can tell the two apart when black hole spin is counted. A Fisher matrix study then forecasts how tight a mass bound LISA can set.
arxiv-2511-18535:
Alexander Moretó, Noelia Rizo, and Gabriel A. L. Souza prove a stronger form of a classic group theory claim. For a finite group and a prime p, Brauer's height zero conjecture ties the heights of characters in the main p-block to a local structure. Their form adds the action of a set of Galois symmetries on the characters.

The result answers a recent conjecture by Malle, Moretó, Rizo, and Schaeffer Fry. As a payoff, the team derive a Galois form of the Itô-Michler theorem, a structure result about which primes can divide character degrees. Height zero claims have guided block theory for decades. A form that tracks symmetry action sharpens that guide.
arxiv-2511-18635:
Shireen Chand, Faith Baca, and Emilio Ferrara ask whether fixing one bias in a language model can worsen others. Models inherit social biases from training data, and many fixes target a single dimension at a time, with success judged only on that dimension. The team studies four mitigation techniques across ten models from seven families. They track racial, religious, professional and gender bias together, along with the coherence of the model's answers on a standard stereotype benchmark.

Targeted fixes sometimes lower the intended bias, but they often raise bias elsewhere or make answers less coherent. The pattern holds broadly enough that the authors call it a no free lunch problem for debiasing. Their advice is plain: any bias fix should be audited across categories and for general quality before it is trusted, not scored on its target alone.
arxiv-2511-18735:
Zhantao Gong, Liaoyuan Fan, Qing Guo, Xun Xu, Xulei Yang, and Shijie Li define foresight intelligence, the ability to anticipate and interpret future events. They also build a question answering data set to measure it in vision language models. Such foresight matters for driving and other real tasks, yet existing research largely overlooks it.

Using their FSU-QA data set, they find current leading models still struggle to reason about the future. The data set also grades world models by whether their predicted futures help a vision model answer better, checked with control experiments. Fine tuning even small models on the data lets them surpass much larger models by a wide margin.
arxiv-2511-18935:
Peng-Cheng Lu, Zong-Guo Si, Han Zhang, and Xin-Yi Zhang study the creation of tau particle pairs when two photons collide, keeping full track of the taus' spins. The work covers two settings: lead nuclei passing at a distance in ultraperipheral collisions, where their light fields interact, and dedicated lepton colliders. The authors compute cross sections and spin correlations at next-to-leading order in electroweak precision, a refined level of calculation.

The refined contributions turn out numerically small for the measures they examine, which simplifies future analyses. Using their spin correlations, they then test quantum entanglement in the tau pair and find a genuinely entangled configuration near the threshold where the pair's mass is smallest. The results support using photon collisions to probe tau physics and quantum effects together.
arxiv-2511-19035:
Kai Zheng and eight co-authors assess building damage in Gaza from paired satellite images taken before and after strikes. Swift, sound damage maps guide aid and steady recovery. Conflict zones are hard: building styles repeat, damage patches are small, and edges blur, so labels are scarce and classes look alike.

Their MC-DiSNet starts from the pre-trained DINOv3 vision backbone, whose rich features suit thin data. A siamese pair of branches compares the two dates; multi scale cross attention between them localizes subtle semantic change. The design targets small damaged zones with soft borders. Humanitarian mapping from orbit is the use case.
arxiv-2511-19535:
Ilán Carretero and six co-authors classify spitzoid tumors from DNA methylation data that is often incomplete. Getting this diagnosis right matters, since errors lead to under- or over-treatment. Methylation profiles carry useful signals, but real clinical data have missing entries from limited coverage and lab artifacts, which earlier studies ignored.

Their method, ReMAC, extends a masked autoencoder approach called ReMasker to handle classification on high-dimensional data with or without gaps. Masked learning lets the model fill and use partial profiles in a principled way. On real clinical data, ReMAC performs strongly and robustly against competing classifiers in sorting these tumors.
arxiv-2511-19835:
Xuewen Liu, Zhikai Li, Jing Zhang, Mengjuan Chen, and Qingyi Gu work on making video generation faster. Diffusion transformers lead this field, but their attention step grows costly as videos get longer. Sparse attention cuts the cost by focusing on key tokens, yet earlier sparse methods lost much quality.

The authors trace the loss to two biases: key tokens get too much weight, while ignored tokens lose weight they should keep. Their Rectified SpaAttn fixes both problems, using pooled weights to reset key-token scores and a gain-aware step to restore the rest. A custom Triton kernel speeds up two major video models while keeping generation quality high, and the code is open source.
arxiv-2511-19935:
Songlin Zhao, Michael Pitts, and Zhuwei Qin present EfficientXpert, a way to specialize large language models cheaply. Low-rank adaptation cuts training cost but leaves a dense model, while pruning done apart can remove weights that adaptation later needs. The aim is a sparse expert that still runs on limited hardware.

EfficientXpert adapts the low-rank updates and the sparse weight set together. Its ForeSight Mask scores weights through a reconstruction stand-in that uses the changing adapted weights, and a Partial Brain Surgeon step realigns the adapter in closed form. At high sparsity, the best variant keeps nearly all dense-adaptation performance on the tested models, with modest extra training time and memory. The study also guides how much adapter recovery capacity to choose.
arxiv-2511-20035:
Fangyang Zheng surveys two open conjectures in non-Kähler geometry for a broad audience. The setting is complex geometry where the usual Kähler condition fails, a field many readers know only slightly. The two problems are the constant holomorphic sectional curvature conjecture and the Fino-Vezzoni conjecture, both described as typical questions for the field.

Zheng assumes no expertise in the area and writes the essay as an entry point. He traces the history of each conjecture and reports recent developments on both. Readers get the statements, the background story, and the current state of progress, in a form meant to be followed without specialist training.
arxiv-2511-20135:
Amano, Hirata, Togawa, and colleagues put a new ion trap to work for X-ray astronomy. Their 2025 paper reports first results from the JAXA-EBIT. An electron beam ion trap makes highly charged ions. Controlled lab plasmas benchmark the atomic data astronomers need. Space telescopes now deliver very sharp X-ray spectra.

The trap was newly introduced to Japan's astronomy community. Dielectronic recombination tests used highly charged argon ions. Performance matched Heidelberg's compact EBIT closely there. Photoexcitation experiments ran at the SPring-8 synchrotron. Its BL17SU beamline supplied soft X-ray light. Resonance transitions were detected for two key ions. Helium-like oxygen O6+ showed its expected lines. Neon-like iron Fe16+ transitions appeared as well. Such data pin down transition energies and probabilities. Interpreting XRISM telescope spectra depends on them. Over ninety-five percent of baryonic matter is hot plasma. Lab benchmarks keep cosmic conclusions grounded.
arxiv-2511-20535:
Bastos, Caprio, and Raizzaro study fractal sets in a number system built from a prime. Their 2025 paper examines backward Julia sets of p-adic Hénon-like maps. The map sends a pair (x, y) to (xy + c, x) over p-adic numbers. Backward orbits that stay bounded form the filled Julia set. Whether that set stays bounded hinges on the constant c.

When the p-adic size of c is at most one, boundedness holds. The backward set then sits inside the p-adic integer pairs. When the size of c exceeds one, all changes. The backward set becomes unbounded in that regime. Its Haar measure is infinite there too. Fibonacci numbers enter the scaling of special orbit sets. No p-adic norm lies between one and p, which simplifies some cases. The work extends classic complex dynamics into p-adic territory.
arxiv-2511-20635:
Fu, Zeng, Lan, and co-authors retrain a video model into an all-purpose image studio. Their 2025 paper presents iMontage for many-to-many image generation. Video models learn strong priors for smooth, coherent sequences. Image data carries far wilder variety than video frames. Merging both promises consistent yet dynamic picture sets.

The framework takes variable-length image sets as input and output. One model then covers generation plus many editing tasks. The adaptation is deliberately light and minimally invasive. Curated data plus a staged training recipe teach image skills. Original motion priors survive the retraining intact. Outputs keep strong consistency across images in a set. Scene dynamics exceed what single-image models usually manage. Best quality currently comes with up to four inputs. Long-context many-to-many cases remain unexplored so far. Code and weights are promised publicly.
arxiv-2511-20735:
Amedeo Romagnolo introduces in 2025 StarEstate, a Python package that builds fake galaxies full of stars so astronomers can test theories. Mock catalogues help read telescope data, but generating each star by numerical integration can take hours. StarEstate assigns positions, ages, and chemical makeups from statistical distributions and stellar evolution models, for the Milky Way or for elliptical galaxies.

Its speed comes from pre-calculated integrals, solved once, stored, and reused, cutting generation time by orders of magnitude. A signature feature is dynamical temperature, the spread of stellar velocities, which decides how tightly each population hugs the spiral arms. Stars younger than 100 million years are dynamically cold and trace the arms tightly; those aged 100 million to a billion years spread more; older ones drift into a smooth pattern. One showcase run generated a spiral disk of 100 million stars, with star types assigned by the Morgan-Keenan classification.
arxiv-2511-20935:
Henry Marichal, Joaquín Blanco, Diego Passarella, and Gregory Randall release in 2025 UruDendro4, a public dataset for automatic tree-ring detection. Rings record each year's wood growth, but measuring them by hand along a few radii is slow and imprecise. The dataset holds 102 cross-section images of Pinus taeda, a plantation pine, each with annual rings delineated manually. Uniquely, samples come from several heights along the stem, so models can reconstruct yearly wood volume, not just width.

The authors benchmark current detectors on the data. The best method, DeepCS-TRD, reached a mean average precision of 0.838 and a mean recall of 0.782, with an adapted Rand error of 0.084 on the test images. Ablation studies validate the chosen settings. Adding UruDendro4 to training improved a model's generalisation to other ring-detection data, the point of a benchmark: better tools for judging which forestry practices grow wood best.
arxiv-2511-21135:
Ziyi Chen and a large team train in 2025 SocialNav, a foundation model that teaches robots to move through crowds politely, not just efficiently. Shortest-path planners ignore social norms, like not cutting through a conversation. SocialNav uses a hierarchical brain-action design: a high level that understands norms and explains its reasoning, and a low level that emits compliant trajectories. Its SocNav dataset holds 7 million samples, mixing chain-of-thought social reasoning data with an expert trajectory pyramid drawn from internet videos, simulators, and real robots.

Training first injects skills and norms by imitation, then refines them with SAFE-GRPO, a flow-based reinforcement learning method that rewards socially compliant behaviour. The video layer alone contributes 2.0 million pseudo-trajectories reconstructed from urban exploration footage. Against the previous state of the art, SocialNav raised success by 38 percent and social compliance by 46 percent in the authors' benchmark of nine social scenes.
arxiv-2511-21235:
Daniel Berend and five coauthors at Ben Gurion University present two new rules for deciding what a computer cache keeps and what it throws out, in 2025. Classic rules like Least Recently Used need heavy bookkeeping or react slowly when demand shifts. Their AdaptiveClimb instead adjusts one number, the promotion jump an item earns on each hit, based on recent hits and misses, with no per-item statistics to maintain.

Berend and his coauthors extend the idea in DynamicAdaptiveClimb, which also grows or shrinks the cache itself as workloads change. Across 1067 real-world traces from 6 datasets, the dynamic policy lifted hit ratios by up to 29 percent over the FIFO baseline. It also beat the next-best rivals, AdaptiveClimb and SIEVE, by roughly 10 to 15 percent, with the largest gains where working sets fluctuated most.
arxiv-2511-21635:
Anantha Padmanaban Krishna Kumar explains why deeper vision transformers can see worse, in 2025. Tracking token representations layer by layer on ImageNet through ViT-S, ViT-B, and ViT-L, Kumar finds a consistent three-phase pattern he calls Cliff-Plateau-Climb. Representations first decorrelate sharply, then process at low similarity for a long plateau, then re-correlate in the final layers.

The plateau stretches with depth, lasting 6, 12, and 14 layers in the three models, and simply adding layers extends diffusion rather than skill. In ViT-L, that same trade-off, between spreading information and scoring well, only shows up about 10 layers deeper than where ViT-B reaches it. Better models progressively marginalize the CLS token, the designed aggregation hub: in ViT-B its centrality fell by 99.2 percent during processing. Kumar's Information Scrambling Index quantifies the mixing, giving architects a diagnostic for choosing depth that completes clean phase transitions.
arxiv-2511-21835:
Fang continues a study of metrics, ways of measuring sizes of sections, on ample line bundles in non-Archimedean geometry, where distances obey a stronger triangle rule than usual. This second part follows an earlier paper on the same normed sections. The central objects here are semipositive metrics and the measures they spread over the associated analytic space of the variety.

The main theorem proves an arithmetic Hilbert-Samuel formula at a single local place. A normalized limit built from the metric equals an integral against an equidistribution measure, and for continuous semipositive metrics that measure becomes the Monge-Ampère measure. Fang also proves continuity properties for Shilov finite metrics and solves the Monge-Ampère equation with prescribed finite equidistribution measure there. The results suggest the theory can be rebuilt from more analytic steps, separating the measure's construction from the underlying geometry.
arxiv-2511-21935:
Collina and colleagues ask whether algorithmic collusion, AI agents tacitly keeping prices high, survives when some sellers price by hand. They model repeated pricing games, the classic Bertrand setup where sellers undercut each other round after round and the lowest price wins the sale. AI agents play equilibrium strategies, while a defecting human uses a simple no-regret learning rule.

Their main theoretical finding is that even a single human defection can destabilize collusion and drive prices down, and multiple defections push prices closer still to competitive levels in their model. That contrasts with two-player games, where earlier work showed high prices can persist despite a heuristic player. They also study defection-aware AI agents, characterizing exactly when collusion is fragile and when it persists as sellers and prices grow.
arxiv-2511-22635:
Bradd, Higson, and Yuncken complete the re-proof's second half. The principle organises the tempered dual of a real reductive group. Every tempered irreducible representation is either square-integrable modulo the centre, a discrete series representation, or embeds in one parabolically induced from a square-integrable representation on a smaller Levi subgroup. It is one of two pillars under the Plancherel formula, and unlike the discrete series, studied for decades, had received geometric attention.

The proof runs through operator algebras. Tempered representations correspond exactly to representations of the reduced C-star-algebra. The authors take the C-star-algebra built from the Satake compactification in the first paper, choose an ideal in it, and use the fact that an ideal splits C-star-algebra's spectrum in two. That partition separates discrete series from induced representations, yielding the principle rather than by case analysis, showcasing how noncommutative geometry organises harmonic analysis.
arxiv-2511-23235:
Gatla and colleagues build the first question-answering system for Hindi tourism, focused on Varanasi, the pilgrimage city on the Ganges. Visitors ask about rituals, temples, food, and travel in Hindi rather than English. No Hindi QA resources existed for this culturally specific domain. The team hand-built 7,715 question-answer pairs through fieldwork across ten subdomains, from Ganga Aarti ceremonies to ashrams, public toilets, and river cruises.

They expanded the set to 27,455 pairs with Llama-generated questions, then fine-tuned BERT and RoBERTa variants two ways, full supervised tuning and the parameter-light LoRA method. LoRA reached an F1 score of 85.3 percent while training 98 percent fewer parameters, and the fully tuned Hindi-RoBERTa did best overall at 89.75 percent F1 in the merged evaluation, handling culturally embedded words like aarti and kund better than the BERT variants did.
arxiv-2511-23435:
Prevedel speeds up Fabry-Pérot photoacoustic tomography, an all-optical biomedical imaging method, not with better hardware but by reordering the scan itself. The imaging sensor's cavity thickness varies across its surface. The ideal laser wavelength differs at each scan position and the laser must retune between positions, which throttles speed in time-critical experiments where fast imaging genuinely matters for living samples.

His new approach sorts scan positions by their optimal bias wavelength and then optimizes the visiting order with traveling-salesman-style algorithms. This cuts how often the laser must retune and shortens the path. Tested under realistic imaging conditions, the optimized trajectories deliver roughly an overall sevenfold increase in effective imaging speed and work with any interrogation laser and sensor quality. They come with a quantified trade-off between scan frequency and sensitivity for users to choose from in the study.
arxiv-2512-00035:
Mislav Has, Tao Xiong, Fehmi Ben Abdesslem, and Mario Kušek test WebAssembly on resource-constrained Internet of Things devices. IoT hardware and software vary widely, which hurts portability and maintenance. WebAssembly, built for the web, is a portable, secure, and efficient runtime that could unify deployment.

Their study measures its performance, efficiency, and portability on limited devices. Evidence like this tells builders whether one binary can truly serve many tiny platforms. Portable runtimes would ease updates and security patching across device fleets. Portability across heterogeneous hardware is the problem statement, with WebAssembly tested as the unifying runtime answer.
arxiv-2512-00335:
Large language models consume enormous energy on graphics processors, which limits where they can run. Takuto Ando and Yu Eto study accelerating them on a coarse-grained reconfigurable array in 2025. Such arrays offer a trade-off between energy efficiency and programmability.

The authors work on efficient kernel mapping, placing the model's core computations onto the array's structure. They also carry out a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system, not just its peak speed. Hardware like this could bring capable language models to settings where power and cooling are tight. Coarse-grained arrays sit between fixed circuits and general processors in flexibility. Mapping is where such hardware usually succeeds or fails in practice.
arxiv-2512-00635:
Cryptographic chips can be mathematically secure and still leak secrets through power use and electromagnetic radiation. Archisman Ghosh surveys circuit-level countermeasures and proactive detection techniques for side-channel attacks in 2025, in an extended abstract. Internet-connected embedded devices make the exposure widespread.

Side-channel analysis exploits timing, cache behavior, photonic emission, and other physical traces. Buildable, low-overhead countermeasures can be added to designs without exotic fab steps. Proactive detection aims to catch leakage during design rather than after deployment, protecting devices from keys extracted by simply watching them work. Extended abstracts announce work in progress, inviting scrutiny before the full study lands. Low overhead matters because consumer devices cannot spare much power for defenses. For folks who ship small smart gear, the gain is a shield they can add at the fab stage. It is not a patch they must beg users to put on later.
arxiv-2512-00735:
A large team led by S Ivanov and A Kireev reports on light trapped by defects in a 2025 physics paper. They study topological dislocations, flaws that run through a material that is otherwise a neat periodic lattice. Far from the flaw, the lattice keeps its regular pattern.

Such dislocations show up in many systems, from crystals and sound-based lattices to light-based ones and matter waves. The team observes light trapping at these defects, in both the linear and nonlinear regimes. Trapped light stays near the defect instead of spreading away. Learning to control that effect could guide new designs for photonic devices.
arxiv-2512-00935:
Hunseok Kang, Doowon Koh, and Dung The Tran extend a classic partition theorem in a 2025 math paper. Raimi's theorem concerns splitting a space into parts with a surprising covering property. The authors move the result from its classical setting to the continuous world of the circle. Their new setting is the n-dimensional torus, a doughnut-like space in any dimension.

Building on recent work in finite groups, they prove that measurable partitions of the torus exist with a strong property. For any finite measurable cover, some shifted piece of the cover meets every part of the partition in positive measure. Such results link combinatorics, measure, and symmetry.
arxiv-2512-01735:
Marius Tacke and co-authors let language models design physics-constrained networks for mechanics. Agentic frames now spawn task-specific agents on demand. The team extends that idea to software modules. A module for a science task can be generated when needed, not hand-built.

Their case is constitutive modeling in solid mechanics. The generated networks must obey physics laws by construction. If the demo holds, labs could order bespoke solvers in plain words. Each solver would still respect the physics its task demands. Generated modules ship with their constraint code visible, so engineers can audit the physics before a design rests on its output.
arxiv-2512-01835:
Milo Bechtloff Weising studies a vast algebraic object: the infinite Hecke algebra of type A, built over a field where distance is measured in a non-archimedean way. His 2025 paper focuses on the case where the algebra's parameter is a pseudo-uniformizer, a special element of that field.

Weising looks at a family of representations called almost-symmetric, which must obey extra conditions from both topology and algebra. He then gives a complete classification of the irreducible ones, the basic building blocks that cannot be broken down further. For representation theorists, the work pins down exactly which building blocks this infinite algebra allows.
arxiv-2512-02135:
White dwarfs often show heavy elements in their atmospheres, pollution that should sink quickly, so something must keep delivering rocky debris. Isabella Trierweiler, Konstantin Gerbig, and Malena Rice test in 2025 whether slow orbital oscillations driven by a distant companion can do the delivering.

These von Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai oscillations need a three-body system tipped at a large mutual inclination to switch on. The authors add dissipative precession, a gradual swivel of the orbits, and check how often the mechanism triggers pollution. The result constrains a leading explanation for how dead stars come to eat their own planetary systems.
arxiv-2512-02435:
Zhongjian Qiao and seven co-authors work on teaching agents from logged data when the world changes. An agent trained for one setting may be deployed in another that moves in different ways. Logs from the new setting may be scarce, while logs from the old one are plentiful.

Mixing both datasets naively can hurt, since the old data follows different dynamics. The team's method filters the data, keeping samples that align in both dynamics and value. Cleaner training data should help agents adapt to a new setting without fresh trial and error in the real world. The filter keeps what helps and drops what would pull the agent off its course.
arxiv-2512-02735:
Anna Rodum Bjøru and four co-authors frame a causal way to explain black box AI models with concepts. Concept based explanations describe a model's choice in human ideas, like stripes or wings, rather than pixels. Good explanations must be understandable and faithful to what the model truly does.

Their framework intervenes on concepts and computes the probability that the concept suffices for the outcome. Both local explanations, for one case, and global ones, for the model overall, come from the same causal logic. Faithful concept explanations could build trust in AI used for lending, hiring, and care. A cause based score can be shown to a judge or a board in words they can grasp and probe.
arxiv-2512-02835:
Yifan Li and six co-authors make video segmentation explain its reasoning instead of hiding it. Referring video segmentation finds an object described in words, often involving motion, cause, or change over time. Past systems compress that reasoning into opaque embeddings, leaving the chain of thought untraceable.

ReVSeg uses reinforcement learning to reward a visible reasoning chain for each segmentation. Step by step reasoning can be checked, corrected, and trusted more easily. Transparent segmentation helps editors, annotators, and safety reviewers who must know why a system tracked one object and not another. Steps shown in the open can be taught, marked, and fixed, which is more than a lone black box score can give a class.
arxiv-2512-02935:
L. de Souza and four co-authors study clustering in active matter where particles slow down in crowds. Self propelled particles can pile up through simple excluded volume effects. Quorum sensing adds a second route: propulsion drops where local density runs high.

Using kinetic balance theory and simulations, the team finds the two routes interact in a reentrant way. Clustering dips through a clear minimum as sensing strength or persistence time varies. Non monotonic clustering warns designers of synthetic swarms that more sensing does not always mean more grouping. A dip, not a climb, is the shock here. More of a good thing can mean less of the clumps that labs have long taken as its mark.
arxiv-2512-03035:
Ibrahim Laiche and three co-authors learn control ready models of mechanical systems without ever measuring acceleration. Lagrangian systems describe machines from robots to vehicles through energy based equations. Non conservative forces, like friction, complicate both modeling and control design.

Their hybrid method derives and identifies physically consistent models, which model based control synthesis requires. Skipping acceleration measurements removes a noisy, costly sensing step. Consistent models learned from gentler data could widen model based control to machines where accelerometers are impractical or unreliable. Gentle data needs are a door for small labs. They lack the racks of big names but hold much of the skill that real world rigs need to work at all.
arxiv-2512-03135:
Bosons may host protected states at their edges, like fermions do. Alan Gardin, Emilio Cobanera, and Giuseppe Carlo Tettamanzi study that idea in this 2025 work. For fermions, a famous ten-fold scheme sorts insulators and superconductors by symmetry.

The authors seek a bosonic scheme as close as possible to the fermionic one. They focus on synthetic photo-magnonic crystals, systems that mix light and magnetic waves. They report symmetry-protected zero modes at the boundary that involve many bodies. Such modes could matter for future quantum devices. Bosonic edge modes could store quantum states in ways that resist local noise.
arxiv-2512-03335:
Designers build work step by step, refining as they go. Faizan Farooq Khan and co-authors model that process in this 2025 work. Most AI design tools treat synthesis as a single-step task, which understates how complex creative work is.

The authors present a layered design generation method that proceeds step by step. Each layer adds detail while keeping earlier choices in view. Stepwise tools fit how designers actually work. They could make AI help in layout, graphics, and product design feel more natural and controllable. Layered steps also let users intervene mid-design, not just judge the final output.
arxiv-2512-03735:
Measuring temperature with a quantum probe sounds exotic, yet the limits of such sensing in noisy conditions are still unclear. Pritam Chattopadhyay addresses that gap in a 2025 quantum physics letter. The focus is on probes in non-Gaussian states, which lack the smooth bell-shaped statistics of familiar quantum states, while energy leaks into the surroundings.

Working in the short-time regime, Chattopadhyay derives exact bounds on the quantum Fisher information, the quantity that caps how precise any temperature estimate can be. The analysis shows Fock states, which contain a definite number of energy packets, gain precision linearly with time. Gaussian probes improve only with the square of time, which is weaker at short times. Exact simulations back the formulas. The author maps the scheme onto circuit quantum electrodynamics hardware, sketching a realistic route to sharper thermometers in noisy devices.
arxiv-2512-03835:
Drones acting as flying base stations could fill coverage gaps in crowded cities and remote countryside alike. Ghoshana Bista and colleagues study how to run such a fleet in a 2025 systems preprint on 5G network slicing. Slicing lets one network serve premium, silver, and bronze users at different quality levels, and the drones must position themselves and share resources wisely.

Their framework trains several learning agents together but lets each act on its own, comparing three multi-agent algorithms head to head. MAPPO gave the best balance between service quality and energy use, especially where interference was heavy. MADDPG offered finer continuous control and slightly cleaner signals in open rural scenes, at higher energy cost. MADQN served as an efficient baseline for discrete choices. No algorithm won everywhere: the right pick depends on terrain, user density, and service demands.
arxiv-2512-04035:
Judging a company's financial danger from its published statements is a ranking problem with several competing risks at once. Marwa Abdullah, Revzon Oksana Anatolyevna, and Duaa Abdullah apply multi-criteria decision-making tools to that problem in a 2025 finance preprint. Their case company is the AL-Ahliah Vegetable Oil Company, and their evidence is a decade of its ratios.

Two established techniques do the analysis. The Analytical Hierarchy Process organises the risks and weights their relative importance through structured pairwise comparisons. Simple Additive Weighting then scores the alternatives on those weighted measures. Together the methods cover 2008 to 2017, letting the authors rank the risks faced and single out the years of greatest exposure. The study is presented as a worked example of how formal tools can discipline a judgement that managers often make by feel.
arxiv-2512-04235:
Estimating a probability density from data sounds routine until the data refuse to be Gaussian, skewing and decaying with long tails instead. Shantanu Sarkar, Mousumi Sinha, and Dexter Cahoy benchmark the options in a 2025 preprint, and propose a faster contender. Six made-up unimodal datasets with realistic irregularities serve as the proving ground.

Their Dual Polynomial Regression method splits a density at its mode. Each side of the split gets its own fit, capturing asymmetry directly. Training uses GPU-accelerated kernel or histogram estimates implemented in TensorFlow, both faster than the standard SciPy routine. Competitors span parametric fits, histograms, and kernel methods. They are scored by squared error, divergence, correlation, normalisation, and runtime. Validation on blood pressure data from three hundred thousand patients crowns a fourth-order version, trained on kernel output, as the best balance of accuracy and overhead.
arxiv-2512-04535:
Zhenzhen Ren, Xinpeng Zhang, Zhenxing Qian, and co-authors built GTM, a small model that pretends to be any software tool an AI agent might call. Agents gain real power by using outside tools, from search engines to payment apps. Training them live on real tools is slow, costly, and hard to maintain. Their 2025 arXiv paper offers a stand-in: one model that mimics tool behavior on demand.

GTM holds about one and a half billion parameters. Given a tool's description and call arguments in a prompt, it returns output that closely matches the real tool. The team trained it with a pipeline that faked training data across tens of thousands of tools in hundreds of domains. Prompt-level setup swaps tools without new code. Agents can then practice at high speed against the simulator. The approach cuts training bills while keeping practice realistic.
arxiv-2512-04735:
Herbert Jordan, Kamil Jezek, and Pavle Subotic introduce a state database built for modern blockchains that never fork. A chain's state database stores account data and proves who owns what. Ethereum's version was designed for a forking chain that keeps many state versions alive. Newer chains copy Ethereum's standards so apps can move over, yet they finalize blocks without forks, making the old database wasteful. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts fresh.

The new database is a native build, not a layer over a generic key-value store. It keeps full Ethereum compatibility while dropping multi-version baggage. For validators, the team reports tenfold speed gains and state storage shrunk by about ninety-nine percent. App-facing queries also run several times faster. Leaner state storage lowers the hardware bar for running a validator, which helps keep fast chains decentralized.
arxiv-2512-05035:
Philipp Mertsch reviews what a decade of sharp measurements has taught us about the cosmic rays that rain through our galaxy. Instruments in space now record the makeup of these particles with high precision up to very high energies, and ground arrays take over beyond that. The energy spectrum, long drawn as one smooth slope, turns out to have several breaks, and the arrival directions show patterns of their own.

On the theory side, the breaks can be explained by shifts between classes of sources or by changes in how particles wander. What limits every prediction, Mertsch argues, is our poor map of the galaxy's magnetic fields, large and small. He flips the problem around: because cosmic rays respond to those fields, their measured paths can serve as a probe. The talk sums up what is known, what is not, and what future data could reveal.
arxiv-2512-05335:
Yuxiang Liu and Shengfan Cao tackle visual domain transfer for robots that learn by imitation. The hard version of the problem is realistic: the target environment offers only scarce recordings, none of them expert demonstrations, and none collected by the current policy. The authors first prove a bound. The imitation error in the target domain is at most the source-domain error, plus a measure of how differently the two domains' observations distribute, state by state.

Guided by that bound, their method, State-Conditional Adversarial Learning, aligns the latent representations of source and target observations, conditioned on the system's state. A discriminator estimates the divergence term in the bound. Experiments in visually diverse simulated driving environments show robust transfer and strong sample efficiency. The work offers a principled route for self-driving policies trained in one visual world to keep working in another they have barely seen.
arxiv-2512-05535:
A. Katherina Vivas and seven co-authors ask whether the Crater II dwarf galaxy is being torn apart by our Milky Way's tides. Crater II is an odd neighbour: enormous for its faintness, extremely diffuse, and sprinkled near its core with variable stars. The team mounted a deep, multi-epoch imaging campaign across its outskirts with the Dark Energy Camera, sweeping a wide swath of sky.

The survey confirms tidal tails streaming from the galaxy. It catalogs dozens of periodic variable stars, most of them members — RR Lyrae stars and anomalous Cepheids whose pulses make them distance markers. Those markers reveal a strong distance gradient running along the tails, plus a notable clump of stars in the leading tail. Despite covering less area than earlier surveys, the deeper photometry sharpens the tails' definition. The answer to the title's question, the evidence says, is yes: Crater II is disrupting.
arxiv-2512-05635:
Georgy Perevozchikov, Nancy Mehta, Egor Ershov, and Radu Timofte tackle a bottleneck in smartphone photography. Camera software that turns raw sensor data into finished pictures learns well only from paired examples. Such pairs are costly to gather. Their 2025 framework trains these image pipelines with unpaired data instead, using optimal transport to map between the raw and finished domains.

A key piece is the unbalanced form of transport, which can discount odd samples in the target set rather than forcing a match. A committee of expert critics guides the mapping, each one watching for a known failure: off colors, broken structure, or unreal fine detail. The team retrained leading camera pipelines with the method. In paired mode it beat the original results on all measures. In unpaired mode it rivaled, and at times topped, models trained the costly way.
arxiv-2512-05735:
Paula Mellado, Francisco Muñoz, and Javiera Cabezas-Escares follow the motion of the charge pattern in their moiré ladder. In their charge density wave, charge piles up in a rhythm that does not match the crystal lattice. The pattern can slide at almost no energy cost, a motion carried by excitations called phasons. Their 2025 model is a four band tight binding ladder whose legs are shifted against each other.

The shift comes from pairing up sites along one leg, and it builds a large moiré cell with modulated hopping between legs. Bands flatten near the Fermi level. With Coulomb repulsion added, a charge wave forms with opposite bumps on the two legs. Its phasons are long lived, neutral, and sound-like, and their speed is set by the shift and the inter-leg hopping. The model clarifies how small layer mismatches bring such sliding order into stacked materials.
arxiv-2512-06035:
Ana Isabel Lopez Murillo and five co-authors listen for planets tugging on each other's schedules. When planets transit, gravity between them shifts the crossing times. Those transit timing variations can weigh planets, precious where star wobble methods drown in young star noise. The team searched thirty nine young systems hosting fifty three transiting planets, using Kepler, K2, and TESS data, for timing wobbles.

Known variations were recovered for eleven planets; four new candidates appeared. The surprise is the rate: about twenty eight percent of young planets show timing evidence, against roughly seven percent in older Kepler systems. Starspots, the obvious confounder, explain little of it. Young systems look dynamically busier, still settling. The paper ends practically: a priority list for ground based follow up.
arxiv-2512-06435:
Mara Sherlin Talento, Jordan Richards, Raphael Huser, and Hernando Ombao look for the brain channels that drive extreme events, such as seizures, rather than everyday activity. When brain signals spike to very large values, the links between regions in those extreme moments may carry clues that normal links miss. Standard tools sum up pairwise ties or fit fixed models, but they cannot say which channels drive the strongest extreme links between two groups of signals.

The team extends a classic method, canonical correlation, into the tails of the signal spread. A new matrix of pairwise tail ties feeds an efficient estimator of their measure, and plots show which channels add most to the extreme link. The payoff is sharper spotting of extreme events in EEG records from epilepsy patients, where a few channels are known to spark seizures. Better spotting supports better seizure risk care.
arxiv-2512-07335:
Paul Wilsens, Katrien Antonio, and Gerda Claeskens nowcast with machine learning inside a classic statistical loop. Nowcasting means estimating what has already happened but not yet been reported, the daily reality of disease surveillance. Insurance claims, and economic statistics, where delays make the present look rosier or grimmer than it is. Their framework runs expectation-maximisation, alternating between guessing the missing reports and refitting the model, but lets neural networks and gradient boosting machines do the fitting.

Both halves of the problem are learned: how events occur, and how they get reported, each with its own covariates about timing and about the entity involved. In simulations with high-dimensional information and nonlinear effects, the method models both processes well and beats existing EM nowcasters built on linear models. Applied to the reporting of Covid-19 cases in Argentina, the gradient boosting version again performed best.
arxiv-2512-07535:
John O'Hara and nine co-authors wrote this 2025 quantum technology paper. Quantum photonic chips could power future computing and communication at large scale. Their growth has been held back by light sources that appear at random places.

The team instead grows quantum dots at controlled sites, in neat arrays. They align an array of ten gallium arsenide dots to ten silicon nitride waveguides. The coupling works at the chip's edge and holds at cryogenic temperatures. Tiny nanopillars, self-aligned around each dot, guide the fabrication. An on-chip beamsplitter confirms that single photons enter the chip as triggered. The dots emit at close wavelengths, so neighbors overlap spectrally across the array. Light collection stays consistent and repeatable from waveguide to waveguide. Simulations suggest the coupling efficiency can still grow from its current level. The result is a regular, high-yield bank of single-photon sources.
arxiv-2512-07635:
Yusuke Nishinaka wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on vertex algebras, structures that encode quantum field symmetries. Costello and Gwilliam built a route from prefactorization algebras to vertex algebras. Their theorem demanded a discreteness condition.

Nishinaka rebuilds that route in a bornological setting, a flavor of complex analysis. That version drops the discreteness demand. He then feeds the machine a suitable Lie conformal algebra. From it he constructs a prefactorization algebra the extraction accepts. The resulting vertex algebra matches the algebra's enveloping vertex algebra exactly. The construction runs through an object he calls a factorization envelope. It extends earlier work on affine and Virasoro vertex algebras. A super version of the story comes along as well. New such algebras appear for famous vertex superalgebras. The Neveu-Schwarz example is named among them.
arxiv-2512-07735:
Shi Jin, Qi Shao, and Haitao Wang wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on gas dynamics under uncertainty. The Boltzmann equation tracks how a gas of particles moves and collides. Real problems feed it uncertain starting data and an uncertain collision rule.

The authors ask how the solution's sensitivity behaves as time runs on. Whole space, with no walls to complicate matters, is their setting. A Green's function method drives the central analysis. Higher derivatives of the solution in the random inputs decay over time. That decay is polynomial, steady rather than sudden, in their results. They then turn the same lens on a numerical scheme. Stochastic Galerkin approximation replaces the randomness with a computable system. Its numerical error also decays polynomially as time advances. Uncertainty, in this setting, washes out of the solution's fine structure. Long-time forecasts inherit a calmer error picture than feared.
arxiv-2512-07835:
Eun Park wrote this 2025 dissertation in algebra on taking group algebras apart. A group algebra blends a group's symmetry with a field's arithmetic. Over a field of positive characteristic, that blend has a rich block structure.

The goal is an explicit split into projective indecomposable modules. Those modules are the algebra's basic building bricks. Park finds the radical series of each brick for the algebras studied. Projective covers and injective envelopes serve as the construction tools. Cyclic group algebras turn out to be uniserial, a simple chain. A p-group algebra is itself a single projective indecomposable module. The worked examples live over characteristic two in the dissertation. The Klein four-group and the alternating groups on four and five letters are done fully.  The topic then widens to blocks, the algebra's coarsest split.
arxiv-2512-07935:
Myrann Baker-Rasooli, Nathan du Toit, Nicolas Pavloff, and Quentin Glorieux wrote this 2025 physics paper. In a fluid of light, photons flow like a superfluid inside a nonlinear medium. Vortices in that flow can chase and overtake each other, a dance called leapfrogging.

The team imprints two vortex-antivortex pairs and films what follows. Phase-resolved imaging tracks the swirls' real-time evolution in the lab. A point-vortex model, set in an outward background flow, matches the dance well. Careful control of the starting gap separates success from breakdown. Two distinct dissipation mechanisms explain where leapfrogging fails. At high injected speeds, phase slips tear through the pattern. Multi-charged vortices instead spawn a dispersive shock wave. That wave acts as a steady source of further phase slippage.  Light-based fluids offer a clean stage for watching vortices misbehave. The work maps how quantum fluids lose perfect flow.
arxiv-2512-08435:
Yadikaer Maitiniyazi and Masatoshi Yamada, theoretical physicists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about composite models of gravity. In such models, the graviton is not a basic particle but emerges from more fundamental fermions or scalars, bound together. The authors ask whether a dynamical tensor field with the right properties really appears.

Working with the functional renormalization group, they study two prototype models, one fermionic and one scalar. In both, an auxiliary tensor field is introduced in the channel of the energy momentum tensor, exactly where a graviton should form. Following the flow equations, they show a finite kinetic term for that field is generated dynamically at low energies. In the spin two sector, the result matches the structure of the Einstein Hilbert action. Other sectors keep extra terms, which the authors are careful not to mistake for a gauge fixing artifact.
arxiv-2512-08535:
Xinyue Liang, Zhinyuan Ma, Lingchen Sun, and colleagues, computer vision researchers in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their framework, Photo3D, tackles a weak point of three dimensional generation: shapes are sound, but surfaces look fake. Real three dimensional assets with rich texture are scarce, because precise scanning is slow and hard.

Photo3D instead learns from images made by a strong image model. Since generated pictures can warp the underlying structure, a structure aligned pipeline makes several views that agree with a given shape, building a detail rich dataset. An enhancement stage then transfers realistic appearance onto a generated object, using perceptual features and semantic matching to keep the look consistent without bending the structure. The scheme plugs into different generators, and across tests it reached top photorealistic quality. Image models, the authors argue, can supply the texture richness that three dimensional datasets lack.
arxiv-2512-09335:
Seonghwa Choi and colleagues present RnD-Avatar, a framework for building human avatars that can be relit and re-posed from a single camera video. Reconstructing a moving person in three dimensions is a long-standing problem. Recent radiance field and Gaussian splatting methods often lose the fine geometry tied to motion, such as clothing wrinkles, so their results look less than photorealistic.

RnD-Avatar attacks that weakness with dynamic skinning weights, which define how the avatar bends with pose while also learning extra deformations caused by body motion. A new regularization term helps recover fine geometric detail even when visual cues are sparse. The authors also release a multi-view dataset recorded under varied lighting for testing relighting. Their framework renders new poses and viewpoints realistically and holds up under arbitrary lighting, reaching leading results on view synthesis, pose rendering, and relighting tests.
arxiv-2512-09435:
Xufan He and colleagues present UniPart, a system that generates 3D objects part by part. Many applications need models that come apart into meaningful pieces, not single fused shapes. Existing generators either segment parts implicitly, with little control over detail, or depend on external segmenters trained on labeled datasets.

The key observation is that a model learning whole-object geometry naturally becomes aware of parts along the way. Building on that, the authors design a unified latent representation that encodes an object's geometry and its part structure together. UniPart then runs a two-stage diffusion process guided by an image: first it generates the whole geometry while segmenting the latent parts. Then it refines each part using both whole-object and part-specific information, predicting part shapes in both global and canonical spaces. In experiments, UniPart gave better segmentation control and part-level geometric quality than existing approaches.
arxiv-2512-09535:
Yves Ruffenach explores a way to build a language model, moving sequence order out of the neural network's operations and into the geometry of its hidden space. His model is a variational autoencoder whose latent variables evolve under a Gaussian process, a probabilistic model of smooth trajectories. A non-autoregressive decoder generates all words of a sentence in parallel.

The paper gives the formulation: a causal Gaussian process prior over the latent sequence, and a structured approximate posterior for training. Its training protocol is built on a regularized evidence bound. The evaluation is framed as a constrained proof of concept rather than a bid for state-of-the-art scores. Within that frame, the model trained stably, and its sampling variants behaved consistently with each other. Ruffenach concludes that part of language's structure can be carried by the probabilistic geometry of a latent space instead of neural machinery.
arxiv-2512-09735:
Marialuisa Aliotta and colleagues review how underground laboratories have advanced nuclear astrophysics, the study of the fusion reactions that power stars and forge the chemical elements. Those reactions happen at energies so low that their rates are extraordinarily hard to measure on the surface, where cosmic rays swamp the signal. The review marks thirty years of activity at LUNA, the first underground laboratory for the field.

Going deep underground removes much of the background noise, letting detectors count the rare events that mimic stellar burning. The authors recount the major breakthroughs achieved this way, explaining how understanding of how stars form, shine, and die was built from the interplay of observation, theory, and these experiments. They also survey the instrumentation and detection techniques the challenges forced into existence. The review closes by anticipating future opportunities at LUNA and at other underground laboratories worldwide.
arxiv-2512-10335:
Anna Ohorodnyk and Chen-Hsuan Hsu study a pair of parallel helical channels, wires along which electrons move in a twist-linked way, joined to superconducting pairing. Their paper notes that tidy theory predicts special zero-energy modes at the corners of such a system. But real samples are never tidy, and flaws change the story.

Using renormalisation group analysis, the authors add uneven pairing and interaction between the channels, plus random spin-flip flaws from magnetic or charge disorder. They find a richer map of phases, including one holding a single Majorana zero mode per corner, and cases where lost zero modes revive. Disorder, usually treated as pure harm, becomes a knob that can reshape the topological behaviour, with signs a scanning tunnelling microscope could see.
arxiv-2512-10635:
Klaus Jansen, Kai Kahler, and Corinna Wambsganz shrink hard scheduling and packing problems without changing their answers. Two instances of a parameterised problem are equivalent when they share the same solutions, or when one instance's solutions can be rebuilt from the other's plus some precomputed pieces. A small equivalent instance is as good as a kernel: solve the little one, keep the answer.

The authors construct such equivalents for scheduling and knapsack problems and improve a known bound on the size of an equivalent vector for integer linear programs. That improvement cascades into compact equivalents for feasibility problems generally, a small one for knapsack in terms of its item count. And a kernel for integer programs in terms of their constraint matrix. For load balancing, a generalised scheduling problem, they reach an equivalent instance whose size depends only on the distinct processing times.
arxiv-2512-10935:
Jay Karhade and co-authors present Any4D, a system that rebuilds a moving three-dimensional scene, with real-world scale, in one forward pass. Earlier tools usually chose between dense flow for two views or sparse tracking of points in 3D. Any4D instead predicts motion and geometry for every pixel across all frames at once, and it is not limited to ordinary video.

When extra sensors are available, the transformer can also consume depth frames, inertial motion readings, and radar Doppler data. The trick is a modular description of the scene: each view carries egocentric factors, depth maps and camera intrinsics in local coordinates. While allocentric factors, camera poses and scene flow, live in global coordinates. Across varied setups the authors report errors two to three times lower than prior work at fifteen times the speed, opening doors for robotics and other applications that need metric 4D understanding.
arxiv-2512-11035:
José Benavides and colleagues count how many galaxies are intrinsically thin, and find far more flat dwarfs than simulations produce. Using large galaxy catalogues, they infer true shapes from the spread of apparent flattening seen on the sky. Thin systems turn out to be common across a wide range of galaxy masses.

Among mid sized galaxies, a large share are flatter than one to five in thickness, and even small dwarfs include many very flat systems. Three leading cosmological simulations, by contrast, produce almost no thin dwarfs at all. The authors blame limited resolution and imperfect treatment of gas and star formation physics. Their census challenges modellers to explain how small disk galaxies form and stay so flat.
arxiv-2512-11135:
Karthik Garimella and colleagues work on running transformer language models on encrypted data, so cloud servers never see private queries in plain form. Fully homomorphic encryption allows computation directly on scrambled data, but its limited instruction set makes standard operations slow and awkward. The team focused on the linear algebra kernels at the heart of transformer inference.

Using the Orion framework, they benchmarked two ways of packing matrix operations and found one clearly faster at transformer scales. Network level pruning then cut the run time of feed forward layers by more than tenfold. They also added encrypted matrix multiplication between two ciphertexts, a missing piece for attention blocks. A roofline analysis showed the implementations are limited by memory traffic, pointing to new encodings as the route to scalable private inference.
arxiv-2512-11335:
Yixuan Zhang and a large team improve ultrasound image segmentation by teaching a vision base model to respect boundaries. Ultrasound guides many medical choices, but speckle noise and artefacts blur organ edges. The powerful DINOv3 model, trained on natural images, segments medical images well yet is insensitive to the specific way ultrasound boundaries degrade.

Their FreqDINO setup works in the frequency domain, splitting images into low frequency structure and high frequency boundary detail at several scales, then aligning the parts with learned attention. A refinement module builds boundary prototypes from the high frequency components, and a decoder keeps boundary and region predictions steady with each other. Extensive tests show the method surpassing leading alternatives with strong generalisation to new data. The authors release their code for medical and research use.
arxiv-2512-11535:
Licheng Zhang, Yuanqiu Huang, and Zhangdong Ouyang prove a route guarantee for the densest graphs that can be drawn with limited edge crossings. A 2-planar graph can be drawn so each edge is crossed at most twice, and an optimal one packs the maximum possible edges under that rule. The question is how connectivity of such dense drawings translates into Hamiltonian paths that visit every vertex.

The authors show every optimal 2-planar graph that is 4-connected is Hamiltonian connected, meaning a spanning path exists between any chosen pair of vertices. The connectivity demand cannot be relaxed. They construct infinitely many 3-connected optimal 2-planar graphs with no Hamiltonian cycle at all. The note pairs a clean positive theorem with matching counterexamples, a satisfying form of sharpness in graph theory.
arxiv-2512-11635:
Keerthana Murugaraj and co-authors teach computers to pull themes from huge piles of old newspapers. Historians face real hurdles: topics drift over decades, scan errors garble words, and the volume is vast. Older tools like LDA often miss how talk changes over time.

The team uses BERTopic, a neural method built on transformer word vectors. They apply it to news stories from 1955 to 2018 about nuclear power and safety. The method tracks how themes rose, fell, and merged, and shows how talk of power and weapons overlapped. It scaled well and read context better than older tools. The work gives historians a sharper lens on public debate.
arxiv-2512-11935:
Jaehyung Lee and co-authors present AGAPI, an open platform that wires language model agents to materials science tools on AtomGPT.org. Agents can call many web tools for data on crystals, forces, band gaps, and protein shapes. Eight open models are linked to the tool set.

The key question is whether tool access truly helps or just looks busy. The team splits error into agent error and error baked into the source data. On fresh test cases, agents with no tools missed band gaps by more than one electron volt. Agents with tools stayed near exact. The platform also ran ten step defect design jobs on its own, start to finish.
arxiv-2512-12135:
Lucine L Oganesian and co-authors at the University of Southern California presented BaRISTA at NeurIPS 2025. BaRISTA is a transformer model for brain signals recorded from inside the skull. Such recordings track many brain areas at once, at scales from one channel to whole regions.

Earlier models mostly coded each channel on its own. BaRISTA lets users choose the scale for coding and for masking during training. Tests on public data show that larger scales beat channel level coding on later decoding tasks. The model can also rebuild single channel signals well while using region level codes.
arxiv-2512-12335:
Anup Kushwaha and Om Prakash study hulls of linear codes over a special ring in a 2025 math paper. A code's hull is the overlap between the code and its dual code, and it matters for building quantum codes. Their ring, called E, lacks a multiplicative identity, which makes the theory less standard.

They first work out residue and torsion codes for the hulls, then give the hull's generator matrix in explicit form. Four build-up methods grow longer codes with larger hull rank from shorter ones. They also study when two codes are the same up to reordering, and how hulls can vary. As a use case, they classify optimal free E-linear codes up to length 8.
arxiv-2512-12735:
Zhimin Chen, Bryan Kelly, and Semyon Malamud characterize a hard limit on machine learning in finance in a 2025 paper. Learning methods are flexible, but finite samples cap how closely they can match the true data generating process. The authors define a universal lower bound, the Limits-to-Learning Gap, for the gap between a model's fit on observed data and the population benchmark.

Across variables like excess returns, yields, credit spreads, and valuation ratios, the implied gaps are large. Standard methods can thus substantially understate true predictability in financial data, they argue. They also refine the classic Hansen and Jagannathan bounds with the gap, study parameter learning in general equilibrium settings, and show the gap can naturally generate excess volatility in prices.
arxiv-2512-12835:
Eyal Kaplan writes a short note in set theory about two ways to order ultrafilters, which are tools used to compare very large collections. The two orders are called the Ketonen order and the Lipschitz order. Both extend an older order first used for normal measures.

Earlier work by Goldberg showed that the Lipschitz order extends the Ketonen order. He also noted that under a strong claim called the Ultrapower Axiom, the two orders are the same. Kaplan shows the orders can in fact differ. Even a weaker form of that axiom does not force them to match. The note settles an open question left by Goldberg.
arxiv-2512-12935:
Thanh Toan Le Ngo and co-authors build a system that finds a requested moment inside a video using text, sound, and image cues together. Video libraries are growing fast, so search by moment matters. Past systems used fixed mixes of cues, modeled time poorly, and forced users to pick a cue type by hand.

Their design first retrieves broadly with two vision models, then reranks with a third. A time aware score favors event chains that hang together over scattered frames. A GPT-4o based agent splits vague queries into visual, text, and speech sub-queries and adjusts the mix. Tests showed gains on vague queries and on temporal coherence.
arxiv-2512-13035:
Fran Ilcic and Indrakshi Raychowdhury build a digital quantum circuit that checks whether a simulated state stays physical. Their setting is a loop-string-hadron description of SU(3) gauge theory in one space dimension, a simplified form of the strong force theory. The description uses fewer qubits than older bases.

Even so, leftover constraints on flux numbers must hold link by link, and noise can push a state outside the allowed sector. Their oracle circuit tests the local constraint at a chosen link. They report its cost in qubits, gates, and circuit depth. The check could help keep future gauge theory simulations honest.
arxiv-2512-13235:
Jianyuan Bo and Yuan Fang present CORE, a self-supervised method for learning from graph data without labels. It builds on masked feature reconstruction, where a model restores the hidden features of masked nodes. The authors show the goals of that method and of contrastive learning can coincide under set conditions.

CORE pairs each masked node's original features only with its reconstructed ones, pushing the encoder to use context rather than the node itself. Masked nodes also serve as negative examples for contrast. The fusion beat prior masked methods on node and graph classification, gaining up to about 3.8 percent over GraphMAE variants in their tests.
arxiv-2512-13435:
Thomas Bsaibes and co-authors build a torsion pendulum from a lithographed silicon nitride ribbon, aimed at sensing extremely weak gravitational effects. Torsion pendulums can hold sizable masses in a very soft trap. If cooled near their ground state, faint quantum effects, possibly including gravity, might appear in their decoherence.

Thin ribbon suspensions bring the needed low dissipation but are hard to fabricate. Their wafer-scale method defines the ribbon by lithography, opening the way to extreme aspect ratios and multi-strand designs. A centimeter scale, 37 milligram device showed a fundamental frequency of 162 millihertz and a quality factor of 12,000 in vacuum.
arxiv-2512-13535:
Antonin Chodron de Courcel proves results for nonlocal conservation laws in several space dimensions. These laws track a quantity that moves based on values at a distance, not just nearby. His case allows a nonlinear mobility and a bounded force, with weak conditions on the kernel that links distant points.

Unlike the linear case, solutions here can form shocks in finite time, even with a smooth kernel. Courcel builds entropy solutions by a vanishing viscosity method, a limit of slightly smoothed problems. He also gives a rate for how fast that approach reaches the true solution. The results pin down when a solution exists and is the only one, at least for a short time.
arxiv-2512-13835:
Hilario Espinós and co-authors present a microwave-free way to measure magnetic fields with nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond. These centers are a solid-state platform for quantum sensing. Standard optical methods are sensitive but need microwaves, which heat samples and add stray fields that can disturb what is measured.

Their framework works at near-zero field and uses cross-relaxation between differently oriented centers, so no microwaves are needed. Past optical versions required strict alignment of the field with crystal axes. Bayesian inference on photoluminescence maps now extracts both the field vector and the crystal orientation under arbitrary configurations. An analytic model of the resonances speeds the inference. Tests show robust orientation finding and field reconstruction, toward compact, alignment-free magnetometers.
arxiv-2512-13935:
Qi Chen, Fabio Ramos, Alán Aspuru-Guzik, and Florian Shkurti speed up Bayesian optimization for molecular discovery with foundation model priors. It searches for the best molecule, learning how structure maps to properties. It struggles when data are scarce, priors are weak, and the candidate space is vast.

Their likelihood-free method skips explicit surrogate models and uses priors from general LLMs and chemistry foundation models to shape acquisition functions directly. It learns a tree-shaped partition of the search space with local acquisition functions, searched by Monte Carlo Tree Search. Coarse LLM-based clustering limits checks to promising clusters, improving scale. Experiments and ablations show large gains in scale, robustness, and sample efficiency for LLM-guided molecular search.
arxiv-2512-14635:
Martin Lang, Alexander Lenz, Ali Mohamed, Maria Laura Piscopo, and Aleksey Rusov compute B meson decay widths in a 2025 paper. They work in the heavy quark expansion, which predicts B meson lifetimes and lifetime ratios from quark level decays.

Starting from the most general effective Hamiltonian for non leptonic b quark decays, they compute analytic matching coefficients for two quark operator contributions up to mass dimension six. They also calculate weak annihilation contributions for four quark operators at dimension six, which were previously missing. The results complete the calculation of beyond Standard Model effects in tree level non leptonic decays tied to lifetimes. As a by product, they give new matching coefficients for the chromomagnetic operator at dimension five and the Darwin operator at dimension six.
arxiv-2512-14735:
Yuqun Zhang, Yuxuan Zhao, and Sijia Chen present PyFi, a 2025 framework that teaches vision language models to read financial images step by step. Questions are arranged like a pyramid, starting with simple perception and rising toward expert judgment. The work comes with PyFi-600K, a dataset of 600K question and answer pairs built around that pyramid.

The dataset is made without human labeling. A challenger agent and a solver agent compete under a Monte Carlo tree search setup, producing chains of harder and harder questions for each image. The team graded leading vision models level by level, then fine-tuned two Qwen2.5-VL models on the chains. Accuracy rose by 19.52% for the 3B model and 8.06% for the 7B model, showing how staged questions help models handle hard financial charts.
arxiv-2512-14835:
Alejandro Cruz-Osorio and seven coauthors improve the models used to picture the black hole in galaxy M87. The Event Horizon Telescope saw a glowing ring around the hole at 230 gigahertz, and other radio views at 86 gigahertz show a wider jet. Models of these views need the temperature of electrons in the hot gas.

Past models used simple formulas for that temperature and assumed a purely thermal spread of electron energies. The new method takes the temperature from tiny scale plasma simulations instead, with no knobs to tune. It matches the jet's shape and width at 86 gigahertz better, and fits the full spread of light well. The work credits magnetic reconnection, the snapping of field lines, with heating the electrons.
arxiv-2512-14935:
Nnamdi Philip Okonkwo and a coauthor build an AI boosted security center for cloud systems. Cloud security teams must sort huge, mixed streams of alerts from short lived resources on tight budgets. Their system, an AISOC built on AWS, watches three machines cast as attacker, defender, and monitoring host.

The team staged a reverse shell intrusion with Metasploit, then sent the defender's logs to an Elasticsearch and Kibana stack. Two classifiers were trained: one to spot malware, and one to flag odd log behavior, using synthetic logs that include attack variants. Their scores are calibrated and fused to sort events as normal, suspicious, or high confidence attack. On held out tests the fusion scored a macro F1 up to 1.00 under controlled conditions. The authors note real world noise will lower that, but simple fusion still helps small teams.
arxiv-2512-15235:
Claudio Savelli and three coauthors build FAME, a benchmark for testing whether language models can be made to forget. Models trained on web scale data raise privacy worries and right to be forgotten claims. Machine unlearning aims to remove set information without retraining from scratch, but existing tests cover only English and only whole person forgetting.

FAME uses synthetic data: 1,000 fictional actor biographies with 20,000 question answer pairs, in English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish. Each biography spans 20 topics in structured categories, from career to personal details. That design supports two tests: erasing a whole identity, and erasing single facts while keeping others. Two dataset splits back the two scenarios. Since the actors are invented, no model met them in pretraining, so unlearning scores stay clean and comparable across languages.
arxiv-2512-15335:
Chenxiang Zhang and five coauthors ask whether shrinking a neural network's numbers also shrinks its privacy leaks. Quantization lowers the precision of a model's parameters to save memory and computing cost. Privacy studies had mostly ignored it, focusing on full precision models and leaving the effect of bit width untested.

The team attacks quantized models with membership inference, which guesses whether a given record was in the training data. They test three post training quantization methods, AdaRound, BRECQ, and OBC, at 4 bit, 2 bit, and 1.58 bit precision on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet. Lower precision consistently leaked less, with up to ten times lower membership vulnerability than full precision models, at some cost in utility. Keeping only the last layer at higher precision gave fine control of the trade off.
arxiv-2512-15435:
Stefan Edelkamp studies computer play in multi player trick taking card games in a 2025 paper, using the German game Skat as the test case. Early choices, such as bidding, game choice, and the first cards kept or dropped, often matter more than later play. Those early choices rely on statistics drawn from large sets of expert human games.

Edelkamp presents an outer learning framework that grows that data set with millions of self played AI games, then merges the new statistics with the old. Perfect hash functions keep the large tables compact. The system keeps learning from its own play, and the approach can support several kinds of decisions in the game.
arxiv-2512-15535:
Christian Rohde and Florian Wendt derive an effective model for compressible liquid vapor flow with rapidly oscillating starting density in a 2025 paper. Such flow, with very many phase boundaries, arises in spray like settings. Tracking each boundary directly is hopeless, so a model for the average behavior is needed.

Starting from a parabolic relaxation of the Navier Stokes Korteweg system, they take a sequence of solutions whose starting densities oscillate ever faster. Reading densities as Young measures, they prove the solutions converge to an effective model. That model pairs standard fluid equations for the bulk quantities with a kinetic equation for the limit Young measure, which encodes the mixing dynamics.
arxiv-2512-15835:
Luigi Caputi and Francesco Vaccarino study diagrammatic Hochschild cohomology in a 2025 paper. It measures deformations of an algebra, and Gerstenhaber and Schack extended it to diagrams, where algebras sit at the nodes of a category and maps link them. Concrete worked cases remain scarce.

The paper pursues three aims. It revisits the link between the founders' chains and the Baues Wirsching theory of settings. It analyzes how the diagram version behaves under special algebra maps.
