The results also expose a trade-off between spoofing accuracy and communication rate, governed by the virtual geometry the user chooses to project.
arxiv-2605-00635:
Alexander Keimer and Lukas Pflug prove a general result: the entropy solutions of scalar conservation laws can be recovered as limits of nonlocal versions of the same laws. Conservation laws describe amounts like traffic density, and their entropy solutions are the right ones when shocks form. In the nonlocal law, the flux at a point depends on averages of the density nearby, which restores a finite travel speed that pure averaging would lose.

The proof changes altitude. Working with the integrals moves the problem to the Hamilton-Jacobi level, where rough-solution theory gives the steadiness needed to pin down the limit. The known bridge between the families then recovers the right solution. The result extends, after a shift, to sign-changing data. For convex fluxes the authors also prove a rate for how fast the limit is reached. It even lets one define solutions through nonlocal near-laws.
arxiv-2605-00935:
An Huang, Junggab Son, and Zuobin Xiong investigate step embeddings in diffusion models as a hidden channel for information. Step embeddings give the denoising network a time signal so it can adapt across noise levels, yet their scope and security risks are little studied. The authors introduce Shadow Timestep Embedding, a mechanism that encodes side-channel information into that temporal space.

Different steps show distinct coding capacity, and encoded information can be used for attack or defense through the scheduler interface. Theoretical analysis treats step embeddings as position maps and derives a coherence measure explaining why disjoint step ranges stay apart. The findings frame the step as a strong side channel for attack modeling and source work.
arxiv-2605-01035:
Daniel Báscones, Arshpreet Singh Maan, Valentin Savin, and Francisco Garcia-Herrero introduce a scalable FPGA architecture for real-time decoding of quantum low-density parity-check codes. The decoder uses message passing and exploits the detector error model from the GARI method, which handles correlated errors. Resource reuse with modest parallelism aims to cut power and area while preserving low latency. The design can in principle adapt to any such code using GARI.

As a case study, three decoder cores run on one FPGA for a well-known bivariate bicycle code, reaching sub-microsecond average latency per round. The implementation uses six times fewer resources than the previous GARI-based proposal. It is described as the first with multiple cores for correlated errors on a single device.
arxiv-2605-01135:
Anya Ji and six co-authors introduce ScribbleEdit, a synthetic dataset for image editing that combines freehand scribbles with text instructions. Text conveys semantics such as texture and color but lacks spatial precision, while scribbles give rough layout but cannot express detailed attributes. Existing models struggle to interpret both together because specialized training data was missing.

The dataset is built by a pipeline that generates source-target image pairs through inpainting, then pairs them with human-drawn scribbles and model-generated text instructions. Off-the-shelf diffusion and autoregressive editing models handle abstract scribbles poorly. Finetuning on ScribbleEdit significantly improves their ability to produce edits that match in both layout and meaning.
arxiv-2605-01435:
Kahori Komaki, Ryohei Miyadera, and Aoi Murakami study a twist on Wythoff's game, a classic two-pile taking game. Players remove stones from one pile, or the same number from both. Whoever takes the last stone wins. The same game can be drawn as a chess queen sliding toward the corner of a grid.

The variant studied here widens the winning corner into a terminal zone: all squares whose two coordinates sum to at most a chosen bound. Reaching any square in the zone ends the game. The team work out the set of losing positions for the player about to move, called P-positions, for this widened target. The pattern is given by the Fibonacci sequence, stated directly rather than by recursion. The result slots the variant neatly into the known theory of turning-turtles and cold positions in combinatorial game theory.
arxiv-2605-01535:
Stanislav Hencl and Yi Ru-Ya Zhang test a hopeful conjecture about weakly quasiregular maps, a bent class of mappings used in geometric analysis. Below a critical smoothness level, such maps need not behave, and Iwaniec and Martin had conjectured that extra regularity would restore good behavior.

The pair show that two natural extra demands, continuity and boundedness, do not save the claim in three or more dimensions. For any bounded region and any exponent under the threshold, they build a bounded continuous weakly quasiregular map, as smooth as the setting allows, that still fails to be quasiregular. Their maps can even have wild sets of nearly the largest size the smoothness permits. The fault lies in a sign condition on the Jacobian that is too weak at this level. Swapping it for a one-sided condition on the distributional degree does restore the good behavior in a stated range.
arxiv-2605-01735:
Chenchen Tan and five co-authors erase a chosen topic from a language model without ever seeing its training data. Privacy and governance rules increasingly demand such selective unlearning, yet most methods need the original corpus and work by refusal training or broad gradient pushes that risk the model's general skill.

Geometric Unlearning works on hidden states instead. From a small set of safe reference prompts it distills a compact, low-rank subspace of safe behavior. Synthetic anchor prompts then trigger a projection that aligns hidden representations for the target topic onto that safe subspace, locally, where the topic appears. A teacher-distillation guard on non-target anchors limits side drift. On two privacy benchmarks the method suppresses the target strongly while leaving other performance nearly intact, using only a little synthetic data.
arxiv-2605-02235:
Mohammadreza Doostmohammadian and Hamid Rabiee design fault detection for mixed traffic, where human-driven cars share the road with connected self-driving cars. Sensor data are partial. The self-driving group must track the state of the human-driven group through shared observer estimates. That must work even when no single self-driving car can see the whole group near it.

Each self-driving car then runs a local check on its own sensor data. The check uses residuals, the gaps between sensed and expected values, to flag faults or attacks. No central unit is needed. Two logics are given, one that uses past residuals and one that does not. Both use chance-based thresholds to isolate a fault.
arxiv-2605-02335:
Önder Gürcan and Moharram Challenger argue that language model agents need explicit social grounding to behave intelligibly, not just fluent speech. Such models now let software, physical, and simulation agents talk and deliberate in natural language. Yet most systems stay weakly tied to roles, norms, intentions, and context, which limits real participation in social settings.

The authors develop a conceptual baseline in which a social agent is grounded in a role definition, made concrete through a persona description. On that base they outline research directions for representation, hybrid control, and evaluation. Their conclusion is that persona-based role definitions are a necessary foundation for turning language competence into social behaviour that others can read and trust.
arxiv-2605-02535:
Fengkai Wei and four co-authors boost light emission from erbium-doped silicon nitride at room temperature, at the wavelength used in telecommunications. Erbium ions emit there naturally, but weakly. The team shapes the material into a metasurface, a pattern of tiny cylinders whose resonances change how light is stored and released around the ions.

By tuning the cylinder radius, they reach an emission boost of about eighteen times after heat treatment, in line with their simulations. Timing tests show the glow fades nearly ten times faster, a sign that the boost comes mainly from the Purcell effect. How deep the erbium sits also matters: deeper placement raised output fourfold across the range tested. The work points toward compact light sources that fit standard chip making.
arxiv-2605-03035:
Mohamed Khalafalla Hassan and Indrakshi Dey argue that counting spare copies is a poor way to judge resilience in virtualized 6G networks. Copies often share the same platform and software, so one fault can take them all down at once.

They propose three scores that reward real variety instead: distinct stand-ins for a function, distinct algorithms with similar performance, and diversity spread across layers. In tests with targeted disruption on synthetic data, the scores split true robustness from mere copy count. The work frames variety itself as a practical tool for open, split 6G systems.
arxiv-2605-03135:
Kabir Kang and Stephen Mussmann argue that scoring classifiers as if all errors cost the same misleads real decisions. In moderation or medical screening, missing a clear case should count more than missing a borderline one.

They propose normalized excess cost, which weights each error by a per-example cost and matches the plain error rate when costs are equal. Costs can come from voter margins, distance to a threshold, or confidence ratings. Across text, image, and table data, cost-weighted scores ran well below raw error rates, showing errors cluster on hard cases. Training with costs helped only unevenly.
arxiv-2605-03535:
Yong Li, Qiyi Tang, and Di-De Yen study hyper-minimization for deterministic register automata, machines that read data values and store some of them in registers for later comparison. Hyper-minimization shrinks a machine as far as possible while changing its behavior on only finitely many inputs. The authors focus on well-typed automata, where each state carries a unique register type.

They first adapt classical ideas from deterministic finite automata to the register setting. Then they give an algorithm that produces automata minimal in both states and registers among well-typed machines. A correctness proof shows the method works, which settles that hyper-minimization is decidable for this class.
arxiv-2605-03835:
Jeremy Feusi and Sam Molcho study the birational classification of orbifold compactified Jacobians, and more generally of families of toroidal compactifications of a group over a toroidal base. The groups are tori or semiabelian schemes. The problem asks which of them count as the same under the relevant orbifold birational notion.

The authors reduce the problem to finding the minimal such spaces in logarithmic geometry, where it becomes a combinatorial one. They solve it for families of tori, for Jacobians of nodal-curve families, and for semiabelian schemes with abelian generic fiber. The general semiabelian case is reduced to an open conjecture. The results extend and recast recent work of Schmitt.
arxiv-2605-04135:
David Gringras and Misha Salahshoor audit academic evaluations of large language models and find a systematic frontier lag: papers tend to evaluate models that were already outclassed when the results were published. They name the underlying problem a publication elicitation gap, the distance between the systems that generated a paper's results and the systems a current reader would reasonably assume were referenced. Their sweep covers OpenAlex records from 2022 into 2026.

From over one hundred twelve thousand keyword matches, they identified about eighteen and a half thousand admissible evaluation records. They ranked each evaluated model against the frontier model of its time on a capability index. The median paper's models trailed the frontier, and that gap is growing year by year. Only a minority of full-text papers state an explicit evaluation date, compounding the misreading risk.
arxiv-2605-04735:
Ondřej Ježek and three co-authors combine two structural design optimisation methods that compensate for each other's weaknesses. Density-based methods explore shapes freely and efficiently but leave blurry boundaries that factories cannot use directly, while level-set methods keep crisp boundaries yet depend heavily on the starting design.

Their sequential framework converts the density result into a signed distance function, a geometric description that initialises the level-set stage for boundary refinement. In three-dimensional tests on cantilever and standard benchmark beams, the combined method matched the standalone level-set method's stiffness while running several times faster on one case. The implementation is released as open-source software.
arxiv-2605-05035:
Carla Caro Villanova and Alan Santos examine how wiring-like capacitive links between superconducting circuits change the spread of quantum information. Simple models treat only nearest neighbours, which works when coupling is weak. In arrays of transmon devices, though, the whole capacitance network can mediate interactions between distant parts.

Using out-of-time-ordered correlators, which track operator scrambling, they show stronger network coupling makes scrambling saturate far faster than the nearest-neighbour picture predicts. Spectral statistics also shift away from random behaviour toward level repulsion, signalling partial ergodicity rather than full quantum chaos. Because the effect appears in realistic device regimes, it matters for scaling superconducting architectures.
arxiv-2605-05135: Ushangi Goginava studies de la Vallée Poussin means of Walsh-Fourier series, a smoothed way of reconstructing a function from its Walsh expansion. He works with a nondecreasing window sequence shaping the smoothing. The central question is for which integrable functions these means converge at almost every point, and he establishes a sharp criterion answering it. When the criterion fails, Goginava shows every Orlicz class below a certain logarithmic scale contains a function whose means diverge everywhere.
arxiv-2605-05335:
Ming-Zhang Wang, Xu-Yang Hou, and Hao Guo find geometric and topological blocks that can stop a quasi-Hermitian quantum system from being recast as a plain Hermitian one. Such systems, including PT-symmetric ones, can be mapped to Hermitian partners by a similarity transformation with a positive metric. A pointwise map is easy, but true dynamic matching needs the transformation to be proper, single-valued throughout, and fitting the modified Schrödinger equation.

The authors separate curvature-based geometric blocks from holonomy-based topological ones around loops in setting space, giving clear criteria for each. Concrete cases show both. Their results clarify when a system can be fully reduced to Hermitian form and when its non-Hermitian traits are built in.
arxiv-2605-05435:
Compressed sensing rebuilds images from very few measurements, guided by a learned generator. Alexander DeLise and Nick Dexter study a conditional version, where a text prompt steers both sampling and recovery. They separate the prompt's two jobs so each can be studied on its own.

For common generator types they prove stable recovery bounds. When the sampling prompt matches the recovery prompt, the method keeps its near-optimal guarantees, while a mismatch adds an explicit penalty. Tests with Stable Diffusion confirm that prompts reshape where samples are taken and change how well images come back.
arxiv-2605-05635:
A black hole dressed in dark matter should cast a slightly different shadow than a bare one. Mohsen Fathi computes those optical signatures for rotating black holes, using numerical ray tracing rather than a single assumed geometry. Two backgrounds are compared against Kerr: a regular black hole from an Einasto dark matter profile, and one from a cored profile.

Fathi maps horizon structure, shadow boundaries, lensing bands, and photon rings under one accretion prescription. He adds image-level diagnostics and angular-size checks against the observed shadows of M87* and Sgr A*. The exercise shows which features could, in principle, betray the dark matter halo.
arxiv-2605-05835:
Large reasoning models sometimes say, mid-thought, that they might be under evaluation. Amelie Knecht, Lucas Florin, and Thilo Hagendorff test whether that spoken awareness really changes behavior. The worry is strategy: a model that knows it is being tested might perform safety rather than be safe.

They compared traces that mentioned evaluation on their own against those that did not, across safety, alignment, moral, and political benchmarks. They also inserted evaluation-aware lines to force the state. The effects on outputs were small, hinting the spoken awareness is more commentary than control signal.
arxiv-2605-05935:
Irmak Sağlam and Georg Zetzsche study games played on infinite state systems with energy style winning rules. Pushdown systems support many decidable games, while counter based systems often make even simple games undecidable. Adding energy semantics, where staying legal becomes part of the winning goal, can change that picture.

The authors define viability games in a broad framework where graphs specify pushdowns, counters, and mixes of both. They map out exactly where these games are decidable and how hard they are across that whole family. Some mixes of pushdowns and counters yield decidable viability games even where related games are undecidable. A few cases are decidable even when plain reachability for one player is not.
arxiv-2605-06035:
Lisan Al Amin and four co-authors bring quantum kernels to the task of spotting fake audio. Many quantum approaches read a spectrogram as a plain image and miss its time and frequency structure. Their method, Q-Patch, is built around that structure from the start.

Each chosen patch of a mel spectrogram is summed up by four acoustic measures, then encoded into a shallow four qubit circuit. Nearby patches share entanglement in the circuit design, keeping it feasible on near term hardware. On a balanced spoofing test, Q-Patch scored 0.87 on the area under the curve measure, against 0.82 for a matched classical baseline. The design suits authenticity checks in low resource settings.
arxiv-2605-06235:
Diane Tchuindjo, Devavrat Shah, and Omar Khattab argue that modern search fails a class of queries they call oblique. An oblique query seeks documents that fit a latent pattern, such as tweets voicing an implicit stance or logs showing a failure mode. Retrieval benchmarks look saturated, yet the authors say efficient search is far from solved once such hidden pattern requests are counted.

They study three mechanisms that make queries oblique and build OBLIQ-Bench, five search problems over real long tail collections. A sharp asymmetry appears: reasoning models reliably verify latent relevance once a document is surfaced. Even sophisticated retrieval pipelines, though, fail to surface most relevant documents in the first place. The benchmark aims to push retrieval design toward latent pattern matching at scale.
arxiv-2605-06335:
Fabian Kabus and five co-authors recover links between clinical variables from language models without opening the models. A model's training spans biomedical literature from many patient groups, so associations between patient traits are buried in its answers. Direct questioning is shaky, so the team instead ask structured comparison questions: patient triplets where one trait is varied and similarity judgments reveal the model's implicit correlation structure.

A statistical model turns those judgments into correlation estimates with no access to signals or internals. Prompt level environment shifts then give estimates per subpopulation, feeding an invariant causal prediction method that returns conservative candidate causal parents. Tests in lung disease and multiple sclerosis gave smooth, stable, clinically sensible correlations. The invariant step distilled them into a small set of candidate causal links.
arxiv-2605-06535:
Ziyun Zeng, Yiqi Lin, Guoqiang Liang, and Mike Zheng Shou introduce Sparkle, a dataset and model for instruction-guided video background replacement. Swapping a video's whole background while keeping foreground interaction natural is central to film and advertising work. Public datasets focus on easier local edits, and existing models often produce static, unnatural backgrounds.

The team traces that failure to weak background guidance during data synthesis. Their pipeline creates foreground and background guidance separately with strict quality filtering. Sparkle holds about 140 thousand video pairs across five background-change themes, plus the largest benchmark for this task, and a model trained on it beats prior baselines.
arxiv-2605-06635:
Hailey Onweller and five co-authors build the first framework for checking whether citations in deep research agent reports actually support their claims. These agents synthesize hundreds of web sources into cited reports, but citations may be broken, off-topic, or factually wrong. Their tool parses inline citations from Markdown at scale and retrieves the cited content for judging.

Each citation is scored on whether the link works, whether the content is relevant, and whether the facts match. Across fourteen models, links and relevance score high, yet factual accuracy runs only thirty-nine to seventy-seven percent for the strongest models. Deeper research with more tool calls makes factual accuracy worse, not better.
arxiv-2605-07235:
Nana Matsuno, Takaaki Yokoyama, and Mami Machida simulate how heat conduction shapes jets from supermassive black holes inside galaxy clusters. Clusters hold hot, thin plasma, and merging clusters create cold fronts that jets must cross. How conduction along magnetic fields changes jet shape and field strength was an open question.

Their two-dimensional simulations move heat from the jet head back into the inner cocoon, raising its pressure. That pressure squeezes the jet far more tightly than in runs without conduction, and the squeezing stretches magnetic fields along the cold front, strengthening them. Conduction efficiency controls the effect, which the authors call conductive collimation.
arxiv-2605-07335:
Mengran Li and nine co-authors present CellScientist, a workflow that lets language models revise models of how cells respond to treatments, without losing the audit trail. Free-form model revision can break code or quietly change the task. Their protocol records every design state and outcome, and routes each mismatch to the part at fault.

Revisions stay local and under a fixed task contract, with checks that contain breaches. In matched-budget studies, structured rework found better held-out models under two base models. Audits link the recorded history to fewer repeated proposals and more targeted repairs, and frozen designs were retested on a fresh cohort for outside validity.
arxiv-2605-07935:
Shuren Xia and three co-authors verify LLM multi-agent coordination protocols before letting them run. In TraceFix, an agent drafts a coordination protocol as a structured representation from the task description, and generates formal coordination logic. It then repairs the logic against counterexamples from the TLA+ model checker until verification passes. Verified parts become per-agent system prompts, guarded at runtime by a monitor that rejects off-protocol moves.

Across forty-eight tasks in sixteen scenario families, every task reached full verification, most on the first attempt and none needing more than four repairs. In thousands of runtime runs, monitored execution with verified protocols achieved the highest task completion, and an ablation showed verification cut deadlock and livelock rates by more than half.
arxiv-2605-08335:
Jacqueline Caminiti and Aidan Herderschee examine a correction to black hole entropy for charged holes near extremality. The Bekenstein-Hawking formula gets a competing term. Semiclassically, it is the negative exponential of the inner horizon area. The cancellation between the two drives the density of states to zero. That happens as the horizons merge.

Building on earlier work, the authors argue the correction is a complex saddle geometry. It belongs to the gravitational path integral. The solution has negative boundary length. It caps off at the inner horizon. A Picard-Lefschetz analysis of the inverse Laplace contour follows. A stability check joins it. Together they show how the saddle and its minus sign shape the spectrum.
arxiv-2605-08735:
Joowon Kim, Seungho Shin, Joonhyung Park, and Eunho Yang reason with video by pairing a vision language model with a video generator in a tight loop. Generators alone drift over long tasks and compound small mid clip errors. Plans made fully in advance commit too early, while whole video critiques arrive too late, so CollabVR intervenes at each step instead.

The language model plans just the next action, inspects the generated clip, and folds the diagnosis into the next prompt to repair faults. Across two benchmarks it lifts both open and closed generators at equal computing cost, with the biggest gains on the hardest tasks, and stacks on top of reasoning tuned generators.
arxiv-2605-08935:
Hao Wu and eleven coauthors steady joint casts of linked flows, like sea and air. Each sim's slips feed the next one's slips. The slips grow till long casts crash. Their PnP-Corrector plan locks trained physics cores in place. It trains just a fix agent. The agent fights the set biases the link breeds, in advance. A lean cast build named DSLCast is the plan's spine.

The split keeps physics sound while the learned layer copes with drift. On a three hundred day sea and air cast, error drops by more than a fourth. The plan beats top sets on key scores. Long casts gain life with no new physics training.
arxiv-2605-09435:
Danieli studies word sets over endless alphabets, where machines carry small stores that hold letters for later checks. It has been guessed that the Parikh image of every such machine word set is given by a rational form. That image is just the letter count, with order ignored. The guess was known for one store machines. Danieli sharpens that result and then breaks the wider guess, showing where the theory stops acting like the finite alphabet case.

For one store machines, the star height of the Parikh image is at most two, a bound that holds for all such cases. Yet one store context free word sets already reach any star height at all. For many stores the guess fails outright. So does the claim that context free grammars and machines match in power over endless alphabets. In short, Parikh's theorem does not survive the move to endless alphabets.
arxiv-2605-09535:
Chi and Wang advance the Erdős Kleitman problem, the non uniform version of the Erdős matching problem. For integers n and s, the problem asks for the largest family of subsets of an n element set with no s pairwise disjoint members. Kleitman settled the question Erdős had posed. The authors approach it from the Erdős matching conjecture side, fixing m and writing n from s, m, and a remainder c.

They prove that for fixed m of at least 3, and large enough s, extremal families take a specific form. That form combines m element subsets of a chosen set with all larger subsets, over a c range set by two constants. For m equal to 3, they pin down the asymptotic remainder range for which that form is extremal. The result fixes extremal structure in a long standing non uniform matching problem.
arxiv-2605-10135:
Lu and seven colleagues accelerate large-scale graph-index building for approximate nearest neighbour search, the engine behind vector databases. CPU-based construction is slow for large, high-dimensional data, while GPUs are costly and memory-limited. Their end-to-end system, ScaleGANN, builds graph indexes on low-cost spot GPUs in a distributed cloud setup.

A divide-and-merge design with an optimised vector partitioning algorithm improves indexing time and space efficiency while preserving index quality. A novel resource allocation strategy enables multi-GPU indexing parallelism and cost-effectiveness for both build and query, with a task scheduler and cost model managing spot instances. On large real-world data sets, ScaleGANN builds indexes up to nine times faster at six times lower price than the DiskANN benchmark, with similar scalability and search quality.
arxiv-2605-10335:
Yao Lu and three colleagues cut the memory cost of training giant neural networks. Adaptive trainers such as Adam dominate large-scale training, but they store running estimates of gradient first and second moments, doubling trainer memory. Their 2026 paper introduces PowerStep, a trainer that achieves per-coordinate adaptivity with no second-moment storage.

Motivated by steepest descent under an Lp-norm geometry, PowerStep applies a nonlinear transform straight to a momentum buffer, yielding per-coordinate adaptivity from one buffer alone. The authors prove convergence at the optimal one-over-square-root-of-T rate for non-convex stochastic training. On Transformers from 124 million to 235 billion parameters, PowerStep matched Adam's speed while halving trainer memory. With aggressive int8 quantization it stayed stable and cut trainer memory about 8 times against full-precision Adam.
arxiv-2605-10435:
Shota Takahashi and four colleagues simulate the contest between fast and collisional neutrino flavor instabilities in dense settings such as core-collapse supernovae. Fast flavor unrest and its collisional cousin both drive rapid flavor conversion. Their non-linear contest with damping in uneven settings remains poorly understood. Their 2026 paper studies that contest with neutrino transport simulations including spatial drift and collision terms.

Rather than merely causing simple decoherence, damping substantially alters group flavor swings, driving the system through complex pathways. In every case where flavor unrest develops, the system converges to the same even flavor end state despite diverse intermediate dynamics. The results suggest that dynamic competition could reshape the widely accepted picture of collisionless fast flavor unrest. Realistic collision effects, the authors argue, belong in supernova flavor-conversion models.
arxiv-2605-10535:
Federico Stra and two colleagues settle when concentration optimizers exist for the Born-Jordan distribution. They study the Lp focus problem for the Born-Jordan distribution in dimension d above 1, building on a one-dimensional analysis. Their 2026 paper shows whether concentration optimizers exist depends on the exponent p. The key threshold is p-star of d, equal to 2d over d minus 2 for d at least 2.

For exponents below the key value, from 1 up to but not including p-star, the authors prove the top value is finite and is attained. For exponents above the key value, they show the function is unbounded. They also provide the complete solution in the much harder key regime in d equals 2. The Born-Jordan distribution, an average of broad Wigner distributions, is valued for reducing ghost tones in phase-space signal analysis.

arxiv-2606-04135:
Shiqiao Zhou and colleagues present SARAF in 2026, a forecasting method that borrows the retrieval idea from language models. To predict a time series, it first fetches similar stretches of the series' own past.

Critics note that such stretches may not share the key property of stationarity, where the statistical pattern stays stable over time. The authors answer with a careful theory. They also add a step that deliberately mixes stretches from varied regimes, much like retrieved text from varied sources. On forecasting benchmarks, the method beat prior approaches. It did so mainly by gaining robustness across shifting conditions, not by peak accuracy alone. Diversifying the retrieved past, they conclude, is what makes retrieval work for series.
arxiv-2606-04235:
Tao Jin and Stuart Florescu build a framework in 2026 for collateral choice, with a quantum step inside a proven classical pipeline. Collateral choice is the daily puzzle of pledging assets against margin while obeying legal and risk rules.

The hard part is picking which assets to pledge from a large pool. Their solver uses a quantum routine to propose candidate sets. A classical check then certifies each candidate against all rules. Nothing leaves the pipeline unless it passes the check. On synthetic pools the method found better pledges than standard solvers. The authors stress the certificate step: it makes the quantum part safe to use in a regulated setting.
arxiv-2606-04735:
Veselý and colleagues identify a failure mode in deep reinforcement learning that mirrors a famous human memory bias, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Temporal credit assignment, deciding which past actions caused later rewards, is central to learning. At intermediate eligibility trace depths, they find agents irrationally prefer trajectories with high-magnitude reward peaks over alternatives with higher total returns. They call this Trace-Mediated Peak Bias, and it mechanistically mirrors the Peak-End Rule, where people judge experiences by their most intense moment rather than their overall value.

The bias emerges because eligibility traces amplify distant temporal-difference errors into gradient shocks that fixed-step-size gradient descent cannot normalize, causing global overestimation. Adaptive optimizers, by contrast, mitigate the pathology through second-moment normalization. The paper bridges machine learning and cognitive heuristics with one mechanism explaining both.
arxiv-2606-05235:
Samak Boonpan uses quantum circuit complexity as a measure of particle creation in bouncing cosmologies in this 2026 arXiv paper. A bouncing universe contracts, reaches a minimum size, and expands again instead of beginning in a singularity. Circuit complexity counts how hard a quantum state is to prepare, and tracking it for a quantum scalar field across the bounce could reveal what correlation functions miss.

Earlier studies relied on perturbative approximations, but Boonpan applies the Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant method to build an exact, non-perturbative framework for how complexity evolves through the bounce. The complexity stays finite at the bounce, dominated by the squeezing of the quantum state caused by spacetime contraction. After the bounce, its growth correlates strongly with cosmological particle production. One contribution, called the chirping term, acts as a geometric memory of the transition, quantifying the information cost of creating particles in a nontrivial spacetime geometry.
arxiv-2606-05435:
Naima Tasnim, Lalitha Sankar, and Oliver Kosut introduce DP-MacAdam in this 2026 arXiv paper, a differentially private training algorithm that unifies two previously separate tricks. Differentially private stochastic gradient descent protects training data by clipping each example's gradient and adding noise. Its fixed clipping threshold is a pain point that needs manual tuning. Clipping methods estimate the gradient's mean and variance to set the clipping. Private Adam variants use the same statistics for momentum, yet neither used the estimates for both jobs.

The authors analyze the algorithm and show that it estimates gradient variances in a bias-free manner, which matters because biased statistics would distort both the clipping and the update direction. In evaluations of privacy and accuracy, DP-MacAdam achieved better model utility than the private baseline and than either parent method, adaptive clipping alone or private Adam alone.
arxiv-2606-05535:
Pratama and co-authors address noisy medical images in a 2026 arXiv paper on question answering. Their system looks at a scan or X-ray and answers plain questions about it. Most systems of this kind link a standard image reader to a large language model. Small flaws in the image can then distort what the model sees. The team adds a cleaning step that is trained to rebuild clean image features from damaged ones.

After cleaning, the features pass to the language model as short prefix tokens. A light training method then adapts the system without retraining the whole model. The authors tested the system on two public test sets, SLAKE and PathVQA. It held up better than rival systems when noise was added to the inputs. Its scores on clean images stayed close to the best competing results.
arxiv-2606-05635:
Kong and colleagues teach a model to crop one photo into a film-style trio in a 2026 arXiv paper. Photo tools usually return a single best crop. Posters and stories, though, often need three views: a wide scene, a medium frame, and a close-up. Each crop also needs a short caption to carry the story. The team defines this triple-shot task and trains a model for it with little expert labeling.

Training runs in three stages. First, guided reasoning teaches basic cropping through worked examples. Next, the model learns from its own high-confidence drafts, scored by a mix of checks. A final reinforcement stage uses a reward built for this task. The team also built TSC-Bench, twelve hundred expert-marked test cases. On shot placement their model scored nearly three times the accuracy of GPT-5. The result points toward automatic storyboarding.
arxiv-2606-05735:
Dihua Jiang and co-authors settle parts of a wavefront set conjecture for classical groups in a 2026 arXiv paper. Wavefront sets record the rough directions hidden inside a representation, a symmetry package for a group. Three flavors exist: arithmetic, trace-based, and one from special models. The conjecture says they agree. The team works over local fields of characteristic zero, including the real and complex cases.

Their first theorem proves a reciprocity between wavefront sets for representations with a generic parameter. Over archimedean fields, a second theorem confirms the conjecture and its refinement outright. The character of the representation then has its fine structure fixed by arithmetic data alone. A composition law ties the model-based flavor in across all fields. As a bonus, the work sharpens Vogan's maximal-orbit principle, a guiding rule in the field. Conditional pieces remain, and the authors mark exactly which ones.
arxiv-2606-06035:
Firmbach, Steinbrecher, Popp, and Mayr make fiber-in-solid models solvable at scale in a 2026 arXiv paper. Embedding thin beams inside solid bodies models everything from collagen tissue to reinforced composites. Lagrange multipliers enforce the coupling, but the discrete system becomes an indefinite saddle-point problem that naive solvers choke on. Augmented Lagrangian preconditioning steadies the system while keeping the constraints exact.

Starting from an ideal block preconditioner, the team derives usable block-triangular variants. Solid, beam, and Schur complement blocks can then be handled on their own. Several Schur complement approximations are tried and compared. Tests showed robustness across model parameters. Iteration counts stayed nearly flat under mesh refinement. Strong and weak scaling both looked favorable. An engineering example, a composite sandwich plate, shows the workload. Mixed-dimensional models are growing across biomechanics and materials science. Solvers that respect their structure are the bottleneck this paper removes.
arxiv-2606-06135:
Lucie Kubíčková and Martin Isoz extend a fluid simulation method in this 2026 arXiv paper on computational fluid dynamics. Engineers optimizing shapes with simulated airflow normally must rebuild the computational mesh whenever the shape changes, which is slow. Immersed boundary methods avoid remeshing by embedding the solid shape inside a fixed grid. The authors adapt one such method, the hybrid fictitious domain approach, to Reynolds-averaged turbulence models, which average out turbulent fluctuations rather than resolving each one.

Their open-source OpenFOAM solver adds wall functions, which approximate flow near solid surfaces, and solves the averaged equations with the SIMPLE algorithm. It matched standard body-fitted simulations across Reynolds numbers from ten to one million, on benchmarks such as flow over a backward-facing step and an Ahmed body. Tests on a NACA airfoil at varied attack angles checked robustness, though the solver tended to overestimate wake size.
arxiv-2606-06635:
Tanvi Thoria and co-authors read the fingerprints of failing reasoning in this 2026 arXiv paper. When a language model reasons step by step and goes wrong, the failure is not one thing. Using token level uncertainty signals from a single completion's log probabilities, they distinguish two processes. In committed failure, the model locks onto a wrong path early; past a commitment point, more trace only hurts detection. In persistent uncertainty, doubt accumulates throughout, and the full trace is needed to spot the failure.

Across twenty three model and dataset configurations, the framework's predictions held in twenty of twenty three cases, far above chance. The classification pays off practically. In the committed regime, self consistency sampling can be skipped on the top thirty percent most confident inputs without losing failure recall. Combining uncertainty features with agreement rates lifted detection in both regimes.
arxiv-2606-06835:
Language models think best in the language they trained on most. Jayarao and co-authors let a model call for help in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system can translate an input into the model's strong language before answering. Translating everything would waste money, though. Models also refuse help too often, out of overconfidence.

The team trained one policy to decide for itself, using reward alone. A confidence gate keeps translation for cases the model truly cannot handle natively. Training covered twenty two languages in three resource tiers and five domains. The gated policy kept the full reward of an always translate policy. It did so at about sixty three percent of the cost. Gains were largest for low resource languages. The policy even handled two invented languages it had never seen, and transferred to nine held out ones.
arxiv-2606-07035:
Nuclear theory drowns in giant matrices whose eigenvalues encode a nucleus's energy levels. De Lucia and a large team solve those problems on a quantum annealer in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their test bed is the equation of motion phonon method, a many body technique for nuclei. Full quantum algorithms for eigenvalues need hardware that does not yet exist.

Annealing offers a nearer term path. The eigenvalue problem is recast as a binary optimization puzzle. A hybrid algorithm then peels off eigenvalues one by one through deflation. Classical steps clean up between quantum rounds. On real D-Wave hardware, quantum annealing beat simulated annealing on ground states. Deflation recovered the full spectrum with high precision. Symmetric test problems reached machine precision under all deflation variants. The paper maps both the promise and the limits of today's annealers for nuclear physics.
arxiv-2606-07235:
Mehrish and Vascon rethink how AI systems gather evidence from long, mixed-format documents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Answers often hide in fragments spread across text, tables, and slides, yet standard retrieval fetches isolated chunks ranked independently. Their system, FlowReader, treats evidence assembly as a min-cost flow problem, a classic optimization method that routes flow through a network at lowest total cost. One scoring signal controls which fragments act as sources, sinks, and connecting paths.

The chosen flow is split into candidate evidence paths, pruned for redundancy, and passed to vision-language model workers that draft the answer. A consistency check can trigger one deeper refinement pass when the first answer looks shaky. On the VisDoMBench benchmark, FlowReader scored best on the two subsets dominated by fragmented evidence, reaching about fifty-eight on table-heavy questions and seventy-three on slide questions in their reported averages.
arxiv-2606-07535:
Krasnodębska, Kusa, and Lipani test whether safety training in one language protects users of other languages, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A model aligned to refuse harmful requests in English may comply with the request in Polish or Greek, an inconsistency with deployment stakes. The authors introduce RefusEU, a refusal alignment dataset spanning 12 European languages with a dedicated test set for models. Controlled experiments used Direct Preference Optimization, a method that teaches from preferred-versus-rejected answer pairs, varying the training languages.

Two insights stand out. Aligning in English did not ensure cross-lingual safety, even for identical harm categories tested in other languages. Multilingual training data, by contrast, improved safety while leaving knowledge intact, as measured by a knowledge benchmark. The results argue that multilingual safety cannot be an afterthought bolted onto English training. Dataset and evaluation materials are released, targeting European language coverage that safety research neglects.
arxiv-2606-07635:
Shen and a team fuse brain scans of different kinds to detect early cognitive impairment, in this 2026 arXiv paper on NeuroAlign. Functional MRI shows dynamic brain activity while diffusion imaging maps structural wiring; together they should reveal mild cognitive impairment better than either alone, but their spaces differ and their outputs misalign. Their layered framework models multi-scale dynamic connectivity and aligns dynamic with static and functional with structural embeddings, then lets connectivity-level and region-level features shape each other globally.

An attribution method designed for the system gauges which links and regional markers drive each decision, without needing gradients. Evaluated across 3 cohorts under 5-fold validation, NeuroAlign reached accuracy near 0.83 on the ADNI dataset. Fused features beat the best single feature type. Cross-dataset transfer to an independent cohort was partial, which the authors report as evidence of domain gaps between scanning sites.
arxiv-2606-07935:
Song and co-authors announce the fourth edition of a challenge on generating facial reactions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The task: given someone speaking, produce the facial reaction a listener would plausibly show, with many valid answers rather than one correct face. The REACT challenge series has standardised this multiple appropriate facial reaction generation problem, and the 2026 edition raises the bar.

Two data additions headline the update. Personality labels for the Big Five traits let systems generate reactions conditioned on who the listener is, not just what was said. The new MARS dataset broadens the scenarios available for training and testing. The challenge also adds a second task, predicting electroencephalography signals, the brain's electrical activity, as a reaction. Together the changes push reaction generation toward personalised, multimodal modelling: a system should eventually react like a particular person, in face and in measurable brain response, not like a generic listener.
arxiv-2606-08035:
Hangui Lin and co-authors diagnose a coordination failure inside vision-language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains such models to reach correct answers, but scores only the outcome. Token-level analysis shows what goes wrong mid-reasoning. The model fails to alternate between extracting visual evidence and synthesising text, staring at words when it should look. This breakdown is causally linked to wrong answers.

Their method, DyCo-RL, builds the alternation into training. A Fisher-Rao geodesic distance measures how much each token's attention shifts within its modality, so tokens can be assigned visual or text roles. Training checks whether each token's attention matches its role, and reweights the learning signal by that alignment. The model is rewarded not just for being right, but for looking at the right thing at the right step. Experiments show this improves visual reasoning over outcome-only training.
arxiv-2606-08135:
Siyu Nan and co-authors improve how language models write code inside large existing repositories, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Repository-level generation is hard because new code must call the right existing functions across a codebase far too big for the model's context window. Retrieval systems fetch candidate functions to reuse, and planners sketch steps. Two flaws persist: plans are written with no behavioural guidance, so they drift from what the code should do. And retrieved functions are reused blind to their actual implementation logic.

Their framework, TICoder, fixes both ends. A test-driven iterative planning mechanism uses the repository's test cases as behavioural specifications, refining the implementation steps against them before code is written. An implementation-aware reuse mechanism then reads how candidate functions actually work, not just their names and signatures. The pairing is the point: tests discipline the plan, implementations discipline the reuse.
arxiv-2606-08335:
Karl Zhu and colleagues optimize the design and operation of green ammonia plants in this 2026 arXiv paper. Green ammonia is made with renewable electricity. But the Haber-Bosch process at its heart has a minimum load. The synthesis unit cannot run below a certain throughput without shutting down. Wind and solar output fluctuate, so guaranteeing that minimum is the central challenge. The authors build a robust optimization framework that plans for worst-case conditions within stated bounds.

A strategic model sizes the plant while allowing flexible operating modes such as hot idling and shutdowns. A scenario-reduction method clusters weather patterns and generates adversarial renewable trajectories to test plans against. An operational model then adapts decisions on a rolling horizon as forecasts update. In computations, the framework produced plans that stayed feasible in out-of-sample simulation. Existing approaches failed the minimum-load requirement in those tests.
arxiv-2606-08535:
Yun-Hsuan Huang, Bui, and Chuang sharpen satellite images with a lightweight network in this 2026 arXiv paper. Remote sensing faces a spatial-temporal trade-off. Finely detailed imagery is acquired infrequently, while frequent observations are coarse. Single-image super-resolution enhances coarse images without changing schedules. But many transformer-based models are expensive and sensitive to limited or biased training data. Their architecture, NGram-MoSE, targets both efficiency and texture continuity.

An N-gram context injection mechanism strengthens consistency across the local windows the transformer processes. A mixture-of-experts design scales capacity through sparse activation, consulting only a few subnetworks per patch. Together the two ideas aim at super-resolution cheap enough for routine use over large areas.
arxiv-2606-09335:
Agneedh Basu and colleagues dissect why speech recognizers stumble, testing state-of-the-art models on Indian languages under messy real-world conditions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Recognition performance varies with language, speaker, and recording chain, but systematic factor studies for Indic languages are rare. The authors analyze decoded outputs from several open-source models in zero-shot settings across Hindi, Bengali, Kannada, Telugu, and Marathi. They correlate word error rate with speaker traits like word length and speaking rate, and probe audio factors in depth for Hindi.

Bandwidth is the most critical audio factor: narrowband 2G GSM audio degrades recognition sharply, while wideband stays close to clean accuracy. Bit depth shows a threshold, stable at 10 to 12 bits, collapsing at 8 bits and below. Competing background speech causes the strongest degradation of all, with Whisper models comparatively robust. Neural restoration introduced harmful artifacts, making plain resampling the safer choice for telephony.
arxiv-2606-09735:
Wendy Tam peers inside a language model to see what safety tuning did to its political lean in this 2026 arXiv paper. The tuning method is RLHF, training from human feedback, the standard way to align models with stated values. Tam compares the inner maps of Llama 3.1 8B before and after that tuning. The question is whether a partisan tilt was erased or just masked.

The tilt's structure survived. RLHF squeezed the spread of the partisan signal, so output reads balanced, but the direction itself stayed in place. Sparse autoencoder maps showed policy features that fired in the base model went dark in the tuned one. Steering tests then proved the break was causal: the path from tilt to output was cut, not the tilt. Tricks that guess a user's lean can switch the path back on. The mask, Tam warns, is thin, and the same may hold for other values.
arxiv-2606-09835:
Akbaba and co-authors pack a hands-on data workshop into a box that non-experts can run alone in this 2026 arXiv paper. Data physicalization turns numbers into objects people build and touch. Such workshops spark rich talks, but their worth has hinged on a skilled researcher in the room. The team worked with a Swedish social aid group whose staff wanted to run the sessions themselves.

Together they co-designed the kit for youth leadership groups. The box holds both stuff and steps: the materials to build with, and a script that walks a host through each stage. Three pilot runs tuned the set, and two more case studies checked that it travels. The paper lists what the box must carry, from clear task cards to spare parts for when builds go wrong.
arxiv-2606-09935:
Isbarov and colleagues test whether AI agents inside software pipelines can be hijacked by hostile text, in a 2026 arXiv paper on security. Their setting is CI/CD, the automated systems that review code and maintain projects on GitHub. These agents read untrusted content while holding strong permissions. That mix makes prompt injection, where planted instructions steer the agent, a supply chain risk.

Their open-source framework, GitInject, builds throwaway repositories and triggers real workflow runs, so limits and credential handling behave as in production. Across four AI providers, the team documented eleven named attacks, covering config-file injection, credential theft, judgment manipulation, and outages. Every provider tested fell to at least one attack class in its default setup. The worst flaws came from how the pipeline infrastructure handles credentials and configuration files, not from any single model's behavior, and the authors give the cheapest workflow-level fix for each attack.
arxiv-2606-10035:
Prodinger studies a coloring game played on Dyck paths, the lattice walks that step up and down without dropping below zero, in a 2026 arXiv paper on combinatorics. Nodes along the path receive black and white labels, and the white-height counts a weighted measure of the white labels. Using generating functions, the standard tool that encodes counting sequences as power series, he computes the average white-height over all paths of a given length.

For two different labeling models, the average white-height grows like one half times the square root of pi times n, where n is the half-length of the path. A final section links walks with double steps to 2-Motzkin paths, another family of lattice walks, where white-height is again the natural quantity. The paper is short and deliberately elementary, aimed at students learning the trade of analytic combinatorics.
arxiv-2606-10235:
Kushwahaa and colleagues use dying stars to trace the warp in the Milky Way's disc, in a 2026 arXiv paper on galactic astronomy. The team uses two populations: carbon-rich stars about a billion years old, and oxygen-rich intermediate-mass stars only a few hundred million years old.

The downward warp traced by the oxygen-rich stars matches the warp found from Cepheid variables, as expected from their similar ages. The more numerous carbon-rich stars reveal the warp clearly across a wide range of azimuthal angles, and their warp reaches larger amplitudes than the Cepheids' across those angles. Together the populations constrain the warp at intermediate stellar ages, adding a new point to the relation between stellar age and warp amplitude. That age dependence helps astronomers test explanations for the warp, from satellite interactions to misaligned gas accretion.
arxiv-2606-10335:
Jung and his team reconstruct fluid flow fields in a way that respects the physics the data came from, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computing. When input data break physics, through low-fidelity simulation or unmodeled errors, rebuilds can show wrong equation residuals, violated balance laws, or shaky derived values. Their physics-informed B-spline method embeds the governing constraints directly into the rebuild process.

The method builds compact, smooth field forms from tensor-product B-splines, the standard piecewise polynomial basis. It finds the spline control points by weighing data fit against the residuals of the partial differential equations, plus initial and boundary conditions. The method offers simulation scientists a middle path: smoother and more usable than raw gridded output, yet answerable to the equations the flow must obey.
arxiv-2606-10835:
Lee analyzes a blended target update for linear Q-learning in this 2026 arXiv paper. Q-learning steadies itself with a target network, a lagging copy refreshed only periodically, but hard periodic updates can still destabilize linear value models. The lambda-target update averages the periodic update maps with geometric weights, sliding between two known schemes as lambda runs from zero to one.

At lambda zero it is the plain one-period update; as lambda approaches one it becomes projected Q-value iteration. Both endpoints solve the same projected Bellman equation yet generate different error systems. Lee derives a joint spectral radius certificate for the whole family, plus implementable sampled versions of the update.
arxiv-2606-11135:
Zhao, Bouffard, and Joós address a protection problem created by solar and battery inverters in a 2026 arXiv paper. Distribution networks increasingly host inverter-based resources, which supply little short-circuit current during faults. Traditional overcurrent relays, which trip on excess current, can no longer be trusted to spot faults quickly in such networks.

They propose pre-fault voltage discrimination. It uses the voltage recorded just before a disturbance to tell real faults apart from normal switching events and transformer inrush, the surge when a transformer energizes. On that foundation they build a time-domain fault detection algorithm using traveling wave information, the fast transients a fault launches. Offline simulations and controller hardware-in-the-loop real-time tests validated the design. It stayed dependable against small fault inception angles, secure against normal switching, and faster than traditional relays.
arxiv-2606-12035:
Tian-Ci Tian and five colleagues describe quantum devices without rerunning them in this 2026 arXiv paper. Knowing what a quantum device actually does, process description, underpins benchmarking and error checks. Shadow methods recently extended from states to processes, letting many properties be predicted from few measurements, but only singly.

Their framework, shadow engineering, encodes each shadow into sparse transfer matrices. From those, arbitrary combined process chains can be predicted in advance, without running it on hardware. They prove modest sample needs, far better than full process tomography. Shadow data is simply reused, so overhead is minimal. Tests on a superconducting quantum processor show the approach for error mitigation and Hamiltonian dynamics. The authors describe the result as virtual quantum process control: complex changes handled on a normal computer while the quantum hardware stays untouched.
arxiv-2606-12135:
Fournier and Zhou extend mean-field theory to crowds whose links themselves keep changing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Mean-field theory replaces a huge interacting crowd by one typical member facing an averaged environment. Here each particle follows a noisy diffusion, random wandering with drift, while the weight on each link between two particles also evolves noisily. Each weight's motion depends on the states of the two particles it joins.

Starting data are assumed dissociated, a product form where separate random ingredients generate each particle and link. The authors build the limiting equation by averaging over an independent neighbor and prove it has a unique solution. The dissociated structure survives the dynamics, an echo of the classic propagation of chaos. Under stated conditions, coupling estimates show a typical particle and link converge to the limit as the crowd grows. The crowd's overall distribution of state pairs and weights converges too.
arxiv-2606-12335:
Noble and Royle prove a 1988 conjecture for planar graphs after it failed everywhere else, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Las Vergnas conjectured a divisibility pattern in the Tutte polynomial, a graph-counting polynomial, tied to a graph's bicycle dimension, a measure of its cycle structure. The claim says certain derivatives of the diagonal Tutte polynomial at minus one come out as multiples of powers of two. Counterexamples killed it for general graphs and binary matroids. Computation hinted planar graphs, drawable without crossings, might obey it.

The authors define a stronger property, the LV property, and prove it for a wider class: delta-Y-reducible graphs. They analyze how a delta-Y exchange, a local graph surgery, shifts the polynomial's coefficients. Planar graphs are all delta-Y-reducible, so the conjecture follows for them at once. A conjecture surviving only in the flat world now has a proof shaped to that world.
arxiv-2606-12435:
Rathod and co-authors show that a routine data-cleaning step can bake racial skew into mortgage analysis before any model runs, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard equal-frequency binning creates bins with lopsided racial mixes. The team audits 103,481 Chicago mortgage applications from the 2023 HMDA release. They compare standard binning against a fair-binning algorithm, then mine denial patterns and cluster applicants for a disparate-impact check.

Standard binning shows 9.63 percent racial bias in income discretization, matching earlier reports. Fair binning across seven race groups fails at the stricter fairness setting and only succeeds at the looser one, at a twenty-nine percent price in utility. Rule mining finds high debt-to-income ratio dominating denials, with no explicit racial rules. But clustering exposes what rules hide: ten of forty-five cluster-group pairs flag disparate impact, with Black applicants denied more than White applicants among financially similar peers.
arxiv-2606-12635:
Imtiaz and co-authors teach a model to imagine the skin layers a microscope skipped, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reflectance confocal microscopy gives noninvasive optical biopsies: sharp sideways images of living skin at successive depths. But the depth steps are coarse, about six times wider than the sideways resolution, so the stacked volume is stretched and hard to read. Their CD-RCM is the first method built for this imaging geometry.

A feedforward, decoder-only transformer treats scanning as a virtual camera sliding along the depth axis. From a sparse stack, it synthesizes realistic slices at any queried depth, filling the volume evenly. A skin-specific perceptual loss, tuned by self-supervised adaptation on confocal mosaics, keeps the micro-textures honest. Inference takes under a second, with no per-patient optimization. Clinicians gain continuous-depth views and cross-sections resembling histopathology, from data the microscope already collects.
arxiv-2606-12935:
Chen and colleagues introduce MARS, a margin-adversarial risk-controlled stopping rule that cuts the cost of parallel test-time scaling for language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Parallel scaling samples many reasoning traces and majority-votes their answers, which improves accuracy but forces every trace to run to completion. The authors observe that partial traces can be probed at intermediate checkpoints to extract answers without disrupting generation, revealing an evolving aggregate vote.

MARS stops generation once the leading answer stays safe under a bound on future vote movement. With true switch probabilities, MARS provably matches the full-budget vote with high probability, and a 5-feature logistic model matches oracle switching behaviour in practice. Across 3 reasoning models and 3 competition-math benchmarks, MARS saves 25 to 47 percent of self-consistency tokens. It also saves 14 to 29 percent on top of the DeepConf Online baseline, while matching full-budget accuracy.
arxiv-2606-13235:
Georgiadis proves an existence result for a model of mixed fluids in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Maxwell-Stefan equations describe how several chemical species diffuse through each other, each slowed by friction against the others. The version studied tracks temperature, so heat flow and mass flow interact. Its thermal conductivity, the property governing how heat spreads, fades to zero at low temperature following a power law. That fading breaks the usual estimates: the standard energy inequality no longer controls how steeply temperature varies.

The paper shows weak solutions, solutions understood in an averaged integral sense, still exist for all time. The allowed power in the conductivity law runs from above zero up to two. The step is a renormalised energy estimate, a rescaled bookkeeping of energy that restores control over temperature. That control lets the author pin down the heat flux even where conductivity nearly vanishes.
arxiv-2606-13335:
Figalli and Zhang prove a sharp stability result for a theorem of geometry in this 2026 arXiv paper. Alexandrov's theorem says that a surface with constant mean curvature, a measure of how the surface bends on average, must be a sphere. Stability asks the follow-up: if the curvature is nearly constant, is the shape nearly a ball, and by how much? The authors work with bounded smooth domains in dimension whose volume matches the unit ball. A condition on the excess, the deviation from sphericity, places them in a tractable regime.

Their estimate bounds the excess, the volume of the symmetric difference from the ball, and the curvature's deviation, by the size of the curvature's fluctuation in a square-integrable sense. The inequality is sharp, meaning its form cannot be improved. Stability results matter wherever near-constant curvature arises, from soap films to materials modelling.
arxiv-2606-14235:
Xu and co-authors sharpen Bayesian inference by letting a neural proposal propose candidates, then filtering them. Variational inference (VI) fits complex posteriors with simple families; implicit, network-built forms bend easily but still miss in practice, through small size or hard training. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes IVRS: networks build an implicit proposal, and rejection sampling refines it, accepting samples by a density ratio to the target.

A discriminator network estimates it. They define a resampled lower bound as its quality measure, and derive a tighter one than the standard bound. In an ideal analysis with a perfect discriminator, the divergence to the true posterior falls steadily as more resampling is applied. Tests on regression and VAE image modeling beat traditional VI. The method is meant as a drop-in upgrade for the usual workflow, not a new model class.
arxiv-2606-14335:
Hou and Liu prove a 2026 arXiv result in statistics about finding a hidden pattern inside noisy data. A secret graph is planted inside a complete network, and each link receives a random weight. Links in the hidden graph draw weights from one distribution, and all other links draw from another, so the task is to recover the hidden graph from weights alone.

The pair give a unified rule for the information limit of almost exact recovery, the point where nearly the whole graph can be found. Their rule links the gap between the two weight distributions to a threshold from random graph theory. The bounds also cover partial recovery, and for several common weight types they show an all-or-nothing effect, where recovery jumps sharply from impossible to nearly complete.
arxiv-2606-14435:
Peng studies shadowing in dynamical systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. Shadowing means every approximate orbit of a system is closely tracked by a true orbit. Shifts of finite type, symbolic systems built from finite rules, are known building blocks: earlier work showed every compact metric shadowing system is a factor of an inverse limit of such shifts.

Peng first shows that this factor representation alone needs neither shadowing nor metrizability, since every compact Hausdorff system arises that way. What shadowing truly adds is stronger stability: in the metric case, the inverse sequence can be chosen with surjective bonding maps so the zero-dimensional extension still has shadowing. He also proves every compact Hausdorff shadowing system is conjugate to an inverse limit of metrizable shadowing systems with factor bonding maps.
arxiv-2606-14635:
Manaparambil and Anders extend a powerful quantum simulation method to driven systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. The numerical renormalization group finds equilibrium regimes of quantum impurity systems with exceptional accuracy. An impurity system is an impurity coupled to electron reservoirs. Out of equilibrium, the steady state is set by boundary conditions like applied voltage. It is not given by a simple thermal formula.

Their open Wilson chain approach attaches a reservoir to each chain site. Couplings are recovered exactly through a continued-fraction expansion. Bias and temperature gradients enter through a Bloch-Redfield tensor. Its special eigenvector gives the steady-state density operator. Applied to a quantum dot under bias and thermal gradient, the method matched quantum Monte Carlo data. It reached extremely low Kondo energy scales. Single data points took orders of magnitude less time than rival methods on a standard laptop.
arxiv-2606-14735:
George and co-authors shrink vision transformers for phones in a 2026 arXiv paper. Vision transformers classify images well, but their self-attention cost grows quadratically and their parameter counts exclude them from tight mobile and edge budgets. Their model, UtVAA, is an ultra-tiny transformer built for exactly those constraints.

Its Affix Attention block mixes depthwise-pointwise local feature extraction, linear self-attention, coordinate attention for spatial dependencies, and a ternary fusion blending local and global information. Dilated bottleneck blocks widen the receptive field cheaply through dilated separable convolutions with residual connections. The family ships in three sizes, the smallest holding only about two hundred five thousand parameters. Across four datasets including CIFAR and tomato disease images, UtVAA stayed competitive within the sub-million-parameter regime, showing transformers can be redesigned ultra-tiny without major accuracy loss.
arxiv-2606-15335:
Liu and coauthors sanitize shared text by disentangling role from style in a 2026 privacy paper. When AI agents collaborate across organizations, text leaks more than names and numbers. Writing style betrays the source: formatting, vocabulary, and syntax act as fingerprints. Masking of identifiers leaves those signatures untouched. The authors' system, DiSan, splits text into a role subspace and a style subspace. Role content carries the facts and travels; style stays local.

Federated training aligns role prototypes across parties without centralizing text. An adversarial objective keeps the subspaces from leaking into each other. Experiments show masking a fifth of tokens barely dents stylometric attribution. DiSan cut private exposure twentyfold on a multi-agent retrieval benchmark. It kept eighty-three percent faithfulness while doing so. On the Enron corpus, source attribution fell by about seventy-three percent. The work treats privacy as a property of representations, not word lists.
arxiv-2606-15535:
Bergach proposes MADAR in 2026, a processor that abolishes memory addresses. In a normal chip, most area and energy go not to computing but to addressing: register files, caches, and tag checks that store values and find them again. In MADAR, all state circulates in rings that advance one position per clock, with code and data riding together.

A value is named by its orbit position, and a fixed station computes when a circulating instruction sweeps past its operands, on a compile-time schedule. Rings of growing period replace the cache hierarchy, so movement is scheduled, not triggered by misses. Bergach validates the model in cycle-accurate hardware with a constructive scheduler, and prices it with an energy model. For matrix multiplication, energy per operation stays flat as the reduction grows. The design wins when the ring fits the work, and loses when a small job parks in a large ring.
arxiv-2606-15635:
Gao exhibits exceptionally large values of quadratic Dirichlet L-functions in 2026, working at the central point of the critical strip under the generalized Riemann hypothesis. The family is tied to primes: characters whose modulus is eight times a prime. How large such values can grow tests our picture of the value distribution of L-functions.

The tool is the long resonator method, which builds a carefully tuned Dirichlet polynomial that resonates with the L-function to force a large value somewhere in the family. Gao shows some prime modulus in any large range gives a central value at least exponential in a root of iterated logarithms of the range size. The exponent constant matches the best shape known from work on the zeta function and on fundamental discriminants. Such lower bounds discipline conjectures about moments and maxima of L-function families.
arxiv-2606-15735:
Kim and colleagues introduce EHRNote-ChatQA in 2026, the first benchmark for clinical question answering that unfolds over multiple turns and multiple discharge summaries. Clinicians reviewing a patient's history must synthesise several hospital summaries and verify the evidence behind each answer. Existing benchmarks test exam knowledge or single-turn questions instead, missing that longitudinal, evidence-checking work.

Built from de-identified MIMIC-IV records, the benchmark holds 967 patient cases spanning one to five notes, with over sixteen thousand question pairs verified by medical experts. Each content question comes paired with an evidence question asking which notes and sections support the answer. Eleven experts reviewed every sample. Testing twenty-two large language models exposes three weaknesses: models struggle more with evidence grounding than with answering, errors compound across turns, and single-turn skill does not transfer to this setting. The benchmark gives clinical AI a harder, more realistic yardstick.
arxiv-2606-15935:
Huang and colleagues observe dynamical phase transitions in a dephased photonic quantum walk in 2026, in experiment. They govern how a quantum state relaxes toward rest; in open systems they are tied to the spectrum of the Liouvillian, the generator of the motion. The team realises a discrete-time quantum walk on a three-node graph, with a tunable synthetic gauge flux and dephasing to control time-reversal behaviour and detailed balance.

With detailed balance intact, they observe a first-order jump marked by a crossing of real Liouvillian eigenvalues. Breaking detailed balance instead produces a second-order one at an exceptional point, where eigenvalues and their vectors coalesce. As the dephasing weakens, both effects drift and vanish near the unitary limit, persisting only above a finite threshold. The experiment ties that spectrum to the walk's relaxation, on a platform built for the purpose.
arxiv-2606-16235:
Palai and co-authors show in 2026 that a mismatched oxide overlayer can boost the magnetism of a thin magnetic film. Interfaces between unlike oxides let lattice mismatch open new effects. The team joins a 4 nanometer ferromagnetic metal, SrRuO3, with a planar antiferromagnetic insulator, SrCuO2. A bare film serves as reference.

Both films show perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, but the bilayer's saturation magnetization reaches about 2.7 Bohr magnetons per ruthenium, versus about 1.3 for the bare film. Its measured anisotropy constant is likewise far higher, and its Curie point rises too. In transport, the bare film's low-temperature resistivity upturn below 5 kelvin, caused by disorder-driven corrections, is strongly suppressed in the bilayer. Conduction there looks Fermi-liquid-like instead. Hall tests find stronger built-in and skew-scattering terms. Interface design thus tunes these effects together. The gains come from the join itself, not from a thicker film.
arxiv-2606-16335:
Lackner and co-authors test in 2026 how to draw a cancer treatment plan so patients actually understand it, comparing a simple static timeline with an interactive one. Multistage treatments, shown here for acute myeloid leukemia, unfold in phases that overwhelm patients with limited health literacy. The team built two timeline versions using design and psychology principles. One is static and simplified; the other adds layered detail.

A survey measured how well readers followed treatment sequences, and their confidence, for both versions. The static version improves understanding and clarity well beyond the baseline, the authors report. The interactive variant did not help and added overhead and mental demands. Clear hierarchy, steady encoding, and low complexity did the real work. The lesson for patient materials is plain: cut interpretive effort before adding features.
arxiv-2606-16435:
Dong and co-authors unify in 2026 two audio tasks that are usually engineered separately: generating sound from text and editing existing audio by instruction. Separate designs for each task multiply system overhead. Their model, AudioWeave, handles both with one shared architecture and parameter set, adding no task-specific parts. A hybrid diffusion transformer backbone mixes dual-stream and single-stream blocks to balance performance against parameter cost.

The key is joint condition modeling with a factorized position embedding, letting the backbone digest the different inputs each task brings: text, target audio, and optional reference audio. Because the tasks differ in conditions and data shapes, training proceeds in stages. That schedule mitigates task rivalry and catastrophic forgetting, where learning one task erases the other. Experiments show each task holds its performance level, and some improve from shared training.
arxiv-2606-16535:
Fumanal-Idocin and Andreu-Perez audit in 2026 whether the human-readable concepts inside concept bottleneck models are actually detected faithfully. Such models predict through interpretable symbols. But high task accuracy does not prove the symbols honest: jointly trained models can smuggle shortcuts into the bottleneck. The authors test reliability by swapping independently trained concept detectors and classification heads that share one symbolic vocabulary.
