On the CUB-200-2011 bird dataset with full concept supervision, the swap test is reassuring. Performance drops by under one accuracy point, retention stays above 99 percent, and no concept falls below chance detection. Concept-level metrics and symbol-wise uncertainty estimates still flag individual concepts prone to spurious firing. The authors then propose reliability-aware training: one shared detector serves multiple classification heads and is penalized for leaning on unreliable symbols, globally or per instance. Explanations earn trust here by surviving component swaps, not by reading well.
arxiv-2606-16935:
Klein and colleagues present CrossMaps in a 2026 robotics workshop paper on rover mapping. A rover needs maps that record not just what is where, but how trustworthy each observation is, since range errors, lighting artifacts and sparse data all distort fusion and navigation.

CrossMaps builds language-queryable semantic maps from color and depth data in real time. Multi-scale image embeddings from a vision-language model are fused with confidence weights drawn from geometric, semantic and time cues. A dual-memory design separates fresh, noisy sightings, held in short-term memory, from stable landmarks promoted into long-term memory once they look confident and coherent. The system runs on a Jetson-powered ground vehicle alongside standard localization and mapping. Its semantic heatmaps answer natural language queries to steer the rover. The proof of concept points toward shared multi-rover maps and safety-critical navigation as next steps.
arxiv-2606-17135:
Wu presents a 2026 arXiv paper on the quantum fate of the Choptuik naked singularity. In classical relativity, tuned collapse of matter would expose a singularity directly to distant observers. The paper asks whether quantum backreaction changes that stark outcome. Its setting is the Einstein-scalar system, poised between dispersal and black hole formation.

Building on semiclassical interior work, Wu studies controlled exterior models in two space-time settings. In one, boundary conditions pick a vacuum state whose backreaction cloaks the naked region. In the other, horizon tracing finds finite-mass trapped surfaces near a shifted threshold. The upshot is that naked singularities seem to share the fate of ordinary black hole singularities. That reduces a deep loss of predictability to the standard black hole evaporation problem.
arxiv-2606-17235:
Tep and Bernacki present a 2026 arXiv paper on deep learning models that predict how crystal grains grow over time in metals. Such models are usually trained on clean synthetic data, yet real use demands they cope with conditions far from training. The study tests a model from the authors' earlier work on three hard cases, with no retraining or fine-tuning allowed.

The test cases were real experimental microstructures, a bimodal mix of grain sizes, and abnormal grain growth. A new physics-informed attention design was also tried, one that limits attention to grain boundary pixels only. Both models coped with all three cases, but the boundary-focused model did clearly better on the bimodal case, raising image similarity scores and cutting mean grain size error by more than half. Its attention maps also matched curvature-driven growth physics.
arxiv-2606-17735:
Wang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on self-healing reasoning for language models, attacking what they call the autoregressive curse. In long chains of thought, one early slip poisons every later step, since generation never looks back. Their method watches the model's own local cross-entropy as a built-in gauge of uncertainty, rising where the reasoning is shakiest. Segment-level thresholds then flag the defective stretches so they can be cut out and regenerated, reusing the cached context instead of restarting the whole chain from scratch.

Trained on a large mathematics corpus, the approach lifted scores on hard benchmarks for both model sizes tested, passing prior best results. Sample efficiency improved while memory overhead stayed linear, the authors report. The framing treats uncertainty as an internal coordinate the model can act on directly. That is a systems-level route to reasoning that repairs itself mid-flight.
arxiv-2606-17935:
Pu and colleagues present MoonSplat, a system that rebuilds 3D scenes live from a single camera's video, in a 2026 graphics paper. The scene is stored as 3D Gaussians, a representation that renders fast and in high quality, which suits robotics and augmented reality. Online methods, though, often lose track of the camera because they never optimize the whole trajectory at once, and they slow down on long sequences.

MoonSplat adds a global optimization step over similarity transforms that jointly refines camera poses and the voxelized Gaussian map. That enables reliable loop closure, where revisiting a place snaps the reconstruction back into consistency. A color residual learning trick speeds convergence while lifting rendering quality. Experiments on indoor and outdoor scenes show the system stays robust where earlier online methods drifted or stalled.
arxiv-2606-18135:
Gurny and Quinn release a field-recorded dataset of gunshot sounds built for telling calibers apart by ear, in a 2026 paper. Much earlier work trained on audio scraped from the internet, where quality varies and labels can be wrong. Their Certus Caliber Classification Gunshot Dataset instead captures muzzle blasts under controlled field conditions, with rich metadata on every recording.

The collection holds more than eight thousand data points from twenty-eight firearms across sixteen calibers, with multiple cartridge variants, barrel lengths, and action types. Microphones of several kinds, from dedicated recorders to lavaliers and phones, sat at varied positions, mirroring the mess of real deployments. While caliber classification is the headline task, the authors also target gunshot detection, audio separation, and general signal processing research that needs trustworthy real-world reference data.
arxiv-2606-18235:
Chai and colleagues give a house-hunting robot a memory that improves while it searches, in a 2026 paper. Zero-shot object-goal navigation sends an embodied agent to find a named object in a new building with no prior training. Foundation-model agents usually lean on static priors, repeat their mistakes, and burn steps on trial and error. EvolveNav instead learns from its own past episodes at test time.

The system distills finished trajectories into an agentic rule memory of actionable lessons. A retrieval rule based on the upper confidence bound picks which lessons to trust, weighing how relevant each is against its track record. Before acting, a preflection module forecasts how a candidate move will play out, steering the agent away from unpromising rooms. On standard indoor benchmarks it beat zero-shot rivals on success rate by about a tenth, with fewer wasted steps.
arxiv-2606-18635:
Xie offers a heuristic scheme for the 3D Ising model in a 2026 physics paper. The Ising model is the classic open problem of critical phenomena. It resists exact treatment, though modern bootstrap methods pin its critical exponents well.

Xie maps the model's field theory onto an operator-valued matrix taken from anisotropic elasticity. A symplectic algebra governs it, and he imposes a topological constraint that yields a bootstrap equation. A classical projection gives one bound on the anomalous dimension, landing on the known two-loop perturbative value. He then adds a cascade conjecture, in which dimensional reduction steps add framing charges to a rational tangle invariant. That gives a value matching strict bootstrap bounds to a fraction of a percent. The author reads the left-over gap as a measure of the quantum fluctuations the geometry leaves out.
arxiv-2606-18835:
Allahverdyan and Bisharyan propose doing the unstructured database search with a physical system, in a 2026 physics paper. Grover's algorithm made searching an unstructured database the emblem of quantum speedup. A classical digital computer must check elements one by one. The authors instead encode it in an analog system of interacting spherical spins.

In their build, the data set lives in the spin-spin couplings. The selected element is marked by a ferromagnetic coupling between two spins. At low temperature, the equilibrium magnetization piles up strongly on the chosen spins, which completes the search. The search time is the relaxation time from a homogeneous initial state, worked out from Langevin equations. That time grows slower than the square root of the database size. The authors present this as evidence that a dissipative classical analog machine can outrun a unitary quantum computer on this task.
arxiv-2606-19035:
Stenger and colleagues present a 2026 method for splitting quantum circuits across machines with controlled approximations. Exact distributed quantum computing needs an exponential amount of classical data to rebuild the full process, which quickly becomes infeasible. Bigger machines will still have qubit limits, so splitting large circuits into smaller parts run on separate processors is a key path to scale beyond any single device.

The key is weak coupling. When a circuit can be split around a qubit that couples only weakly to the rest, the classical cost falls from exponential to polynomial. The authors show this reduction formally and demo the method on a layered circuit modeled on those used for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm. That case matters because optimization circuits are a prime target for near-term quantum use. Accept a controlled approximation, and distributed runs become far cheaper.
arxiv-2606-19135:
Sander and colleagues build a technical taxonomy of communication protocols for language model agents in 2026. As multi-agent systems grow, agents need shared rules to talk, use tools, and fetch data. The protocol landscape is fragmented, though, which creates a mismatch problem for agent networks. The study sets out to classify the main open-source protocols in a structured, comparable way for builders choosing among them.

Using an established method, the team ran five rounds of building on nine active protocols with real adoption. The final scheme has five dimensions covering counterparty, payload, interaction state, discovery, and schema flexibility. All sampled agent-to-agent protocols pair hybrid payloads with persistent session state. Most support several predefined schemas, while two negotiate schemas at run time. Decentralized discovery stays rare.
arxiv-2606-19235:
Cheng and colleagues propose CodeSentinel in 2026, a three-layer defense against indirect prompt injection in code contexts. Code models increasingly read external context from repositories, docs, and issue threads. Attackers hide instructions in comments, strings, identifiers, or decoy code within that context. The hidden text can steer the model once it is retrieved, turning code reading into an attack surface.

CodeSentinel sanitizes context at inference time before it reaches the model. It parses code with Tree-sitter to extract high-risk nodes, then combines syntax-guided pre-filtering, dynamic scoring guided by the syntax tree, and node perturbation analysis. Flagged nodes are removed or neutralized in place. Across six recent attack families, the system reaches a strong average node-level score. It beats three rival defenses in the comparison. Layered, syntax-aware cleaning of this kind fits how code attacks actually hide, inside structure rather than plain prose.
arxiv-2606-19635:
Xilun Chen and eight colleagues present Token Factory in 2026, a way to feed rich signals into large recommendation models. Transformer-based recommenders excel at industry scale, but classic signals fit them awkwardly. Spelling signals out as text or discrete item codes inflates prompts, memory, and compute.

Token Factory turns traditional signals into soft tokens the model can process directly. Heterogeneous features compress into a compact token stream. Prompt length explosion stops while model performance improves. The design slots into production-scale recommendation settings. Experiments in such a setting validate the gains. Soft tokens give one shared format for signals that once needed bespoke handling. Recommenders can then weigh user history, item traits, and context inside one architecture. The approach aims at practical deployment, not just benchmark wins.
arxiv-2606-19735:
Bhavan Vasu and Rajesh Mangannavar build GLARE in 2026, a chat-style interface for questioning vision model explanations. Global summaries state how an image classifier acts across data and classes as a whole. Their size and complexity make them hard to explore directly.

Users usually want targeted answers, not static explanation artifacts. GLARE places a language model between the user and local explanation data. Questions become structured SQL queries over that data, so users can group and sum the facts as they wish. Replies come back as natural language enriched with statistics. Supporting local explanations and intent-matched visualisations accompany each answer. Tests cover intent reading, query match scores, and coping with unseen queries and datasets. Robustness to wording errors also faces testing. Chat-based access makes global summaries far more usable for staff who audit models.
arxiv-2606-19835:
Roberto Pellerito, Daniel Gehrig, Shintaro Shiba, and Davide Scaramuzza compress event camera streams into neural events in 2026. Event cameras report single brightness changes with microsecond timing. Each lone event says almost nothing, so downstream tools drown in the torrent.

The framework re-tokenises the stream into a small set of rich neural events. Each one encodes a local space-time window through a discrete learnable code. When that code flips, a neural event fires, yielding a far smaller stream. Detection and classification networks train on the compressed stream directly. They match or beat leading methods on those tasks. The event rate falls by a factor of two at the same time. Sparser, smarter tokens ease the load on fast vision systems like drones and robots.
arxiv-2606-20435:
Yechan Park and Yuya Sasaki help applied researchers choose a headline estimand from matching, difference-in-differences, and hybrid designs. Their 2026 paper addresses a routine panel-data dilemma: how to use past outcomes when estimating causal effects. The three designs lean on different assumptions and can deliver different answers.

The authors frame the choice as a minimax-regret problem, picking the design whose worst-case regret against the alternatives is smallest. The framework turns a judgment call into an explicit trade-off that can be computed and defended. Replications guided by earlier work anchor the comparison in real estimation practice. For policy-facing research, a principled rule for the headline number beats habit or taste.
arxiv-2606-20535:
Itai Arad and four colleagues give a near-optimal algorithm for learning local Lindbladians from black-box access to a quantum system's evolution. Their 2026 paper targets the coefficients of the Hamiltonian and dissipative terms that govern open quantum dynamics. Learning them is a first step for verifying and debugging quantum devices.

The algorithm runs the unknown evolution for short times, estimates Pauli transfer matrices from classical shadows, and converts them into Lindbladian coefficients by stable local Fourier steps. For fixed locality and bounded local loss, the number of evolution uses and the total evolution time scale near-optimally with the target precision. Open-system tomography becomes practical at the scales near-term hardware needs.
arxiv-2606-20835:
Istiaq Fahad, Mridha Fuad, and Kazi Sakib propose PromptMark in 2026, a framework for watermarking code generated by large language models. Watermarks support provenance and accountability for AI-written code. Most developers use commercial model services as black boxes. Older watermark methods need access to the decoding process, which those services do not give. PromptMark instead works through structured input instructions alone.

Prompts steer the model toward subtle naming patterns in identifiers and comments. Functional correctness and code structure are preserved. Detection uses statistical tests designed to stay reliable across code lengths and outputs. An iterative feedback loop updates prompts based on detection scores, refining the mark. Experiments test the approach under black-box limits. A prompt-only watermark could help teams prove code origin without changing their model provider or gaining special access to model internals.
arxiv-2606-21035:
V Torres-Gomez and a large DESI team present an unsupervised AI pipeline in 2026 to assess quality in spectra from the DESI survey's second data release. Large surveys collect spectra at scales where visual inspection is impractical. Their pipeline needs no labeled training data. Dimensionality reduction with UMAP is combined with friends-of-friends clustering to isolate anomalous spectra for targeted review.

The pipeline processes tens of millions of spectra tile by tile. A dense core of typical spectra separates from small isolated groups. Over one million outlier candidates result. A sampled visual inspection estimates how many are real faults. Automating triage matters. Rare reduction failures can masquerade as exotic discoveries if no one flags broken spectra first.
arxiv-2606-21335:
Rinku Sebastian, Simon O'Keefe, and Martin Trefzer test whether raw audio can be classified directly in 2026, skipping the handcrafted feature extraction that audio pipelines usually depend on. Features such as MFCCs compress sound into tuned summaries, but designing them costs effort and compute. Reservoir computing offers an alternative: a fixed, random recurrent network whose rich internal dynamics transform the signal, with only a simple readout trained.

The team compares shallow, sequential deep, and parallel deep reservoir designs on their ability to build layered views of sound. The parallel design beats the other two in every test while keeping model complexity low. Skipping feature engineering points toward deployable, low-power acoustic systems, from always-on listening devices to embedded monitors that cannot afford heavy prep work.
arxiv-2606-21435:
Luca Passarella and four colleagues ask in 2026 whether the densest stars in the sky come in two families: ordinary hadronic stars and strange quark stars, coexisting under different equations of state. The team runs the first detailed Bayesian comparison of the two-families scenario against the single-family view, folding in astrophysical observations and laboratory data. Their hadronic models allow hyperons and delta resonances, while quark matter may enter a color-superconducting phase.

Bayes factors favor the two-families picture, though both scenarios still fit current data. Two families ease a real tension: small-radius stars want soft matter at moderate density, while the heaviest pulsars demand stiff matter at high density. Future finds, such as even heavier objects or twin stars with equal radii and different masses, would sharpen the verdict.
arxiv-2606-21535:
Lorenzo Moriondo and Ilias Azizi propose in 2026 that vector search should read embedding spaces as energy networks, not just as geometry. Search engines rank stored vectors by closeness to a query, usually cosine similarity, which ignores the corpus's own structure, so results can be geometrically near yet topologically scattered. Their Graph Wiring framework builds a spectral graph from the feature columns of the embedding space and uses its spectrum as extra signal.

Spectral Indexing, the search version of the idea, couples geometric similarity with spectral information, improving coherence between top and tail results and semantic alignment. A modulation parameter tunes search behavior on the fly, a flexibility that retrieval-augmented generation pipelines increasingly need. The authors ground the method in a theory of epiplexity and test it on benchmarks and industrial data with their open-source arrowspace library.
arxiv-2606-21635:
Monir Nasser-Eddine, Paul Magron, and Romain Serizel rework the training loss for neural speech enhancement in 2026. The standard signal-to-distortion ratio treats every time-frequency region alike, yet intelligibility rides on fine spectral cues: consonant bursts and other short transients carry outsized weight. Their framework weights the loss by local speech presence, speech-to-interference ratio, and spectral flux, all inside a differentiable objective.

The weighting stresses bins where speech and noise compete hardest, while still crediting transient cues. Tests show gains in frequency-weighted quality metrics and in phoneme recognition accuracy, especially for consonants. Spectral checks show cleaner rebuilding of mid-frequency structure at milder interference levels. For hearing-assistive and communication systems, losses that respect phoneme-level detail promise speech that is not just cleaner on paper but easier to understand.
arxiv-2606-21735:
Orchid Chetia Phukan, Girish, Mohd Mujtaba Akhtar, and Chi-Chun Lee expose an age blind spot in speech-deepfake detection in 2026. Detectors for codec-synthesized speech, trained on existing benchmarks, generalize poorly to elderly voices, a worrying gap given fraud targeting older people. The team defines the Elderly CodecFake Detection task and releases the Elderly-CodecFake dataset in English and Chinese.

Their hypothesis: multimodal foundation models, exposed to elderly content in cross-modal pretraining, transfer better than specialist detectors. Experiments back it up. Their BONSAI framework fuses LanguageBind and ImageBind using Jensen-Shannon divergence as the fusion mechanism. The fused system reaches an average equal error rate of 1.66 percent, beating single foundation models and strong baselines, and sets the benchmark for the new task.
arxiv-2606-22235:
Shmayev and colleagues study, in 2026, the non-equilibrium orbital response of chiral carbon nanotubes, hunting for selectivity by angular momentum. Chirality, the handedness of the tube's wrapping, links structure to electronic response. The team surveys a broad set of chiral tubes, both metallic and semiconducting, in and out of equilibrium.

The orbital Edelstein response, meaning current-induced orbital magnetization, depends strongly on both chirality and diameter. No universal scaling law captures it. Instead, distinct families of tubes form characteristic response branches fixed by the chiral wrapping vector. Metallic tubes quickly recover their intrinsic response away from contacts. Semiconducting tubes show pronounced ripples from interference between channels carrying different angular momenta. By adding angular structure to the contact self-energy, the authors show chiral tubes can act as efficient orbital-angular-momentum filters.
arxiv-2606-22335:
Herrera and colleagues present, in 2026, a multi-vehicle system for tracking tagged marine animals with single-hydrophone autonomous underwater vehicles. Acoustic transmitters on animals are usually localized by large multi-hydrophone frames, whose drag limits tracking speed. Stationary receivers, meanwhile, lose animals that swim out of range. The team's design equips several small vehicles with one compact hydrophone payload each.

A particle filter with a hidden Markov model of animal behaviour fuses the vehicles' measurements to estimate the transmitter's position. The behaviour model is fitted to historical movement data. In real-world deployments the system achieves a position error of about ten metres over short-term tracks. A larger simulated dataset gives about fifteen metres over longer deployments in a wider area. The fitted behaviour model beats a generic velocity model, and both beat a random-walk baseline.
arxiv-2606-22435:
Shaodong Wenren, Dingyan Cao, Zhiheng Jiang, and Chenyu Li present a practical statistics tool in this 2026 paper. Their subject is sample size calculation for survival endpoints, the trial outcomes that track how long patients live or stay event-free. Choosing that size well matters, since too few patients can leave a trial unable to detect real effects.

Freedman first proposed such calculations based on the logrank statistic. Later statisticians added factors such as dropout rates and delayed treatment effects, but the professional functions involved are complex to use. Wenren and colleagues built a visual web application on two existing R packages, lrstat and powerSurvEpi. The app turns those calculations into a point-and-click tool for trial planners. They tested its functions and program against known cases. The outputs matched those cases closely, which the authors take as proof that the tool works as intended.
arxiv-2606-22535:
Grzegorz Kowal, Gabriel Ferreira-Santos, and Diego Falceta-Gonçalves develop a theory of tearing instability in anisotropic plasmas in this 2026 paper. The tearing mode rips and reconnects magnetic field lines in a current sheet. Weakly collisional plasmas, common in astrophysics, sustain pressure differing along and across the field, yet standard scalings assume uniform pressure.

The authors build a linear theory in gyrotropic MHD for a force-free Harris sheet, tracking plasma beta and the pressure difference between directions. In the outer region, anisotropy changes the decay rate and matching parameter, and sets an upper cutoff on unstable wavenumbers. In the resistive inner layer, anisotropy enters the leading momentum balance directly. They derive FKR and Coppi branches and match them at their crossover to find the fastest growing mode. The fastest growth rate keeps the Lundquist exponent, its prefactor now set by the anisotropy, beta, and closure indices.
arxiv-2606-22735:
Sara Colando examines how student writing changed after chatbots arrived in this 2026 education paper. Communicating statistical results clearly is a stated goal of undergraduate statistics and data science courses. Educators worry that students now offload that thinking to generative AI.

Colando assembled a corpus of over 1,600 undergraduate data analysis reports written from 2021 to 2025, spanning the period before and after large language models became widely accessible. Comparing style and verb usage across the years, she finds students' writing has become measurably more similar to that of language models. The shift is strongest in the first and fifth quintiles of reports, roughly the introduction and conclusion sections. Surprisingly, students' writing also became more similar to that of statistics experts over the same period. Colando discusses what this means for educators and proposes assessments that still force statistical thinking, such as targeted assignments on structuring a report's introduction.
arxiv-2606-22835:
Zijie Meng separates camera motion from subject motion in generated video in this 2026 paper. The two are tangled in ordinary two-dimensional conditioning, because both kinds of flow scale with inverse depth in the same way. Meng first proves the tangle is representational, not a flaw of any one architecture: from image evidence alone, the split cannot be recovered.

His method, OrthoMotion, therefore rebuilds the controls inside the attention operator. Camera motion goes into a geometric channel, a rotation of the rotary position embedding's phase that preserves norms. Subject motion goes into a semantic channel, a gated value injection in cross-attention. A light regularizer provably drives the two response subspaces to orthogonality, so the controls stop interfering. Meng reports the best camera and subject accuracy together, with cross-talk between the controls cut by more than half and no loss of fidelity.
arxiv-2606-23535:
Bengtsson and McConnell trace a surprising bridge between quantum measurement theory and deep number theory, in a 2026 mathematical physics paper. A SIC is a highly symmetric set of quantum states whose pairwise overlaps, inner products measuring their alignment, take one fixed size. Those overlap values turn out to be algebraic units, special numbers built from Stark units, quantities that Stark's conjectures extract from zeta functions to generate certain number fields.

Mixing exact arguments with numerical evidence, the authors argue that overlap units are always products of powers of square roots of Stark units. In the non-minimal case, a whole lattice of ray class fields, layered number fields, enters the picture. In every second dimension, counted in a specific way, some overlap units collapse to plus or minus one. They trace this pattern to one special property of those ray class fields.
arxiv-2606-23635:
Mustafa examines how particles orbit and how gravitational waves would sound around an exotic compact object in an alternative gravity theory, in a 2026 paper on gravitation. The setting is Freund Nambu scalar tensor gravity, which adds a scalar field to Einstein's tensor description of gravity. Its exact vacuum solution generalizes a known naked singularity case, where the singularity is not hidden behind a horizon. Two extra couplings reshape the geometry.

Mustafa tracks how those couplings move the innermost stable circular orbit, the closest orbit that stays stable, and the marginally bound orbit. For one sign of the scalar coupling the stable orbit shifts inward. Classifying bound orbits isolates extreme zoom whirl cases, where a particle whips around the center before swinging out. Simulated inspirals then show a clear timing drift in the wave bursts, a signature future observatories such as LISA could detect.
arxiv-2606-23735:
Koshkin and Lee identify the algebraic structure hidden inside panmagic squares built from permutations, in a 2026 paper on combinatorics. A panmagic square keeps the same sum along every row, column, and diagonal, including broken diagonals that wrap around the board. The matching permutations picture maximal sets of queens, none attacking another, on a toroidal chessboard. Some panmagic permutations are affine, given by simple modular formulas, and scattered cases were known to close under multi way multiplication.

The authors show these collections are N ary groups, structures whose basic operation combines N elements at once instead of two. Using the Post coset theorem, they identify each panmagic N ary group with a coset of the dihedral group. That group holds the symmetries of a polygon. Its extensions inside all affine permutations are included too. A cycle study links the topic to square free numbers, special primes, and counting formulas.
arxiv-2606-24035:
Ojha studies a puzzling flaw in diffusion-based speech cleaning, where a computer removes noise from recorded speech. Systems such as StoRM, which pairs a first-guess predictor with a learned score network, show a sharp kink in quality once test noise rises past the level used in training. Writing alone in 2026, Ojha uses a variational-flow analysis, a way of tracking how tiny changes flow through the system, to locate where that kink begins.

Careful factorisation of the sensitivity shows the roughness must come from the predictor stage, not from the learned score network downstream. Ojha proves the output loses smoothness exactly when the predictor output does, under three stated assumptions about the reverse process. The result also extends to the step-by-step sampler used in practice. Instead of running experiments, the paper lays out a concrete testing programme, leaving hands-on validation to a planned companion report.
arxiv-2606-24235:
Yuan and colleagues build an autonomous agent that runs spatial proteomics analysis end to end. Spatial proteomics maps protein expression at single-cell resolution inside intact tissue. That matters for tumour biology and precision medicine. Real workflows, though, are fragmented: experts hand-orchestrate specialised tools from imaging to phenotype discovery, limiting scale and reproducibility.

SP-Mind, presented in 2026 as the first agent built for this pipeline, carries expert-curated biological analysis skills and dedicated tools. It converts plain-language questions into complete analytical workflows, with no task-specific fine-tuning. To judge it, the team also releases SP-Bench. The benchmark holds just over a hundred tasks in eighteen categories, across diverse tissue types. On that benchmark and on established downstream tasks, SP-Mind outperforms open-source biomedical agent baselines. Yuan reads this as agent-run pipelines making spatial proteomics routine.
arxiv-2606-24335:
Meivar and colleagues deliberately choose a task no model can truly solve, to watch how vision-language models use evidence. Judging an object's real-world size from one uncalibrated photograph is ill-posed. The information is not in the picture. Any answer must lean on imperfect cues, from category priors to scene geometry. Their 2026 benchmark, Metric VQA, gathers dimension queries from the Objectron dataset, plus hundreds of tape-measured real-world scenes.

Twelve open-weight models, from small to enormous, face counterfactual tests decomposing six evidence channels. Even the largest models trail a text-only frontier system on the in-the-wild split. Target identity proves the most load-bearing cue. The target's own pixels and nearby context help only some models. Apparent size moves answers in no readable direction. Global scene geometry goes largely unused. LoRA fine-tuning is examined as a remedy.
arxiv-2606-24535:
Margalit and colleagues treat shared memory for fleets of AI agents as a governed distributed system, not a bigger notebook. As agent fleets work together, shared state raises problems single chatbot histories never face. Scoped access, temporal correctness, provenance, and policy controlled spread are among them. Their 2026 design defines the fleet memory problem. It names four failure modes: unauthorised leakage, stale propagation, contradiction persistence, and provenance collapse.

Primitives for scoped retrieval, temporal supersession, provenance tracking, and policy led spread answer each failure mode. The primitives are built in MemClaw, a live multi tenant memory service. Testing uses ArgusFleet, a shared harness exercising the live API along four control dimensions. The authors stress the test measures one production service, rather than comparing baselines. Its negative results are central to the point. Provenance is the cleanest success: every one of fifty depth four chains rebuilds with correct writer naming.
arxiv-2606-24735:
Yi-yuan Zhang, Hou-Zun Chen, and Xi Kang ask how a dark matter halo's past shapes the gas around its galaxy, beyond the known dominance of halo mass. The gas halo, called the circumgalactic medium, may also remember when the halo formed. Using the IllustrisTNG simulations, the team computes formation times for TNG50 halos and splits them into early and late forming groups.

Early formed halos host galaxies with more stellar mass and higher metallicity. Their surrounding gas is lighter, and their star formation rates are lower today. Below a certain mass, early halos also show richer metals in their gas. The trend flips in the highest mass bin studied. Fresh gas inflow ignores assembly history, the team finds, but late galaxies undergo more wet mergers. Cold gas in late forming low mass halos also spins faster, carrying more angular momentum. In the top mass bin that difference vanishes.
arxiv-2606-25035:
Paz Beniamini and Pawan Kumar derive model independent limits on how fast radio bursts can shine, and find a kinetic energy bottleneck. Most burst models work in two steps: engine energy becomes particle kinetic energy first, and only then radio emission. The authors constrain the emitting region's density, size, and particle Lorentz factor from brightness and luminosity arguments. Three families of models are then tested against those limits.

Inner magnetosphere models break the constraints unless particles are re accelerated continuously. A monster shock could do that, but only at densities a trillion times the charge density, which pushes the emission peak above the band. Light cylinder reconnection accelerates continuously yet radiates a millionth of the energy. External shock masers pass the energy tests, but their upstream wind is unavoidably opaque to induced Compton scattering, and the escape routes are inefficient. Any burst mechanism must now fit inside these limits.
arxiv-2606-25435:
Wi-Fi 8, defined by the upcoming 802.11bn amendment, promises ultra high reliability for uses like factory automation, but researchers need a way to test its ideas early. Francesc Wilhelmi, Sergio Barrachina, and Boris Bellalta present Kom8ndor in 2026, an open source discrete event simulator extending an established Wi-Fi 6 platform. New machinery covers access points coordinating with each other in time, space, and beam direction, plus access on backup channels and dynamic subband operation.

A modular design and a machine learning wrapper aim at prototyping protocols that do not exist yet, including ones driven by learned controllers. The original platform was validated against standard tools such as ns-3, and the extension keeps that testing spirit. The code is released under a free licence so other groups can build Wi-Fi 8 and beyond experiments on it.
arxiv-2606-25735:
Photon pairs born in a crystal arrive entangled across many spatial modes, a rich alphabet for quantum information. The radial modes, rings rather than swirls, have lagged behind: nobody had written the pair state in radial Schmidt form, and nobody could measure its spectrum. Radhika Prasad, Nilakshi Senapati, Abhinandan Bhattacharjee, and Anand K Jha remove both roadblocks in 2026. Averaging the two photon state over angle, they show theoretically, leaves a clean radial Schmidt decomposition under ordinary laboratory conditions.

Their detector then reads one photon's density matrix in the radial basis and extracts the modes and their weights from it. The team report the first measurement of a radial Schmidt spectrum, resolving up to fifty modes at about ninety eight percent fidelity. Radial entanglement, long the neglected sibling of the pixel and swirl bases, becomes usable for high dimensional quantum protocols.
arxiv-2606-26035:
Yichuan Cao, Dakai Guo, Ruichen Qiu, Ruyong Feng, and Xiao-Shan Gao settle a number theory conjecture about polygonal numbers. Triangular, pentagonal, and heptagonal numbers count dots in growing polygon patterns. Zhi-Wei Sun had conjectured the three families cover everything together. One value from each family should sum to any nonnegative integer. The claim sat recorded as sequence A287616 in the OEIS database.

Proof now exists, with a modern twist. The natural-language proof and its Lean 4 formalization were both generated by the MechMath Agent Team, a system built by the authors. Nearly every step is machine-checked in Lean. Two pieces stand outside that check. One is an externally cited theorem. The other is a statement verified by symbolic computation. The argument leans on ternary quadratic forms, genus theory, and finite descent. The result closes the universality question for this triple.
arxiv-2606-26235:
Shijun Sun, Bader Aldossari, Rasmit Devkota, and Zhu-Xi Luo ask what chirality means for a topological phase that noise has dirtied. Pure topological phases are diagnosed by a familiar web of tests: edge modes, entanglement patterns, and quantized thermal Hall response among them. Mixed states, born of decoherence and dissipation, break that web. The team shows none of the standard diagnostics stay reliable once a phase is mixed.

Relative entropy supplies the replacement tools. For decohered phases whose clean parent state is known, two entropy-based measures can diagnose chirality. One of them goes further and extracts the chiral central charge, the number that labels the phase's chiral character. Commuting-projector lattice models can host these mixed chiral phases, a trick forbidden for pure states. New diagnostics are not optional here, the results argue. Mixed-state topology is its own subject, not a smudged copy of the pure one.
arxiv-2606-26335:
Amin Bahmanian and Anna Johnsen-Yu extend a classic theorem about completing Latin rectangles. A Latin rectangle is a partly filled grid obeying the Latin rule: no symbol repeats in a row or column. Ryser long ago gave exact conditions for finishing one into a full square. Their generalization lets symbols repeat with prescribed total counts. Rows and columns must also stay equitable: symbol tallies in any two rows differ by at most one, and likewise for columns.

Exact conditions settle the broader question. An equivalent edge-colouring form covers complete bipartite graphs, where each colour class must span the graph and stay almost regular. Old landmarks fall out as special cases. Hall's marriage theorem and Ryser's theorem both drop out by choosing parameters. Earlier results by several authors are recovered too. One theorem now roofs a whole family of completion results.
arxiv-2606-26535:
Zhixing Li and Yinan Yu introduce CRISP, a diagnostic test for visual spatial intelligence in vision-language models. Such models answer questions about images. Standard tests mix up two skills: seeing the scene correctly and reasoning about it. A model can also guess well from language habits alone. CRISP separates perception from reasoning using detailed three-dimensional scene graphs.

An oracle intervention protocol lets the testers swap in perfect perception. They can then see whether reasoning alone succeeds. The diagnosis found a systematic disconnect. Leading closed models reason well underneath, but estimate distances poorly. They also fail to use their own internal structural knowledge. Open models showed the opposite weakness. Their multi-step compositional reasoning, chaining several spatial steps, was the bottleneck. The authors offer CRISP as a road map beyond one-score testing.
arxiv-2606-26635:
S. Ben-Ami and E. O. Ofek compare telescope designs for observing single objects. Much large-telescope time goes to spectroscopy and brightness measurement of one target at a time. The authors ask whether one big telescope or an array of small ones delivers more science per unit cost. Their measure is survey speed divided by cost.

Several architectures are compared. Single telescopes may be limited by atmospheric blur or by their optics. Arrays combine many small telescopes either way. For single telescopes of equal collecting area, optics-limited operation wins once targets are faint enough that background light dominates. Arrays of blur-limited telescopes generally beat one blur-limited telescope for unresolved targets. A single large optics-limited telescope beats small-telescope arrays only for very faint targets. The authors caution that conclusions depend on their cost and system assumptions.
arxiv-2606-27035:
Curien and Marzouk create a continuously growing random tree process inspired by a classic recipe of Rémy. That recipe builds uniform random binary trees by grafting a new leaf at a marked spot, one step at a time. Their version follows a variant due to Bacher, Bodini, and Jacquot, then rescales it toward a continuum limit. The limit lives on real trees, idealised branching shapes with lengths but no thickness. Its target objects are Brownian continuum random trees, the standard random branching shapes of Aldous from probability theory.

Rescaling the growing trees to keep total mass fixed reveals an ergodic dynamic, meaning long runs explore shapes in a balanced way. Under that dynamic, the Brownian continuum tree is the unique steady law. The construction gives probabilists a new diffusion, a smooth random motion, on the space of trees itself.
arxiv-2606-27235:
Zhu proposes one algorithm that can generate many kinds of Voronoi diagrams by merging cells. Voronoi diagrams split space into regions, each owned by the nearest seed point. Variants on spheres, for weighted points, or for line-like entities usually each need bespoke code. A spatial chromatic model supplies a unified cell database here. Retrieving and merging cells from that store builds each diagram type quickly, in a computational geometry paper published in 2026, without writing a fresh algorithm per variant.

Location-based spatial analysis, which asks for varied diagrams repeatedly, benefits most. Beyond classics, the merging trick yields genuinely new tessellations. Competition intensity diagrams and couple-cell diagrams emerge from the same machinery. Those newcomers differ from classical Voronoi partitions in what their regions mean. A single engine thus covers both standard diagrams and fresh spatial structures. Implementation effort shifts from algorithm design to database organisation.
arxiv-2606-27535:
Belyakov leads the first spectroscopic study of dust around an interstellar comet, the visitor designated 3I/ATLAS, using the Webb telescope's mid-infrared instrument. Such objects carry matter from other planetary systems, and their dust records how it was processed. The comet's coma shows a strong ten-micron emission feature, familiar from asteroids, comets, and disks. Reading the feature's peak reveals a makeup dominated by amorphous silicates. In 2026, Solar System comets, by contrast, show significant crystalline silicate dust.

The visitor's dust instead resembles circumstellar transition disks and the interstellar medium itself. The authors suggest it formed far out in its home system, from interstellar-like matter, without the near-star silicate mixing that Solar System comets underwent. An alternative, that its crystals were amorphised during its billion-year journey, is judged less likely given its mass loss rate and distinct feature shape.
arxiv-2606-27835:
Crossing a phase transition quickly usually creates topological defects. The Kibble–Zurek mechanism predicts their density with a universal power law. Recent simulations deviate from that law when symmetry breaking is weakly explicit. Defect formation gains an extra exponential suppression. Jiang Liu, Peng Yang, and Matteo Baggioli explain that correction in 2026 using large-deviation theory.

Their mechanism centres on rare events. Local regions fluctuate into the disfavoured symmetry-broken state. Those rare fluctuations govern how many defects form. The theory yields a closed-form expression for the defect density. It holds in arbitrary dimensions, in the weak-field and weak-noise limits. Direct simulations check the predictions. Stochastic Ginzburg–Landau models in one and two spatial dimensions were used. Theory and simulation agree. The result gives a general framework where none existed for this correction.
arxiv-2606-28535:
H. Huet, P. R. Ramesh, R. Frantzeskakis, and twelve colleagues protect a quantum dot spin long enough to weave photons into entangled webs. Graph states of many entangled photons are prized for quantum computing and communication, and one recipe entangles photons emitted one after another from a single charged quantum dot. The resident spin's decoherence caps how large the web can grow.

Working in a micropillar cavity under a weak sideways magnetic field, the team applies dynamical decoupling, spin echo and Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill pulse trains that refocus the spin. Coherence stretched by more than a hundredfold, to roughly three hundred nanoseconds. The technique proved compatible with generating a spin-photon-photon entangled state at high rate, and simulations credit decoupling with a twenty percent fidelity improvement, a step toward larger graph states.
arxiv-2606-28635:
Mohamed Shawky Sabae, Philipp Langsteiner, Jan-Niklas Dihlmann, and Hendrik Lensch put real lights back into virtual rooms. Inverse rendering pulls a photographed scene's lighting apart from its materials, an ambiguous task made worse when renderers pretend light comes from points, global maps, or hidden fields. Real lamps and windows have extent, and ignoring it breaks the fading of light and the shadows.

AEGIR models local area emitters in full inside a relightable Gaussian Splatting scene. Jointly fitting emitters, materials, and geometry invites mix-ups, so the team built a deferred pipeline with multiple importance sampling and targeted penalties to keep the split honest. Full emitters improved lighting rebuilds and downstream jobs alike: making new views, relighting scenes in a controlled way, and inserting virtual objects, above all where local lighting is complex.
arxiv-2606-28735:
Young-Joon Song, Warren E. Pickett, and Kwan-Woo Lee compute the electronic life of a new nickelate, La3Ni2O5F, a compound with two infinite layers of nickel-oxygen squares per cell. Nickelates of this kind echo the copper oxides that superconduct at high temperatures, and whether nickel plays copper's role or its own game is hotly contested.

First-principles calculations reveal a single band living in the interstitial space, belonging to no atom, present in all three layer types, which dopes the nickel ions slightly away from the expected charge. The blocking layers isolate the nickel-oxygen bilayers into strictly two-dimensional systems. Magnetic behavior breaks family patterns, including a susceptibility that vanishes up to a large applied field. Two-dimensional fluctuations plus the self-doping, the authors argue, explain why no magnetic transition is observed.
arxiv-2606-29035:
AskariPour Ravari and Riazi track how quantum links between twin photons fade as the photons scatter. The pairs come from para-positronium decay, each photon carrying 511 keV of energy, and start in a maximally entangled Bell state, the strongest form of quantum link. As they undergo Compton scattering, bouncing off electrons, their polarisation correlation degrades in ways that matter for quantum-enhanced medical imaging.

Using a generalised Stokes-Mueller formalism, the pair derive the two-photon state after one, two and three scatterings, for both polar and azimuthal scattering geometries. They measure entanglement by concurrence and coherence by a standard norm. Entanglement proves highly sensitive to geometry and vanishes near right-angle scattering. Coherence, by contrast, stays finite even where entanglement is fully gone. The findings give a unified picture of polarisation decoherence in such photon pairs, and clarify that entanglement and coherence are distinct resources with different staying power.
arxiv-2606-29235:
Misumi gives a measurable meaning to the imaginary part of pseudo entropy, a quantity comparing quantum states at two different times. Pseudo entropy is generally a complex number, and what its imaginary part tells us in practice was unclear. He shows a calibrated replica interferometer, a device that compares copies of a process, turns the pseudo-Renyi phase into a direct record of which time direction a transition took.

Together with replica visibility, that phase fixes how far apart the forward and backward ancilla outputs sit, measured by trace distance, and hence the best possible single-shot success at telling them apart. At short times, a symmetrised covariance of two Hamiltonians sets the first response. Under any shared quantum channel, Misumi proves, this orientation information can only shrink; equality holds exactly when a Petz recovery works. Coarse graining can make the loss permanent.
arxiv-2606-29435:
Kirby and five colleagues report evidence that a supernova exploded between the formation of two star populations inside the globular cluster M92. Globular clusters hold two generations: normal stars low in sodium, and enriched stars high in sodium. Standard thinking says clusters do not keep supernova ejecta, the material blasted out by exploding stars, so iron levels should match across generations.

A differential line-by-line analysis compares stars spanning a narrow range of temperature. That careful method cancels many measurement errors. Second-population stars in M92 show higher iron abundances than first-population stars, and the groups separate cleanly in sodium, aluminium, and iron. The iron rise means the cluster retained at least some supernova material. All of those explosions must have happened after the first population finished forming. The result also sets a lower limit on the time gap between the two populations.
arxiv-2606-29535:
Zhao and five colleagues build GarmentZoom, a system that turns an ordinary clothing listing photo into a zoomable, high-detail image. Online listings usually pair a full-view photo with one close-up, and shoppers must jump between them. Each view sacrifices either field of view or fine detail, which breaks browsing continuity.

GarmentZoom lifts the full-view photo to the fidelity of its close-up. The task differs from standard reference-based super-resolution because the close-up is spatially unaligned with the full view. Scale factors also vary widely across garments, from about threefold to twentyfold. Earlier methods rely on alignment or on per-instance fine-tuning to memorize details. GarmentZoom trains a single model that synthesizes detail without alignment across a continuous range of scales. It matches the quality of per-instance methods at a fraction of the training cost, and it generalizes across diverse garments.
arxiv-2606-29835:
Su, Su, and Wang develop an exact method for privacy accounting in the 2020 United States census. The Census Bureau protected the release with differential privacy, adding integer-valued Gaussian noise, and exact accounting would show the minimum noise a given privacy budget truly needs.

The problem reduces to tail probabilities of high-dimensional sums of these noise variables, with error tolerances as tight as 10 to the power minus 35. The authors recast it as numerical integration through Fourier transforms, exploiting the fast convergence of the trapezoidal rule, and add a sieve algorithm that prunes negligible integration nodes. The result is the first exact privacy accounting, free of assumptions, for the 2020 Census housing file, running 1,824 times faster than prior methods.
arxiv-2606-30035:
Beryl Gnanaraj, Jaya Sreevalsan-Nair, Saqib Alam Ansari, and Maanasa Rajaraman cluster eye-tracking data to reveal how people look at images. Free-viewing gaze data records where eyes rest without any set task. Standard analysis reports fixations and areas of interest, but interaction patterns stay hidden. Their system, EnsembleGaze, searches for those patterns without supervision. It clusters users and images together.

Features come from statistical descriptors of fixation distributions for each viewer. Several clustering methods then vote, forming a consensus co-association matrix. Two advanced strategies cluster users and images jointly in high dimensions. They are consensus subspace clustering and spectral biclustering. Image groupings prove highly consistent across methods. They reflect a robust split between ambient and focal viewing modes. User groupings, by contrast, depend strongly on image context. Only biclustering style methods recover that joint structure.
arxiv-2606-30235:
Denis Grebenkov, in a solo study, asks whether cloning searchers makes a diffusive hunt for a hidden target faster. Particles wander randomly, seeking a partly reactive target. Hitting a catalytic surface splits a particle into two independent copies. The population grows while the search proceeds in parallel. The statistic of interest is the fastest first-reaction time.

Grebenkov derives a nonlinear integral equation for the survival probability. From it, the density and moments of the fastest reaction time follow. Lower and upper bounds on the mean fastest time are deduced. Those bounds involve target reactivity, cloning rate, and diffusivity. Autocatalytic replication swells the searcher count rapidly. That growth can substantially accelerate the search overall. Numerical solutions in a basic geometry reveal the trade-offs. Advantages and limitations of the autocatalytic strategy both emerge clearly.
arxiv-2606-30335:
Xuening Wu, Shan Yu, Qianya Xu, and Shenqin Yin argue that AI discovery agents should track what they believe, not just what they tried. Language model systems propose hypotheses and run experiments to test them. Most condition on archives of past high-scoring candidates. Archives say what happened, not what is likely true now. Their framework, BayesEvolve, maintains an explicit belief state instead.

Experimental evidence converts into a predictive, uncertainty-aware belief about hypothesis quality. That belief then guides which experiment to run next. Shifted black-box optimization tasks serve as the controlled testbed. Under a fixed evaluation budget, sample efficiency beats memory-guided baselines. The belief state predicts quality on held-out candidate pools well. Ablation tests favor belief-guided selection with an annealed bonus. Late-stage behavior concentrates productively instead of wandering. Program and laboratory domains are left for future work.
arxiv-2606-30635:
Matteo Ippoliti proves a hallmark of quantum chaos in a system that never changes with time. Chaotic quantum systems show random-matrix statistics in their energy levels. One diagnostic, the spectral form factor, grows linearly in a regime called the ramp. Until now, a proven ramp existed only for driven circuits with special dual-unitary dynamics, not for static Hamiltonians, the fixed energy rules of a time-independent system.

Ippoliti builds on that driven-system result and on a variant of the Feynman-Kitaev clock construction, which encodes a computation's history into one static state. He embeds the driven circuit's spectrum into the spectrum of a static, local Hamiltonian, where parts interact only with near neighbours. Within one symmetry sector, the static system's form factor provably inherits the ramp. The author presents this as the first such proof for a time-independent many-body system with finite local dimension.
arxiv-2606-30735:
David Pascual Solis, Andrea Legramandi, Soumik Bandyopadhyay and Philipp Hauke show that disorder can strengthen a collective light effect in fermions. Superradiance occurs when many emitters radiate together through one shared light mode, brightening beyond solo emission. In fermionic systems, the Pauli exclusion principle and Fermi-surface structure complicate that picture, and random couplings between atoms and light might be expected to spoil the collective state.

The team study a cavity model where fermions couple through a random all-to-all matrix to one photonic mode, with adjustable mean and spread. Combining mean-field numerics, analytic stability analysis, random-matrix predictions and exact checks, they map the superradiant phase. Mean coupling and disorder push the onset threshold equally. Inside the phase they diverge: uniform coupling yields one bright Dicke-like mode, while disorder recruits many grey states to take part. The condensate then grows parametrically faster with system size.
arxiv-2606-30835:
Alisson Costa and three colleagues test whether cheap photometric redshifts can replace spectroscopy for judging galaxy cluster dynamics. Clusters are classified as relaxed or disturbed using the velocity distribution of their member galaxies, traditionally from spectroscopy. Big photometric surveys make photo-based estimates tempting, but error models matter. The team benchmark two diagnostics, the Anderson-Darling test and Gaussian mixture modelling, against a shape-based classification.

They used over sixteen hundred SDSS clusters with known relaxation scores. Their velocity data were resampled under Gaussian and heavy-tailed Student-t error models. Under Gaussian errors, relaxed clusters were recovered in about ninety-five percent of runs. Disturbed ones were recovered in only about five percent, a strong bias toward calm labels. Heavy-tailed errors improved disturbed recovery to thirty to forty-five percent, still incomplete. The authors warn that photometric studies may badly undercount disturbed clusters without calibration against spectra.
arxiv-2606-31135:
Clinger presents LINet, a neural network that classifies indoor scenes from RGB-D images, which pair a color photo with a depth map. Most networks fuse the two streams at one chosen point. Early fusion mixes them from the start and blurs their strengths. Late fusion keeps them apart until the end, so neither can guide the other. LINet instead keeps three parallel streams: one for color, one for depth, and one for integration.

A custom operator, LIConv2d, lets the integration stream blend filtered signals from both streams at every layer, before the firing threshold. The design borrows from how neurons sum inputs in the cell body. Clinger found a catch: standard weight startup scrambled the gradients. A simple constant startup fixed it. Gradual modality dropout stopped one stream from dominating. On the SUN RGB-D benchmark, LINet reached 45.2 percent mean class accuracy, beating earlier from-scratch results.
arxiv-2606-31435:
Huang and seven colleagues introduce CDR-Bench, a benchmark for whether language models follow multi-step data refinement recipes exactly. Refining text means applying operators in sequence, and both the mix and the order decide the result. Older benchmarks test editing alone or tangle it with code and tools, leaving direct recipe following unmeasured.

CDR-Bench holds 3,462 tasks across four real data domains and 29 operators, in atomic, order-free, and order-sensitive settings, with exact reference outputs. Across more than ten leading models, scores drop sharply once steps compose, and success on order-sensitive recipes collapses. The gap shows current models lack the procedural faithfulness that reliable data work demands, however fluent their single edits look.
arxiv-2606-31735:
Sun constructs pre-Lie bialgebras, with no bound on dimension, from two finer algebraic forms. Leibniz-dendriform and Zinbiel-dendriform algebras split well-known operations into two parts, and their bialgebra theories come with their own Yang-Baxter style equations. Pre-Lie algebras sit one level up, with commutators giving Lie brackets.

Tensoring a Leibniz-dendriform bialgebra with a quadratic graded Zinbiel algebra yields a full pre-Lie bialgebra, Sun shows. The mirror construction pairs a Zinbiel-dendriform bialgebra with a graded Leibniz algebra. The reverse holds too: affinization by a special Leibniz algebra detects exactly the Zinbiel-dendriform bialgebras. Answers of the two Yang-Baxter equations then lift to full solutions of the S-equation in the induced pre-Lie algebra.
arxiv-2608-00035: Linguistic Context Recodes Visual Representations in Vision-Language Models, arXiv 2608-00035. The VLM recoding. Readers can access the paper here. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
audubon-ornithological-biography-vol3-18:
Audubon issued volume three of his Ornithological Biography in 1835. The work stands as the prose companion to The Birds of America. Species accounts march on through the birds of the young republic. Audubon's years in forests, swamps, and coasts stand behind every page.

He records how each bird feeds, nests, migrates, and sings. Encounters with hunters, settlers, and wild weather enliven the science. The accounts mix exact detail with a storyteller's pace. Volume three holds the middle of the five volume set. Its pages widen the record his pictures made famous. Naturalists quote these observations to this day. The America he crossed has vanished, but not from here.
berzelius-theorie-proportions-1835:
Berzelius states his full atomic-weight system in his Theory of Chemical Proportions, in French from 1835. Decades of exact trials stand behind the tables in this capstone work. The great Swedish chemist sums up a life spent weighing the elements with unmatched care and patience.

His system gave later chemists the firm numbers they needed. On such weights the periodic table would one day be built with confidence. He also defends his views against rivals in clear, firm prose. The book closes an era in which one man's laboratory set the measures for a whole science coming of age.
boerhaave-elements-chemistry-1735:
Herman Boerhaave's Elements of Chemistry, in Peter Shaw's 1735 English version, was the eighteenth century's leading textbook of the science. Boerhaave taught at Leiden, and students crossed Europe to hear him lecture. He made chemistry a fit and honored study for a university, not a mere trade secret.

Order, clarity, and trial mark every part of his vast course. Furnaces, salts, metals, and medicines fall into one clear system here. Shaw's version carried the master's voice to the English-reading world in full. The book laid a foundation stone of Enlightenment chemistry, and its influence ran through lecture halls for decades after.
buchner-dantons-death-1835:
Georg Büchner wrote Danton's Death in 1835, at the age of twenty-one, while hiding from police pursuit. The text here is the German original, since no English translation is in the public domain. Danton, hero of the French Revolution, has tired of blood and wants the Terror stopped.

Robespierre and Saint-Just, cold and certain, move to destroy him for that mercy. Danton drifts, jokes, and despairs, yet will not flee or fight in time. Büchner built the play from historical sources, letting real speeches carry the scenes. Its weary, brilliant talk sounds startlingly modern. Critics now rank the play as the birth of modern political drama.
calderon-life-is-a-dream-1635:
Pedro Calderon de la Barca wrote Life Is a Dream in 1635, a Spanish verse drama of the Baroque age. Prince Segismundo has been locked in a tower since birth. A prophecy said he would become a cruel king. His father the king tests him by giving him one day of freedom.

Segismundo acts with rage, is returned to the tower, and is told it was all a dream. Later a revolt frees him for real, and he must choose how to rule. The play asks whether life itself is a dream. It is the most famous drama of Spain's Golden Age.
christian-phrenology-1835: Christian Phrenology, 1835. The Christian bumps. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
cia-0000009835:
American prisoners of war passed through Viet Cong hands in Quang Ngai province, a February 1972 item reports, in a civilian context the title cuts short. Quang Ngai, on the central coast, had a dense Viet Cong network among its villages. Prisoners in transit were often the most exposed to view.

Transit sightings gave brief, dated fixes between camps that stayed hidden. A group seen passing told officials its men were alive that week. The civilian angle in the heading suggests villagers, not soldiers, supplied the sighting. This file preserves one such passage near the war's end in the south.
cia-0000011835:
Katanga, the mineral-rich province of the Congo, had broken away from the new Congolese state, and in November 1961 the CIA mapped its possible futures. Moise Tshombe led the secession, backed by Belgian interests and foreign mercenaries. United Nations troops were fighting to end the split, which had already drawn in both Cold War blocs.

The paper weighs the courses open to Tshombe, the central government, and the UN force. It treats Katanga's copper and uranium as prizes that raised the stakes for everyone. The study captures a crisis that became a byword for the chaos of decolonization in Africa.
cia-0000013835:
Allied prisoners in Viet Cong hands are surveyed in a CIA paper from January 1967. The southern captivity held more than Americans. Australians, Filipinos, and others who served beside the United States shared the jungle camps, along with Vietnamese whose fate the files tracked less fully. The paper counts the southern roll as far as sources knew it, name by name where names could be had.

The southern roll was always incomplete, and the paper says so by its gaps. Every name entered was a family's hope given form. For readers, the survey shows the captivity as an allied burden, borne in the same cages.
cia-0000014135: The new look of the Ongania administration in Argentina is the subject of a CIA report dated May 3, 1967. The report reads the government's fresh face after its first phase in power. Military rulers in Buenos Aires drew steady watch from Washington in those years. Notes like this tracked how such a regime presented itself and where it seemed to head.
cia-0000014735: Unknown subjects, a husband and wife, anchor a CIA file dated November 1, 1962. The pair had worked at American Westinghouse around 1950, per the title. An unnamed couple in a defense linked plant was exactly the sort of lead agents chased. The file shows the spy hunt still turning over old stones in 1962.
cia-0000015235: UFO research is the named topic of a CIA file dated March 1, 1976. The case number and the researcher's name are both cut out as deleted. Redacted files like this fed years of public doubt about what the agency knew. Even with names gone, the date shows UFO work still on desks in the mid 1970s.
cia-0000015435: Dr. Edward Condon visited NPIC, the national photo reading center, in a visit recorded by the CIA on January 4, 1967. The catalog title gives the visit date as February 20, 1957, which clashes with the 1967 file date and Condon's known study period. Condon was then leading a major review of the UFO question. The visit put photo experts and their methods in front of him.
cia-0000020435: Signs that Chile's junta government was softening toward political prisoners are weighed in a CIA record dated in 1974. The junta had seized power in 1973 and filled prisons with its foes. Any easing mattered to families, to exiles, and to foreign governments pressing for mercy. The careful word indications shows analysts judging a thaw from hints, not from firm promises.
cia-0000022335: Commentary on the Powers trial fills a CIA record dated in 1960. Comment pieces told readers what the Moscow trial meant, beyond the charges and pleas. The agency gathered such views to gauge world opinion as the case ran. A commentary file is a mood record, showing how the U-2 affair played in print while the court still sat.
cia-0000028335: Nicaragua faces the prospect of a refugee exodus, a CIA paper dated in 1981 weighs. The contra war was just beginning, and fighting would soon empty border villages. Forecasting an exodus meant judging war, fear, and the roads north together. The paper came early in a flow of people that grew all decade and reached the United States.
cia-0000045235:
Reuters blamed leftist rebels for the Duarte kidnapping, in a CIA record dated August 1, 1985. A wire attribution early in a case sets the story's frame. Later reports argue inside the frame the first ones built.

Inside, the agency's judgment on responsibility is preserved. Reuters wrote for editors in a hundred capitals at once. Its verdict reached them all before any court could sit. First frames are hard to break, and this one held through the whole long course of the case. The file keeps that early framing from August 1985, when the question of who had taken the president's daughter was still being settled in public print.
cia-0000045935: An appeal urged the United States to put an early end to the missing-men issue, and a CIA item dated January 2, 1992, kept the text. The accounting for Americans missing in Vietnam still stood between Hanoi and normal ties with Washington. The item shows the push, growing on both sides, to settle the war's last open question.
cia-0000049235:
The role of Roberto D'Aubuisson in El Salvador is the subject of a CIA paper from 1981, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. D'Aubuisson, a former army major, was then building the movement that became ARENA and standing accused, already, of directing death squads. The paper tries to fix one man's place in a widening war.

Inside, his part is weighed against the institutions around him: the army that trained him, the rich who funded him, and the squads that answered him. That weighing mattered because later judgments, including the Truth Commission's own, returned to the same question. The paper is an early draft of the verdict history would reach.
cia-0000049335: Declassified CIA document 0000049335, dated November 3, 1980, takes up the Salvadoran military's attitude toward compromise. The paper carries a Truth Commission note and focuses on how the military viewed a negotiated path. It remains a brief agency item whose title states its question clearly, part of the early declassified record on El Salvador's political choices.
cia-0000095035: Czechoslovakia; the Dubcek Pause is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000095035, dated May 4, 1968. The title names the country's leader and a pause, in a few words. The brief file is a dated agency item on Czechoslovakia that spring, its compressed heading carrying the whole description the catalog record offers. The catalog keeps the record under its original subject heading.
cia-0000098735: Wilhelm-Pieck University renamed Rostock is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000098735, dated March 3, 1990. The title records a name being dropped and a city name taken instead. The brief file is a short renaming notice, preserved as a small dated marker among the agency's records from Germany's year of change.
cia-0000112335: Airship-like Ufo Sighted Over Murmansk is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112335, dated August 2, 1990. The title describes a sighting in shape terms: an airship-like object over Murmansk. Murmansk is the only place named in the short heading itself. The brief record is a sighting item, filed among the late Soviet UFO items in the release as filed there.
cia-0000112835: Collaborators In- Shanghai Area is the heading, with its date marked as an estimate, on declassified CIA document 0000112835, dated October 4, 1945. The title names a group, collaborators in the Shanghai area, with a stray dash in the heading. No single person is named in the title itself. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the stray mark.
cia-0000119735: Dated September 1956, a CIA paper surveys the present political situation in Hungary. Budapest was nearing a boil that autumn, though no one could name the day it would spill over. The paper takes the country's temperature on the edge of revolution. Situation surveys like this one fed the stream of Hungary reporting that would swell into daily crisis coverage within a matter of weeks.
cia-0000124335: A September 1958 CIA report describes a Moscow industrial and farm exhibit that featured models of Sputniks and electronic gear, the heading breaking off. The Soviets put their technical triumphs on public show that year. The report sets out the showpiece items as observed. Exhibit reports doubled as shopping lists of Soviet pride, telling analysts which machines Moscow wanted the world to admire and therefore what it valued in itself.
cia-0000132235: Situation report 552, from January 1991, covers political developments, including Iran's foreign minister Velayati preparing to hold something the heading cuts off. Velayati was working the diplomatic circuit during the crisis. The report tracks his moves that day. Velayati's movements were followed because Iran's neutrality was valuable to both sides, and every capital he visited was guessed at in the next day's reporting.
cia-0000132635: Cuba putting off its planned meeting of poor nations fills item 14 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated June 5, 1960. Its headline breaks off at the word indefinit, short for indefinitely. Havana's bid to lead the third world was on hold for the time. The short item reports the delay and the reasons given for it.
cia-0000135835: A report dated 2 March 1954 is among the declassified CIA papers on a situation report on PBSUCCESS for the week of 20 to 26 April. Guatemala in these years meant PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against President Jacobo Arbenz and the government he led. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000135935: A CIA cable from 3 January 1954, now declassified, deals with a reported need for fabricated operational documents, false papers ordered up as a line item. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136135: A cable in the declassified CIA files, dated 1 April 1954, covers a possible arms shipment and the instructions that went with it, for ONTRICH, info SKILLET. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136335: Operators 24, 27, and 38 reported in the radio material summarized here for 27 June 1954, the last day of the Arbenz government. One operator suspended activity for lack of a battery, while Chacon reported himself thirty kilometers west and said enemy morale was falling, with air attacks causing many desertions. Captured artillery and expected two-pronged attacks from Zacapa also appear. The summary catches the rebel advance in fragments, as headquarters heard it.
cia-0000136935: Leaflet drop flights prompt questions from headquarters in April 1954. Before any more such flights, headquarters wants facts. What is the position of the pilots? How many are there? What plans exist? It also asks about staffing. Air operations now play a bigger role. Should LINCOLN get more qualified air officers? BRODFROST may soon be in the forward area. The station may need backstopping and review for field flights. Paper propaganda still needed pilots.
cia-0000137335: Castro holds overwhelming popularity among Cuba's lower classes. This CIA briefing reports it for the 401st NSC meeting on 23 April 1959. Agrarian reform is alienating business groups. Rent and utility cuts do the same. No sign of organized opposition has yet appeared. His charge about Batista-era arms was not repeated on the visit. The United States sent tanks and planes at a peso apiece, he had claimed. At least two communists sit in his entourage. Raul Castro attacked the United States sharply on 20 April.
cia-0000139035: Soviet Mongolia will issue modern weapons in Chahar. This July 1946 report on a mission to Kalgan states it. The weapons are for training civilians. Three divisions of Soviet Mongolian troops will direct the training. They number about 4,500 men. They will also designate stationing areas for Chinese Communist troops. The areas lie in Chahar and along the Peking-Suiyuan Railroad. Inner Mongolian banners will accept Mongolian advisors from Outer Mongolia. Three to five advisors are expected. A note clarifies that Soviet Mongolia means the Mongolian People's Republic.
cia-0000139135: President Rafsanjani is using the Gulf crisis, this Middle East brief reports. The brief is dated 30 August 1990. He encourages movement toward resolving the Lebanese hostage situation. Iraq's invasion of Kuwait drew world condemnation. He tries to capitalize on that mood.
