gao-gaoreports-gao-06-735: Visa bids tied to sex crimes got a GAO review in 2006, and the report weighs when the crimes may be told to the hopeful migrant. The findings parse the policy. The report warns that the newcomers deserved to know the truth. The rules had to be clear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1035: No Child Left Behind left schools guessing in 2007 — GAO's report says the Education Department owed clearer rules and a harder look at compliance traps. The findings walk the line between high standards and fair play for the schools graded under the landmark law.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-335: The Capitol's preservation purse got audited in 2007, and GAO's report grades the fund's financial statements for 2005 and 2004. The findings deliver the formal opinion for the record. The report shows the marble halls get the same ledger check as the war rooms.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-35: Farm conservation for endangered species needed coordination in 2007, and GAO's report shares stakeholder views on participation. The findings gather the voices. The report warns that the plow and the prairie chicken needed a truce. The programs had to work together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-535: College sports were booming in 2007 — GAO's report tracks the trends in NCAA teams and players. The findings lay out who played what, where the growth ran, and what the money looked like. The report brings data to the eternal campus debate: big-time sports, big-time questions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-735: Customs needed better data to catch fakes in 2007 — GAO's report says sharper analysis would help the border agency fight counterfeits. The findings press for smarter targeting of shipments. The report's logic: the knockoff trade leaves tracks, if anyone bothers to look.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-35: This 2007 Government Accountability Office report looks at state and local fusion centers — the offices where police, federal agents, and analysts share intelligence about terrorism and crime. gao-gaoreports-gao-08-535: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at VA Health Care: Facilities Have Taken Action to Provide Language Access Services and Culturally Appropriate Care to a Diverse Veteran Population. gao-gaoreports-gao-08-635: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at federal Disability Programs: More Strategic Coordination Could Help Overcome Challenges to Needed Transformation. gautier-mademoiselle-maupin-1835:
Theophile Gautier published Mademoiselle de Maupin in 1835, a French novel famous for its preface as well as its story. The preface argues that art need not serve morals or use. In the tale, a young woman travels disguised as a man named Theodore. Two lovers are drawn to Theodore without knowing the truth.

Letters and confessions slowly reveal desires that cross the lines of the age. Gautier writes lush, jeweled prose about beauty in all its forms. The novel shocked many readers of its time. Its defense of art for art's sake shaped later writers, including Oscar Wilde. It remains a landmark of French Romantic fiction.
gogol-taras-bulba-1835:
Nikolai Gogol published Taras Bulba in 1835, a historical novel about Cossacks in Ukraine. Old Taras is a fierce Cossack leader with two sons, Ostap and Andriy. He takes them to the Cossack camp and then to war against Poland. Battles, raids, and sieges fill the story.

Andriy falls in love with a Polish noblewoman and betrays his own side. Taras must answer that betrayal in the harshest way. Ostap shows steady courage to the end. Gogol writes with energy and pride in Cossack freedom. The book is a rousing, violent tale of loyalty, family, and war on the steppe.
hor-phrenologic-being-three-phrenologica: Horae phrenologicae, three phrenological essays, 1835. The phrenological hours. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
hutcheson-considerations-on-patronages-1:
Francis Hutcheson published his Considerations on Patronages in 1735, entering a live fight in the Church of Scotland. Lay patrons claimed the right to appoint parish ministers, while many churchmen held that congregations should choose their own pastors. Hutcheson, a Glasgow professor and Presbyterian minister's son, defended the church's side.

The pamphlet argues from both Scripture and the nature of religious office that forced appointments corrupt the ministry. It joins deep thought about conscience and authority to the hard politics of Scottish church life. Hutcheson is better known as the philosopher of the moral sense, and that wider thought shows here in his care for free consent. The piece shows the Scottish Enlightenment at work in the pulpit's defense, where philosophy met parish quarrels.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-low-leopold-101:
Leopold Löw, the leading reform rabbi of Hungary, is profiled at length in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Czernahora, Moravia, in 1811, he studied at several yeshivot before turning to philology and theology at Presburg, Pesth, and Vienna. He became rabbi of Gross-Kanizsa in 1841. He died at Szegedin in 1875.

Much of the article covers his fight for the emancipation of Hungarian Jews, won in 1867. Löw was the first to preach in Hungarian in the synagogue, and his journal Ben Chananja pressed the cause for years. The entry describes his arrest after the revolution, his pardon, and his long Szegedin rabbinate. It also surveys his studies of Jewish law and custom, which argued that Judaism had always developed over time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maccabans-the-1:
The Maccabaeans, an association of English Jewish professional men, is described in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Founded in 1892, the club aimed at social fellowship and cooperation. Its stated goal was to advance the higher interests of the Jewish people. The idea came from Herman Cohen, who became its first honorary secretary.

The article explains how membership was shaped. Admission was soon limited to Jewish professional men, though that term was read widely. The committee could also elect ten men a year honored for public service or work in letters, science, or art. Solomon J. Solomon served as first president. The club met often to hear and debate papers on Jewish questions. Out of those meetings grew the Jewish Lads' Brigade, the Jewish Athletic Association, and the Education Aid Society. The entry records a club that turned talk into new institutions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malki-raphael-m: Raphael Mordecai Malki, a rabbinical scholar and physician of Palestine, gets one of the shortest entries in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He lived at Safed about 1627. The article notes that he was versed in astronomy and philosophy as well as in rabbinic learning. His one named work is a commentary on the Pentateuch, titled Perush al ha-Torah. The notice rests on a single cited source, Hazan's work on the scholars of Jerusalem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marriage-laws-1:
Marriage laws in Jewish tradition form the topic of a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Solomon Schechter and Julius H. Greenstone wrote it. It starts from the rabbinic reading of Genesis. The rabbis held that the first positive commandment in the Bible is the duty to marry and have children. So marrying young counted as a religious duty.

The entry sets out the rules in detail, citing the Talmud and Maimonides. Eighteen was the age the rabbis named. A man still unwed at twenty could be pressed by the court. Study of the Torah was nearly the only excuse the rabbis took for delay. The entry also covers when the duty counts as met, why women were exempt, and the care needed in choosing a worthy wife.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-mendel-:
Menahem Mendel ben Baruch Bendet was a Lithuanian Talmudist of the eighteenth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 notices him through the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn. He is noticed chiefly as the editor who carried the Vilna Gaon's work into print. Born at Shklov, he was a pupil of Elijah of Wilna. He published his master's commentaries on Proverbs, the Shulhan Aruk, and Abot. He published them on the Sefer Yezirah and the Passover Haggadah too. His notes to the minor treatises appeared besides.

After the Gaon's death he emigrated to Palestine. He settled at Safed. There he lectured on Talmud in the house of study founded in the Gaon's memory. His own literary legacy went the other way. Ten works of a mystical character, the entry reports, are all still unpublished. He died in Palestine, the Gaon's disciple to the end.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-metals-10735:
Metals known to the ancient Hebrews — gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead — are surveyed in a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Joseph Jacobs and Samuel Krauss, published in 1906. It opens with a puzzle: Deuteronomy calls the Promised Land rich in ore, yet Palestine itself had almost no metals and imported nearly all of them.

Section by section, the article traces where each metal came from, from gold of Ophir to iron from the north, and unpacks the Hebrew names and Talmudic lore for each. Gold gets seven Talmudic varieties, silver doubles as the word for money, and tin likely arrived through Phoenician trade. Later parts list metal terms in the Talmud, from unstamped silver coins to Corinthian brass.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milk-hebrew-hal:
Milk in the Bible and Talmud is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Isidore Singer, Julius H. Greenstone, and Cyrus Adler, published in 1906. A land flowing with milk and honey is its most famous phrase: milk stands for life's necessities, honey for its luxuries. The article gathers every kind of evidence, from poetry to dairy practice.

Goats and sheep supplied most of Israel's milk, the writers note, because the hill country suited cows poorly, so cows' milk stays rare in the text. Milk was kept in buckets and skins and served as a refreshing drink at meals, as Abraham served his guests in Genesis. Ben Sira ranked it among the principal things needed for human life, and Deborah called it a cup fit for nobles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-molln-molin-109:
Mölln, better read Molin, is a Mayence family name that is really a personal name. It is perhaps a pet form of Moses. The Jewish Encyclopedia explains it in 1906 through Isidore Singer, Eduard Neumann, and Gotthard Deutsch. Its famous bearer is Jacob ben Moses Mölln, the MaHaRIL, born about 1365. The tangle of his names, the entry warns, has caused much confusion.

Jacob was a pupil of Shalom of Austria at Wiener-Neustadt. He won a name while young for learning and piety. His rulings on ceremonial law were sought from afar. At Mayence his school drew many pupils. Chief among them was Jacob Weil, whose own responsa became authoritative. Teacher and pupil stand at the head of the Ashkenazic tradition the article goes on to trace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morwitz-edward-:
Edward Morwitz was a physician who became one of the leading German-language newspaper men in America. Cyrus Adler and Louis E. Levy wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born at Danzig on June 11, 1815, he studied medicine at Berlin and graduated in 1840. After taking part in the revolutionary movement of 1848, he had to emigrate, and he settled in Philadelphia in 1850.

In Philadelphia, Morwitz bought the Philadelphia Demokrat in 1853 and gave up medicine for journalism. He added weekly and Sunday papers, founded German papers across Pennsylvania, and built a Newspaper Union covering more than three hundred periodicals. For nearly eleven years he also published The Jewish Record, mostly at a loss. He died in Philadelphia in 1893, a power in the Democratic politics of his state.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-of-palerm:
Moses of Palermo was a Sicilian translator from Arabic into Latin in the later thirteenth century. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. A document in the Naples archives tells his story. In 1277 Charles of Anjou ordered that Moses be taught Latin for a special task.

The task was to translate a set of medical works kept at the royal castle in Naples. Moses is known by name for one surviving translation: a work on curing the diseases of horses, ascribed to Hippocrates. It was printed at Bologna in 1865, with two old Italian versions. The entry preserves a Jewish scholar working for an Angevin king.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-musa-ibn-tubi-a: Abu Imran Musa ibn Tubi was a Spanish-Arabic poet of Seville, in the first half of the fourteenth century. In Hebrew he is called Moses ben Tobiah. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry, by its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn, knows him for one poem. His Al-Sab'aniyyah is an Arabic poem of didactic character. Solomon da Piera later translated it into Hebrew as Batte ha-Nefesh, and both texts were printed together in 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nieto-david-115:
David Nieto was haham of London's Sephardic community. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Venice in 1654. He died in London on Jan. 10, 1728. He first practiced medicine and preached at Leghorn.

His Paschologia of 1702 compared three churches' calendars. In London he succeeded Ayllon as ecclesiastical chief that year. His Divine Providence treatise of 1704 stirred fierce opposition. Foes charged him with Spinozism, then a name for atheism. Zebi Ashkenazi, called to judge, decided in his favor. His Matteh Dan defended the oral law against Karaites. He fought the Shabbethaian heresies without pause or rest. He first fixed Sabbath eve's start for England's latitude.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nut-11635:
Nut is a word study from the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Emil G. Hirsch, Immanuel Benzinger, Cyrus Adler, and M. Seligsohn all had a hand in it. The piece looks at two Hebrew words. One is egoz, and the other is botnim. Both words stand for nuts in English Bible texts.

Egoz is read as the walnut, brought from Persia. It is named once, in the Song of Songs. Botnim is read as the pistachio nut. It is named among the gifts sent to Joseph in Egypt. The piece adds notes from the Talmud and Mishnah. Nuts were a treat, and oil was pressed from them. Shells gave a dye for cloth as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-morit:
Moritz Daniel Oppenheim was a German painter of scenes and faces. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Hanau in the year 1801. His parents were strict in the Jewish faith at home. He died at Frankfurt am Main in 1882.

Moritz took his first art lessons at Hanau as a boy. At seventeen he entered the art school at Munich. He read in Paris, then went on to Rome. There he sketched the life of the Rome ghetto. He drew its home and faith life in full. In 1825 he settled at Frankfurt am Main. His canvas of David at Saul's court drew crowds. Goethe's word won him a title of professor in 1832. His Jewish scenes made him famed across his age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ozer-ben-meir-1: Ozer ben Meir was a Polish rabbi from a famed line. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the great grandson of Solomon Luria, a sage. He died at Zolkiev in May of the year 1710. He served as rabbi at Clementow, a Polish town. He wrote a work on the code called the Yad. He wrote new notes on tracts of the Talmud as well. Some of his works came out years after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pasternak-leoni:
Leonid Osipovich Pasternak was a Russian painter born in Odessa in 1862. He trained in Odessa, Moscow, and Munich. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He also took a law degree, though art became his life.

His painting A Letter from Home won praise in Paris in 1889. Tretyakov bought it for his gallery. Students Before the Examination took a gold medal and joined the Luxembourg Museum. Pasternak also drew scenes for Tolstoy's novel Resurrection. From 1894 he taught at the Moscow school of painting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perizzites-1203:
The Perizzites were a tribe of Canaan in the Bible. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They lived in the south of Palestine. Abraham found them there when he entered the land.

Jacob feared them after the crime at Shechem. Later, Simeon and Judah beat them in battle. Solomon never made them pay tribute. Ezra still lists them among the peoples of the land. The name is missing from the table of nations. Newer scholars think it covers all folk of unwalled towns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pick-arnold-121:
Arnold Pick was an Austrian psychiatrist of Moravian birth. He was born at Gross-Meseritsch on July 20, 1851. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied medicine at Berlin and Vienna. His field was the pathology of the mind.

Pick took his degree in 1875 and entered asylum work. He served at Wehnen, then at the Prague state asylum. In 1880 he became chief physician at Dobrzan. Six years later Prague made him professor of psychiatry. His books map diseases of the brain and nerves. One was written with Kahler in 1880.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polak-jakob-edu:
Jakob Eduard Polak was an Austrian doctor who worked in Persia. Isidore Singer and Emil Jelinek wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Bohemia in 1818, he studied medicine at Prague and Vienna. In 1851 he sailed to Teheran to teach at a new army school.

Polak soon won the trust of Shah Nasir-ed-Din himself. He first taught in French through a helper who translated. Within a year he could lecture in Persian. He wrote a Persian book on the human body. He also made a medical word list in three tongues. He founded a state clinic with sixty beds. His book on Persia and its people came out at Leipsic in 1865.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-precedence-1233:
Precedence means the rank and first place given to persons by rule. The Editorial Board and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Such rank can rest on custom or on set law. The Bible shows a clear order of rank in the home. The husband stood above the wife, they note.

The male was put before the female in that order. The first-born son took a double share of the estate. The child of a bondwoman ranked lower than others. In Egypt the whole tribe of Levi stood apart. Its men were freed from bondage there, the article says. The entry works through rank in home, court, and synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pul-12435:
Pul was a king of Babylonia in the eighth century B.C. Emil G. Hirsch and Samuel Fuchs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He seized the throne in the year 745. He held it until the year 737. He is one and the same as Tiglath-pileser the Third. King lists name him as Pulu in short form.

Rawlinson first put that link forward in 1863. Lepsius proved it on his own six years later. On taking power, Pul brought peace back to Babylonia. In 738 he took Kullani, thought to be Calno of the Bible. He laid tribute on Syria as far south as Samaria. His own stone records name the kings who paid him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rahab-broad-125:
Rahab of Jericho hid the two spies sent by Joshua. Emil G. Hirsch, M. Seligsohn, and the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Her house stood in the city wall. It had a window facing outward.

The article retells Joshua chapter 2 in close detail. Rahab hid the men on her roof and misled the king. She asked that her whole family be spared in return. She then lowered the spies by a scarlet cord. When Jericho fell, Joshua kept that promise to her. A second part covers how later rabbis discussed her.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ricardo-david-1:
David Ricardo was an English political economist born on April 19, 1772. Joseph Jacobs and J. H. Hollander wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in London. He died on September 11, 1823.

The article traces his family from Italy to Holland to London. His father Abraham grew rich on the stock exchange. David was the third child of a large family. His schooling was sound and practical, the writers say. His father designed him for a financial career. At fourteen David joined his father's exchange business. Even young, he showed a taste for abstract reasoning. He pressed for final analysis in every question. He held opinions firmly yet stayed open to proof. The entry introduces a thinker formed by the market.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenau-william:
William Rosenau was an American rabbi born at Wollstein, Germany, on May 30, 1865. Cyrus Adler and I. George Dobsevage wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He trained at Hebrew Union College and earned a doctorate at Johns Hopkins.

Rosenau led Temple Israel in Omaha, then Congregation Oheb Shalom in Baltimore from 1892. He held office in the Central Conference of American Rabbis for years. At Johns Hopkins he taught rabbinica, and he sat on Baltimore's board of education. His books cover Hebrew turns in the English Bible and Jewish ceremonial customs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rules-of-elieze:
The Thirty-Two Rules of Eliezer b. Jose ha-Gelili are rules for reading the Bible's non-legal passages. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Many of the rules also serve in legal interpretation.

The entry lists and explains all thirty-two rules one by one. Some turn on small particles: one word can widen a verse, another narrow it. Others cover arguing from lesser to greater, or repeated words bearing special meaning. Still others treat shortened speech and clauses split across a passage. Together they form a toolkit for drawing teaching out of Scripture's wording.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sabeans-11435:
The Sabeans were the people of Sheba, an ancient kingdom in southeastern Arabia. Joseph Jacobs and Louis H. Gray wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. They are known from the Bible, classical writers, and native inscriptions.

Genesis gives Sheba, their ancestor, three different pedigrees in its genealogies. One line makes him a grandson of Cush, through Raamah of Arabia's coast. Another makes him a descendant of Shem, through Joktan the patriarch. A third makes him a grandson of Abraham by Keturah, his later wife. The Psalms and prophets stress Sabean wealth and busy trade in gold.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salomon-haym-13:
Haym Salomon was an American financier born at Lissa, Poland, in 1740. Cyrus Adler and Herbert Friedenwald wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He left Poland after its partition in 1772 and settled in New York.

When the Revolutionary war began, Salomon sided with the American cause. The British jailed him as a spy after taking New York in 1776. His languages won him a post in the Hessian commissariat instead. From there he helped French and American prisoners escape their captors. In August 1778 he fled New York, leaving property, wife, and infant behind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ha-nasi-:
Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel ha-Nasi. He was an exilarch, the official head of the Jews, in Bagdad. He probably held that post sometime between 773 and 816. Until recently, scholars knew he existed only from one hard manuscript passage. Part of that passage was printed in the Maẓref la-Ḥokmah.

The passage says the pious took the groundwork of the prayer book from Aaron ben Samuel ha-Nasi. Aaron had left Babylon. A fourteenth-century Paris manuscript adds more. It says Moses, who wrote a prayer work, was Aaron's pupil. The Chronicle of Ahimaaz gives Aaron a large role in Italy. Taken together, these scraps prove that Samuel himself was real.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-savannah-13235:
Cyrus Adler and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Savannah. The Georgia city stands on the Savannah River. General James Oglethorpe founded it in 1733. Georgia was meant as a refuge from religious persecution. The colony's trustees warned Oglethorpe not to encourage the Jews. The general ignored them.

The first Hebrew settlers arrived in 1733 itself. Among them was Dr. Nuñez, whose good work Oglethorpe praised. Savannah's Jews prospered in peace until the Revolution. Many scattered then, and several enlisted in the rebel army. After independence they returned and rebuilt. Their president, Levy Sheftall, sent greetings to President Washington. The letter was warmly answered. The Mickwa Israel congregation, founded soon after the first landing, anchors the community's story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwab-moise-13:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Moïse Schwab. He was a French librarian and author. Schwab was born at Paris on September 18, 1839. He studied at Strasburg's Jewish school and Talmud Torah. From 1857 to 1866 he served as secretary to Salomon Munk. Since 1868 he has been a librarian at the Bibliothèque Nationale.

Schwab's chief work renders the Jerusalem Talmud into French. It runs to eleven volumes, printed from 1871 to 1889. He began it before Frankel's introduction existed. Critics praised and blamed it in turns. He finished the huge task alone. His other books cover Jewish history and the ethnography of Tunisia. He wrote a bibliography of Persia and studied early Hebrew printing. In 1880 the ministry sent him to Bavaria to hunt old Hebrew presses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-serah-13435:
Serah was the daughter of Asher, one of Jacob's twelve sons. Wilhelm Bacher and Isaac Broydé wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on her. She is counted among the seventy who went down to Egypt with Jacob. Her name appears again in a census taken in the wilderness.

Serah stands alone as the only woman in those family lists. That odd fact made rabbis build legends around her. One tale says she first told Jacob that Joseph still lived. Jacob then blessed her with life without end. Another tale has Moses ask her where Joseph's remains lay. The entry shows how a brief name grew into lasting story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shekanzib-13535:
Shekanzib was a small town near Nehardea in Persia, perhaps on the Tigris. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its women were famed for beautiful songs of mourning. They sang those songs at burials in the town.

Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi barred his children from living there. He called it a town of mockers, the entry reports. Yet Rab Nahman married a woman from Shekanzib. Sherira Gaon tells that Rabba fled there for safety. He ran when Papa ben Nazar captured Nehardea. The brief entry mixes praise, blame, and refuge around one little-known Babylonian town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sid-sidi-arabic:
Sid, or Sidi, meaning lord or noble in Arabic, is a common Eastern Jewish family name. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the name. Several rabbinical authors bore it across the Balkans. Abraham Moses Sid was born at Nish in 1842.

Abraham wrote many works, though few reached print. His printed books cover ethics, Passover law, and Ruth. The Nish synagogue library kept four more works in manuscript. Judah Sid served as chief rabbi at Philippopolis under Ottoman rule. He headed its tribunal as president there as well. His Ot Emet treats rules for reading the weekly Law lessons. His Ner Mizwah comments on the Pentateuch itself. The entry gathers one name's learned bearers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simhat-torah-th:
Simhat Torah, the Rejoicing over the Law, is the second day of Shemini Azeret. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It falls on the 23rd of Tishri and closes the Feast of Sukkot. The name came into use only in later times. It marks the day the yearly Torah reading ends.

As soon as Deuteronomy ends, Genesis begins again at once. All the scrolls are taken from the Ark in the morning. A hymn is sung for each scroll in turn. Those who read the last and first parts are honored. Gifts, dinners, and even dancing in the synagogue grew around the day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sofia-the-triad:
Sofia, once called Triaditza and Sredec, is the capital of Bulgaria. Gotthard Deutsch and M Franco wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It lies 350 miles from Constantinople. Jews lived there before the ninth century. In 811, Jewish prisoners from Thessaly joined that early community.

More Jews came from the Byzantine empire in 967. Others arrived from Germany in 1360 and Hungary in 1367. When Murad I took Sofia about 1389, four synagogues stood there. They served Byzantine, Ashkenazic, Italian, and native Jews in turn. Spanish Jews founded a Sephardic synagogue after 1492. The false Messiah Shabbethai Zebi later wrote to his brethren of Sofia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-max-emanu:
Max Emanuel Stern was a Hungarian Hebraist born at Presburg on November 9, 1811. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. His father taught at the Jewish primary school in Presburg. When his father went blind, Max took over his classes at fourteen. He died at Vienna on February 9, 1873.

Stern studied at night and wrote Hebrew poems and translations of Proverbs. In 1833 he became a corrector for a Vienna printing press. He later led the Jewish-German school at Eisenstadt. His epic poem on Elijah appeared under a pen name in 1840. From 1845 he published a Hebrew periodical backed by the Imperial Academy. The emperor gave him a gold medal for literature and art. The entry traces a Hebrew writer honored by the state.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sussmann-ezra-b: Ezra ben Jekuthiel Sussmann was a Polish scholar of the eighteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. His one known book is Hoshen Yeshu'ot, printed at Minsk in 1802. It comments on the Pirke Abot, the rabbinic ethics tractate. Bibliographies by Benjacob, Fürst, and Zedner record the work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanhuma-b-abba-:
Tanhuma ben Abba was a Palestinian amora famed for sermons. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He belonged to the fifth generation of amoraim. Huna ben Abin was his main teacher. He likely lived at Nave in Perea.

Tanhuma ranked among the foremost haggadists of his time. One Talmud tale shows his wit before an emperor. The ruler proposed that all become one people. Tanhuma answered that circumcision divided them by Rome's choice. The emperor threw him to wild beasts for winning. The beasts left him unharmed in the story. A bystander who mocked was not so lucky. Tanhuma also ordered a public fast in his town. The entry blends legend with a preacher's public record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-terni-mattathia:
Mattathiah Nissim ben Jacob Israel Terni was an Italian rabbi and poet. M. Seligsohn wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Terni served congregations at Florence, Urbino, Pesaro, and Sinigaglia. He worked in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

His writings center on Jewish law and marriage rules. Sefat Emet collects his halakic decisions, printed at Leghorn in 1797. Midbar Mattanah gathers responsa in four parts. An appendix in Italian appeared at Urbino. He also left a volume of poems. The entry is brief, drawn from standard bibliographies. It still fixes his posts, dates, and main books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-toledo-14435:
Toledo, capital of Old Castile, held one of Spain's oldest Jewish communities. Joseph Jacobs wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jews lived there by the sixth century at least. The Toledo Council of 589 already legislated against them. Later councils banned intermarriage and public office for Jews.

Jews reportedly helped the Arabs take Toledo in 715. Under Arab rule their position seems to have been strong. Congregation minutes stayed in Arabic into the late 1200s. Judah ha-Levi and Abraham ibn Ezra were born in Toledo. The city became Europe's hub for translation from Arabic. Alfonso X granted Jews full equality with Christians. Friction between the faiths soon followed anyway.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tubal-cain-1453:
Tubal-cain, brother of Jabal and Jubal in Genesis, stands at the dawn of metalwork. Emil G. Hirsch, Ira Maurice Price, and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The Lamech sons founded several industries and arts. Scholars dispute the exact Hebrew text of Genesis 4. Some call part of it a marginal gloss.

The Septuagint omits one key word of the verse. Dillmann and others think Tubal once stood alone. Cain, they argue, was added later as a title meaning smith. Tubal matches an Assyrian people southeast of the Black Sea. The Tibareni traded bronze goods with Phoenicia, Ezekiel notes. That trade supports the older reading. Later tradition adds still more inventors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-valls-raphael-1:
Raphael Valls was a Spanish Marrano put to death by the Inquisition. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Valls was burned at the stake at Palma, Majorca, on May 6, 1691. The court treated him as the rabbi of the Chuetas, Majorca's hidden Jews.

Two of his followers died with him. They were his pupil Raphael Terongi and Terongi's sister Catalina. All three held fast to Judaism. Local poets wrote verses about their deaths. Women on the island still sang those verses years later. The entry keeps their names and story from being lost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weill-mathieu-1:
Mathieu Weill was a French mathematician and school leader. He was born at Hagenau, Alsace, on May 24, 1851. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at Burg, Strasburg, and the Polytechnique. He trained at the military school of Fontainebleau. He rose to lieutenant of artillery.

Weill resigned his commission in 1877. In 1881 he began teaching math at Collège Chaptal. In 1898 he became the college's principal. He published essays in French math journals. His textbooks cover analytic geometry in one course. A four volume set treats arithmetic, geometry, algebra, and trigonometry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wurzburg-15035:
Wurzburg is the chief town of Lower Franconia in Bavaria. Gotthard Deutsch and Moses Lob Bamberger wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The town ranked as a city from the year 741. A Jewish group lived there from the 1000s at least.

The first firm proof of Jews there dates to 1119. The Crusade of 1147 brought great pain to them. Fresh attacks came in 1298 and again in 1349. In that last year Jews died by fire in their synagogue. Men, wives, and small children chose death that way. In 1565 a bishop cast the Jews out of the town. The grave yard was seized and shut soon after. The group at Heidingsfeld took up the work from there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zemah-ben-hayyi:
Zemah ben Hayyim was gaon of Sura from 889 to 895. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the stepbrother of Nahshon ben Zadok of note. He came to the chair on the death of that man.

He is known most of all for one court reply he made. Men of Kairwan had asked him of Eldad ha-Dani then. Eldad was a far guest who claimed a lost tribe root. The reply of Zemah treats that guest in nine points of law. It ends with a plea for the gaps in Eldad's tale. Zemah held those gaps to be mere slips of mind in age. One more reply of his lives on in a law book. No facts of his own life are known to men now at all.
mellon-ms-6-alchemical-miscellany-1435:
Mellon MS 6 is an Italian paper manuscript of about 1435. Yale's Beinecke Library holds the slim book, with 17 leaves. One hand wrote most of it, in a gothic antique script.

Two known works treat the magic traits ascribed to gems. They also treat the meaning held to sit in carved stones. Mixed in are steps to mend spoiled wine and tint glass. One step claims to ripen grapes early, and one to make an ass bray loud. Red ink marks most heads, capitals, and paragraph signs. Damp has marked the lower edges through the whole book.
nasa-tm-19680016260-lunar-explorer-35:
Norman F. Ness of Goddard Space Flight Center reports on Lunar Explorer 35 in this May 1968 paper, presented at COSPAR in Tokyo. The spin-stabilized spacecraft entered lunar orbit on 22 July 1967. It weighed about 104 kilograms and circled the Moon in about eleven and a half hours.

Its instruments included magnetometers, plasma probes, and detectors for energetic particles and cosmic dust. Bi-static radar tests probed the electrical properties of the lunar surface using reflected radio signals. Ness reports that the spacecraft operated continuously after launch. Its data gave scientists new views of the Moon's space environment and surface properties.
on-the-functions-of-the-brain-and-of-eac: Franz Josef Gall wrote this work on the brain, printed in 1835. Winslow Lewis translated it from the French. Gall argues that head shape reveals talents and traits. The hosted sample preserves only Google Books boilerplate text. It gives no readable pages of Gall's work itself. Readers can confirm the title, author, and translator from the metadata alone. Volume one treats the origin of moral and mental faculties in man.

The team compared shop-bought DNA extraction kits on herbarium specimens. They judged each method by DNA purity and yield. They also checked success at copying three DNA markers of different sizes. Methods differed a lot in performance. Clean DNA mattered more than the amount gained. Short DNA pieces copied far more often than long ones. How a specimen was prepared also affected success. The results help researchers choose methods for old plant material.

One shortcut uses overlap between confidence intervals. If two intervals do not overlap, the values differ. The authors simulated how uneven intervals behave. They searched for an interval level that mimics a standard test. Intervals at the eighty-four percent level worked well. They matched the usual five percent test level. openalex-w2076380535:

One soybean type tolerates drought better than the other. The team imposed short water stress on both. They measured growth and nitrogen fixation in the plants. A lab method profiled their small-molecule chemistry. The two types differed sharply in body responses. Certain chemical pools changed most under drought. The work shows which pathways help tolerance. Breeders can use those clues for hardier soybeans.

Megan Adams, Jennifer Carpenter, Jess Housty and colleagues argued for deeper partnership between scientists and Indigenous communities. Their paper appeared in Ecology and Society in 2014. Ecological research increasingly touches social questions. Indigenous peoples hold deep knowledge of their territories. Their governments are gaining more decision power in Canada.

Research can confirm and strengthen local ecological knowledge. That knowledge guides care of land and resources. Community-level studies offer many chances for joint work. Yet academic habits can still exclude local partners. The authors draw on coastal British Columbia experience. They suggest ways to share authority and credit. True partnership improves both science and local decisions.

Jorge Salluh, Márcio Soares, Jose Teles, and colleagues published this study in Critical Care in 2010. The DECCA study measured how common delirium is in intensive care units around the world. Delirium, a sudden state of confusion, harms many ICU patients, but most earlier data came from single hospitals.

On one study day, teams screened patients in over a hundred ICUs across eleven countries. About a third of patients who could be assessed had delirium. Those patients were sicker on arrival and faced higher death rates in the ICU and hospital. They also stayed far longer. Prior use of the sedative midazolam was more common among patients with delirium.

Polina Perelman, Warren Johnson, Christian Roos, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Genetics in 2011. They built a family tree of living primates from fresh DNA sequence data. The team gathered about eight million DNA letters from one hundred eighty-six primates. The animals covered about nine in ten known primate genera, plus relatives as outgroups. The resulting tree is unusually robust and clears up many taxonomic disputes. It reveals ongoing speciation, mixed ancestry in places, ancient survivor lineages, and uneven rates of change across branches. It also adds new data on human evolution.

Betty Abelev and colleagues in the ALICE Collaboration published this measurement in Physical Review C in 2013. Particle yields at each momentum test rival pictures of the cooling fireball: fluid flow, thermal models, and quark recombination.

ALICE covered a broad momentum range near the collision's midline for each species. Spectra and yields were tracked from glancing to head-on collisions. The results were set against hydrodynamic, thermal, and recombination expectations. Such data pin down the fireball's freeze-out conditions, when particle counts stop changing. They also feed the debate over whether standard thermal assumptions fully hold at this energy.

It also yields design principles specific to collaborative settings. The paper bridges a respected learning theory into the social settings where much learning now happens.

Julie Cagliero, Sharon Y. A. M. Villanueva, and Mariko Matsui reviewed leptospirosis and cytokines in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology in 2018. The review gathers the cytokine evidence for leptospirosis specifically. If a storm drives severity, calming it could save patients that antibiotics alone cannot. That makes immune monitoring a clinical priority, the authors imply.

With no approved RSV vaccine at the time, the gut-lung link points to a possible low-cost therapy route.

During that run, the collider's brightness rose fourfold and each crossing held far more collisions. Trigger rules had to be tuned to hold data rates down while keeping a high catch rate for real physics. The authors measured the triggers' success rates for electrons and photons in both proton and heavy-ion collisions. The rates stayed high, showing the system coped with much harsher conditions.
openalex-w3190974535:

Such lessons can shape screening programmes that more women actually use.

The roadmap aims to turn known science into everyday practice worldwide.

The authors suggest that even gentle weekly training may help the oldest adults keep lower-limb function.

Cristina Aguayo-Mazzucato, Carmen Sanchez-Soto, Victoria Godinez-Puig, and co-authors studied the insulin system in the first days of life for a 2006 paper. Pancreatic islets are the small clusters of cells that make insulin. After birth they are rebuilt as the body shifts from life in the womb to feeding on its own.

The team tracked that restructuring inside a postnatal critical window, a short period when the islets change shape and reset how they release insulin. Windows like this matter for diabetes research: faults laid down in the first days can echo for a lifetime. The study maps what normal development looks like so that abnormal development can be recognized.
plos-pone-0000135:
Priya Chikhlikar, Luciana Barros de Arruda, Milton Maciel, and colleagues published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2006. They built a DNA vaccine that joins an HIV-1 protein, Gag, to a human protein called LAMP-1. The team tested this chimera in rhesus macaques, monkeys used as a stand-in for human immune responses.

As the title reports, the vaccine drew out a broad immune response, both cellular and antibody-based. Blending a viral protein with a routing protein is a trick meant to show the virus to more parts of the immune system. The results informed later work on DNA vaccine design against HIV.
plos-pone-0000235:
Javier Pérez-Tris, Olof Hellgren, Asta Križanauskienė, and colleagues published this parasitology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies within-host speciation of malaria parasites, the splitting of one parasite lineage into distinct species inside a single host animal. That idea challenges the usual picture of species splitting across separated places.

If new malaria species can arise side by side in one bird or mammal, parasite diversity may grow faster than expected. The authors present evidence bearing on that process. The work matters for tracking the many malaria relatives in wild animals, some of which can cross into new hosts.
plos-pone-0000335:
Stefan Wuchty published this network biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The interactome is the web of interactions between a cell's proteins. Studying the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum, the author examines its rich-club phenomenon. This is a core of highly connected proteins that also connect to each other. He asks whether it is an artifact of the data or a signature of the parasite's lifestyle.

Malaria parasites live inside host cells and rewire them, which could shape their protein web. Distinguishing a real signature from a data artifact is the paper's task. The answer bears on using network maps to find drug targets in the parasite.
plos-pone-0000435:
Bjoern Seidel and colleagues tested whether a prion disease can wait in soil and still infect, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Scrapie is a fatal brain disease of sheep caused by prions, misfolded proteins that resist breakdown. The team used strain 263K and asked whether it can transmit disease by the oral route after persisting in soil over years.

Their title states the answer: yes, it can. Soil-bound prions would explain how pastures stay infectious long after sick animals are gone, a serious problem for farmers and wildlife managers. The work adds hard evidence to fears that prion contamination of land is durable and hard to clean.
plos-pone-0000535:
Toomas Timpka and colleagues wrote a protocol for spotting toddlers headed for lasting obesity, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their high-precision protocol identifies preschool children at risk for persisting obesity, the kind that does not resolve as the child grows. The aim is to target help where it will matter most.

Most heavy toddlers slim down; a minority carry obesity into adult life with its disease risks. A precise protocol avoids both missing that minority and labeling the majority wrongly. Prevention programs are expensive to run for everyone, so risk identification decides whether early intervention is practical at all.
plos-pone-0000635:
Keizo Sugaya, Shiro Matsubara, Yasuhiro Kagamihara and colleagues studied a mutation tied to Huntington's disease onset, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The mutation stretches a polyglutamine tract, a run of one amino acid repeated too many times. Stretched proteins can change shape, misfold, and gather into aggregates such as amyloid fibrils, which are toxic to cells.

The team reports that the expansion creates a pathological epitope, a distinctive patch the immune system can recognize. That patch is linked to nucleation, the first seed from which aggregates grow. Pinpointing the seed step matters, because blocking nucleation could, in principle, delay the disease whose onset this patch helps set.
plos-pone-0000735:
Mathias Streitz, Lydia Tesfa, Vedat Yildirim and colleagues looked for a blood-cell sign of active tuberculosis, in PLOS ONE in 2007. T-cell responses to tuberculin have low diagnostic specificity in populations vaccinated with BCG. Tests using subunit antigens such as ESAT-6 and CFP-10 can diagnose latent infection. No reliable immunological test, though, could confirm active pulmonary tuberculosis.

The title reports their marker: tuberculin-reactive T cells lose a certain surface receptor in active disease. A test separating active from latent infection changes treatment decisions and contact tracing. Patients with active disease need urgent therapy and isolation; latent carriers need a different path entirely.
plos-pone-0000835:
Tomohisa Horibe and Nicholas J. Hoogenraad found a control switch for the cell's response to stress inside its mitochondria. Mitochondria are the cell's power plants. When bad, unfolded proteins pile up inside them, the cell nucleus turns on genes for helper proteins that clean up the mess. The team had helped find this response, called the mitochondrial unfolded protein response, in mammal cells.

Their title reports that the Chop gene holds an element that boosts this response. One stretch in one gene's control zone thus helps run a whole stress program. That is a firm handle on a pathway that counts in aging and in diseases where nerve cells die. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2007.
plos-pone-0000935:
Miriam Podtschaske, Uwe Benary, Sandra Zwinger and colleagues showed how T cells turn a graded signal into an all or none reply, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Making interleukin-2 is a key step when helper T cells switch on. It drives their growth and shapes both attack cells and the regulatory cells that calm them.

The team found that inside each cell, activation of the factor NFATc2 is digital: fully on or fully off. Stronger stimulation recruits more cells rather than pushing each cell harder. That design keeps responses decisive instead of half hearted. It also changes how immune drugs and vaccines should be judged, cell by cell.
plos-pone-0001035:
Matthew Loza, Charles McCall, Liwu Li and colleagues assembled a gene set for studying inflammation genetics, in PLOS ONE in 2007. New links keep appearing between inflammation gene variants and common diseases. Testing those genes fairly requires a systematic list, not a grab bag of favorites.

The team gathered inflammation related genes into a pathway focused panel for genetic analysis. A defined panel lets studies compare results on the same ground. It also keeps attention on genes with a plausible shared role, rather than scattered single hits. Their assembly work is infrastructure: unglamorous, and exactly what later association studies stand on.
plos-pone-0001135:
Cutting out a tumor is not always possible, so doctors look for ways to kill one in place. Bassim Al-Sakere and co-authors report an early test of such a method in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The method is irreversible electroporation, which uses short, strong electric pulses to destroy tissue without heat.

The team reports the first successful use of the technique against aggressive skin tumors implanted in mice, with minimal invasion. Because the pulses do not cook tissue, nearby structures may be spared in ways heat-based methods cannot manage. The paper is a proof of concept in animals, not yet a human treatment.
plos-pone-0001235:
Rice feeds half the world and serves as the model plant for cereal genomics. Kouji Satoh and colleagues mapped the full-length copies of its genes and measured their activity, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Rice has a considerably smaller genome than other monocots, which made it the first cereal sequenced.

Accurate genome sequences of the indica and japonica varieties existed, but knowing where genes start and end, and when they switch on, needed more work. The authors combine full-length cDNA mapping with microarray expression analysis to describe gene organization in rice. Such maps underpin breeding and functional studies.
plos-pone-0001335:
Some tuberculosis is smear-negative: the standard microscope test cannot see it, and diagnosis is hard. Blood-based immune assays had shown promise for such cases. Ronan Breen and colleagues combined immune tests and sputum checks in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Lung fluid sampling lets both kinds of test run at once. Until now, that had only been possible with invasive procedures.

The authors report rapid diagnosis of smear-negative tuberculosis using this combined approach, in people with and without HIV. With HIV, such disease is more common and more deadly. A fast route to diagnosis that avoids invasive sampling fills a real gap.
plos-pone-0001435:
Jeffrey Bhasin and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on sex based gene control in mouse immune cells. Many trait gene sites act in one sex but not the other. Why that is so was not well known. The team read gene use in immune cells from a cross of mouse strains, split by sex.

They mapped sites where gene variants steer gene use in a sex linked way. The maps show that males and females run some of the same genes on unlike settings. That helps explain why some ills and drug effects split by sex. It also urges care in pooling male and female data in gene studies.
plos-pone-0001535:
Say Viengchareun and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on milk hormones and brown fat in newborns. The hormone prolactin and kin drive breeding and milk making. Their receptor is rich in brown fat, the tissue that burns fuel for heat. Yet its job in fat was not known. The team tested mice that lack the receptor.

They show the signal is vital for brown fat work around birth. A growth factor acts as a key go between in that path. Newborns rely on brown fat to hold body heat. The work thus ties a breeding hormone to a core survival task in the young.
plos-pone-0001635:
Jacob N. Barney, Thomas H. Whitlow, and Arthur J. Lembo rebuilt the invasion history of two non-native plant species for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Records of where invading plants spread, and when, are rarely kept well, which makes invasion patterns hard to study at the scale of whole regions. The team turned to herbarium records, the pressed plant specimens stored by botanical collections.

By mapping dated specimens and studying the spatial trend, they traced how each species moved across the landscape over time. The full text gives the maps, the likely entry points, and the places the authors flag as at risk of future invasion. Land managers can use such reconstructions to spot where a plant will spread next and where control work is best spent first.
plos-pone-0001735:
Simone Kurt, Anke Deutscher, John M. Crook, and their co-authors modeled how the hearing brain separates sounds in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The brain breaks the world into discrete objects of perception. When similar objects appear at once, it must segregate and selectively address them. Models aim to solve this with winner-take-all circuits, where the strongest signal suppresses the rest.

The team studied global winner-take-all inhibitory interactions in auditory cortex and how they enhance contrast between sounds. The full text gives the model and the neural data it explains. Sharper contrast in hearing helps listeners follow one voice in a crowd, and the same principle guides design of hearing devices and speech software.
plos-pone-0001835:
Dick S. J. Groenenberg, Albert J. Beintema, René W. R. J. Dekker, and their co-authors used ancient DNA to settle a bird dispute in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. A persistent controversy surrounds the flightless island hen of Tristan da Cunha, Gallinula nesiotis. Some believe it went extinct by the end of the nineteenth century; others suppose it still inhabits Tristan. The status of the related name Gallinula comeri was also disputed.

DNA from museum specimens let the team test the hens' identity and relationships. The full text gives the sequences and the family tree. Ancient DNA turns museum skins into evidence, resolving extinction questions that field surveys alone cannot answer.
plos-pone-0001935:
Yoni Haitin and co-authors probed how a heart and nerve channel senses voltage, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The channel, Kv7.1, opens and shuts in response to electric charge, and faults in it cause disease. Its voltage sensor is a helix called S4 that moves when the charge shifts, which in turn works the channel gate.

How S4 moves was unclear. The team swapped single building blocks of S4 for a tagged form and tracked the effects. They report that a second helix, S1, constrains S4 in the sensor. A clearer picture of the sensor helps explain channel faults and may guide drugs that tune them.
plos-pone-0002035:
Jing-xin Zhang, Gretchen Diehl, and Dan Littman worked on making mouse T cells host HIV, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A small animal model of HIV would speed drug and vaccine work, but the virus fails to copy itself in non-primate cells. Most past work used fibroblast cell lines, not the T cells the virus attacks in people.

The team relieved a block that stops HIV before it joins the host genome, and charted further blocks in primary mouse T cells. Each block named is a step a model must clear. The study shows how many locks keep HIV a primate virus.
plos-pone-0002135:
Yuyan Zhu, Huayan Hou, William Nikolic, and co-authors studied brain immune cells in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Microglia are the brain's own defense cells, and in this disease they switch on in ways that may harm nerve cells. Signals through pathways called MAPK drive much of that response when the cells meet amyloid-beta, the protein that builds up in patients' brains.

Earlier work by the group showed that a surface protein called CD45 calms this response. Here they point to a related form, CD45RB, as a drug target. Adjusting it might lower the harmful side of microglial activity while leaving the brain's defenses in place.
plos-pone-0002235:
Petra van der Stoop and co-authors asked what a chromatin protein does for mouse embryonic stem cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Ring1b, also called Rnf2, is a core part of Polycomb repressive complex 1, a system that switches genes off by marking histone H2A. Embryos cannot develop properly without it.

To learn its role in early development, the team studied Ring1b in mouse embryonic stem cells, the cells that can form any tissue. They report that it helps keep those cells stable in their undifferentiated state. The finding ties a gene-silencing machine to the balance stem cells strike between staying young and growing up.
plos-pone-0002335:
Jacques Prudhomme, Eric McDaniel, Nadia Ponts, and co-authors mined sea bacteria for new malaria drugs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Malaria kills about 2 million people a year. Rising drug resistance and the lack of an efficient vaccine make fast, broad antimalarial drug discovery urgent.

The team turned to marine actinomycetes, bacteria famed for producing antibiotics, as a new source of compounds against the human malaria parasite. Ocean microbes make chemical defenses unlike those of land species, so their extracts may hold scaffolds the parasite has never met. Screening programs like this widen the pipeline for a disease that keeps outrunning its medicines.
plos-pone-0002435:
Huurman and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Volkert A. L. Huurman, Robert Hilbrands, Gabriëlle G. M. Pinkse, among others. Its subject is cellular Islet Autoimmunity Associates with Clinical Outcome of Islet Cell Transplantation. Islet cell transplantation can cure type 1 diabetes (T1D), but only a minority of recipients remains insulin–independent in the following years.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002535:
Siawaya joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Joel Fleury Djoba Siawaya, Teri Roberts, Chantal Babb, among others. Its subject is an Evaluation of Commercial Fluorescent Bead-Based Luminex Cytokine Assays.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002635:
Jason Ivanoff and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was fMRI evidence for a dual process account of the Speed-Accuracy tradeoff in Decision-Making. The catalog record names Jason Ivanoff first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The speed and accuracy of decision-making have a well-known trading relationship: hasty decisions are more prone to errors while careful. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002735:
A 2008 study by Patricia Chastagner and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up AIP4/Itch regulates notch receptor degradation in the absence of ligand. Authorship is credited in the record to Patricia Chastagner and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The regulation of Notch signaling heavily relies on ubiquitination events. It goes on to note a further point. Drosophila Su(dx), a member of the HECT family of ubiquitin-ligases, has been described as a negative regulator of Notch signaling. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002835:
K. Mathias Wegner and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on clustering of drosophila melanogaster immune genes in interplay with recombination rate. The full author list in the catalog record begins with K. Mathias Wegner, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Gene order in eukaryotic chromosomes is not random and has been linked to coordination of gene expression, chromatin structure and also recombination rate. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002935:
José Rodríguez, Victoria Jones, Masashi Tabuchi and co-authors studied new neuron growth in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease in 2008. In adult mammals, new neurons are added mainly in two brain areas. One is the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus, a region central to learning and memory.

In a triple transgenic mouse carrying Alzheimer's-linked changes, growth of new neurons in that region was impaired. The title states that result plainly. Published in PLOS ONE, the finding links the disease model to a loss in the brain's own renewal, which may worsen memory failure.
plos-pone-0003035:
Tarja Sironen, Jonas Klingström, Antti Vaheri and co-authors described Puumala hantavirus pathology in macaques in 2008. Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and a lung syndrome in people worldwide. Leaking capillaries sit at the center of these diseases, but how the leak develops had remained unknown.

Macaques offer a close model of human infection. The PLOS ONE study sets out the pathology of Puumala infection in them, testing ideas about how the disease unfolds. A faithful animal picture is a step toward treatments for a virus group with few options. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003135: Igor F. Tsigelny and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on how hybrid oligomers, mixed clusters of proteins, form. The title links that process to the joint development of Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease in the brain. No abstract text beyond the title was supplied, so this record states no methods or findings.
plos-pone-0003235:
Yuji Yoshiike, Ryoichi Minai, Yo Matsuo and colleagues study amyloid oligomer shape in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Recent in vitro and in vivo studies suggest that destabilized proteins with defective folding induce aggregation and toxicity in protein-misfolding diseases. One such unstable protein state is called amyloid oligomer, a precursor of fully aggregated forms of amyloid. Detection of these oligomers was the challenge addressed.

The authors examine amyloid oligomer conformation in a group of natively folded proteins. Readers learn how a toxic intermediate can arise even from proteins that normally fold well. That idea widens the search for what makes proteins dangerous in diseases like Alzheimer's.
plos-pone-0003335:
Ismael Galván and Carlos Alonso-Alvarez link an antioxidant to a bird signal in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. To understand how traits used in animal communication evolved and are maintained as honest signals, researchers need to understand mechanisms that prevent cheating. It has been proposed that honest signaling is guaranteed by costs associated with signal expression. The team test a cellular cost mechanism.

The title reports that an intracellular antioxidant determines expression of a melanin-based signal in a bird. Readers learn how a bird's internal chemistry could keep its colour badge honest. Costly signals are a central idea in how animal displays can be trusted.
plos-pone-0003435:
Kuo-Liong Chien and co-authors followed heart risk in Chinese adults for this 2008 study. They measured the wall thickness of the carotid artery in the neck. They also noted plaque, fatty buildup inside that artery. Data on these measures were still limited for Chinese groups.

The team ran a community cohort and tracked new disease over time. Thicker walls and plaque each pointed to more heart disease and stroke ahead. Both signs came before illness, not after it. Simple neck scans may flag at-risk adults early in this population. Both measures can be taken with a painless neck scan rather than any surgery.
plos-pone-0003535:
Tamara E. King and co-authors built a model of prostate cancer in bone for this 2008 paper. Cancers of prostate, breast, and lung often spread to bone. Tumor cells grip bone using adhesion receptors called integrins. That spread also causes severe, hard-to-treat bone pain.

Their new xenograft model placed human cancer in mice for study. A receptor, alpha 6 integrin, played roles in migration and bone pain. The model lets drug hunters test pain relief in a living system. It ties tumor movement and suffering to one molecule. Bone pain is often the worst part of late prostate cancer for patients.
plos-pone-0003635:
Akira Katoh, Peter J. Chapman, and Jennifer L. Raymond published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Good movement needs control of both force and timing, and timing can improve with practice. The team asked which molecules let animals learn that timing. They worked with mutant mice.

Mice with faulty P/Q-type calcium channels could not adjust the timing of their movements through learning. Normal signaling through these channels was needed for that change. The result ties a basic skill, learning when to move, to one type of channel in the brain's motor circuits.
plos-pone-0003735:
Benjamin J. Dubin-Thaler, Jake M. Hofman, Yunfei Cai, and colleagues published this cell mechanics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Actin-based movement and force drive immune response, tissue building, and cancer spread. Cell spreading is a favorite model for studying that machinery. The team measured it with care.

They quantified how fast cell edges move and how hard cells pull on their substrate. The numbers revealed distinct motility modules, separate units of the spreading process. Breaking crawling into parts gives researchers targets for work on immunity, development, and metastasis. Each module can now be studied, and perhaps tuned, on its own.
plos-pone-0003835:
So-ichi Tamai, Kamon Sanada, and Yoshitaka Fukada published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2008. New neurons are born throughout adult life in a few brain regions, including the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus. There, progenitor cells keep dividing and giving rise to fresh neurons. Brain clocks shape much of this tissue's activity.

The team found that adult neurogenesis in the hippocampus depends on the time of day. The birth of new neurons rose at certain hours and fell at others. The rhythm suggests the brain schedules its own renewal by the daily clock.
plos-pone-0003935:
Stefan Kempa, Julia Krasensky, Silvia Dal Santo, and co-authors studied a plant stress hormone in 2008. Dryness, salt, and cold all harm plant growth and yield. The hormone abscisic acid, or ABA, guides how plants respond to such stress. Its role in switching genes on was already well established.

Their PLOS ONE article gives ABA a central role in sugar handling under stress. Plants shift how they store and use carbohydrates when conditions worsen. Linking that shift to ABA helps explain how plants budget energy in drought. Crop scientists can use the insight in breeding tougher plants.
plos-pone-0004035:
Daniel Rubinoff and Johannes J. Le Roux examined sudden leaps in moth evolution in 2008. Saltational evolution means a lineage changes fast and far beyond its relatives. Gradual change is the dominant model in evolutionary biology. Sudden leaps are rarely invoked as an alternative.

Their PLOS ONE article reports evidence in the sphinx moth genus Proserpinus. Repeated and independent leaps appear in that peculiar group. Documenting such events tests the limits of gradual models. The moths offer a rare case where rapid change left clear traces. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004135:
Wai Fook Leong and colleagues published this bone study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Osteoporosis, a disease of weak bones, is among the most common of all diseases. Drugs can slow bone loss or build new bone, and finding targets for bone-building drugs requires knowing how bone-forming cells, called osteoblasts, mature.

The study looks at palmitoylation, the attaching of a fatty molecule to proteins, and its effect on osteoblast growth. The authors report that this process controls how a signal protein called BMP switches on Osterix, a factor osteoblasts need to mature. The result names a possible new target for drugs that build bone.
plos-pone-0004235:
Yonatan Mahller and colleagues published this childhood cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neuroblastoma, a tumour of young children, often goes into remission but commonly relapses. The cancer stem cell theory blames rare tumour-initiating cells that resist conventional therapy and regrow the tumour.

The team report that neuroblastoma cell lines contain pluripotent tumour-initiating cells, cells able to make many cell types and seed new tumours. They also show these cells are susceptible to a targeted oncolytic virus, a virus engineered to attack cancer. A therapy that reaches the relapse-causing cells could change this disease.
plos-pone-0004335:
Elsa Youngsteadt and colleagues published this Amazon ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Across lowland Amazonia, arboreal ants collect the seeds of specific plants and cultivate them in nutrient-rich nests. These ant-gardens are diverse yet obligate and species-specific symbioses: the ants depend on their plants for nest stability, and the plants depend on the ants.

The team studied species-specific seed dispersal in this mutualism, asking how ants choose the right seeds. A gardener that plants only its own crop keeps the partnership pure. The study shows the precision inside one of the tropics' neatest arrangements.
plos-pone-0004435:
Routine liver blood tests are among the most common checks in medicine. Nilufer Rahmioglu, Toby Andrew, Lynn Cherkas, and co-authors asked how much of their variation is inherited, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Doctors use these tests to judge liver health, track disease, judge treatments, and spot liver harm from drugs. Levels differ from person to person for many reasons.

The study splits those reasons into genes and life experience, a field called genetic epidemiology. Knowing how strongly genes set each test protein helps doctors read odd results. A level that looks abnormal may be normal for someone's family line. The work also points to gene hunts that could reveal new facts about how the liver works and fails.
plos-pone-0004535:
The worm C. elegans can show gene interactions more clearly when its diet is tuned just right, show William Mair, Siler Panowski, Reuben Shaw, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dietary restriction, eating less without malnutrition, lengthens life in many species and lowers the risk of age-related disease. Its lifespan effect is conserved from worms to mammals, which makes the small worm a useful test bed.

To find genes behind the effect, researchers combine dietary restriction with gene changes, a method called genetic epistasis analysis. The trick is choosing a restriction level strong enough to reveal interactions but not so harsh it swamps them. The authors optimize that level for C. elegans. A well-set dial makes gene discovery faster and cleaner for the whole aging field.
plos-pone-0004635:
Premature babies breathe in measurably different patterns from full-term babies, show Philipp Latzin, Stefan Roth, Cindy Thamrin, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Preterm infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia, a chronic lung disease of prematurity, have structural changes in their lungs. Those changes have functional consequences for lung volume, ventilation inhomogeneity, and respiratory mechanics.

Some studies had shown lower lung volumes and increased ventilation inhomogeneity in these infants. The team measured lung volume, breathing pattern, and ventilation inhomogeneity in preterm and term infants for direct comparison. Precise measurements matter in neonatal care: they show which babies' lungs are coping and which need more support, and they give trials of new therapies an objective yardstick.
plos-pone-0004735:
Megan Sellick and colleagues tested how isotope levels vary in bird tissue by place, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Isotopes in tissue can reveal where a bird has been, since food and water differ by site. In theory, a single capture could show past moves and spread of that bird.

In practice, the basic maps of how isotopes vary were still thin. The team measured strontium and hydrogen isotopes across places. Better base maps make bird tracking from feathers more trusty. That helps guard migrants whose routes cross many lands. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory.
plos-pone-0004835:
Maj-Britt Pontoppidan and colleagues studied spatio temporal spread of dead Ophiocordyceps infected ants, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Parasites likely play key roles in structuring host groups. Many adaptively manipulate host behavior, so extended phenotypes of parasites and their distributions in space, and Time are potentially key ecological variables for knowledge transmission dynamics in tropical forest ecosystems.

Infected ants die in clustered graveyards above ground. Fungal positioning maximizes spore spread to new hosts. Graveyard patterns reveal manipulation precision. Rainforest ecology includes such hidden control. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0004935:
Some chemicals can mimic hormones and disturb development. They can come from industry or from plants themselves. Genistein is one such plant-made compound, found in soy. Sana Sassi-Messai and colleagues studied it in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked how genistein affects zebrafish development. Zebrafish are a standard model for early growth.

The team found the compound acts through two different pathways. A single natural chemical can scramble development by two routes at once. The work adds zebrafish evidence to wider concerns. Hormone-like substances are reaching water and wildlife. Studies like this show why their effects deserve close tracking.
plos-pone-0005035:
Membrane proteins run the cell's exchanges with the outside world. They are hard to study because they shun water. Myriam Reffay and colleagues tracked them in model membranes. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They followed how membrane proteins associate with each other. The setting was artificial membranes that mimic real ones.

The tracking reveals rules of protein matchmaking in the membrane. Association depends on the membrane setting as much as the proteins. The work offers a window into stubborn machinery. Membrane proteins include many drug targets. Understanding their partnerships helps design better medicines. It also helps explain how receptors and channels organize themselves.
plos-pone-0005135:
Prochlorococcus is a tiny ocean microbe. It has the smallest genome of any photosynthetic organism. Erik Zinser and colleagues tracked its daily routine in PLOS ONE in 2009. They followed its transcriptome across the day. They also measured its photophysiology and cell cycle. At temperate latitudes, sunlight varies predictably each day.

The microbe choreographs everything to that light cycle. Genes, light use and division march in step. A minimal cell times its life to the sun with precision. The work is a masterclass in doing more with less. Prochlorococcus fixes vast amounts of carbon in the oceans. Its daily rhythm shapes ocean productivity. Understanding it matters for the planet's carbon budget.
plos-pone-0005235:
Daily body clocks run on gene feedback loops, but nerve activity may tune them too. Kilman and colleagues tested that tuning in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. They disturbed dynamin, a protein that handles membrane traffic inside cells.

The team used a temperature-sensitive, faulty form of dynamin to perturb the system on demand. The title states the result: perturbing dynamin has potent effects on the fly's circadian clock. That finding ties everyday cell traffic to the timing system, a link that clock research had left unclear. The fruit fly is cheap and fast to breed, so a clear result there can guide work on clocks in larger animals and in people.
plos-pone-0005335:
Polycomb proteins keep gene patterns locked in as an embryo develops. In plants and animals, a complex called PRC2 marks genes with a chemical tag, H3K27me3. Exner and colleagues studied the plant protein LHP1, which reads that tag, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

LHP1 resembles the animal reader of the same mark. Its chromodomain proved essential for binding H3K27me3 and for normal Arabidopsis development. A single reading domain thus carries much of the plant Polycomb system's memory, showing how deeply this gene-silencing machinery is conserved. Corn, wheat, and rice all use this same lock-and-key gene system, so a plant model result here can guide work on the crops that feed most of the world each year.
plos-pone-0005435:
Michael Long and Fabio Rossi reported a warning for mouse genetics in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. A widely used system lets scientists switch genes on or off in chosen tissues of mice. Reporter strains show where the switch has worked by turning on a visible marker.

The authors found that gene silencing can block the switch in adult cells for two common reporter strains. When that happens, the marker stays dark even though the system should have worked. Workers who use these mice need to know that a dark result may mean silencing, not a failed gene change.
plos-pone-0005535:
