Alessandra Burgio and four colleagues project how many Italian babies will be conceived with medical help by 2050, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Italy is famous for very late childbearing, which pushes more couples toward fertility treatment. The team combined official 2023 data with nine scenarios, varying how fast mothers' ages rise and how fast treatment rates grow.

Changes in the age mix of women, they found, would barely move the share of assisted births. Later childbearing and wider use of treatment mattered far more, lifting the share from a little over four percent in 2023 to roughly eleven or twelve percent by mid-century. Planners, they argue, should prepare for that growth.
plos-pone-0354235:
Postler and colleagues, in a 2026 study, compare outcomes when the lower thigh bone is replaced with a prosthesis after a break versus as a planned revision. This operation is often the last chance to save a leg when the bone above a knee replacement is badly damaged. The two routes to it may carry very different risks.

Ninety-three patients at one center were followed for about five years on average. Patients whose bone broke had fewer earlier operations and reported higher satisfaction afterward. Yet their death rates were much higher, reflecting the frailty that comes with such breaks. Planned revision patients needed far more repeat surgery by five years, but died less often. Being female lowered repeat-surgery risk, while an earlier stiffer knee implant and a planned indication raised it. The authors advise surgeons to weigh these opposite patterns when counseling patients.
plos-pone-0354335:
Bashar Al Qaroot and colleagues ran a randomized trial to find the best height for wedge insoles, a simple shoe insert prescribed to unload the painful inner side of arthritic knees. Their 2026 study gave thirty-four patients with mild to moderate inner knee osteoarthritis either escalating custom wedges or standard care, tracking X-ray alignment, joint space, and symptom scores.

A mid-height wedge performed best. It straightened the bowed alignment in the non-dominant leg, stopped the joint space from narrowing further while untreated knees kept thinning, and eased pain and overall symptoms. The tallest wedge was abandoned because most patients could not tolerate it. The dose lesson is practical: enough wedge to correct, not so much that patients quit wearing it.
plos-pone-0354635:
Lin Tao and co-authors surveyed young breast cancer survivors in China about existential distress during rehabilitation. Existential distress, anguish over meaning, death, and identity, can shadow recovery long after treatment ends. Their 2026 survey covered several hundred women under fifty within five years of treatment, using standard scales for adaptation, support, resilience, and distress.

Poorer adjustment to life after cancer came with clearly higher distress. Two stepping stones carried much of that effect. Social support alone passed along about half of the indirect influence, and resilience formed a second route, including a chain through support into resilience. Tao and colleagues say rehabilitation should build support networks and coping strength, not only treat the body.
plos-pone-0354735:
Ratchanok Phonyiam and three colleagues published this 2026 study protocol on life after childbirth for Thai women with type 2 diabetes. Income, housing, work, and support shape health after delivery as much as medical care does, yet nobody had studied these women's postnatal experience. The plan first adapts a well-being questionnaire into Thai, then surveys women, then interviews selected mothers in depth.

The two strands will be merged to show how social conditions drive well-being scores. As a protocol, it reports intentions, not results. Phonyiam aims to guide fairer postnatal care for diabetic mothers.
plos-pone-0355335:
Jijie Fan and colleagues present in 2026 a method to judge whether heart tracings from wearable devices are clean enough to trust. Noise from movement, power lines, and drifting baselines can spoil readings and mislead later diagnosis. Their method needs no hand labelled training set, a common limit in real use.

Fake noise was added to clean tracings to teach the system what damage looks like. A rebuilding step then highlighted the damaged zones, and scores from the whole signal and from those zones were combined. Tests on four public sets gave strong scores, suggesting the joint view generalises better to unseen noise.
plos-pone-0355735:
Weilue He, Julie Osborne, and Megan Frost test a new way to sterilize medical equipment in their 2026 paper. Hospitals and device makers now rely heavily on ethylene oxide gas, which works well but is highly toxic to people and the environment. Their candidate replacement is nitric oxide gas, used at ordinary room temperature and normal air pressure.

The team exposed hardy bacterial spores, the standard test for sterilization, to nitric oxide and tracked how fast they died off. The gas killed the test spores in a steady, predictable pattern and also inactivated two bacteria that commonly cause infections. The dose that workers or users might encounter stayed well below the level classed as immediately dangerous, pointing to a safer, greener option.
plos-pone-0355835:
Dan Kuang and colleagues measured how temperature shaped deaths and costs in Chengdu, a basin megacity in southwest China. Both heat and cold raise mortality, but their local weight was unquantified. Their 2026 study modelled seven years of daily death records across twenty-three counties against weather, then priced the burden for a recent year.

The risk curve was U-shaped, with a safe middle band. Just over seven percent of non-accidental deaths were tied to temperatures outside that band. Cold accounted for most of the share, several times the heat portion. Kuang and colleagues argue basin cities should plan for cold snaps as seriously as heatwaves when protecting public health and budgets.
plos-pone-0355935:
Holly Tuten and co-authors report the first years of a public tick reporting programme in Illinois. Tick-borne illness is rising in the United States, and two biting species are spreading into new ground. Their 2026 account covers submissions from residents between 2018 and 2023, with lab testing of a subset.

Residents sent in eight tick species, led by the lone star tick and the blacklegged tick. Submissions arrived nearly all year and came mostly from people, dogs, and deer. Testing found six disease agents, including the Lyme disease bacterium in about one in seven adult blacklegged ticks. The authors say public submissions widen surveillance cheaply and reveal year-round exposure risk.
plos-pone-0356235:
Leila Verena da Conceição and six colleagues develop artificial seeds for cassava, a staple crop that feeds hundreds of millions, in this 2026 study. Cassava is normally planted from stem cuttings, which multiply slowly and carry disease. Their synthetic seeds wrap tiny axillary buds in beads of sodium alginate gel. The team varied the gel strength and the chemical used to set it. They then measured how well buds pushed through and grew outside sterile conditions.

The setting chemical proved decisive. Beads set with calcium chloride hardened into tight networks that strangled emergence, stopping it entirely at higher gel strengths. Beads set with calcium hydroxide let up to four fifths of buds emerge with strong growth, though plain uncoated buds still did slightly better. A dilute gel near one percent balanced sturdiness and emergence best. Storage and field trials come next.
plos-pone-0356735: Chagonda and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a review on early signs of a dangerous pregnancy condition. Preeclampsia can strike without warning later in pregnancy. The planned review covers tests that measure two urine chemicals, glycolic acid and methylsuccinic acid, in the first trimester. A cheap early urine test could flag risk months ahead, when watchful care helps most.
plos-pone-0357035:
Chia-Wei Tsai and co-authors break a recently published quantum messaging scheme that claimed ironclad security. The scheme let two parties exchange secret bits both ways under a controller's supervision, using four-particle quantum states, and its proof leaned on wiretap channel theory. The critics assume the controller is fully untrusted, exactly as the original design allowed, and show how that controller can cheat with a classic Trojan horse trick.

By sneaking probe light into the equipment, the controller can quietly read off the private keys and then reconstruct every secret bit both parties sent, the attack shows. Because the probes leave the checked particles untouched, the scheme's own error alarms never fire. Tsai and colleagues argue the proof failed by ignoring the physical layer, a warning for quantum security claims generally.
plos-pone-0357735:
Sidra Rashid leads a team of six teaching self driving systems to guess where cars will go next, in PLOS ONE in 2026. A vehicle's future path depends on its neighbors, but not equally: one close truck matters more than five distant sedans. Earlier models either watched a small neighborhood or treated every neighbor alike, and their errors grew over longer horizons. The team's model pairs a memory network with a multi head attention system that ranges across the scene.

Attention scores let the model weight the vehicles that influence the target, and position aware features capture long range patterns. On a public highway dataset, the model beat every established rival. At the five second horizon its prediction error fell by more than half compared with the next best method. For a car planning a lane change, that margin is the difference between a calm decision and a late swerve.
plos-pone-0358135:
Aleksandr Diachenko and Detlef Gronenborn wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article in archaeology. It looks for signals of social dynamics in archaeological time-series, long sequences of finds ordered by age. The authors study how the way culture is passed on, and the biases of makers, shape the diversity of assemblages, the collections of artifacts found together.

How people copy each other's styles, and how makers favor certain forms, can raise or lower the variety in the record. Untangling those forces matters because archaeologists read past societies from exactly these patterns. If bias alone can create a trend, social conclusions drawn from artifact counts need extra care.
plos-pone-0358235:
Weilong Zheng and Huanhuan Zheng mapped cell states inside melanoma tumors, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. A tumor is not uniform; where a cancer cell sits shapes how it behaves. The pair studied the spatial layout of melanoma cell states and the neighborhoods formed with support cells called fibroblasts.

Their map reveals tumor cells beside cancer-associated fibroblasts that show enhanced capacity to multiply. That geography points to where the tumor grows fastest and where therapy should strike. It also suggests that cutting the support fibroblasts provide could slow growth. Spatial studies like this are changing cancer from a list of cell types into a map, and maps suggest routes of attack.
plos-pone-0358335:
Lingzhu Huang led a team of seven authors studying a fast, deadly heart illness in children, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fulminant myocarditis is severe heart inflammation that can kill within hours, yet it can look like a stomach bug at first. The team searched emergency department records for warning signs.

Huang's group described the clinical traits of children with the condition and flagged signs visible early in the emergency visit. A short list of red flags helps emergency doctors act before the heart fails, with intensive care and heart support ready. For parents, the wider lesson is that rapid worsening after a seeming stomach illness deserves urgent care.
plos-pone-0358535:
Joseph Resch and Mark Handcock wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article in statistics. It assesses variational likelihood estimation, an approximate computing method, inside network formation models. Those models explain how social and other networks form their links, one tie at a time.

Exact likelihood calculations for networks grow impossibly slow as networks enlarge, so researchers lean on approximations. Assessing one approximation honestly shows when its answers can be trusted and when they drift. Statisticians who model networks, from friendships to trade, are the audience for this check on a common shortcut.
plos-pone-0359335:
Yongwei Fan and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It aims at diagnosing Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia early, a lung infection common in children and young adults. The authors develop and test a model that predicts the illness from signs and tests taken in a routine examination.

A model built from ordinary examination findings could flag this pneumonia before specialized tests return, guiding early treatment choices. Development plus validation means the model was built on one set of patients and checked on another. Clinicians who treat children and lung disease, facing look-alike pneumonias, are the audience for such a model.
plos-pone-0359535:
Tiffany Chen and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It works at county level in the United States. The authors study links between walking and bicycling data gathered automatically by devices, and self-reported data on activity outside work, what people say they do.

Passive data from phones and counters could give health officials cheap, current activity maps if it matches what surveys show. Comparing the two sources tests whether the automatic stream can stand in for costly surveys. Public health agencies planning activity programs county by county are the readers for this check.
plos-pone-0359635: Viktorisson and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on work absence after a mini-stroke in Sweden. A transient ischemic attack is a brief stroke-like event that soon passes. The team used national registers to follow working-age adults and their sick leave. Knowing how long people stay off work after such an event helps doctors, employers, and insurers plan support and return-to-work steps.
plos-pone-0359835:
Ting Zhang, Sheng Ye, Liang Ye, and Zekai Qian published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns the tomb of Yue Fei, a famous Chinese general from the Song dynasty. Stone relics at the tomb need cleaning, and the authors evaluate that cleaning with infrared thermography.

Infrared thermography uses heat images to reveal surface conditions that the eye may miss, such as damp or hidden damage. A non-destructive check suits fragile heritage stone, where testing must not harm the object. Conservators caring for stone monuments can apply this evaluation approach before and after cleaning other historic sites.
pmc-13196835:
Varvara Pantelidou and colleagues offer a 2026 case report on two cancers found at once. A 58-year-old woman came in with a lump in her right breast. Scans showed growths in both breasts, and biopsies found distinct breast cancer types on each side.

A full-body scan then flagged a spot in her left lung. A needle test showed it was a separate lung cancer, not spread from the breast. A joint care team chose staged surgery. Both breasts were removed first, then part of the left lung a month later. Two years on, the patient stays free of disease. The authors stress joint team review, since no shared rulebook covers such paired cases.
pmc-13196935:
Shaoguang Ren and colleagues report a 2026 cohort study on mobile phone use and rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis is an immune disease that swells and harms the joints. The team used UK Biobank data, a large health database, to test whether phone habits link to new cases.

They tracked close to 480,000 adults for a median of about fourteen years. Just over six thousand new cases appeared in that span. Phone users had a modestly higher risk than non-users. Risk was also higher for people who talked on a phone more than thirty minutes a week. The authors note that habits of use, not just owning a phone, may matter, and that more work is needed on cause.
pmc-13197435:
Moritz Berger and colleagues present a 2026 methods study on measuring emotional intelligence in elite swimmers. Emotional intelligence means reading and managing feelings, a trait tied to sport success. Ratings on scale questions can be skewed when athletes answer by habit, such as always picking extremes.

The team applied latent trait models, math tools that infer a hidden trait from answers. Richer models also accounted for each swimmer's response style and doubt. Those models fit the data better than simple scoring models. Ignoring answer habits, they argue, can distort how a swimmer's emotional skill is judged. Better models may sharpen mental support in elite sport.
pmc-13198035:
Lakshmi Sravanti and Hesham M Hamoda share lessons on social media for child mental health in a 2026 commentary. They draw on running the accounts of IACAPAP, a global body for child and adolescent psychiatry. Social media can spread mental health literacy and fight stigma, yet it raises ethics and trust risks with young audiences.

They describe the group's aims: health promotion, teaching, and advocacy across platforms. Content is tailored to each platform's style. From this work they propose the ABLE-GA framework. Its six parts cover alignment, boundaries, language, ethics, governance, and adaptation. The guide aims to help peer bodies use digital platforms with care.
pmc-13198635:
Émile Blanchette and Laurent Fradet present a 2026 case report on a rare bone growth in the tongue. A lingual osseous choristoma is mature bone found where it does not belong, in tongue soft tissue. Just over one hundred cases appear in print, and vague signs make it easy to miss.

Their patient was a 45-year-old woman with a slowly growing lump on the back of her tongue, spotted at a routine dental visit. She had no pain, bleeding, or trouble swallowing. The firm, pale lump looked like a benign fiber growth. Removal under local numbing gave both diagnosis and cure: lab study showed mature bone in the tongue tissue. Two years on, no return appeared.
pmc-13202435:
Tiny gaps in metal ion size steer crystal design in a 2026 study headed by Kenika Khotchasanthong on lanthanide coordination polymers. The research article makes ten compounds from lanthanide chlorides and chloranilic acid, forming two-dimensional layered networks whose patterns depend on which lanthanide is used.

Larger early lanthanides produced a honeycomb network, while smaller later ones formed a brick-wall pattern, a direct effect of lanthanide contraction. Adding a bridging molecule to the brick-wall form created a pillared, guest-filled three-dimensional layout in two cases. The ytterbium brick-wall material also captured more carbon dioxide than the honeycomb form, linking ion size to gas storage performance.
pmc-13213335:
Kaipeng Zhang and colleagues explore in 2026 whether fat-based nanoparticles can help largemouth bass handle sugary feed. Bass digest carbohydrate poorly, so cheap high-starch diets often cause liver trouble, and particle size might decide how well any additive works.

The team made particles in five sizes and dosed fish on high-glucose feed. Sugary feeding disturbed liver sugar pathways, switching on genes that make glucose while disrupting storage genes. Middle-to-large particles, roughly 150 to 200 nanometres across, switched on an intestinal sugar transporter gene, with the 150-nanometre size performing best in the reported tests. Tuning particle size could make functional feeds practical for bass farms.
pmc-13214435:
L. Zimniak and colleagues run a 2026 trial on whether smartwatch nagging gets bowel surgery patients moving sooner. Early walking after colorectal operations speeds recovery, yet patients in a traditional ward without a formal enhanced-recovery programme often stay in bed.

Sixty-two patients were randomised to hourly active reminders on a smartwatch or to passive step tracking alone, with everyone wearing a tracker. The reminded group took significantly more steps across the first five days and reported stronger motivation to move. Complications and hospital stay length did not differ between groups. Cheap wearable prompts, the authors conclude, can substitute for some missing programme structure after surgery.
pmc-13217435:
Hacer Alataş and co-authors present a 2026 cross-sectional study of how the antioxidant power of women's diets relates to inflammation and insulin resistance in polycystic ovary syndrome. In that condition all three problems intertwine.

The study compared 129 women with the syndrome against 135 matched controls. The syndrome group ate a diet with clearly lower total antioxidant capacity, scoring 11.8 against 14.3, while showing higher inflammatory markers and insulin resistance nearly double the control level. The models found that richer antioxidant intake was tied to lower insulin resistance both directly and through reduced inflammation. Syndrome status, inflammation, and low antioxidant intake each predicted worse insulin resistance on its own, backing antioxidant-rich diets as a management lever.
pmc-13218135:
Ling Ding and colleagues outline a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of subgroup claims in sepsis trials. Sepsis is life-threatening organ failure driven by a disordered response to infection, and immune-modulating drugs are a hopeful treatment family. Trial after trial has failed to show a benefit, partly because patients respond unevenly. That unevenness makes subgroup findings tempting but easy to overread.

The review will gather randomized trials of immunomodulatory drugs in adult sepsis, plus their published secondary analyses, searching five databases and trial registries. Four reviewers will screen studies independently, extracting one subgroup analysis per trial with standardized forms. Credibility of each claimed subgroup effect will be rated with a dedicated instrument for effect modification analyses. The team summarizes which drugs show differing effects across patient groups and pool effects where studies overlap. It will compare subgroup reporting between trials with significant main results and those without.
pmc-13218235:
Yue Pan and colleagues present a 2026 study on raising the projection contrast of an infrared scene projector. Such projectors display infrared scenes to test thermal imaging systems in the lab, a method called hardware-in-the-loop simulation. Diffraction from the mirrors of a digital micromirror device scatters light and washes out contrast, capping how demanding the test scenes can be.

Working with a dual-micromirror infrared optical engine, the team calculated the diffraction directions of the orders, aiming to use as much light as possible. They tuned a two-element prism group so light strikes at the angle the diffraction math requires. Tracing the stray beams from mirrors in the off state showed the irradiation stayed close to the level expected without diffraction. Bench tests matched the simulation results. The authors note the same contrast-boosting approach can be carried over to other devices built on micromirrors.
pmc-13219435:
Shreyas Indurkar, Betül Kayacik, Peng Liu, and Esther Kuehn ask where the brain files touch memories in a 2026 study. We recognize objects by feel and carry emotional touch memories, but their code was unresolved. Memory could be stored in body-centred coordinates, pinned to skin. Or it could sit in external coordinates merging touch with where the hand sits in space and what the eyes see.

Volunteers learned patterns delivered, then retrieved them with hands in the same posture or crossed over, and in matching or changed surroundings. If outside coordinates ran the system, crossing hands or shifting the scene should have hurt accuracy. Performance showed no such influence, fitting body-centred storage: the pattern is remembered on the body, not one in the room. The authors connect the result to experience, where memories in trauma and somatic symptoms stay tied to body sites instead of remapping outward.
pmc-13219935:
Seetha Radhakrishnan and colleagues, writing for a Canadian Society of Nephrology working group in 2026, examine how the 2025 KDIGO guideline on childhood nephrotic syndrome fits Canadian practice. Nephrotic syndrome is the commonest glomerular disease of childhood, a filter disorder that leaks protein into urine, and the guideline was refreshed. The working group paired its reading with a survey of pediatric kidney centres.

The group endorsed most of the recommendations and praised standardizing definitions of the disease and of treatment response, along with prednisone induction protocols. Two areas were flagged as muddy: how relapses should be treated, and which drug to choose for children who relapse frequently or depend on steroids to stay well. Canadian data informed the discussion. The authors are candid about one limitation: they did not grade the quality of proof behind the guideline, so the commentary is an applicability exercise rather than a re-appraisal.
pmc-13220835:
Javier Domínguez-Ortega and colleagues test whether sampling compartments sharpens the inflammatory fingerprint of severe asthma in the 2026 BRISA study. Sorting asthma by its inflammation type guides biologic therapy, and nasal cytology, scraping cells from the nose, would be a painless substitute for inducing sputum. Whether the nose mirrors the lower airways in severe disease was the open question.

Twenty-two patients with severe asthma gave nasal samples, induced sputum, and blood for inflammatory proteins, and were split by their blood eosinophil count. Patients with higher eosinophils had worse lung function, more exacerbations, and higher periostin levels. Only sixteen produced sputum, spanning eosinophilic, neutrophilic, mixed, and quiet patterns. Nasal cytology agreed weakly with the sputum pattern, while blood and sputum eosinophils tracked each other well. The authors conclude nasal sampling cannot replace sputum for phenotyping severe asthma, though it may add information beside blood markers.
pmc-13222635:
Zeyu Zeng and co-authors build an early warning model for severe Mycoplasma pneumonia in children, in a 2026 single-center records study from Shanghai Children's Hospital. Records covered 2,381 children treated between late 2019 and late 2023. A drug-resistance mutation common in this infection was tracked with clinical and laboratory features.

About seven in ten children developed severe disease, and nearly half carried the resistance mutation, which clustered in the severe group. A seven-measure model using fever duration and six blood measures predicted severity with strong accuracy. For carriers, early use of other antibiotics shortened hospital stays compared with waiting. The model could help doctors triage children sooner.
pmc-13226135:
Hirokazu Sawamura and colleagues present a 2026 case of stubborn lymph fluid leaking after groin lymph-node removal for melanoma in a 70-year-old woman. The usual fix requires injecting dye through a remaining lymph node, but none were left to puncture. A nuclear-medicine scan instead mapped two disrupted lymph pathways running beside major leg veins.

Guided by that map, the team punctured the fluid collections directly and sealed them with a medical glue mixture. The first sealing was not enough, because leakage persisted along the second pathway. Treating a small pouch there, which proved to connect with the drainage tube, stopped the external leak within several days. The case offers a fallback route when standard access is impossible.
pmc-13226535:
Alnaghaimshi and colleagues ask how mental health phone apps should be adapted for Arabic-speaking migrants in Australia. Apps could widen access to care, but only if their language, faith cues, and family values fit the people using them. Evidence to guide that design has been thin, so the team surveyed a community directly.

They gathered answers from 219 first-generation Arabic-speaking migrants, all recruited outside clinics. The survey covered views on mental health, how people seek health information online, and whether they would use a mental health app at all. The lessons feed design choices: wording, religious fit, privacy, and trust, before any app is offered as support.
pmc-13226835:
Shahin Seidi and colleagues survey a 2026 study of disease-carrying ticks gathered from farm animals in Kerman Province, south-east Iran. Ticks were collected in spring 2022 from 199 cattle, sheep, goats, and dogs across sixty-five villages. Laboratory DNA tests on 707 ticks hunted six groups of bacteria that ticks pass to animals and people.

Two tick species dominated the catch. Rickettsia bacteria appeared in over half the pooled samples, and sequencing named four species, several known to infect humans. Ehrlichia and the Q-fever agent Coxiella burnetii showed up at lower rates, while Bartonella was rare. Mixed infections occurred in a minority of pools, complicating diagnosis and control for local veterinary services.
pmc-13227635:
Bo Wang and Shin Kaneko review a 2026 laboratory programme that manufactures fresh T cells from induced pluripotent stem cells to replace exhausted ones in cancer and chronic infection. Their route began with reprogramming a patient's own T cells into stem cells and growing rejuvenated replacements. The review follows the shift toward donor-based, off-the-shelf products that any patient could receive.

Clinical-grade, animal-product-free manufacturing protocols anchor the practical side. Gene editing then tunes the cells: stronger internal signalling, removal of features that provoke rejection, and receptor designs that cut the risk of graft-versus-host disease. Parallel work grows regulatory T cells for autoimmune disease. Remaining hurdles are translation into routine clinical supply.
pmc-13229935:
George Gaskell and colleagues examine in 2026 whether new genomic techniques for crops can win public acceptance in Europe. Gene editing tools such as CRISPR promise faster breeding for drought tolerance, disease resistance, and better nutrition. Europe long rejected earlier genetic modification after heated public debate, so the reception for newer methods matters.

Media coverage, environmental group views, and opinion data now point to a fairly warm reception in most European countries. A two-tier rule agreed in late 2025 would treat small edits like normal breeding and keep stricter controls on larger changes. Openness about how plants are made is presented as the key to support. Fixed camps among campaigners or populist actors could still stall debate.
pmc-13230935:
Hossam Kotb and colleagues apply in 2026 a dingo-inspired search method to place solar and wind units in power grids. Adding local generators at the right spots and sizes can cut energy lost as heat during delivery. Two standard test grids were used, a small distribution network and a large meshed transmission network.

On the small grid, placed solar units cut active power losses by large shares under normal, light, and heavy loads. Voltage steadiness also improved, with the weakest buses rising well above danger levels. On the large grid, three solar units alone trimmed losses, and adding wind units helped more under heavy load. A dispatch rule for light load kept high renewable shares from hurting performance.
pmc-13232035:
Aboubakr Khazaz and colleagues chart in 2026 last-line drug resistance in urine infections caught outside hospitals in Morocco. Twelve cities contributed nearly thirteen hundred samples of the two bacteria that cause most urinary infections, collected across 2022 and 2023. Resistant samples then had their full genomes read to find the resistance machinery.

Resistance to carbapenem drugs ran far higher in Klebsiella than in E. coli samples. Klebsiella mostly carried enzyme genes that destroy the drugs, including several NDM variants and OXA-48. E. coli more often blocked drug entry or pumped the drugs back out. One global high-risk Klebsiella clone dominated the resistant set. Watching only hospital samples would miss this community spread entirely.
pmc-13232835:
Osita Sunday Nnyigide and colleagues simulate in 2026 how two common soaps pull apart a tiny folded protein that serves as a folding test case. The Trp-cage miniprotein is small, fast-folding, and well measured, which makes it a clean probe. Computer models compared a negatively charged soap with a positively charged one across heat and dose levels.

In plain water the protein sat folded at room temperature and spread out when heated. The negative soap invaded its oily core directly, gathering around it and prying the fold open. The positive soap touched it more weakly, and at high dose its clumps even sheltered the folded shape from heat. Charge and dose decide whether a soap unfolds or protects, a rule useful for drug and detergent design.
pmc-13233335:
Elisa Cantone and colleagues published a 2026 survey study, written in English, on how users of mental health services in Sardinia, Italy judged their care during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Italy's community mental health system grew out of the Basaglia reform, which closed asylums in favor of local services. The team surveyed 118 service users in 2025 and compared answers with a 2021 pandemic-era survey of 200 users.

Overall satisfaction with care stayed very high in both rounds. Perceived respect for users' rights and for staff rights rose after the pandemic, and views of resource adequacy improved as well, though resources remained the weakest area. The authors read the results as evidence that community-based services protected dignity even under pandemic strain.
pmc-13233735:
Cihan Çelik, Fahad Mirre, and İsmail Gedi İbrahim published a 2026 case report of a three-year-old with semilobar holoprosencephaly. In this birth defect, the front part of the brain fails to divide fully into two hemispheres. The child showed seizures, feeding trouble, slow development, and midline facial differences. The mother had poorly controlled diabetes during pregnancy, a known risk factor for this malformation.

Brain MRI showed partly fused frontal lobes and a single fluid cavity. The thalami were partly fused too, and a membrane that should split the two halves was missing. The authors stress that imaging children with developmental delay and neurological symptoms can reveal such malformations early. Recognition shapes follow-up care and helps clinicians guide the family about what to expect.
pmc-13236935:
Mayuko Kawabe and colleagues cut tiny regions from tonsil tissue in 2026 to study IgA nephropathy, a kidney disease driven by misdirected antibody production. Tonsil removal helps some patient groups more than others, hinting that tonsil immune geography differs. The team compared tonsils from five patients with matched samples from five people with habitual tonsillitis.

Inside the germinal centers, the busy zones where antibody cells mature, patient tissue showed a clear rise in a marker called KLRG1. Staining placed that marker inside the centers, most strongly in patients whose kidney biopsies showed crescent-shaped damage. The groups were tiny, so the authors call the pattern a hypothesis. Still, the spatial detail points at where a harmful immune response may be organized.
pmc-13237335:
Khalid B Saleem and colleagues simulated heat flow in 2026 inside a porous, wavy-walled cavity holding a hot star-shaped obstacle, using a hybrid nanofluid of water carrying copper and aluminum oxide particles. Engineers care about such enclosures for solar collectors and reactor cooling. Finite-element runs varied the star's lobe count, flow strength, porosity, and particle loading, and a neural network then searched for the best design.

One trade-off dominated: heat transfer could not rise without entropy generation rising too. The best balance came with a nearly plain obstacle and no nanoparticles at all, under gentle flow. Lobes and particle loading tended to add entropy faster than they added heat transfer. The authors say neural-network optimization can trim irreversibility losses in nanofluid heat exchangers.
pmc-13238535:
Hatem M. Taha and colleagues reported in 2026 a 17-year-old boy with trichohepatoenteric syndrome, a rare inherited disorder causing intractable diarrhea from infancy, woolly hair, and distinctive facial features. After an intestinal amoeba infection, his diarrhea worsened sharply, with exhaustion, weight loss, and stomach pain. His history already stretched beyond the gut.

Over the years he had accumulated recurrent bone inflammation, a fluid cavity in the spinal cord, and bowel inflammation that answered poorly to standard therapy. Antibody tests suggested celiac disease without biopsy proof, muddying the picture further. The authors argue that infections can trigger flares in this syndrome and that its spectrum runs wider than the classic description. Adolescent survivors, they note, need watching for these extraintestinal turns.
pmc-13241435:
Nagler, Zach, and Pock rebuild MRI scans with a diffusion model small enough to stay interpretable. Most diffusion priors are huge black boxes needing pre-estimated coil maps. Their prior multiplies compact Gaussian-mixture experts instead. Image and coil sensitivities are reconstructed jointly, the coils under a smoothness prior.

The method stayed fast and robust when contrast, anatomy, or scan trajectory shifted. A richer parameterization of the prior then improved both denoising and reconstruction quality. No offline coil calibration is needed, freeing acquisition setups. Nagler's team presents it as a leaner route to generative MRI reconstruction.
pmc-13241535:
Brücker and colleagues at Göttingen identify the transcription factor MSX1 as a driver of cervical cancer growth. The homeobox protein guides tissue development, and its cancer role has swung between suppressor and promoter. Healthy cervical lining showed no MSX1 at all. The protein showed anew in precancerous lesions, prompting a closer look.

Cancer cell lines expressing MSX1 formed colonies more readily and migrated faster. The protein switched on an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition program tied to spread. Sequencing pointed to cytoskeletal control pathways and the effector FOS as partners. Blocking both the RHO pathway and FOS control fully undid the aggressive behavior.
pmc-13243135:
Jinyu Lai and co-authors present a 2026 study of a new needle method for easing knee pain from osteoarthritis. Standard heat treatment of knee nerves leaves some nerves untouched, so pain often stays partly in place. Their three-in-one method reaches three nerve branches through one entry point.

The team reviewed 57 patients treated at Taihe Hospital, with 30 getting the new method and 27 the standard one. Pain scores fell in both groups, and the new method group scored lower at one, three, and six months. No severe side effects appeared in either group. At six months, 93 percent of the new method group felt pleased with the result, against 74 percent for the standard group.
pmc-13243335:
Amy Siobhan Millard, Irene Sperandio, and Philippe Chouinard tested a tool so routine in vision labs that nobody questions it: the fixation point. Their study appeared in Attention, Perception and Psychophysics in 2026. Volunteers judged the size and distance of real objects and of afterimages, with and without a central marker to hold their gaze. The two stimulus types differ sharply in how much depth information they carry.

The marker slightly improved size constancy for both kinds of stimulus, backing its reputation as a gaze stabilizer. Distance judgments told a split story: real objects were judged just as steadily either way, while afterimages grew erratic when the marker appeared. Links between focusing ability and size errors hint the marker also frees viewers from relying on eye-muscle signals. The authors warn that a supposedly neutral method choice can bend results for ambiguous stimuli.
pmc-13245035:
Shengnan Du and co-authors reviewed a quarter-century of work on biosensors in traditional Chinese medicine research. Their systematic review appeared in Chinese Medicine in 2026. Biosensors pair a biological recognition element with a physical reader to detect chosen molecules fast and sharply. Searching four databases for studies from 2001 to 2025, the team mapped where these devices now serve herbal medicine and where they stall.

The applications are broad: telling herb varieties apart, measuring and screening active components, hunting drug targets, and quantifying how tightly compounds bind them. Sensors also serve quality control and safety testing of herbal products. The newest gains come from miniaturization, integrated micro-devices, and smarter data processing. Limits remain in stability and real-sample messiness. The authors pitch biosensors as the bridge Chinese medicine needs between a herb's chemistry and its proven effects, the link that could move evaluation from tradition toward measurement.
pmc-13245235:
Antonia Cattle and co-authors survey machine learning across sport in a 2026 scoping review. Teams now use learning models for performance gains, injury control, and selection choices. The review maps where the tools are used and how well they serve real users.

The team charted 270 peer-reviewed studies from 2002 to 2024. Uses spread across 12 broad areas, led by computing, biomechanics, and sport psychology. Action recognition, injury prediction, and talent spotting were the top tasks. Models often scored well yet stumbled on messy data, unclear logic, and hard access for coaches. The authors argue the tools should back human judgment, never swap it out.
pmc-13246635:
Saad Alhumaid and a large team review how long hives tied to viral infection can last in a 2026 systematic review. Viruses commonly trigger sudden hives in children and adults. Whether the rash can drag on, turn chronic, or keep returning was poorly mapped.

Five studies with 596 people met the rules after a search through March 2026. Most cases settled within weeks to a few months of the infection. A small share lasted past six months, and a few past a year. Return and chronic rates ranged widely across studies, though many mixes blurred the infection-only picture. The authors ask for cleaner long-term tracking.
pmc-13246735:
Djaballah and co-authors are the subject of this 2026 retraction note in Scientific Reports: their paper has been retracted. The original article, published in 2024, had proposed a hybrid machine learning model, mixing an LSTM network, a random forest. Grey wolf optimization, to detect multiple faults in machine bearings from vibration data.

After publication, concerns were raised about odd vocabulary and inconsistencies in how the paper described its data, analysis steps, and results. The editors asked for explanations plus the underlying data and code; what the authors supplied did not resolve the problems, so the editors withdrew confidence in the article. Two authors disagreed with the retraction, and three did not respond to the editors.
pmc-13247835:
Chong, Partovi, and McCurry piloted a self-directed online exercise program for anxious older adults in this 2026 BJPsych Open feasibility study. Twenty-one participants aged forty to seventy-seven with clinically significant anxiety used the ExTRA platform for eight weeks: anxiety education, exercise programs, goal-setting strategies. A wearable activity monitor feeding their progress back to them.

Every participant stayed to the end, and acceptability ratings were high. Objectively measured activity rose: daily steps climbed by well over a thousand and active minutes grew substantially, both with moderate effect sizes. Anxiety scores fell by an amount that just missed statistical significance, while stress and depression scores dropped significantly. The authors judge the automated, scalable format feasible and ready for a full randomized trial.
pmc-13248035:
Ranjan, Jain, and Panwar followed kidney injury in critically ill patients with tropical fevers, in this 2026 World Journal of Critical Care Medicine study. In a Rajasthan teaching hospital's intensive care unit during the 2025 monsoon season, they enrolled sixty-eight adults whose laboratory-confirmed tropical febrile illness came with acute kidney injury, recording severity, organ support, and whether kidneys recovered by discharge.

Scrub typhus caused nearly two thirds of cases. Mortality was modest, but many survivors left with incompletely recovered kidneys. Early low oxygen, overall illness severity, and needing dialysis predicted the worst outcomes. The authors argue that judging these patients by creatinine-based kidney staging alone misses the real risk, and that comprehensive severity assessment should guide care in tropical intensive care units.
pmc-13250335:
Milad Dodangeh and co-authors describe a dangerous self-harm case in this 2026 report. A 27-year-old man deliberately swallowed nine razor blades and a full table fork, objects spread across different parts of his gut, raising the risk of tearing and bleeding.

X-rays and scans showed the fork, about 19 centimetres long, stretching from his lower gullet into his stomach, with the blades further down in the small bowel. Pulling them out through the mouth was judged unsafe. Surgeons opened both stomach and bowel under X-ray guidance and removed everything. He recovered well, and mental health follow-up was arranged.
pmc-13250435:
Baur and co-authors compare operations that stabilize athletes' shoulders after repeated forward dislocations. Their 2026 Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine review pools nineteen studies covering about eighteen hundred fifty athletes, mostly young men in contact or overhead sports. The main question was how many athletes fully return to sport after each procedure.

Across all operations, about four in five athletes returned fully to sport, while one in ten stopped altogether. The Bristow-Latarjet procedure, which adds a bone block to the socket, beat Bankart soft-tissue repair on full return rates. The authors note the operations were not offered to identical patients, which clouds direct comparison. Even so, the bone procedure looks strongest for demanding athletes in this evidence.
pmc-13250835:
Anil Kumar presents an Ayurvedic surgical technique for a hard fistula case in this 2026 case study. A 40-year-old man had a returning horseshoe-shaped anal fistula at the front, a complex tunnel pattern where standard surgery risks scarring and loss of bowel control.

The method used, called IFTAK, intercepts the tunnel and threads it with a medicated alkaline thread that cuts and heals tissue slowly while sparing the muscle ring. Checks included finger exam, scope view, dye test, and probing to map the tracts. The fistula healed fully with no return at eight months. The author reports shorter hospital stay and treatment time than older methods.
pmc-13251035:
Zeid and co-authors clean metal-polluted irrigation water with magnetic nanoparticles and rice straw charcoal, then test the water on alfalfa. Their 2026 BMC Plant Biology study targets lead, cadmium, and nickel, which build up in crops past safe limits. Both sorbents are cheap and plant-friendly by design.

The salicylic-acid coated iron nanoparticles removed nearly all lead and cadmium at low contamination levels, and most of the nickel. Charcoal from carbonized rice straw also stripped lead efficiently from the water. Metal stress alone slashed germination and growth and raised damage markers in seedlings. Water cleaned by either sorbent largely reversed that harm, lifting germination above even the clean-water control in one test. The authors recommend both materials for low-cost water cleanup.
pmc-13252735:
Geronimo Bejarano and co-authors test whether easier access to physical therapy cuts opioid use in this 2026 policy study. Many United States states have let patients see a physical therapist directly, without a doctor's referral, a change rolled out at different times.

Comparing states that adopted direct access between 2006 and 2014 with those that did not, the team tracked opioid pill shipments and opioid deaths. After adoption, pill volume fell by about 15 percent relative to control states. Opioid deaths, however, showed no clear difference. The authors argue that referral barriers push patients toward pills, and removing them improves population health even if deaths take longer to move.
pmc-13252835:
Yue Pan and a large team examine kidney disease in people with HIV in this 2026 cohort study from the United States. Kidney disease is common in this group, and both depression and kidney-straining medicines might sit on the path from HIV to kidney damage.

Data came from a long-running combined cohort of men and women, with 2,530 participants at the baseline visit. Kidney disease was nearly twice as common in people with HIV, at about 18 percent versus ten percent. HIV status and use of kidney-straining medicines each raised risk over follow-up visits. The team also tested whether depression or those medicines carried part of HIV's effect.
pmc-13253935:
Amirsajad Jafari, Fatemeh Shams, and Elina Khanehzar propose a new cancer idea in a 2026 article. Cancer often returns because spread tumor cells go dormant, stop dividing, and later wake up. The authors suggest copying the gene-control patterns of hibernation, such as DNA methylation and histone changes, to lock spread cells in dormancy. They coin the name dormostatics for such drugs. A roadmap and open questions are laid out, but the idea is a proposal, not a tested treatment.
pmc-13254235:
Keita Yanagisawa and colleagues report a rare lymphoma presentation in a 2026 case report. An 87-year-old woman with past tuberculosis developed fast-progressing leg paralysis. Scans showed chronic pyothorax, a long-standing pus-filled chest space, with a mass pressing on her spinal cord.

A biopsy confirmed pyothorax-associated lymphoma, an EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that grows in such chronic chest disease. She and her family declined surgery, so she received steroids and two cycles of R-CHOP chemotherapy. No nerve recovery followed. The authors urge early MRI and biopsy when patients with chronic pyothorax develop new nerve signs.
pmc-13254335:
Jonas Hosp and a large team introduce a brain mapping method in a 2026 study. Neurodegenerative diseases harm both gray matter and the long white-matter paths that link brain areas. Their streamline-wise method, yielding what they call a degenerome, maps axon loss along about 20,000 fiber paths from diffusion MRI scans.

Groups included Alzheimer's disease with 81 patients, Parkinson's with 177, and two rarer diseases, plus 26 healthy controls. Each disease showed a distinct fiber pattern matching known anatomy, such as limbic paths in Alzheimer's. The patterns separated the diseases and allowed single-patient views.
pmc-13255635:
Zhuoqun Li and colleagues report a 2026 study building a gene signature from the extracellular matrix, the scaffolding around cells, in diffuse glioma brain tumors. Survival in these tumors stays poor despite surgery and drug treatment, and the matrix's role had been unclear. The team started from 27 matrix-related genes gathered from the literature.

Statistical selection narrowed the list to a six-gene signature that predicted patient survival across three separate cohorts. Tumors with dense matrix features also carried heavy infiltration by exhausted immune cells, an immunosuppressive picture. Tissue staining from a Beijing hospital supported the computational findings. The authors offer the signature as a prognostic tool and a clue that the matrix helps shield gliomas from immune attack.
pmc-13256035:
Jian Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 study of why some Tibetan sows fail to come back into heat after weaning their piglets. The delay, scored as the weaning-to-estrus interval, cuts breeding success head-on. The team set sows that cycled on time against those that stayed in anestrus, profiling hormones, immune markers, gut microbes, and blood metabolites.

Anestrus sows showed out-of-balance reproductive hormones and a shifted immune state. Their gut microbe groups and metabolic profiles also stood apart from the cycling group. Stats linked gut microbes and their products to hormone and metabolic pathways, hinting they may steer recovery. The authors offer the gut-metabolite-endocrine axis as a new lens on sow fertility, with payoffs for breeding and managing this high-altitude pig breed.
pmc-13256635:
Maria Clara Gama de Souza Silva and co-authors review in 2026 how oxidative stress and gut–skin axis imbalance contribute to immune-mediated skin diseases such as psoriasis and atopic dermatitis. Their narrative review looks past inflammation alone to the chemical damage and microbial shifts that help drive these chronic conditions.

The gut and skin microbiomes also lose bacteria that produce helpful short-chain fatty acids. The authors argue that pairing redox and microbial profiling could sort patients into clearer groups and guide more tailored treatment choices.
pmc-13256935:
Elisa Bisconti and colleagues report a 2026 cell study of a beetroot leaf extract tested on human skin cells. Healthy skin depends on balanced fats in its outer layer. The extract came from leaves grown in controlled bioreactors, which keeps its makeup steady.

Treated keratinocytes, the main cells of the outer skin, showed lower levels of reactive oxygen species, a form of chemical stress. pmc-13257035:
Tu and co-authors profiled phenolic compounds in the fruit and peel of three wampee varieties using targeted metabolomics. They compared total phenolic levels, screened for compounds that set the varieties apart, and mapped the pathways behind the gaps. The aim was a chemical basis for telling varieties apart and judging their health value.

One variety led total phenolics in fruit, while another's peel ranked highest. Twelve fruit and nine peel compounds stood out as markers, and several antioxidant, antibacterial phenolics rose in two varieties compared with the leader. Fruit gaps centered on phenylpropanoid and flavone pathways; peel gaps on flavonoid routes. The results support variety naming and breeding choices.
pmc-13257235:
Aktura and a mixed team asked how many hospital clinic visits could have stayed in primary care. Each panel mixed a dermatologist, a family physician, and a general practitioner. Agreement between panels was scored.

Just over half the cases were judged workable in primary care, a quarter directly by a family physician and the rest with teledermatology support. Children were slightly more workable this way than adults, though panels agreed less on pediatric cases. Acne, dermatitis, and surface fungal infections were most common. Few patients had seen a family doctor first, pointing to referral habits worth changing.
pmc-13257835:
Hao Li and co-authors model magnetic polishing for rough internal channels in printed metal parts in a 2026 study. Magnetic abrasive finishing adapts to such shapes, so its removal physics were formalized.

Two wear modes, rolling and sliding, were modeled with rough-surface contact theory and correction factors. Experiments on printed aluminum channels in a combined magnetic field setup checked the math. The process cut defects and roughness as predicted, with gaps blamed on model idealization and uneven fields. Manufacturing engineers gain a systematic theory for a finishing method that industry uses by feel. Predictable removal brings printed cooling channels closer to flight and medical standards.
pmc-13258335:
Heyi Guo and colleagues examined a failed bubble tube pulled from a glass curing furnace. The Inconel 690 tube had spent years bathed in molten glass hotter than a thousand degrees, with gas bubbling through it. Their 2026 failure analysis asks why the metal wasted away unevenly.

Along the outer wall, a chromium-rich oxide skin formed, then tore away where flowing glass scoured hardest. The side facing the bubble flow corroded at more than twice the rate of the calmer side. Each scouring round exposed fresh metal to oxidize again, speeding the cycle. Their findings guide material choices and lifetime estimates for furnace parts.
pmc-13258535:
Fnu Samiksha and coauthors review fungal cell wall sugars called beta glucans in a 2026 article on gut and immune health. Immune sensors on cell surfaces recognize these sugars and switch on defense activity. Eaten glucans also feed gut microbes, which then produce helpful short chain fatty acids.

Evidence links the compounds to support in bowel inflammation, metabolic problems, lung infections, and cancer care. In cancer settings they may strengthen antibody drugs and vaccines. Uneven sources and formulas make human trial results hard to compare. Few large, well standardized trials exist so far. Readers see both the promise and the proof still needed before routine medical use.
pmc-13259135:
Yifeng Huang, Xikang Lu, and Daode Zhang monitor cutting tool wear across changing machine settings in a 2026 study. Vibration and spindle current signals were fused as multi channel inputs. A deep model with attention read those signals for wear states.

Training moved in stages from source settings to target settings with few labeled examples. Fusing three signal channels beat single and dual channel inputs clearly. Repeated tests with random restarts confirmed the advantage held steady. Competing adaptation methods trailed the staged approach on their custom dataset. Factory engineers gain a wear monitor that survives setting changes without full retraining.
pmc-13259435:
Ziheng Xia and colleagues fuse physics with deep learning to recognize aircraft from radar echoes. A high-resolution range profile compresses a target into a one-dimensional signature of peaks. Purely data-driven networks read it well but stumble in noise and explain little. Their 2026 model runs two branches in parallel.

One branch learns features straight from the raw profile, while the other estimates the peaks' positions and strengths explicitly. Cross-attention blends the two views before the verdict. On measured ten-class aircraft data, the fused model classified more accurately and held up better under added noise. Its peaks lined up with real energy hotspots, keeping decisions interpretable.
pmc-13259535:
Maialen Vázquez-Polo and coauthors teach primary school children about celiac disease in a 2026 education study. Nearly three hundred pupils aged ten to twelve in northern Spain joined the month long program or a regular curriculum control. Eight inquiry based sessions covered the disease and gluten free eating.

Knowledge scores rose clearly in the program group and held one month later. Pupils explained the disease better, judged gluten content, and sorted foods correctly more often. Inclusive behavior choices also improved at follow up. Pupils additionally reported understanding scientist work better. Schools gain a tested program that builds empathy for classmates with dietary disease.
pmc-13259735:
Alshimaa S. Othman and coauthors compare premenstrual symptoms and coping in women with menstrual migraine in a 2026 study. Six hundred one women were classed by diary records across at least three cycles. Headache impact, symptom screening, and coping questionnaires supplied the measures.

Menstrual migraine patients scored higher on both symptom severity and headache impact. The severe mood disorder form appeared somewhat more often in that group, though the gap missed significance. Having that diagnosis added several points to headache impact scores in adjusted models. Lower awareness and acceptance coping also tracked with heavier headache burden. Neurologists gain targets for combined cycle and migraine care.
pmc-13260035:
Stephany Rocha Ribeiro leads a 2026 study of tick- and parasite-borne germs in free-living opossums in São Paulo State, Brazil. Blood samples came from 115 opossums of two species, ninety-five white-eared and twenty black-eared opossums. The team used microscope checks and DNA tests to look for three groups of pathogens: Babesia, Hepatozoon, and Ehrlichia. Positive samples were sequenced and placed on family trees to identify them.

Five samples, or 4.35 percent, tested positive for Babesia, all from white-eared opossums collected in Botucatu. Two samples, or 1.74 percent, were positive for Ehrlichia, and no Hepatozoon DNA was found. The sequences matched known South American marsupial strains closely, in one case exactly. The authors call this the first molecular detection of both germs in this opossum species in Botucatu, and urge continued surveillance.
pmc-13260335:
Eike Matthias Wacker and co-authors present a 2026 software study of TOFU-MAaPO, a pipeline for large metagenome datasets. A metagenome is the combined genetic material of a microbial community. Over 600,000 metagenomes sit in public archives such as the Sequence Read Archive, but shared, repeatable analysis tools are lacking. Their single-command pipeline cleans raw reads, assembles genomes, and annotates them, working on local files or pulling data straight from the archive.

In benchmarks against three existing pipelines, the new workflow produced twelve percent, and forty-two to seventy-seven percent, more high-quality assembled genomes, depending on the rival tool. In a large test run, it pulled down 16,462 human gut metagenome samples and classified them against a standard naming database in under fifty-five hours on a cluster of machines. The tool is free online for research groups.
pmc-13260535:
Grigorios Thermos and co-authors present a 2026 case series of cocaine-induced plasma cell dermatomucositis, an emerging inflammatory condition with ulcerated, nodular lesions around the nose and lips. The series looked back at six patients from two United Kingdom pathology archives. Records, medical photographs, and tissue reports were reviewed to define its features and rule out other diseases. Cocaine exposure was confirmed in every case by history or toxicology testing.

The group had five men and one woman, with a mean age of 50.3 years at diagnosis. Patients typically showed raised, ulcerated masses in the nasolabial area. Tissue analysis in every case found dense collections of plasma cells, a type of immune cell, grouped around vessels. Medical and surgical treatments generally brought partial improvement. The authors, in the first UK series, urge thorough clinic and tissue correlation because the condition mimics common lesions.
pmc-13261535:
Elysia Grose and colleagues present a 2026 prospective study of smell outcomes after endoscopic sinus surgery for chronic sinus inflammation with nasal polyps. Loss of smell is a hard-to-treat symptom in this condition. The team measured outcomes with both a symptom questionnaire and an odor identification test.

The single-center study enrolled 36 adults operated on between July 2022 and May 2024; 45% were female and the mean age was 48. Mean SNOT-22 symptom scores fell from 57 before surgery to 22, 15, and 25 at 1, 3, and 6 months. Odor identification improved from 5.2 of 16 odors to 7.9, 8.3, and 7.7 at the same visits. Improvements were statistically significant at every follow-up. The authors conclude surgery can meaningfully improve smell, while noting longer studies must test whether gains last.
pmc-13263035:
Lingbo Liu examines whether hospital telehealth volume tracks with artificial intelligence adoption in a 2026 journal article. Telehealth and AI are both signs of digital change, but their link was unclear. The study covered 6,173 United States acute care hospitals, using national survey and cost data to sort hospitals into three AI adoption tiers for clinical and office work.

pmc-13263335:

pmc-13263535:

pmc-13263735:

pmc-13264035:

pmc-13264135:

pmc-13264235:

pmc-13264335:

pmc-13264635:

pmc-13264835:

pmc-13264935:

pmc-13266035:

pmc-13266135:

pmc-13267035:

pmc-13267535:

pmc-13267835:

pmc-13268435:

pmc-13268935:

pmc-13269035:

pmc-13270635:

pmc-13271435:

pmc-13272035:

pmc-13272335:

pmc-13274235:

pmc-13278235:

pmc-13278735:

pmc-13278835:

pmc-13279435:

pmc-13280735:

But it grew from stray spit gland tissue outside the gland itself, a very rare spot.
