Surgeons took the lump out, and lab checks confirmed the tumor type. The authors say careful scans before surgery can spare patients a wider operation than they need.
pmc-13281335:
Alaa Elsaghir and colleagues reviewed gut germs and joint disease in a 2026 paper. The disease group, called spondyloarthritis, causes pain in the spine and joints and can affect skin and eyes. Gut germ mixes are off balance in many patients. The review asks whether that imbalance helps the immune system turn on the body. It centers on two forms of the disease, one of the spine and one tied to scaly skin.

The authors lay out four paths the gut could drive the attack. Germs may spark a feisty immune arm, mimic body proteins, loosen the gut wall, or send changed chemical signals. Certain self-attack proteins in patients fit those paths. But direct proof in people is still thin, and studies clash. Gut-based cures, like added good germs, remain a research hope, not a proven care.
pmc-13282235:
Bruno Calsa and co-authors report a 2026 mouse study on how low protein intake during pregnancy affects tooth development in offspring. The focus is autophagy, the cell process that breaks down and recycles worn parts. Pregnant mice were fed normal or low protein diets. Their embryos' molar tooth germs, the early buds that form teeth, were checked at three growth stages.

At the earliest bud stage, low protein changed the mix of recycling sacs in two tooth tissues, in opposite directions. Later stages showed shifts in waste-clearing markers in the enamel organ and dental papilla. The bud stage was hit hardest, with slower cell growth and more cell death. The authors suggest low protein blocks or delays the acid step that lets cells reuse their parts, which could disturb how teeth form.
pmc-13283135:
Pregnancy checks based on embryo signal genes lose accuracy after embryo transfer, Japanese Black cattle data from Hitomi Yoshino show in 2026. The test reads genes switched on by a signal from the early embryo. It works well after mating by insemination, but transfer of embryos may differ.

Blood gene levels were checked on days 19 and 21 after embryo transfer. Pregnant cows showed higher gene levels than open cows on day 21. No clear gap appeared on day 19 in this setting. Accuracy was lower than after insemination, above all on day 19. The authors suggest that reasons for failed conception differ by method. Early use of the test after transfer needs caution.
pmc-13283435:
Yellow islands under the dermatoscope hint at skin-only Rosai-Dorfman disease in Maha El Maati's 2026 Moroccan case. The disease is a rare growth of immune cells, usually in lymph nodes. Skin-only disease mimics many other conditions and is hard to spot.

The patient had a growing violet tumor on the back of her thigh for two years. Skin scope views showed blank yellow areas with fine surface vessels in the lesion. Tissue tests showed large immune cells swallowing other cells, a hallmark sign. Full body checks found no disease beyond the skin site. The lump was cut out, with no return at six months. Yellow scope signs may guide diagnosis in darker skin.
pmc-13283635:
Casey Kuka and a large team searched the genome in 2026 for variants tied to knee ligament tears in two ancestry groups. The anterior cruciate ligament is among the most common serious knee injuries in children. Genome-wide scans compare hundreds of thousands of DNA markers between injured and uninjured people to spot risk regions.

The African ancestry cohort held 108 injured cases and 1,080 controls, while the European cohort held 232 cases and 2,320 controls. Thousands of markers passed the study's signal cut-off in each group. Three genes linked to odd kneecap shape, GMNN, RREB1, and TBC1D7, stood out in both cohorts. A risk score built from European markers behaved differently across groups, underlining that genetic risk tools may not transfer cleanly between populations.
pmc-13283735:
Skin clinics in central Kerala were the setting for a 2026 pilot study by Jerene Mathews and colleagues on a hidden drug side effect. Dapsone, a common skin drug, can alter blood oxygen carriage and cause vague symptoms. Formal proof needs blood gas testing that clinics rarely run for outpatients.

Of 41 patients given the drug over 18 months, 28 returned while on it and joined the review. Tiredness, breathlessness on effort, and headache are typical warning clues for the problem. Finger oxygen readings plus symptom checks formed the simple screen under study. The pilot maps how often signs appear and sets up a larger proof study. Early spotting can spare needless tests.
pmc-13284135:
Na Zhu and Chaihong Zhang mapped the research literature in 2026 on immune checkpoint inhibitors for endometrial cancer, a common womb cancer. Checkpoint drugs release brakes on immune cells so they can attack tumours. Using bibliometric methods on two databases, the team charted papers from 2015 to 2024, counting who publishes, where, and on what themes.

One database held 829 papers across 296 journals from 63 countries, and the other held 279. The United States, China, and Italy led output, and the strongest partnership ran between the United States and England. Hot topics included mismatch repair deficiency, the PD-1 and PD-L1 markers, and drugs such as pembrolizumab and dostarlimab. One author and one cancer centre stood out as most influential.
pmc-13284235:
A RISC-V security chip add-on for internet devices is designed by Mohamed Niazy and colleagues in 2026. Connected devices face growing, smarter cyber attacks with tight power budgets. Their co-processor speeds cipher work while staying flexible across algorithms.

A generic port lets cipher blocks plug in without changing core instructions. Blocks run in parallel, and memory moves bypass the main pipeline for speed. The design was built and verified on a Xilinx FPGA board. Encryption throughput reached multi-gigabit rates for the AES block tested. Hashing ran slower, as expected for that algorithm class. Efficiency suits small connected devices.
pmc-13284435:
Mahmood Manshori and co-authors compare two stem cell sources for lung injury after heart failure in a 2026 rat study. Lung damage often follows heart failure through swelling, low oxygen, and weak heart function. Twenty male Wistar rats had a heart attack induced by artery tying, then got menstrual blood cells, bone marrow cells, or a control fluid by vein.

Menstrual blood cells improved heart pumping more than bone marrow cells and cut lung injury and cell death scores in the treated rats. Both cell types reduced lung scarring and a key swelling marker, but only menstrual blood cells lowered iNOS levels. The authors conclude these cells protected lungs through anti-swelling, anti-death, and anti-scarring effects in this model.
pmc-13284735:
Takuro Makiura and co-authors present a 2026 surgical case report after a failed catheter repair of the mitral valve. An 87-year-old man had a MitraClip placed eight months earlier for severe leakage, then worsened four months ago when the clip held only one leaflet. Echo scans showed the loose hold at the P1 segment.

At open surgery, the clip and stuck leaflet tissue were removed as one block, since fibrous cover makes late solo removal hard. The defect was patched, new artificial chords were added, and a ring was placed, ending the leakage. The authors note repair can suit rear leaflet cases, but plans must fit leaflet shape and clip site.
pmc-13285035:
Christian Tague and co-authors give a 2026 narrative review on vaccines as a tool to prevent cancer before it starts. Infections with some viruses and bacteria cause up to fifteen percent of cancers worldwide, with the heaviest load in poorer countries. Shots against human papillomavirus and hepatitis B virus lead the current effort.

HPV shots cut infections, pre-cancer growths, and, over time, invasive cancers, with best gains when given early at high coverage. Wide hepatitis B shots have cut chronic infection and liver cancer, as seen in Taiwan and The Gambia. Barriers stay steep: cost, supply, culture, and missed birth doses. New shots for other agents are in growth, aided by mRNA methods.
pmc-13285635:
Spread breast cancer has turned into a long-term illness for a growing band of women. Virginia González with fellow experts lay out whole-person care advice for Spain in a 2026 opinion piece. Better drugs now stretch response for years, creating patients whose cancer stays quiet while treatment rolls on. Oncologists and primary care doctors wrote the guidance together.

Advice covers sticking with therapy and handling side effects early. It also covers catching spread signs fast and juggling other ills and drug clashes. Mind support, healthy habits, and tight teamwork between cancer and primary teams run through every page. Sharing follow-up with primary care, the experts say, guards both life quality and treatment gains.
pmc-13285735:
Anthony Yii and co-authors review chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in Singapore in a 2026 survey of current evidence. The lung disease is often missed or treated late there, even with strong health services in place. Their review covers how common the disease is, who faces the highest risk, and how care is changing.

Smoking remains the main cause, but cases tied to past tuberculosis, biomass smoke, and allergens are now better known. Most patients show up with moderate to severe disease plus heart disease, diabetes, or airway damage, and hospital stays drive much of the cost. Care rests on quitting smoking, rehab, and inhaled drugs, yet flare-ups persist for many. A biologic drug approved in Singapore in 2025 adds an option for patients with high eosinophil counts.
pmc-13285935:
Fang Cheng and co-authors link blood levels of the leukemia drug flumatinib to results in a 2026 drug monitoring study. The drug, made in China, blocks the faulty signal that drives chronic myeloid leukemia in its chronic phase. Patients vary a lot in response and side effects, so the team asked whether drug levels in blood explain part of that spread.

Higher peak levels two hours after a dose came with deeper responses at the gene level, in first-line and later-line care alike. Cut points drawn from the data marked the level tied to major response and the higher level tied to deep response. Gut side effects also tracked with levels, with diarrhea tied to high trough readings and sickness tied to high peaks. The authors frame the cut points as early guides for dose tuning, pending proof in planned trials.
pmc-13286735:
Annie J DiFrank and a large team hunt liver cancer warning marks in blood DNA in a 2026 biomarker study. Imprinting control regions carry methylation set early in life and stable across tissues, making blood a plausible window on liver risk. Genome-wide scanning of white-cell DNA from 10 cancer patients and 51 controls flagged suspect regions, and a purpose-built array retested them in fresh groups of 29 patients and 36 controls.

The scan found 1,519 differently methylated regions tied to cancer, mapping to 81 candidate control regions, most never linked to this cancer before. The validation array confirmed over half of those it retested. Nearby genes clustered in pathways for liver swelling, hepatitis, fat buildup, and cancer itself. The authors propose these stable marks as candidates for a blood panel that triages high-risk patients earlier.
pmc-13286835:
ShaoXiang Yuan and co-authors review a cell change that may help drive skin scarring. Their 2026 review covers skin fibrosis, where skin grows thick and stiff from long-term swelling, injury, or immune attack. In the change at issue, surface cells lose their traits. They take on traits of the cells that build scar tissue.

Scarred skin piles up stiff fibers and loses its stretch. Work grows hard and life quality drops. Proof now links the cell change to this build-up. How much of the scar it explains, next to the skin's own scar cells, is still not clear. The review maps the signals that drive the change and flags drug targets for future work.
pmc-13286935:
Huasheng Xu and co-authors report two young patients whose tooth roots grew in odd shapes after regenerative treatment meant to restart root growth. The 2026 paper describes immature teeth with dead pulp caused by an extra bump on the chewing surface, treated with procedures that invite the root to keep developing. Both cases were followed for four years.

Instead of straight, even growth, one root curved and another formed in separate segments. A literature review explored why, pointing at prior inflammation and braces worn during healing as possible influences. The teeth themselves did well clinically. Dentists, the authors warn, should expect that even successful regeneration can leave an unusual root shape.
pmc-13287135:
Jhommara Bautista and co-authors review how microbes shape the zone around a tumor. Their piece came out in 2026. Microbe-made chemicals plug into host switches. That traffic tunes how immune cells grow, show targets, and burn fuel in tumors.

Those signals can calm or fire the attack on a tumor. Which way they push rests on dose, the switch hit, and the local cell mix. They also sway how well key cancer drugs work. Body-wide swelling and scarce food in the zone reshape the microbes in turn. The authors flag weak spots in the field: thin human proof, mixed lab methods, and dirt in low-germ samples.
pmc-13287635:
Kohei Nimura, Takamoto Okudaira, and Katsuyoshi Michibayashi examined feldspar crystals in 2026. The rock came from an oceanic core complex in the Philippine Sea. They hunted signs of slow cracking helped along by chemical attack at crack tips. Three mapping methods were layered to read crystal direction, strain, and calcium content together.

Patches poor in calcium ran alongside natural split planes and tiny internal boundaries inside large crystals. The team reads those patches as cracks that later sealed with fresh crystal growth. Such a cycle first opens paths for fluids, then closes them. The authors link the grain-level pattern to how deep ocean crust gains and loses permeability over time.
pmc-13287835:
Mon Ei Ei Moe and co-authors walk through a tricky heart tracing case in 2026: a woman aged 41 with pneumonia whose heart ran fast with a wide signal pattern. The tracing showed a right bundle branch block shape, rightward axis, and backward signals to the upper chambers at a fixed one-to-one pace.

That pattern puts a rare ventricle rhythm high on the list, yet common blocking drugs failed to settle it. Early beats from the ventricles neither reset nor stopped the rhythm. The authors show feature by feature why the tracing cannot cleanly separate a top-chamber rhythm with detoured conduction from the rare ventricle rhythm, and why drug response matters.
pmc-13288535:
Miguel San Sebastian and co-authors measure asthma in Sami people in Sweden. National registers supplied the data. It holds 13,311 Sami people. Each was matched to four non-Sami peers. Matches used age, sex, and home area. Records ran from 1993 to 2018.

Sami men and women got more specialist asthma diagnoses. Rates sat a bit above their peers in both groups. Sami men also had more hospital stays for asthma. Women showed no such gap. Past survey hints of extra burden held up. The authors urge work on causes. They also urge targeted public health steps.
pmc-13288635:
Yifan Xing and colleagues find a hidden translation starter inside a childhood virus genome in a 2026 study. Enterovirus A71 causes hand, foot, and mouth disease and sometimes severe brain complications. Viruses usually start protein building at one entry site near the genome's start. The team screened the whole genome with reporter constructs to hunt for extra entry elements. Two candidate regions turned up inside protein-coding stretches.

One element, between the 2A and 2B coding regions, drove protein production without the normal entry site. It also shifted how much of two viral proteins the cell made and tilted the balance of genome copies. Quiet mutations that changed no protein letters but bent the RNA shape cut replication and virus output. Those changes weakened binding between the RNA and the viral copying enzyme. The authors say such shape-breaking mutations could help design weakened vaccine strains.
pmc-13289135:
Scott Newbould and colleagues give a 2026 study plan on weight change before gut cancer surgery. The study sits in a UK prep service called Active Together. That service blends exercise, food, and mind support. How weight shifts affect surgery is unclear.

The study will recruit 100 adults with obesity. All face curative gut cancer surgery. Visits will run at diagnosis and before surgery. Staff will measure body mass and makeup. Surveys will track food status and life quality. Surgery facts will come from routine records. Stay length and problems will be logged. One-year survival will also be tracked.
pmc-13289235:
Aneesa Vanker headed a 2026 cohort study on indoor air pollution and tobacco smoke before birth in South Africa. The work sits inside the Drakenstein Child Health Study, a birth cohort in a periurban area. Pregnant participants joined between 20 and 28 weeks, and the analysis covered 1143 live births in total.

Exposure checks covered fine particles, carbon monoxide, other gases, and cotinine in urine as a smoke marker. About 17 percent of births were early and 15 percent had low birth weight in this cohort. Active smoking by the mother linked to lower weight-for-age scores in babies. Particle and carbon monoxide levels above ambient standards also tied to more breathing distress at birth, though some links were trends. Cleaner home air in pregnancy emerges as a clear priority.
pmc-13289935:
Emma Michel and colleagues revisit a 2026 puzzle on apathy and impulsivity using a stop-signal task in healthy young adults. Questionnaires show the two traits rise together, defying a simple seesaw theory placing them at opposite ends of one drive spectrum. The authors test whether each trait maps to a distinct action step: stopping versus starting, measured in the same task.

A total of 144 adults did the stop-signal task under consensus rules and filled validated scales for impulsivity dimensions and apathy facets. Bayesian analysis confirmed global apathy and impulsivity scores rose together as expected. Stopping speed did not track urgency impulsivity, and starting speed did not track initiation apathy, against predictions. The paradox survives behavioral testing.
pmc-13290335:
M Daud AK and co-authors characterize foot-and-mouth disease virus in Acehnese cattle in a 2026 study. The virus returned to Indonesia in 2022 and keeps sparking outbreaks. Samples came from sick cattle in Aceh Besar District during 2024. Blood antibody tests and RNA tests targeted different parts of the virus. One positive sample's VP1 gene was sequenced and placed on a family tree.

Antibody tests reacted in some sick cattle and in none of the healthy ones. RNA tests confirmed the virus in seventy percent of swab samples. The sequenced isolate fell in the Middle East-South Asia topotype, Ind-2001e sub-lineage. It matched Indonesian outbreak strains from 2022 at about 96 percent of its letters. Close relatives also circulate in several Asian countries. The authors say combined blood and molecular watch is needed for outbreak tracing and vaccine matching.
pmc-13290435:
A hands-on six-week course turned wary health care educators into more confident AI users, Justin Peacock and colleagues reported in 2026. Their qualitative case study follows a continuing professional development course built to help educators use generative AI in teaching, administration, research, and clinical work.

Drawing on three data sources analyzed with reflexive thematic analysis, the team found that 16 of 21 learners began the course apprehensive or fearful about AI. Working directly with the tools alongside peers shifted their outlook: participants gained confidence, began applying AI in daily tasks, and started advocating for it to others. Peacock and colleagues argue that practice-based, peer-supported training, rather than lectures alone, is what moves educators past fear.
pmc-13290635:
Four doses of a common urinary antibiotic were enough to injure one woman's liver, Mahir Sampat reports in a 2026 case report. Nitrofurantoin is a first-line drug for lower urinary tract infections, and its liver injury is usually tied to long-term use, which makes this early case stand out.

The patient, a 52-year-old woman, developed symptoms after just four doses, and her blood tests showed a disproportionate rise in AST compared with the usual injury pattern. Scored with the updated RUCAM causality tool, her case reached six points, supporting a probable drug cause. Once the antibiotic was stopped, she recovered completely and quickly. Sampat argues the case should put liver injury on the radar even for short nitrofurantoin courses.
pmc-13290835:
A stomach that empties unpredictably wrecks insulin timing, Francesco Galeano and colleagues explain in a narrative review from 2026 of diabetic gastroparesis. The complication, driven by nerve damage in long-standing diabetes, delays gastric emptying without any physical blockage and often goes unrecognized.

The review traces the damage chain: chronic high glucose, oxidative stress, glycation products, and inflammation injure gut nerves and deplete the pacemaker cells that coordinate stomach muscle. The clinical sting is a timing mismatch: food arrives late while injected insulin acts on schedule, causing early low blood sugar and late highs, with wider swings overall. Galeano and colleagues survey diagnosis, diet changes, and drugs, then weigh glucose monitors, automated insulin pumps, and future glucose-responsive insulins as ways to close the gap.
pmc-13291035:
Micayla M. Kane, Sydney E. Sneed, and Erin E. Kaiser sort surgical animal models in a 2026 review. Their topic is vascular cognitive impairment. The illness spans mild memory loss to vascular dementia. It often mixes with Alzheimer’s disease in patients.

Surgical models block or narrow brain vessels in varied ways. Each method sets a distinct harm pattern. Blood flow loss, white matter harm, and memory loss differ by method. No single model fits the whole illness. The review matches each method to a subtype. Labs can then pick a model that fits their question. Better matching should sharpen future drug tests.
pmc-13291135:
Stronger cannabis products and uneven health system readiness across Europe are linked to mental health harm in a 2026 narrative review led by Justyna Śniadach. Use has risen over the past decade alongside high-strength THC goods and more psychiatric presentations, yet monitoring and addiction services vary widely between western countries and the rest of the continent.

Literature, health reports, and national data from 2010 to 2025 show cannabis as the most used illicit drug in Europe, with use now growing fast in central and eastern areas. High-strength products are tied again and again to psychosis, anxiety, panic, and use disorder in the sources reviewed. Western systems spot such cases better, while stigma and thin screening hide much of the burden further east, the authors conclude.
pmc-13291235:
Antibody genes are shuffled to build vast immune variety. Fujung Chang leads a 2026 study on how DNA loops guide that shuffling in young B cells. A protein ring called cohesin pulls DNA into loops. Two forms of the ring carry different parts, STAG1 and STAG2.

Mouse B cells served as the test system. One form kept gene joining balanced at an early stage. Losing it let the other form grab more DNA. Early long loops then formed too soon. Gene use skewed toward near segments as a result. At a later stage, both forms worked together instead. The study shows stage matters in how these rings cooperate.
pmc-13291335:
A tiny laser can now emit clean, single-direction light. Yifan Li leads a 2026 study of a crystal laser with special bound states. Such states give sharp, low-power lasing. Their swirling polarization has blocked clean output for years.

Normal fixes twist the crystal pattern slightly. Real device size still spoils polarization purity. The team used dispersion to tame the swirl instead. Their compact laser kept single-mode output. Beam quality stayed high at the same time. Polarization purity reached a very high ratio. Chip lasers for comms and displays could use this trick. Precision tools may gain a small, pure light source.
pmc-13291735:
Yasue Fukuda and colleagues model mobile health app acceptance in aging Japan in a 2026 survey study. Japan has the world's oldest population, yet only about a fifth of adults use health apps regularly. The online survey reached 960 adults in November 2023, spread across seven age bands. An extended acceptance model added eHealth literacy, self-efficacy, perceived risk, and distrust to the classic drivers. Structural modeling then tested how these pieces connect.

The model explained about 72 percent of the variation in intention to use health apps. Ease of use mattered most, followed by support conditions and expected benefit. Social influence worked upstream, lifting literacy, confidence, and ease judgments together. Age and sex split several pathways in opposite directions. Digital literacy, for instance, raised distrust in young adults yet lowered perceived risk in older ones. Distrust cut intention only among the middle-aged. The authors advise age-tailored promotion.
pmc-13292235:
Chang Chen and co-authors review biomolecular carriers for boron neutron capture therapy in a 2026 article. In this radiotherapy, boron loaded into tumors splits under neutron fire and kills cells from inside. The carrier decides whether enough boron reaches the tumor. The only approved carriers so far are biomolecular, led by boronophenylalanine, cleared in Japan. The review sorts carriers by their biological vehicle.

Amino acid carriers ride a transporter that hungry tumors overuse. Nucleoside prodrugs switch on inside dividing cells and lodge boron in DNA. Sugar-based carriers exploit glucose transporters, while peptides slip in through receptors or direct penetration. Liposomes gather in leaky tumors and can carry targeting decorations. Albumin systems draw rising attention for their safety and high boron loads. The stubborn challenge is sheer dose, since each cell needs vast boron numbers. Protein carriers may finally clear that bar.
pmc-13292335:
Tommaso Piseddu and Fedra Vanhuyse map a 2026 evidence base on how climate risk moves real estate values. Their systematic map coded 130 academic and grey documents published between 2014 and 2023. Coding covered geography, valuation methods, asset types, and whether studies tackled physical hazards or the low-carbon transition.

Physical risk dominates the literature, led by flood studies, mostly American, that lean on official hazard maps and hedonic price models. Adaptation work using damage functions forms a smaller branch. Transition risk research is thinner still, clustering on energy performance rules, labels, and renewable energy side effects. Geographically, Europe's work concentrates in the United Kingdom, Germany, and Italy. The corpus studies one- and two-family houses far more than any other asset class.
pmc-13292435:
Wajahat Mirza and co-authors weigh a 2026 surgical trade-off in a GRADE-assessed meta-analysis: robotic versus open nipple-sparing mastectomy with immediate implant reconstruction. Restricting the pool to prospective studies left just three. The team compared total operating time first, then major complications, nipple tissue loss, and hospital stay, grading certainty with GRADE methods.

Robotic operations ran longer by a mean of 64.01 minutes in the pooled estimate, with wide uncertainty around it. Major complications, nipple-areolar ischemia or necrosis, and length of stay showed no significant differences between approaches. Heterogeneity ran high for operating time, and overall certainty rated low. The authors conclude the robot costs time without proven perioperative gains so far, while stressing how thin and imprecise the prospective evidence remains.
pmc-13292535:
Javaria Waheed and colleagues test how a feed enzyme changes nutrient release timing, in a 2026 laboratory digestion study. Phytic acid in plant feeds locks up minerals and protein for single-stomached animals. The enzyme phytase breaks that lock, but its effect on release timing was unclear. Soybean meal, canola meal, and corn gluten meal were digested in glassware with graded enzyme doses. The team tracked acid breakdown, mineral freeing, and amino acid release curves.

Phytase sharply raised acid breakdown in every ingredient, nearing its ceiling at a mid-level dose. Phosphorus and calcium freed up alongside, rising steadily in canola but plateauing in the other meals. Amino acids escaped fast then leveled in soybean and canola, while corn gluten released them in two waves. Release speed barely tracked acid breakdown, pointing to the ingredient's own matrix as the real governor. The enzyme mainly shifted timing rather than total protein digestion.
pmc-13292935:
Daniel Schneider, Kristen Harknett, and David Arbelaez assess, in a 2026 study, Fair Workweek laws in United States cities and one state. These laws aim to give hourly staff steadier hours and more notice of shifts in shops and food service.

Using survey data and models that compare places over time, the team found more advance notice, more rest between shifts, and fewer last-minute changes after the laws began. Other parts of job quality did not get worse to offset those gains. Effects varied widely by place, which the authors tie to how strongly each local law is enforced. Wider gains may need firmer enforcement.
pmc-13293435:
James C. Barton and co-authors report, in a 2026 study, antibody levels in people with hemochromatosis who carry two copies of a common iron gene change. These carriers face higher infection risk, yet their IgA and IgM levels had not been reported as a group.

Data covered 73 patients, 36 men and 37 women, with an average age of 51 years at diagnosis, an age the authors give. IgA levels matched those in general European groups, with no clear links to patient traits. IgM ran lower than in comparison groups, fell with age, and rose with daily alcohol intake. The work clarifies one piece of infection risk.
pmc-13293735:
Nathan J. Savage and John S. McKell test whether ultrasound measurements of the ulnar nerve can grade a common elbow nerve problem, in a 2026 analysis. Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow is usually staged with electrical tests, which sort patients into several severity tiers. The authors asked whether the nerve's cross-sectional area on ultrasound could separate those tiers, using records from 299 elbows of 262 patients sent for electrical testing.

Ultrasound size separated neighboring severity tiers poorly, shifting the odds only modestly between them. It performed better as a simple yes-or-no guide: very small measurements argued against disease, while large ones, above roughly fifteen square millimeters, argued strongly for it. Age and sex shaped the electrical findings without changing that reading. The authors recommend using ultrasound probabilistically rather than as a grading tool.
pmc-13294335:
Yuriria Cortés-Poza and J Rogelio Pérez-Buendía model flower pattern landscapes with a forest metaphor in a 2026 study. Stable petal and organ identities arise from a gene switch network in Arabidopsis thaliana. Each stable pattern anchors a tree of paths that flow into it, and the full set of trees forms an epigenetic forest. Wild type plants were compared with three single and three double homeotic mutants.

Measures tracked basin size, path depth, fate variety, dominance, and distance from wild type. Mutants warped the forest in distinct ways: one narrowed reachable fates, one deleted a whole identity class cleanly, and one raised fate variety despite losing reproductive organs. Double mutants often broke simple addition rules.
pmc-13294435:
Jamal Kazmi and a large team review atom-thin materials for brain-like computing in a 2026 article. Standard chips waste energy shuttling data between memory and processors, while two-dimensional materials offer tunable gaps, fast switching, and spike-friendly behavior. Resistive, ferroelectric, and phase-change memory cells built from such sheets can mimic synapse strengthening and fading.

Gate control lets one device hold many strength levels, cutting power for learning hardware. Remaining hurdles include growing clean large films, taming defects, and scaling arrays without losing uniformity. Uses in health monitors, edge devices, and quantum-linked systems are sketched as next frontiers.
pmc-13295035:
Boonlom Thavornyutikarn and co-authors improve a printable plastic blend for three-dimensional printing in a 2026 study. Polypropylene random copolymer warps and sticks poorly during printing, limiting its use. Clay nanotubes, a crystal-starting additive, and post-print heating were combined to fix those faults.

Nanotubes up to five percent by weight steadied filament shape and helped prints grip the build plate without glue. The crystal starter sped up solid setting, while nanotubes mainly raised stiffness at some cost to impact strength. Gentle reheating after printing partly restored that strength and refined crystal structure. Together the three steps offer a workable recipe for stronger, steadier prints.
pmc-13295235:
Mohamed I Elsayed and colleagues test gentle anti-mould dips for navel oranges in a 2026 study. Green and blue moulds caused by Penicillium species spoil fruit during cold storage and later shelf display. Silicate salts and a helpful Streptomyces strain were tried alone and mixed.

Fruit were dipped for 15 minutes, chilled for 50 days, then held three days at shelf conditions. Untreated fruit reached heavy mould by the end, while single dips held disease to low single figures. The triple mix showed no visible disease at all across the full period and kept fruit quality measures steadiest, marking it as a strong storage option.
pmc-13295535:
Zhongying Li and colleagues test immune training in whiteleg shrimp in a 2026 study. Shrimp lack the lasting antibody memory of vertebrates, yet a first mild exposure can still sharpen later defence. Two spaced doses of killed Vibrio bacteria were given, and blood cell gene activity was read afterwards.

The second dose switched on wide gene changes in the shrimp blood cells. Growth and division genes rose alongside direct immune weapon genes compared with untrained animals. The pattern supports a memory-like training effect in shrimp defence. Candidate genes named by the work may help breeders select shrimp lines that resist this costly farm disease.
pmc-13295835:
Gillian Flower and colleagues measure heat-linked hospital admissions across England in a 2026 study. Extreme summer heat may send people to hospital for far more than classic heat illness. Records of over four million summer admissions from 2008 to 2019 were matched with fine-grained weather data.

The studied conditions alone accounted for more than 3.7 million admissions, heavily weighted toward people aged 75 and above. Comparing the hottest days with mild ones showed raised admission risk for kidney failure, metabolic upsets, infections, and lung disease flares. Many heart conditions showed the opposite pattern instead. Risk climbed steeply with age across the map.
pmc-13295935:
Tetine L Sentell and a multinational team argue, in 2026, for physical activity rooted in local culture, such as ethnic dance and traditional games. Health guidance often overlooks such activities even though evidence for their benefits keeps growing.

Their narrative review surveys a vast, scattered literature spanning dance, sport, Indigenous health and community design. Because formal searches would return hundreds of thousands of papers, the team first craft a shared definition of culturally relevant activity and set its boundaries. They say clearer concepts will help planners fund and use such activity in population health.
pmc-13296335:
Laura Pérez Sánchez and colleagues present a 2026 method for bioprinting curved corneal tissue without the usual stepped surface. Flat slicing in standard printing loses the cornea's natural dome shape and leaves a stair-like finish. Their approach finds the surface from the model's geometry and generates curved printing paths that follow it.

Corneal constructs printed both ways were compared using micro-computed tomography scans. The non-planar prints matched the intended parabolic profile far more closely than the flat-layer prints. They also showed high optical transparency, which matters for tissue meant to restore sight. The work offers biofabrication teams a route to smoother, better-shaped corneal grafts, though clinical testing remains ahead.
pmc-13296535: Frontiers Production Office issued a correction in 2026 to a study of crop rotation effects on cut chrysanthemums, their soil and root microbes. The notice fixes three back-matter items only. A funding statement that wrongly denied support now names a Ningxia research programme and a flower laboratory. The author contribution list is expanded and corrected. The data statement now points readers to sequence data held under accession PRJNA1468310. The item is a correction notice alone, with no findings of its own.
pmc-13296935:
Jianjun Kang and co-authors devise, in 2026, a bedside test where the target enzyme builds its own detector particles. Acid phosphatase is scarce and fragile in samples, defeating ordinary assays, so the team let it convert a starter chemical into vitamin C, which then sparks iron oxide nanoparticle growth.

The coated particles mimic an enzyme and turn a dye dark in proportion to the target, readable by instrument or phone camera within forty minutes. Detection reached very low levels and worked in human serum. The authors pitch the scheme as a general trick for scarce, fragile markers.
pmc-13297435:
Angela Messina and a large team profile sugar chains on antibodies in people with Ring 14 syndrome, a very rare chromosome disorder, in a 2026 study. The syndrome brings drug-resistant epilepsy, learning disability, and repeated infections, hinting at immune faults beneath. Antibody sugar patterns from six patients were compared with those of healthy peers of like age.

Patient antibodies carried fewer of two sugar types, a pattern also seen in inflammatory autoimmune disease. The shift appeared in antibodies only, not in blood proteins as a whole, which marks it as selective. One patient improved on antibody infusion therapy, a clue the team follows for cause. The profile opens new angles on how the syndrome works and how it might be treated.
pmc-13298235:
Rice bran oil can be gelled into a spreadable fat using natural waxes, show Ali Yassoralipour and co-authors in a 2026 formulation study. They built thirteen oleogels with beeswax, carnauba wax, or blends of the two, and benchmarked them against commercial margarine.

Carnauba gels crystallized and melted at higher temperatures than beeswax gels, and the blends landed in between while forming connected crystal networks. More wax meant thicker, stronger gels, and the hybrids matched the hardness of stronger carnauba gels while binding over 94% of their oil. The gels carried more unsaturated fat than margarine but oxidized faster, a trade-off the authors flag for product development.
pmc-13299735:
Torben K. Heinbockel and Vonnie D. C. Shields review plant essential oils as options besides synthetic insect repellents, in a 2026 survey. These oils mask human scent or throw off insect scent detection, and many also fight microbes. Their green image and healing uses add buyer appeal beyond pest control.

Short protection time remains the chief weakness, since active compounds evaporate quickly. Coating and nano-scale delivery aim to stretch lasting power. Because oils are complex mixtures, resistance may evolve differently than against single-ingredient products. Commercial viability still needs wide safety testing, uniform comparisons against approved repellents, large field trials, and official sign-off.
pmc-13300435:
Nur Oğuz Davutoğlu and co-authors study inflammatory markers in immune thrombocytopenia, a disorder where the immune system destroys platelets, in a 2026 retrospective paper. The single-center review covered 166 adults diagnosed between January 2015 and December 2024, testing routine blood ratios and other laboratory values against complications, death, treatment response, and relapse.

Complications occurred in twelve percent of patients, and about seven percent died during the observation period. Death was tied to older age, male sex, and other illnesses, alongside lower hemoglobin and albumin and higher platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio and D-dimer levels. The standard inflammatory ratios showed little power for predicting complications, though the platelet ratio did track with mortality. Response to immunoglobulin therapy and later relapse each carried their own laboratory signatures. The authors suggest cheap routine tests can help sort patients by risk.
pmc-13300635:
Long exposure to homeopathic Gelsemium dilutions changed how cultured human nerve cells handle energy, Imane Lejri and colleagues report in a 2026 lab study. SH-SY5Y cells were kept for fourteen days with mixes diluted to 9C, 15C, and 30C strength. The team measured cell breathing, oxidant levels, survival, neurite growth, and two signaling proteins.

Treated cells made more ATP and drew more oxygen than untreated controls, while oxidant stress fell. They also survived better and grew longer neurites. Two switch proteins, Akt and mTOR, carried more phosphate tags, hinting at one shared control path behind the changes. The authors frame the work as early groundwork for studying stress-linked brain disorders in a dish.
pmc-13300935:
Andrei Mihnea Rosu and co-authors review catheter closure of paravalvular leaks with Amplatzer devices in a 2026 narrative review. These leaks around replacement heart valves can cause heart failure and blood cell destruction, and reopening the chest is risky after earlier surgery. The authors walk through device design, imaging guided strategy, and the registry and cohort evidence for a device family prized for fitting irregular, crescent shaped defects.

Reported results show high technical success with real relief of symptoms and hemolysis, plus reasonable medium term durability in well chosen patients. Outcomes still hinge on leak shape, the prosthesis involved, access route, imaging quality, and operator experience. The evidence base has no randomized trials, uses inconsistent outcome definitions, and rarely compares devices head to head over long periods. Even so, the authors keep Amplatzer platforms as a practical mainstay for complex leaks in experienced centers.
pmc-13301135:
Kidney care for IgA nephropathy is shifting from blanket support toward targeted attack, Abdulaziz Alroshodi charts in a 2026 review. The disease is the world's most common glomerulonephritis and a frequent road to kidney failure. Older care rested on blood pressure control, renin–angiotensin blockade, and steroids with their heavy side effects.

Newer supportive drugs, SGLT2 inhibitors and the dual blocker sparsentan, protect the kidney without suppressing immunity. Gut-targeted budesonide, complement inhibitors, and immune modulators now cut proteinuria in trials. Missing head-to-head comparisons, thin long-term safety data, and high prices still cloud choices, the author cautions, so careful rollout and more research remain essential.
pmc-13301535:
Heart fitness rebounds on a schedule after a heart attack, Kristina Skroce and colleagues chart in a 2026 rehabilitation study. Stable post-STEMI patients and inactive healthy adults both completed twelve weeks of supervised high-intensity interval training, four four-minute bouts per session, three times a week. Testing at four-week marks tracked fitness, heart function, blood markers, and walking distance.

Peak oxygen uptake rose about twenty-two percent in the heart group and twenty-three percent in controls by week twelve. Ejection fraction in patients jumped early, reaching 57.5 percent by week four, while a cardiac stress marker stayed flat and inflammation eased. Body fat and six-minute walk distance improved in both groups, supporting the program's safety in low-risk patients.
pmc-13301635:
E Efimova and co-authors ask whether switching off resynchronization pacing harms patients on heart pumps in a 2026 study. Most pump patients with these devices never responded, and its benefit on mechanical support is unproven. The center reviewed 158 patients. Forty-eight, about thirty percent, had the pacing switched off, most often for a failing left sided lead, at a median of about eighteen months.

Ventricular arrhythmia rates in the first year matched, near thirty-seven versus forty percent. Survival without transplant, though, favored switching off, with three year estimates around eighty-one percent against forty-nine percent. The link held after adjustment for sex, age, and disease type, while overall survival did not differ. The authors caution that reasons for switching off varied and the design looked back in time. Still, the data give no sign that turning the pacing off costs these patients rhythm safety.
pmc-13301735:
Alessandro de Sire and co-authors compare two rehab styles after steroid injections for chronic shoulder pain in a 2026 randomized pilot trial. Patients with subacromial bursitis and pain rated at least four of ten received three weekly ultrasound guided injections into the bursa. They then had ten sessions of proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation, a hands on technique using diagonal movement patterns, or standard exercise based physiotherapy. Pain, disability, quality of life, and range of motion were tracked out to twenty-four weeks.

Both groups improved, which is the practical news: the injections plus either therapy helped. The facilitation group edged ahead on outcomes at some time points, functional scores and shoulder movement. The advantage never held across all the measures, so the authors refuse to declare a winner. Their summary is that facilitation may add something for certain patients and moments, and a larger trial would be needed to prove it.
pmc-13301835:
A A C Velraeds and colleagues describe the first Dutch experience, reported in 2026, with a leadless pacemaker placed in the heart's upper chamber. The device suits people whose natural pacemaker, the sinus node, works poorly. Older wired systems often pace the lower chamber unnecessarily, which can weaken the heart over time.

Ten patients received the atrial device from October 2024 onward, and every implant succeeded. Most had sinus node dysfunction, and several needed testing at multiple positions before fixation held. Threshold readings settled quickly, average projected battery life was just over nine years, and no complications appeared during short follow-up. No patient needed lower-chamber pacing, though the authors stress that a larger cohort must confirm these early results.
pmc-13302535:
S Kotoulas and co-authors analyse, in a 2026 sub-analysis, the rhythm drug flecainide in patients whose frequent extra heartbeats had already resisted beta-blockers. Heavy extra-beat burdens can weaken the heart, and guidelines place beta-blockers first despite limited effect. All patients in the parent study had declined catheter ablation.

Patients with earlier beta-blocker exposure numbered thirty-two, against fifty-six who had never taken one. Flecainide cut burden by about eighty percent on average in the pre-treated group, and nearly two thirds of them achieved at least a ninety percent reduction. Results in the never-treated group were somewhat weaker, and adding a beta-blocker alongside gave no extra gain. No major side effects occurred during follow-up.
pmc-13303235:
Older heart patients sort into three tiers of medication safety skill at home, Furong Jiang and colleagues map in a 2026 survey from a Sichuan hospital. Three hundred ninety-three patients who had undergone coronary stenting answered scales on medication competence, health literacy, and family functioning between February and June 2025. Latent profile analysis carved the population into competence groups.

Just thirteen percent landed in the high-competence tier, while thirty-one percent sat low and the rest in between. Schooling, age, health literacy, family support, and how often relatives remind patients about pills separated the groups. The authors recommend tiered nursing follow-up that strengthens literacy and recruits the family.
pmc-13303635:
Jinlong Gao, Lulu Yan, and Jun Ma report a 2026 study of magnetic carbon particles designed to split water out of heavy oil mixtures. Stable water-in-oil blends resist separation and slow transport and refining, and earlier magnetic particles performed poorly on heavy oil.

Particles coated with polyethyleneimine were made and tested by the standard bottle method. At a modest dose, the treated blend cleared water well within an hour at moderate heat. Microscope views showed particles rushing to the oil-water boundary and breaking the surface film through charge effects and hydrogen bonding. Better green separators for the oil industry could follow.
pmc-13303935:
Li Dai and Xiaoyan Sun review smart drug carriers that release antibiotics only where infection cues appear, in a 2026 synthesis on drug-resistant infections. Standard antibiotics spread through the whole body, often missing infection sites while exposing harmless microbes.

Infected tissue tends to be acidic, rich in reactive oxygen, and full of germ-linked enzymes, and carriers can be built to react to each signal. The review compares passive carriers, triggered carriers, and free drugs, and weighs barriers such as biofilms, hidden germs inside cells, and drug pumps. Triggered release could raise local doses while sparing the rest of the body.
pmc-13304935:
Yousun An, Nicholas Norris, Donglai Li, and Jenny E. Gunton review ketogenic diets for obesity and diabetes in a 2026 narrative synthesis. Cutting carbs sharply shifts the body from burning sugar toward burning fat and making ketone fuels.

That shift may dull hunger, ease weight loss, and improve sugar control and insulin response. Lower insulin demand could also rest the insulin-making pancreas cells. Pairing the diet with diabetes drugs may add benefit, but one drug family raises a rare acid-buildup risk needing close watching. Gut microbe changes, long-term safety, and staying power remain open questions.
pmc-13305235:
Karol Skotniczny leads a 2026 randomized comparison of how sweat loss during exercise affects thigh muscle tissue by starting hydration level. Hard exercise drying the body by a few percent can dull performance, but resting tissue effects were unclear.

Thirty active men were split between guided drinking and normal habits, checked weekly by urine strength. All cycled at half power until losing about three percent of body weight. Ultrasound stiffness measures and twitch tests covered the front thigh muscle and nearby layers before and after. Only the deep wrapping layer softened after exercise, regardless of group. Twitch traits held steady.
pmc-13306035:
André Pereira and a large Portuguese team test in 2026 whether an invasive freshwater clam can polish municipal wastewater for reuse. Corbicula fluminea filters large volumes, so the team exposed clams to real secondary-treated effluent carrying drug residues and resistant bacteria. They also tracked changes in the clams' own tissues and microbes.

Within a day, clams removed more than seventy percent of three tracked chemical contaminants, with average removal near thirty-nine percent overall. Counts of multidrug-resistant bacteria fell significantly despite real wastewater slowing clearance. Clam tissues recovered their microbe counts and community mix after exposure. Giving an invasive species a useful treatment role could aid control efforts, the authors argue. The work frames biofiltration as a low-technology polishing step for water reuse.
pmc-13306135:
Victoria Fleming-Batayneh and a large consortium examine inflammation in 188 adults with Down syndrome in a 2026 analysis. Adults in this group often carry extra weight and face early Alzheimer disease pathology, both tied to inflammation. Blood markers were compared with body mass, age, and brain amyloid measured by PET scans.

Most participants met criteria for obesity, and higher body mass linked consistently to higher levels of several inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein and interleukin-6. Older age related mainly to higher beta-2 microglobulin. Amyloid burden showed a narrower link, with interleukin-6 only. They call for later work on brain inflammation as Alzheimer pathology advances.
pmc-13306735:
Sharafa Bankole modelled signal distortion in 5G transmitters with two linked neural networks in a 2026 study. Power amplifiers bend signals in ways that shift with past input, and one giant network wastes computing power on field hardware.

The cascaded design splits the job between two smaller real-valued networks, each handling part of the dynamic behaviour. Accuracy held while total parameter count fell sharply against a single large model in reported comparisons. The authors argue the split approach suits base stations and other gear where space and energy stay tight.
pmc-13307635:
Castilla Bolanos and co-authors measure the chemistry of lab grown mini brains in this 2026 paper. Cerebral organoids are small brain like tissues grown from human stem cells. They identified and quantified 17 metabolites in organoids aged from 85 to 312 days. The chemical profile resembled fetal rather than adult human brain. Lactate ran high, two amino acid signals sat at near equal levels, a maturity marker stayed low, and an unusual compound called hypotaurine was abundant. pmc-13308035:
Magda López Saldaña and colleagues report in 2026 a seventy-eight-year-old man whose oesophagus turned black and necrotic a week after heart attack care complicated by cardiogenic shock. Care rested the gullet completely with intravenous feeding, strong acid suppression, and support for cardiac output. A repeat endoscopy seven days later found the lesions fully healed. The condition kills often, but deaths usually stem from the underlying illnesses rather than the gullet itself. The authors credit fast stabilisation of blood flow plus conservative treatment. Their review places the case within the two-hit idea of poor perfusion meeting acid injury.
pmc-13308235:
Stephanie Ali Fairbairn and colleagues link a gene regulator called Kaiso in 2026 to why some triple-negative breast cancers hide the androgen receptor that drugs could target. Removing Kaiso in cancer cells raised receptor expression, weakened a metastasis-linked target gene, and made cells more sensitive to the receptor blocker enzalutamide. pmc-13309235:

Heavier left ventricles correlated with larger right volumes and weaker right pumping on both measures used. pmc-13309635:

Tumor cells, immune cells, and support-cell precursors formed clear groups in grade III tumors, new glioblastomas, and returned tumors alike. Six genes stayed shared and steady across all stages, with activity tied to tumor persistence and return. Path modeling showed support-like cells shifting toward cancer cells. The authors flag the shared genes as leads.
pmc-13309835:

pmc-13310635:
Ruchik Kevadiya and co-authors report appendix tissue disease that imitated appendicitis in a young woman in a 2026 case article. Blood tests showed no infection signal, and scans suggested either appendicitis or a burst ovarian cyst. Surgery found blood in the belly, endometriosis spots, and a likely burst follicle, and tissue study proved endometriosis on the appendix surface. The authors urge keeping the diagnosis in mind for young women.
pmc-13310735:
Chunli Lu and colleagues study how parenting passes across three generations in Chinese families in a 2026 survey. Grandparent style may shape parent style, which then links to child behavior. Data came from 2,120 families with children, parents, and reports on the oldest generation. Warm and firm parenting passed on through family affection, then linked to fewer child problems. Harsh control passed on through family conflict, then linked to more child problems. Strengthening warm firm care and breaking harsh cycles may help the youngest group.
pmc-13310835:
Amr Ali Mohamed Abdelgawwad El-Sehrawy and co-authors review clot risk in blood cancers called myeloproliferative neoplasms in a 2026 paper. Mutant stem cells, swollen white cells, sticky platelets, and vessel walls form what the authors call a thrombotic niche. Standard cell lowering care leaves much risk behind. pmc-13310935:
Máté Krisztián Kardos and a large team publish river basin chemistry data from Central Europe in a 2026 dataset paper. Sampling covered calm flows and flood peaks, with grab and automatic river sampling plus passive sediment traps. Labs measured major ions, nutrients, toxic elements, rare earths, and stable and radioactive isotopes. Fine soil and sediment parts were used for solid tests. Open data support checks of transport models at catchment scale.
pmc-13311135:
Jia Hui Megan Loh and co-authors report pregnancy care in a woman with a rare sugar processing disorder in a 2026 case study. Proof for pregnancy care is scarce, and mannose is often stopped for safety doubts.

pmc-13311935:

The discussed study by Bertrand and Morvillers gathered nurse views inside psychiatric settings. Finch draws practice lessons: staff need quality supervision plus training and backing to use proven behavior change methods. For research, she urges multi-site, long-term studies that can weigh the many factors shaping nurse experience. Better support for nurses, the note argues, is a patient safety issue too.
pmc-13312235:
Kap Sum Foong and colleagues write a 2026 letter to the editor on penicillin allergy labels and antibiotic prescribing inside prisons and jails. pmc-13312335:

pmc-13312535:

The authors propose transgenic rotifers as a scalable hatchery platform for antiviral protection.
pmc-13312835:

In a training set of 3,088 visits, stiffness tracked with vessel density, artery-to-vein ratios, curvature, and deposits on the retina. pmc-13312935:

Evidence for fast genome sequencing in adults, as opposed to sick infants, has stayed limited, so the team reviewed a structured program at Mayo Clinic.

Thirteen of those 57, or 22.8 percent, received a genetic diagnosis that matched their presentation, spread across genes including IFIH1, C9orf72, and FGF14. The authors also hunted for clinical features that predict a positive result and tracked how often the answer changed management, aiming to show where rapid sequencing earns its place in adult neurology.
pmc-13313235:

Gene tests, chromosome counts, and probe staining proved the cells truly came from D. willistoni. The lines are expected to aid study of this species and its bacterial partners in many ways.
pmc-13313335:
Connor R. King and colleagues propose a new account of a gene-reading pattern in a class of RNA viruses in a paper from 2026. These nonsegmented negative-strand RNA viruses read their genes in a fading gradient, with early genes read most and later genes read less.

The model matched the fading pattern across many such viruses and in shuffled variants of the VSV virus. Its process measure also tracked with genome length, as the authors report. A shared mechanism across this virus class could sharpen antiviral design.
pmc-13314735:

The team used data from 170 older adults who had planned knee replacement, tracking pain interference over 6 months after surgery. One method draws the recovery path itself; the other grades recovery against what was expected. The 10 people rated high by the path method also beat hopes by the second method, as the authors report. Among 82 people rated moderate, the second method spread widely, and among 78 rated low most matched too, by the counts given. The check helps aging studies pick a measure.
pmc-13315135:

pmc-13315435:

That gap creates doubt for regulators and slows sales across borders. The authors propose a risk-based framework for food-safe cell lines and banking to guide future shared rules.
pmc-13315535:
Xuetao Liu and co-authors asked in 2026 whether a protease enzyme that survives feed pelleting can still lift amino acid use in broilers. Day-old chicks then got normal-protein feed, low-protein feed, or low-protein feed plus one protease, as mash or pellets, for 14 days. Pellet feed raised daily gain compared with mash, and no diet-by-form interplay appeared for growth or digestibility. pmc-13315935:

pmc-13316835:

pmc-13317335:

pmc-13317535:

pmc-13320035:

pmc-13320235:

A chip version kept the sharpness, a step toward cheap point of care checks.
pmc-13320435:
Yanan Sun and co-authors rewire a giant enzyme line that builds a ring shaped antibiotic in a 2026 study. pmc-13322935:
Yehinson Barajas Ramón and colleagues review heat imaging in soccer, in a 2026 systematic review on fatigue, injury risk and recovery. Following PRISMA guidance, they searched major databases to June 2025 and judged study quality with standard tools.

The authors judge the tool valid, reliable and non-invasive for these tasks, while noting that study designs and measures varied. Standard routines for imaging and reading would help teams compare results.
pmc-13323135:
Shuangrui Sui and co-authors relate resilience and social support to mental health in breast cancer, in a 2026 analysis of 1,052 inpatients and follow-up patients. Regression models gave resilience a stronger weight than social support for mental outcomes. The authors propose using that split to target support where both burdens run high.
pmc-13323235:

pmc-13324135:

pmc-13324435:

pmc-13325135:
Nicholas M. Marshall and co-authors design polyurethane foams that fall apart at low heat in a 2026 materials study. Standard foam packaging is a thermoset that resists recycling, which blocks foam-in-place packing for risky cargo.

Cutting the water and isocyanate blowing share improved breakdown a lot. A strong acid catalyst and aliphatic isocyanates in place of aromatic ones helped further. The authors see uses in low-waste packaging and in wrapping hazardous loads that must later be freed cleanly.
pmc-13325735:
Keisuke Tachiyama and co-authors measure fading nerve responses in spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy in a 2026 study. The fading pattern is well known in ALS, but its spread in this slower, X-linked motor neuron disease was unmapped.

Shoulder and upper arm muscles faded most often, with the deltoid at 86 percent and the trapezius at 70 percent of patients. Hand muscles trailed at 37 and 25 percent for the two sites. The deltoid drop was also the largest. The pattern mirrors ALS despite the gentler course.
pmc-13327535:

pmc-13328335:

pmc-13328435:

pmc-13329535:

pmc-13331235:

pmc-13332035:

pmc-13332735:

pmc-13333035:

pmc-13333335:

pmc-13335835:

pmc-13336435:

pmc-13336535:

pmc-13336735:

pmc-13336835:

pmc-13337435:

pmc-13337635:

pmc-13337835:

pmc-13341335:

pmc-13341435:

pmc-13341635:

pmc-13342435:

pmc-13343735:

pmc-13343835:

pmc-13346035:

pmc-13347635:

pmc-13347735:

pmc-13349835:

pmc-13350635:

pmc-13350735:

pmc-13351135:

pmc-13400635:

pmc-13400735:

pmc-13400835:

pmc-13400935:

pmc-13401535:

pmc-13402235:

pmc-13402335:

pmc-13402635:

pmc-13403635:

pmc-13403735:

pmc-13404635:

pmc-13404835:

pmc-13404935:

pmc-13405635:

pmc-13405835:

pmc-13407135:

pmc-13407435:

pmc-13422635:

pmc-13422835:

pmc-13423935:

pmc-13425535:

pmc-13426335:
