Tomohiro Mimura, Yusaku Nakazono, Noriyuki Kida, Hitoshi Koda, and Takaaki Tsunokawa study, in 2026 work, how kick rate reshapes joint coordination in underwater dolphin kicking. Swimmers use this wavelike motion after starts and turns, where race outcomes often hinge. Eight male swimmers kicked at 80 to 120 percent of their best personal rate while 3D cameras tracked motion.

Speed rose with kick rate but flattened past the personal optimum. At high rates, hip and knee moved in opposite phase more often, yet the time needed to reverse the kick stayed nearly fixed. Squeezing that fixed reversal into shorter cycles squeezed trunk wave motion late in the downbeat. Protecting trunk motion may matter more than raw kick speed.
pmc-13507335:
Kannan Swathy leads a 2026 team that tests seed extracts of Annona squamosa, the custard apple, against the tomato leaf miner Tuta absoluta, a moth pest devastating tomato crops worldwide. Chemical sprays face rising resistance, so plant-derived options draw interest. Extracts made with five solvents faced eggs and larvae in bioassays.

The hexane extract performed best, fully blocking egg hatching at the top dose and killing most larvae within two days. Treated larvae showed lowered protective catalase and raised detox enzyme activity, signs of chemical stress. Earthworm safety tests showed minimal harm, unlike a standard synthetic insecticide that killed nearly all worms. Two fatty compounds dominated the extract and docked strongly onto a key insect enzyme in models.
pmc-13508235:
Muaaz Alajlani, Afraa Alnokkari, and Loai Aljerf survey how pharmacy students in Syria use artificial intelligence tools for study, in 2026 work. AI tools are spreading through higher education, yet little is known about their use in war-affected, low-resource settings. The survey ran in January and February 2026 and drew 295 students from public and private universities. Questions covered how often students use such tools, what they use them for, and what support their schools give.

Nearly nine in ten students used AI tools for academic work, and almost all of them favored ChatGPT. Top uses were explaining concepts, looking up drug facts, and making practice questions. Students rated the learning benefits fairly high. Institutional support, though, scored very low, and nearly all students said guidance and training were absent. Almost everyone learned these tools alone. Senior students felt more confident with them than juniors did.
pmc-13508335:
Luca Timoceanu and five co-authors report early vision gains after surgery for a full-thickness hole in the center of the retina, in 2026 work. The operation removes the eye's gel, peels a fine membrane, and fills the eye with gas while it heals. Records covered 193 eyes treated at their center, with vision checked about a month after surgery. Holes were classed as small, medium, or large by a standard scale. The team also weighed which gas was used and how long patients were told to lie face down.

Two thirds of eyes gained at least two lines on the vision chart within that first month. Gains did not differ by hole size, gas choice, or face-down time. Hole closure, though, fell sharply for large holes compared with small ones. The results help set patient expectations for the first month of recovery.
pmc-13509535:
Dmitry Skvortsov, Aliya Khudaigulova, Danila Lobunko, Sergey Kaurkin, and Galina Ivanova test gait training for people recovering from a stroke that blocked blood flow to the brain, in a 2026 pilot study. Twenty patients received nine sessions of visual feedback training paced by a metronome, aimed at making steps on each side mirror each other more evenly, on top of standard care. Twenty other patients received standard care alone.

Detailed walking measures showed the uneven pattern typical after stroke in both groups at the start and at the end. The trained group showed a hopeful trend toward more even stepping, yet the change fell short of statistical proof. The control group showed no change on that measure. The authors call for a larger trial with enough patients to settle whether the method truly helps.
pmc-13509635:
Bulent Mamikoglu, Pankajavalli Ramakrishnan, Fawaz Al-Mufti, and Gerard Gianoli weigh reported outcomes for rebuilding the wall of a large vein near the ear to treat pulsing tinnitus, in a 2026 review. The operation is a skull-base procedure called sigmoid sinus wall reconstruction. The sound in this condition matches the heartbeat and can stem from a thinned or opened vein wall. The authors searched databases and graded the studies by design, group size, follow-up length, and safety reporting.

Ten studies passed into the final set, most small and backward-looking. Only one group was followed for more than five years on average. In that group, the pulsing sound vanished in about two thirds of ears. Most ears kept a good result years later. Direct pressure readings before and after surgery were rare. The authors call the results hopeful yet thin and urge shared standards for judging success.
pmc-13509835:
Pablo Rodriguez and nine co-authors ask how sampling for germs should be handled in children with septic arthritis, a joint infection that needs fast action, in a 2026 review. Drawing fluid from the joint remains the key urgent step, serving both diagnosis and drainage. The review works through nine clinical questions and builds a risk-based plan shaped by age and by how sick the child appears.

The germs behind these infections change with age, with one kind ruling before age four and staph bacteria ruling after. For children under four with a mild picture and a positive throat test for the early-childhood germ, the authors float non-invasive checks as a possible path, with close review within three days. For older children, joint sampling under anesthesia stays the standard. The plan is offered as a hypothesis, not as guidance backed by major societies.
pmc-13512035:
Hanna Vertanen-Greis and colleagues report a field study, published in 2026. It is a proof-of-concept study of Finnish teachers' voice symptoms. It asks whether symptoms track the indoor air quality teachers perceive at work. Teachers frequently blame stuffy classrooms for hoarseness and voice strain. The team compared self-reported symptoms with clinical voice measures. Environmental readings were compared too.

Poorer perceived air quality was associated with more voice symptoms. Longer exposure time was as well. No matching links appeared in the clinical voice examinations, though. The measured environmental data showed no matching links either. Perception and symptoms seem to travel together without simple physical proof. The authors recommend monitoring affected teachers. Longer studies with real-time air data are also recommended.
pmc-13514735:
Maria-Delia Florean and co-authors test in 2026 whether simple blood markers can predict which sinus patients relapse after surgery. Their disease, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, is a long-lasting inflammatory condition that often returns despite a thorough operation.

They followed sixty-nine patients for up to three years after first-time sinus surgery, measuring four blood proteins before the operation. High blood eosinophils, a type of white blood cell, proved the strongest single warning sign of recurrence. Three proteins, periostin, eotaxin, and procalcitonin, also ran higher in patients who relapsed, and procalcitonin separated the groups best in accuracy testing. The authors propose adding a small blood panel to routine follow-up to flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13517935:
Maya Ermakova leads a fourteen-author team building miniature antibodies for polio vaccine testing in a 2026 study. Inactivated polio vaccine works only if its D-antigen, the virus shell in its potent native shape, survives production, so factories need precise measuring tools. The team raised camelid single-domain antibodies, tiny VHH fragments, against the D-antigen of Sabin type 1, the vaccine strain.

The fragments bound the native antigen strongly. One clone, S1-C7, sharpened the test kit enough to tell the vaccine strain from its wild Mahoney cousin. Ordinary antibody mixes could not do that. It even neutralised the virus in a dish. Another clone, S1-D9, recognised all three polio serotypes, hinting at a shared shell feature and a future universal detector. Ermakova's team offers the panel as quality-control instruments for the eradication endgame, where every batch's antigen content matters.
pmc-13518035:
White and colleagues reported a 2026 case of severe tetanus that began with a rooster peck to a finger. The patient was a 65-year-old poultry hobbyist with type two diabetes and no tetanus vaccination in over ten years. Tetanus toxin, made by bacteria in soil and manure, blocks the nerves' braking signals and causes rigid, spasming muscles, and animal injuries are a rarely recognized route of infection.

White describes progressive jaw stiffness, abnormal tongue sensation, and slurred speech at presentation, with scans ruling out stroke and deep neck infection. Worsening respiratory distress needed a breathing tube passed through the nose with a camera's help, followed later by a tracheostomy, an opening in the windpipe. Despite antibiotics, tetanus immunoglobulin, and sedation, spasms returned whenever sedation lightened. The authors use the case to press vaccination awareness for under-immunized agricultural workers and early airway planning in severe disease.
pmc-13518435:
J Weber and three colleagues revisit a long-standing needle taboo after armpit lymph-node surgery in a 2026 German review. Removing axillary nodes for breast cancer or melanoma can damage lymph drainage, and guidelines have long told clinicians to spare that arm: no blood draws, no drips, no pressure cuffs, for life. When the other arm fails, staff resort to foot veins or central lines, both worse options carrying their own pain and clot risks.

Older caution rested on small case reports. Newer data, the authors argue, show that single venous punctures and catheter placements on the operated side are safe when no lymph swelling exists yet. Their practical rule: after a failed attempt on the safe side, try the operated arm before reaching for awkward sites or a central line. Weber's team frames the shift as evidence catching up with a precaution that outlived its data.
pmc-13520235:
Qiongling Zhao leads a nine-author genome scan in 2026 of Phyllanthus emblica, a medicinal and edible fruit tree of tropical Asia whose genetics were barely mapped. Leaf samples from 112 accessions collected in China and India yielded 73,405 high-quality DNA markers through a reduced-representation sequencing method.

Family trees split the accessions into two major groups and four source-based subpopulations. Diversity varied sharply, with one source group far richer than others, suggesting uneven use of the breeding pool. Scans flagged regions under selection holding genes for protein turnover, stress response, and hormone transport. A first association study for leaf shape found 85 linked spots, enriched for leaf development and cell wall genes, seeding marker-assisted breeding.
pmc-13520335:
Elnaz Afshari and Neda Soleimani design on paper in 2026 a single vaccine aimed at both Salmonella and Shigella, two food-borne bacteria with no licensed vaccine yet. Their computer-based design joins short immune-triggering fragments from six shared bacterial proteins.

Fragments were screened for immune coverage, safety signals and stability, then linked onto a bacterial flagellin scaffold that also boosts immunity. Modelling suggested a stable, water-friendly construct of suitable size, with favourable structure checks. Immune simulation predicted a strong response. Because all work so far is computational, laboratory and animal testing would be the essential next step before any health claim.
pmc-13520535:
An and colleagues published a 2026 meta-analysis of nerve injury after total hip replacement, a rare complication that is hard to treat once it happens. Pooling case control studies should reveal which patients and surgical choices carry the most risk. The team searched four databases for work published up to April 2025.

Twelve studies covering nearly 1.18 million patients met the criteria for pooling in this analysis by An. Simple comparisons linked injury to younger age, obesity, female sex, fractures, longer operations, repeat surgery, and spinal disease. After fuller adjustment only three factors stayed clearly linked: female sex, a posterolateral surgical approach, and spinal disease. Arthritis type and diabetes showed no clear link, and the spinal disease result weakened when single studies were removed.
pmc-13520635:
Chailapakul and colleagues built a BRCA1 mutant hamster cell line in 2026 to compare how BRCA1 and BRCA2, two cancer-linked genes, each handle DNA damage. Using CRISPR editing on V79 cells, they created a weakened BRCA1 line missing nine building blocks, and set it beside a BRCA2 mutant and normal cells.

Both mutants failed to gather the repair protein RAD51 at damage sites and lost the high-fidelity repair route, and each grew extra sensitive to damaging agents. With different profiles: the BRCA1 line feared a topoisomerase trap and a PARP blocker most, the BRCA2 line feared other drug classes more. The BRCA1 line also carried an unstable chromosome count, while the BRCA2 line stacked up chromosome breaks and kept them unrepaired longer after radiation. Both lines failed the checkpoint that should pause division. The authors offer the matched pair as a model for mutation-specific drug design.
pmc-13521235:
Alvin P Chan and colleagues find in 2026 that blocking fat absorption in mice prevents obesity yet worsens fatty liver inflammation, separating weight gain from liver harm. The fat-blocking drug orlistat is used for obesity, while effects on steatohepatitis remained unclear.

Mice ate a high-fat liver-disease diet with or without orlistat for 32 weeks. Drug-treated mice stayed leaner through fat malabsorption, yet liver enlargement, fat build-up and scarring still progressed. Liver chemistry showed lost essential unsaturated fats, more saturated fats, plus stronger fat-making and inflammatory signals. Imaging, blood tests and tissue checks all agreed that leanness did not protect the liver here.
pmc-13521935:
Mei and colleagues reported in 2026 a family of ultra-thin metallic materials that pull gold out of waste electronics liquid with striking speed and selectivity. Recovering precious metals from e-waste is valuable but current methods are inefficient. The materials are two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides, sheet-like compounds of metals and sulfur, in their metallic phases, including compounds of molybdenum, tungsten, tantalum, and titanium.

Mei found the sheets removed almost all gold ions from solution in about fifteen seconds. Their pull on gold dwarfed that on rival ions such as copper, nickel, and sodium by a factor of a hundred thousand or more. The titanium compound held the most gold, roughly ten times the capacity of most benchmark materials. Scaling up, the team made membrane sheets and recovered a small amount of high-purity gold from 30 discarded computer processors.
pmc-13522435:
Dong Woo Shin, Sujin Oh, Yun Ji Hong, and Kyoung Un Park profile microbes in blood products collected for cell therapy in a 2026 laboratory study. Forty specimens from eight donors were examined, covering several plasma types, a white-cell layer, and saliva. Genetic sequencing of a bacterial marker gene was used to identify organisms down to species level.

Plasma specimens held a wider mix of microbes than saliva, and the different specimen types formed distinct clusters. One streptococcus type dominated across specimens, while another organism appeared only in plasma. Skin swabs grew nothing after disinfection, suggesting skin carryover alone cannot explain the DNA signals. The profiles may help staff judge molecular test results during cell manufacturing.
pmc-13523235:
Babatunde Ogunmiloro tests an artificial intelligence stroke aid delivered through a messaging app in a 2026 preliminary study. Expert neuroimaging is scarce in many underserved regions, and early stroke treatment is often missed. Two image models were trained on more than six thousand annotated brain CT scans covering normal scans and two stroke types, then checked on a separate public dataset.

The stronger model reached ninety-nine percent accuracy in internal testing and held up well on external sets, with especially strong detection of bleeding strokes, a distinction that guards against dangerous clot-busting treatment. The chosen model was built into a Telegram bot that answers in real time and deletes uploaded data automatically for privacy. The author acknowledges limits, including slice-level data splitting, and frames the results as preliminary.
pmc-13524135:
Kulkarni and colleagues reported in 2026 the first Indian case of antenatal sepsis, a severe infection during pregnancy, caused by Bordetella hinzii, a rare bacterium linked to poultry. The patient was a 27-year-old pregnant woman with sickle cell anaemia and a mild thalassemia trait, both inherited blood disorders that weaken defences. She arrived breathless and swollen, and her unborn baby had stopped moving.

Kulkarni found the baby had died in the womb at 24 weeks of pregnancy. Blood tests showed severe anaemia, high white cell counts, and strong inflammation markers. Cultures grew the rare bacterium, confirmed by an automated lab system. The strain responded to several strong antibiotics, including meropenem, but resisted others such as ceftriaxone. The mother improved on standard early treatment. The authors stress fast, advanced microbe testing for rare infections in high-risk pregnancies.
pmc-13524335:
Yingying Lu and colleagues identify, in a 2026 study, caveolin-1 as a third host factor needed for a Bacillus cereus toxin to kill cells. Hemolysin BL is a three-part pore-forming toxin and a major cause of this bacterium's harm in food poisoning and severe infection. Two host receptors were already known, yet mice lacking both stayed only partly protected.

Genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens in mouse and human cells pointed to caveolin-1, a membrane protein tied to tiny surface pockets called caveolae. Imaging and binding tests showed the protein sits with the toxin at the cell surface and physically associates with it. Mice missing all three factors were completely resistant to toxin challenge. The authors define a three-part host system and propose caveolin-1 as a determinant of susceptibility.
pmc-13526035:
Michela Polici leads a large team in a 2026 study testing whether body composition measured on scans predicts cancer-related death in colon cancer. Patients had stage II or III disease treated with upfront surgery, and baseline abdominal CT scans were segmented automatically by artificial intelligence software. Seventy-six measures covered visceral and under-skin fat, bone, and liver density.

The cohort held 293 patients, and about one third died from their cancer. Higher average density values for visceral fat and under-skin fat correlated directly with cancer-related death in slice-based analysis, and visceral fat density held up in volumetric analysis too. Adjusted survival models confirmed visceral fat density as an independent predictor in both approaches. The authors present fat quality, not just quantity, as a prognostic biomarker worth prospective testing.
pmc-13526135:
Santo and colleagues report real-world results for a radioactive targeting drug in the hardest prostate cancer cases: metastatic, castration-resistant, and visibly hungry on FDG scans, a marker of aggressive disease. The treatment, lutetium-177 PSMA-I&T, delivers radiation to cells carrying the PSMA surface protein. Their 2026 retrospective study covered 25 such patients who had both PSMA and FDG scans before treatment, letting the team test which scan features predicted benefit.

Just under half the men achieved at least a thirty percent fall in PSA, the blood marker of prostate cancer activity. A little over a third halved it, respectable figures in this pretreated group. Two scan ratios predicted that response: strong average PSMA uptake, and PSMA uptake dominating FDG uptake by a wide margin, each reaching statistical significance. Total tumour burden, measured by imaging volume or blood markers, predicted survival outcomes.
pmc-13527235:
Dennis L. Parker and colleagues implement, in a 2026 imaging methods study, a way to measure absolute brain temperature from the chemical signatures of brain metabolites. Temperature guides care after brain injury and during heating or cooling therapies, yet measuring it inside the head noninvasively is hard. Their sequence, called GREPSI, combines a fast spectroscopic scan with a signal-shifting trick.

The shifting method removes the huge water signal and locates metabolite peaks whether or not water suppression is used. Tests on a brain phantom across temperatures from twenty-two to forty-two degrees matched the water bath within two percent at the top end, with precision near two tenths of a degree. Scan time ran two to five minutes for an eight-slice slab, and a healthy volunteer produced values in the normal range.
pmc-13528035:
Jie Zhang and four colleagues mine nursing notes for patterns of problems during outpatient dialysis in a 2026 study. The records came from one center and covered January 2024 to April 2025. The focus was low blood pressure during sessions, a common dialysis complication. Two reviewers pulled the data separately. The team checked which patient traits lined up with ever having the problem.

Older age came with slightly lower recorded odds of in-session low pressure. Kidney failure from diabetes also linked with lower odds than the comparison group. Other complications showed no firm links. The authors stress the limits of chart review. Session settings were not in the notes, so cause cannot be claimed. They propose nurse-led watch protocols built on such notes. Future work should pair live blood flow monitoring with structured checks.
pmc-13528135:
Benjamin Gordon and fifteen colleagues trace how a signal protein helps breast cancer reach lymph nodes in a 2026 study. The protein, Jagged-1, switches on the Notch pathway in nearby cells. Tissue arrays compared first tumors with their matching node deposits. Mouse models tested whether the protein drives spread. Cell barrier tests showed how vessel walls react.

Tumors rich in Jagged-1 invaded lymph vessels and nodes more in mice. A decoy that blocks the vessel growth signal VEGFR3 cut that spread. Jagged-1 loosened the lymph vessel lining in dishes. Tumor cells then crossed more easily, and lining cells turned inflammatory and sticky. Node deposits held more Jagged-1 than the first tumors. High levels there meant higher relapse risk. The authors pitch Jagged-1 as both a warning marker and a drug target.
pmc-13529035:
Aafreen Bari and six colleagues examine infected corneal inflammation after a fast cross-linking treatment in a 2026 study. The treatment stiffens the cornea in keratoconus, where the eye bulges into a cone. Records came from a large Indian eye center. Of 723 eyes treated from 2021 to mid-2024, fourteen developed infiltrative keratitis. That is a rate near two percent.

Cases clustered in summer and rainy months. Patients from upper-middle income homes formed the majority. Being sixteen or younger more than doubled the relative risk. The commonest germ grown was a skin staphylococcus. Scans showed most damage sat in front of the treatment line. Clearing took about eighteen days on average. Three scan patterns appeared, from flattening to brief steepening. Early care, including steroid drops, ended with good vision, the authors report.
pmc-13529635:
Uk-Su Choi and four colleagues size tiny brain hubs tied to hormone and social signals in a 2026 MRI study. The hubs sit in the front hypothalamus and make oxytocin and vasopressin. Deep learning software carved the region into ten parts. The sample was small, twenty-three non-clinical adults. Trait scores for autism and ADHD were collected.

Two neighboring hubs, short-named PVN and SON, grew or shrank together. That pairing fits a shared hormone axis. Smaller SON volume tracked with higher autistic traits. It also tracked with stronger ADHD symptoms. Path checks suggested PVN effects flow through SON. The authors call the results preliminary, given the tiny sample. Still, they offer rare living-brain evidence for a hormone circuit in these traits. Bigger samples must test the claim.
pmc-13529735:
Valero-Cortijo and colleagues went fishing in the medicine cabinet for a drug that protects gut lining cells from a suicide signal gone wrong. In inflammatory bowel disease, the immune messenger TNF-alpha can flip colon cells from survival mode into apoptosis, orderly self-destruction, when an internal safety checkpoint fails. Their 2026 screen ran 2,421 approved compounds through colon cells engineered to lack that checkpoint. They hunted for anything that restored protection rather than merely blocking TNF from outside, as current biologic drugs do.

One winner stood out: potassium dehydroandrographolide succinate, a derivative of a traditional plant remedy. It rescued more than four fifths of the endangered cells by shutting down the caspase-8 death pathway specifically, while leaving a second death route untouched. Two obvious signalling explanations were tested and ruled out, leaving the mechanism open. The authors propose it as a complement to anti-TNF therapy.
pmc-13530135:
Ying Ma and colleagues set soil safety benchmarks in 2026 for an oasis on the Tibetan Plateau, where farming and grazing press on fragile high land. Standard soil checks give no clear cutoff values and handle patchy ground poorly. The team turned to multifractal models, which capture uneven patterns across space.

More than 1,500 samples from the Delingha-Ulan Oasis yielded background levels and screening values for 20 elements. Nine elements showed spiky patterns hinting at local contamination, while iodine stood out with extreme enrichment. Mercury, nitrogen, and phosphorus shifts pointed to wolfberry farming and herding as likely sources.
pmc-13530535:
Epner and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 217, outcomes from a multicenter database for arthroscopic repair of panlabral tears. These are shoulder socket rim tears wrapping 270 to 360 degrees around the joint. These huge tears are rare, inconsistently diagnosed, and feared for recurrent instability.

The series included 63 patients, median age twenty-three and overwhelmingly male, mostly contact and overhead athletes. At two years, median shoulder scores sat in the excellent range, with the standard shoulder score at ninety-five and instability-specific scores similarly high, all significantly improved over baseline. Three quarters returned to play, and over ninety percent of those returned at their previous level or higher. Recurrent instability struck about nineteen percent overall. Only two patients suffered a frank new dislocation and five needed further stabilization surgery, rates the authors note compare favorably with earlier series.
pmc-13531535:
Cecilia Morel and co-authors hunt in 2026 for prescription clues that appear before a pancreatic cancer diagnosis in England. Linked practice and registry records covered 12,990 patients diagnosed between 2011 and 2018. Eight drug groups that treat early disease features were tracked across the five years before diagnosis.

Insulin prescribing rose first, about 19 months before diagnosis, and earlier in women than in men. That timing hints at diabetes caused by the tumor itself. Reflux, pain, and sickness medicines rose in the final year. Each rise marks a window where checking for cancer sooner might help a small share of patients.
pmc-13531735:
Tiia Mönttinen and colleagues compare in 2026 a rapid recovery path with standard care after keyhole appendix removal. Ninety-six adults with uncomplicated appendicitis at one Finnish hospital entered the prospective study in sequence, first standard care, then the fast track. Phone interviews days after discharge captured pain, sleep, and satisfaction.

Fast-track patients went home a median six hours sooner and reported less sleep disruption from pain. Worst and lightest pain scores favored the fast track, while middle pain ran slightly higher, leaving pain verdicts mixed. Satisfaction stayed high in both groups, and nearly all fast-track patients would recommend the approach.
pmc-13531835:
Shi-Wei Lin and co-authors build in 2026 a CT-based prediction model for a rare kidney cancer subtype defined by gene rearrangements. Records and scans covered 746 kidney cancer patients across several centers, including 77 with the target subtype. Thousands of image texture features were distilled from tumor and normal kidney regions.

A chart combining both image scores with age and stage predicted the subtype strongly in training and held up at fresh centers. Calibration and usefulness checks also passed. Such a tool could flag the subtype before surgery without a biopsy, guiding tailored treatment planning for a cancer that imaging alone rarely names.
pmc-13533835:
Chapple and colleagues published a 2026 study on a hidden transport route inside myelin. Myelin wraps nerve fibers in fatty layers that speed up signals. The team found that tiny cargo still moves through channels inside that wrap. They named the route TRAM, short for transport route across myelin.

Live imaging in mice showed cargo moving along fine tubes inside the sheath. Nerve activity sped up or slowed that traffic in their tests. Mice missing key motor proteins saw the traffic stall almost fully. Stalled traffic was followed by damage to the nerve fiber itself. The route likely ferries food and spare parts to the fiber's edge. Feeding the fiber well may matter as much as the signal itself.
pmc-13534435:
Eric Bertrand Kouam and colleagues survey in 2026 cowpea farming across two zones of Cameroon. Cowpea is a key food crop in tropical Africa, yet output faces drought, pests, and poor soils. The team questioned 300 farmers in 15 divisions about their systems, limits, and seed choices.

Most farmers grew local landraces rather than improved types, with improved seed more common in the drier northern zone. Farming styles differed sharply by zone in gender, farm size, and sales. Land purchase, animal traction, group membership, and seed access raised uptake of improved types, guiding breeder and outreach priorities.
pmc-13534535:
Zhaoxiang Zeng and colleagues screen in 2026 for microplastics in the soft core of spinal discs from patients in Wuhan, China. Plastic particles have been found in many human tissues, yet this sheltered disc core was barely studied. Tissue from 51 disc surgery patients was digested, filtered, and scanned with Raman imaging.

Nine polymer particles were confirmed across five patients, most smaller than 100 micrometres, with types spanning foam and rubber-like plastics. Blanks and surgical materials were checked to cut false matches. Readers get early proof that particles can reach this tissue and a method for larger studies.
pmc-13536535:
Esedullah Akaras and Ugur Sozlu survey in 2026 physiotherapy students in Turkey on climate change awareness and anxiety about the future. Young health workers will face climate health effects, yet their readiness and worries were little known. An online survey reached 394 students at state universities with two standard scales.

Students showed moderate climate awareness and notable future anxiety, with a weak positive link between the two scores. Female students, environmental volunteers, and frequent social media users for climate news scored higher on awareness. Prior environmental training showed no clear link, guiding curriculum planners.
pmc-13536635:
Sejoong Ahn and colleagues validate in 2026 the updated SOFA-2 organ failure score in emergency department patients with septic shock. The new score revises cut-offs and adds modern organ support types, but it had been tested mainly in intensive care. Two prospective registries gave over 4,000 patients for head-to-head scoring.

Death risk rose with both scores, yet SOFA-2 separated survivors from non-survivors better at hospital, 28-day, and 90-day marks. Its risk estimates also matched real outcomes more closely with lower error. The update looks ready for emergency use in septic shock.
pmc-13536735:
Jiaxing Wang and co-authors survey eating disorders and suicide risk among Chinese college students in a 2026 study of 18,578 students surveyed in late October 2023. Questionnaires covered background, eating problems, low mood, anxiety, and suicide risk. Statistical models identified factors tied to eating disorders overall, plus factors tied to suicide risk among students who had eating disorders.

About one in seven students met criteria for an eating disorder. Higher weight, town or city living, childhood separation from parents, higher maternal schooling, low mood, anxiety, and prior suicidal thoughts or attempts each tracked with eating disorders. Among affected students, about one in five reported suicidal thoughts or attempts. The authors urge routine suicide checks for students with eating disorders and joint care for mood symptoms.
pmc-13539735:
Jiahong Xu and four co-authors review, in a 2026 article, why triple-negative breast cancer spreads to bone and how printed three-dimensional models might help researchers study that spread. Triple-negative disease lacks the hormone receptors that many breast cancer drugs target, so treatment options stay narrow.

The review first explains the cycle in which tumor cells prompt bone breakdown, then looks at printed scaffolds built from gels that can hold tumor, blood vessel, and bone cells together. Such models offer a place to test new drugs and delivery methods. The authors also note printed implants and surgical guides, plus the technical hurdles that still block wider clinical use.
pmc-13539935:
Yuki Hirai and seven colleagues present a 2026 case report of lung surgery complicated by two rare birth defects of blood vessels in the same patient. A 68-year-old woman had cancer in her right lower lung lobe, plus an extra artery from the aorta feeding its base and upper lung veins draining to the wrong place.

Three-dimensional reconstructions mapped the vessels before a keyhole operation removed the lobe. Surgeons tied off the aberrant artery twice and divided it with a stapler, and recovery went smoothly. The tumor proved to be an early-stage adenocarcinoma. A year later scans showed no return of cancer and no swelling at the cut vessel.
pmc-13540835:
Arezo Khadiv and colleagues compare gut bacteria in a 2026 study. The bacteria are Escherichia coli strains from two groups. One group has irritable bowel syndrome. The other group is healthy. The team hunted genes that help bacteria cling to the gut. They also hunted genes for stealing iron.

Gene tests covered sticking factors and iron systems. They also covered toxins and protective capsules. Six genes were much more common in the syndrome strains. That held true after strict correction for many tests. Two genes ran the other way, turning up more in healthy strains. No strain carried two key adhesion genes at all.
pmc-13540935:
Victor M Cnossen and colleagues compare two kinds of trial volunteers in 2026. One group joined controlled human infection trials. In those trials, healthy people are deliberately given a pathogen. The other group joined standard first-in-human drug trials. The two designs look alike on paper. The infection studies ask more of the body.

Seventy infection volunteers answered a validated questionnaire. Ninety-eight drug trial volunteers did the same. Money motivated the infection group less. Altruistic reasons ran stronger in that group. Infection volunteers also endured more severe symptoms. They said expected symptoms truly shaped their choice to join. Views on fair pay and fair burden matched across groups.
pmc-13541835:
Acton and colleagues run a careful supplement trial on ubiquinol, the absorbable form of coenzyme Q10, a molecule that ferries electrons inside mitochondria, the cell's power stations. The oxidised supplement form has repeatedly disappointed in exercise studies. Their 2026 double-blind trial randomised 54 healthy, recreationally active men to take a daily ubiquinol dose or placebo for six weeks. It biopsied muscle to measure mitochondrial breathing and leak proteins, and tested severe-intensity cycling endurance before and after.

Blood coenzyme levels rose as intended, and one mitochondrial measure improved. A control ratio suggesting tighter coupling between oxygen burning and energy capture fell significantly in the supplemented group against both its own baseline and placebo. The suspected leak proteins did not change, leaving the mechanism open, and the end of the abstract's report gives no performance verdict, so the endurance benefit remains unproven by the headline data.
pmc-13542235:
Jifang Sun, Chengbo Xu, and Fang Xie describe a 2026 computer vision method for spotting teacher behaviour in classroom images, designed as a sensing layer for future virtual and mixed-reality teaching spaces. Their system builds on the YOLOv8 detector, which locates objects in a single pass over an image. Two additions target classroom difficulties: an edge-focused module that sharpens object boundaries, and a dynamic module that gathers detail at several scales.

A revised loss function, named Focaler-Shape-IoU, was added to tighten the fit of predicted boxes around teachers and teaching objects. Tests on a classroom dataset the team collected themselves gave precision, recall, and average precision that competed well with several widely used detectors. The authors present detection as groundwork: reliable perception of what a teacher is doing must come before automated feedback or synchronised virtual classrooms can work.
pmc-13542935:
Mathias Holmsgaard Eskesen and colleagues published a 2026 population study of bloodstream infections in people with B-cell blood cancers in North Denmark. The team linked cancer registry and health records for patients diagnosed between 2013 and 2022. They described which organisms caused infections and searched admission data for factors predicting a positive blood culture or death soon after infection. Statistical selection picked the strongest predictors.

Among 1,592 patients, about one in five had at least one positive blood culture. Gram-negative bacteria overtook gram-positive ones during the decade, driven by Escherichia coli, which caused roughly a quarter of positive cultures. Low neutrophil counts, high inflammation markers, sepsis, low blood pressure, and kidney failure all raised the chance of a positive culture. Older age, kidney failure, and sepsis predicted death within thirty and ninety days. The authors say such routine data could feed prediction tools that tailor infection care.
pmc-13543435:
Laura Braun and colleagues published a 2026 review of inherited risk for lymphoma, the blood cancers arising in lymphoid tissue. Most lymphomas appear without family pattern, yet relatives of patients carry measurably higher risk, and some families cluster strikingly. The review gathers what is known about germline variants, the inherited changes present from birth, alongside environmental and infectious contributors. It also describes a Swiss programme prospectively collecting genetic samples from people with a family history of lymphoma.

Few susceptibility genes are firmly established, and strongly acting mutations explain only a small share of the excess risk, because lymphoma genetics is many small effects spread across families. Finding the weaker variants demands large, well-described case and control sets, which the authors argue family-based cohorts supply better than unselected population sampling. Better risk recognition could steer counselling, watch for treatment toxicity, and prevent second cancers in predisposed patients.
pmc-13544635:
Sebastian Sonnenberg and colleagues present GBAS-GUI, a software pipeline that scales up genotyping by amplicon sequencing, a low-cost method that reads chosen DNA segments in many samples at once. Existing analysis routes were often tied to one marker type, slow at scale, or poor at storing results for long-term monitoring projects. Their system wraps the workflow in a graphical interface with checkpoints, parallel processing, and a relational database tying each genotype to its sample information.

A built-in score rates how informative each marker is, and a rescue strategy recovers usable genotypes from duplicated genome regions whose fragment lengths do not overlap. Tests on several real datasets showed faster processing, cleaner handling of artefacts such as stray amplification, and richer information when full sequences, not just lengths, were used. Large population-genetic and monitoring studies are the intended beneficiaries.
pmc-13545335:
Ismail Sivri and colleagues benchmarked three large language models in 2026 on naming anatomical structures visible in X-ray images. Thirty radiographs from different body regions, drawn from an open atlas, were shown in both normal and slower thinking modes to ChatGPT-5 Plus, SuperGrok 4, and Gemini 2.5 Pro. Two anatomists scored every answer against standard anatomical terminology.

Gemini 2.5 Pro scored highest in both modes, reaching about 86 percent accuracy in thinking mode, while SuperGrok 4 stayed near half correct. Extra thinking time helped only ChatGPT-5 in a clear way, and its answers also became less consistent across repeats. The authors see teaching promise in these tools but warn that reliability is not yet sufficient.
pmc-13545635:
Yaoqin Wang and co-authors tested in 2026 how well two tools separate ovarian cancer that starts in the ovary from cancer that spreads there from elsewhere. That distinction changes treatment and outlook. One tool is the ADNEX ultrasound risk model, and the other is the ratio between two blood markers, CA125 and CEA. Records of patients with confirmed diagnoses of each type were compared.

Most metastases in the group came from the digestive tract, and about half were found at the same time as the original tumor. Each tool worked reasonably on its own, yet combining the marker ratio with the ultrasound model performed best, with an accuracy near 84 percent. The authors suggest the pairing could sharpen decisions made before surgery.
pmc-13546535:
Qianyu Zhu and colleagues investigated in 2026 whether a gene called RAE1, which helps move RNA out of the cell nucleus, helps drive stomach cancer. Antibodies against RAE1 had already hinted at value for early detection. Staining of patient tissue showed RAE1 levels were higher in early cancers than in precancerous or normal tissue, and levels rose with clinical stage.

Turning the gene down in cancer cells slowed their growth and movement, raised cell death, and stalled their division cycle, while turning it up did the opposite. Tumors with the gene silenced also grew more slowly in mice. Gene activity profiling tied the effect to the Hippo pathway, a growth control system. The authors propose RAE1 as a candidate marker and treatment target.
pmc-13547235:
Naraindas Bheel and co-authors tested in 2026 whether ash from groundnut, or peanut, shells can replace part of the cement in concrete, cutting both cost and carbon output. Mixes substituted ash for up to a fifth of the cement, and cubes, cylinders, and prisms were strength-tested after curing periods from one week to three months. Statistical response models were fitted to the results.

A ten percent replacement performed best, lifting compressive strength by about 13 percent over plain concrete at 90 days, with matching gains in bending and splitting strength. Water absorption and drying shrinkage fell as ash content rose, and embodied carbon dropped. The authors recommend the ten percent substitution, backed by models that explained nearly all the variation in results.
pmc-13547335:
Micanaldo Ernesto Francisco and colleagues built in 2026 a cheaper way to find mosquito breeding water with drones. Their approach skips the expensive map-stitching and special cameras that malaria programs in poor regions cannot afford. Their deep learning model outlines water bodies directly in ordinary still photos, using each photo's GPS tags for location. Training used more than 4,400 drone images from Pangandaran Regency in Indonesia.

On held-out images the model overlapped hand-drawn water outlines by 86 percent with color photos and 80 percent with grayscale ones. Field teams then visited 47 predicted sites and found water at every one, with larvae at nearly a third, including the two local malaria-carrying species. The whole workflow ran on ordinary cloud tools.
pmc-13548335:
Laurence E Lee and colleagues surveyed adults with spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy, a genetic condition that slowly weakens muscles, about how often they fall and what surrounds each fall. Falls are suspected to be common in this group, yet nobody had mapped them systematically. Sixty-one patients from a British specialist clinic returned questionnaires covering falls and near-falls over the previous twelve months, describing up to three events of each kind.

Nine in ten respondents had fallen at least once, and more than two thirds fell at least monthly. Most falls happened indoors during walking, reaching, bending, or turning, and patients blamed weakness first, then tripping and balance loss. Injuries were usually bruises or sprains, with fractures rare. Grabbing a stable surface was the commonest rescue in near-falls. The authors urge routine falls attention in this clinic population.
pmc-13548535:
Ji-Yun Zhu and colleagues build a combined nutrition and inflammation score to predict survival after stomach cancer surgery, in a 2026 study of 518 patients from three Chinese hospitals. Standard staging says little about body fat or immune state, both of which shape recovery. The team measured waist size on scans taken before surgery to estimate relative fat mass, then paired it with a blood-based inflammation score.

Patients were split into training and validation groups. Higher fat mass and higher inflammation grade each predicted worse survival on their own. Joined into one score, they separated patients into low, middle, and high risk groups with clearly different three-year survival and complication rates. The combined score beat surgical extent and lymph node stage as a predictor. The authors propose it as an easy preoperative check that flags who needs closer support.
pmc-13548635:
Bridget Murphy Hussain and colleagues review links among disordered eating, food insecurity, and the pandemic for American undergraduates, in a 2026 systematic review. College students face high rates of eating problems, and both unreliable food access and pandemic stress may push vulnerable students toward harmful coping. The team searched seven databases for studies from 2014 to 2024 that used standard diagnostic definitions.

Every included study was a one-time survey, with samples from under a hundred to nearly two thousand students. Different measurement tools blocked pooling the numbers. Still, food insecurity and pandemic disruption each tracked with emotional eating, a possible on-ramp to binge eating disorder, and students showed more depression and anxiety feeding disordered patterns. No study measured all three factors together, a gap the authors flag for future work on student health.
pmc-13550635:
Hatice Yıldırım, Ayça Kurt, and İrem Okumuş published a 2026 study of parenting and child tooth health in Turkey. They enrolled 605 children aged 6 to 12 at a first dental visit. Parents reported habits and diet. A scale scored parenting style. Dentists examined each child, and each child rated dental fear.

Warm, positive parenting linked to fewer rotten or filled teeth. It also linked to less plaque and less fear. Poor tooth health clustered with young age and low parent schooling. It also clustered with weak brushing and high sugar intake. In adjusted models, warm parenting tied only to the tooth decay score. Harsh parenting tied to plaque and gum scores instead.
pmc-13551835:
Alexander Izhaki, with five colleagues, published a 2026 retrospective study of a blunted heart rate response during drug-based heart stress imaging. Dipyridamole stress SPECT scanning is widely used to find poor blood flow to the heart, and a weak pulse rise during the drug challenge may signal risk. The single-center cohort included all adults scanned without added exercise between 2014 and 2017, followed through September 2020.

Of 388 patients, nearly two thirds showed the blunted response and over half had normal imaging in the reported counts. Blunted response tied to cardiovascular death in adjusted analysis, and patients combining it with abnormal imaging carried the highest risks of adverse events and overall death. The authors propose adding the simple pulse measure to routine scan reporting.
pmc-13553635:
Aure Enkaoua and five colleagues refine augmented-reality guidance for pituitary surgery. Good alignment between pre-operative models and live endoscopic views is vital for reliable guidance. Coarse alignment from face scans misses motion between the face and inner targets. Depth at the sella region stays hard to pin down with monocular endoscopy alone. Their 2026 paper tests a depth-based fix.

The team matched monocular depth predictions against depth rendered from the pre-operative model. Normalised cross-correlation proved most robust and became the goal. A continuous optimiser then refined pose frame by frame. Depth-based optimisation lifted DICE from 0.77 to 0.81, IoU from 0.63 to 0.68, and cut centroid error by 36 percent.
pmc-13558535:
Peter Anderson and eleven colleagues charted in 2026 how atopic dermatitis is treated, and how heavily it weighs, on adults across five Middle Eastern countries and Turkey. Real-world practice in the region was poorly documented. Their cross-sectional programme surveyed 209 dermatologists who reported on 736 patients, and more than four hundred patients described their own symptoms, quality of life, general health, and work impact.

Doctors classed about a third of patients as severe. Symptom and quality of life scores showed a moderate burden on average, and overall work impairment approached half of working capacity. Nearly nine in ten patients used topical treatments, while fewer than one in five received immune-suppressing pills and about one in eight received a biologic injection. The authors conclude that more effective therapy is underused and press for wider access.
pmc-13558635:
Panayota Kolypetri and eighteen colleagues test nasal Protollin in early Alzheimer's disease. Protollin, a nasal adjuvant, was studied in a random blinded phase 1 trial of 16 early Alzheimer's patients. Subjects got nasal Protollin or placebo twice over two weeks. Treatment caused few side effects. Their 2026 paper asks whether Protollin can shift immunity and clear amyloid.

Before treatment, patient monocytes showed weak cleanup genes and a strong pro-inflammatory signature. Nasal Protollin reversed these problems from the one-milligram dose upward, inducing a robust cleanup gene signature. A similar pattern appeared in brain monocytes clearing amyloid in a mouse model. Treatment also lowered cell signal molecules and cut CD8 T cell activation and killing.
pmc-13559435:
Yaling Fang and colleagues compare community-acquired pneumonia in patients with and without type 2 diabetes, using gene tests of lung wash fluid to name the germs at work. Their 2026 observational study enrolled 285 pneumonia patients, of whom 213 entered the final analysis: 96 with diabetes and 117 without. Bedside, lab, and gene data were pooled as one set.

Regression methods picked out thirteen candidate features, then cut them to a handful tied on their own to diabetes status. Higher body mass index, raised blood urea nitrogen, COVID-19 and Aspergillus infections all marked the diabetic group. Connective tissue disease, by contrast, showed up less often among them. The authors read the pattern as a distinct clinical and pathogen profile for diabetic pneumonia patients. They advise stricter infection screening, closer kidney checks, and attention to weight and glucose control in this group.
pmc-13559635:
Tana Lin and colleagues investigate RECQL, a DNA helicase that helps keep the genome stable, as a possible driver and marker in gastric cancer. Their 2026 study combines network analysis of public datasets with spatial transcriptomics and knockdown experiments in a gastric cancer cell line. The gene first surfaced through co-expression screening tied to disease progression.

RECQL ran high in tumor tissue and matched advanced stage plus poorer survival. Enrichment analysis linked it to DNA repair pathways. Tumors with abundant RECQL also held more M2-type macrophages and higher levels of immune checkpoint molecules, and spatial data placed the gene in myeloid-rich tumor regions. Silencing RECQL in HGC-27 cells slowed their growth and movement while increasing cell death. The authors propose the helicase as both a prognostic biomarker and a candidate drug target. Validation so far rests on datasets and one cell line's experiments.
pmc-13560235:
Jean-Vincent Lamien and colleagues survey health workers' knowledge and acceptance of the malaria vaccine in Burkina Faso's Nanoro district. Their 2026 cross-sectional study follows the vaccine's February 2024 entry into the national immunization program. Of 340 eligible workers, 257 answered the online questionnaire between April and May 2025.

Acceptance was nearly universal: 98.8 percent would vaccinate their own children in the reported rate. Knowledge lagged behind enthusiasm, with 22.6 percent unaware of the vaccine type used locally or its schedule. Over half said they received no training before rollout. Insufficient information was the main reason the hesitant minority gave. Wanting to recommend the vaccine and positive attitudes traveled with personal acceptance, though independent effects could not be confirmed. The authors urge training for every health worker, not only immunization staff, plus stronger public communication.
pmc-13560335:
Lina Wang and colleagues report long-term outcomes of one-stop hybrid ablation for persistent atrial fibrillation in patients whose earlier catheter ablations failed. Their 2026 retrospective study follows forty-four patients treated between May 2015 and April 2021 with same-day surgical and catheter ablation through one-sided chest access, plus management of the left atrial appendage.

At discharge, 93.2 percent of patients held sinus rhythm, with no deaths or strokes in hospital. Freedom from arrhythmia measured 68.2 percent at one year, then settled near half by three and five years in the reported follow-up. Half the patients recurred, most within the first year. A larger left atrium hinted at higher recurrence risk in exploratory modeling. Appendage tissue showed muscle thickening and inflammation often, with hidden clot in a tenth of specimens. No clot-related events occurred during follow-up. The authors call the strategy viable but exploratory.
pmc-13560435:
Junjun Xu and three colleagues measure what patients know, feel, and do about bowel preparation before sedation-assisted colonoscopy at a Beijing hospital. Their 2026 cross-sectional survey gathers 459 patients who had completed the procedure between June and August 2025. Structural equation modeling then maps how knowledge flows into attitudes and from there into practice.

Scores told an uneven story. Knowledge averaged under ten on an eighteen-point scale, attitudes sat middling, yet reported practice was generally good. First-timers made up two thirds of respondents, and most came because of symptoms. In the model, knowledge was significantly tied to both attitude and practice, with the link to practice the stronger of the two. The authors conclude that education is the lever: structured, evidence-based teaching aimed at knowledge gaps, especially for first-time and lower-literacy patients, should lift preparation quality where it counts.
pmc-13562135:
Susannah Leaver and colleagues review trauma in the very old as its own branch of critical illness, with distinct assessment traps and care pathways. Their 2026 article sets trauma in the oldest patients apart from the young crash victims who shaped trauma systems. Across Europe, aging populations bring more frailty, multiple diseases, and medication loads into emergency care.

Injury here usually means a low-energy fall from standing height, yet brain bleeding, chest trauma, and organ failure follow often enough to fill intensive care beds. Aging physiology and drug effects mask deterioration, and triage tools built on younger cohorts underestimate severity, causing under-triage and delay. Once admitted, care fragments across trauma, geriatric, and general wards. The authors call for early recognition, routine frailty assessment, and multidisciplinary care matched to patient goals.
pmc-13562335:
Sigal Sviri and three colleagues review end-of-life choices for very old people who are critically ill, in a 2026 paper. Patients aged eighty and older now fill a growing share of intensive care beds. Their health before the illness varies widely, so no single score can say who will recover. The authors weigh how frailty, daily function, and the severity of the new illness shape outcomes and treatment choices.

Practical steps run through the review: short trials of intensive care with a set review point, honest talks with families, and shared choices about starting or stopping life support. The writers stress comfort, dignity, and respect for what the patient values. They also cover strain on families and on staff, plus gaps where teaching and research still fall short.
pmc-13562735:
Xiaonan Zhao and colleagues tested a follow-up step that can rescue uncertain genetic diagnoses. Exome and genome sequencing often flag variants predicted to disrupt RNA splicing, the editing of gene messages, yet many stay classified as uncertain. Their 2026 study reviewed cases at one centre where targeted RNA sequencing was run after such variants appeared, to see whether the extra test changed the verdict.

Of 139 eligible variants, most were uncertain at first, and RNA testing helped reclassify variants in 27 of 64 fully tested cases. That yielded positive results in 23 cases and a likely diagnosis for two recessive conditions. Among cases with follow-up, most saw management changes and some saw treatment changes. The authors estimate the step lifts diagnostic yield by about 1.6 percent.
pmc-13563735:
Hong-rou Lin and ten colleagues chart twenty years of scarlet fever in Guangzhou, China, hunting for when and where the disease strikes. Records from 2005 to 2024 held 9,601 cases, a yearly rate of 3.16 per 100,000 people. The 2026 team described the pattern, applied statistics and scanning tools to find clusters across the city. Trends split the two decades into four phases: quiet years, a surge, a COVID-dented stretch, and a post-COVID rebound.

Incidence climbed at 17.26 percent a year. Cases peaked twice yearly, from April to June and again from November into January. Boys and kindergarten children aged three to six dominated early, yet the rebound added schoolchildren aged seven to ten as a near-equal group. Hot spots sat in the central districts and spread toward fast-growing edges like Licheng in Zengcheng. The authors urge control timed to the twin seasons and aimed at those districts and ages.
pmc-13563835:
Yalian Chen and Xianfang Zhang pool trials on a practical question for sinus surgery: does adding corticosteroid treatment after endoscopic surgery for nasal polyps beat surgery alone? The polyps grow back stubbornly, and steroids calm the inflammation that feeds them. Their 2026 meta-analysis, run to standard reporting rules, searched three databases and kept eight clinical studies with 776 patients in total. Recurrence, quality of life on a sinonasal questionnaire, symptom scores, and endoscopic appearance were pooled across the studies, with low disagreement between them.

The combined approach won on every front. Polyp recurrence odds fell to 0.57 of the surgery-only level. Quality-of-life and endoscopy scores improved by margins, and symptom scores dropped by nearly four points. The authors temper the verdict: studies rarely separated polyp subtypes, steroid delivery varied, and symptom relapse went under-reported. Within those limits, adjunctive steroids look like a clear post-surgery gain.
pmc-13571335:
Paul K. Jain and colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a catastrophic air embolism during robotic-assisted bronchoscopy, a camera procedure with an otherwise strong safety record, in a 74-year-old woman. Moments into the procedure she suffered a heart attack pattern, airway bleeding, and cardiac arrest.

Heart imaging showed clear arteries but a large pocket of air trapped at the tip of the left ventricle. Her course grew worse with severe brain swelling, seizures, and loss of blood flow to a limb. High-pressure oxygen treatment, the usual rescue, was ruled out by her underlying lung damage. The report warns teams that this rare complication can imitate a heart attack and defeat standard rescue options.
pmc-13572335:
Ying Hu and colleagues follow, in a 2026 UK Biobank cohort study, 231,148 women to test whether spontaneous miscarriage predicts early death, and whether later lifestyle changes that risk. Lifestyle was scored from diet, smoking, activity, and body weight, and deaths before the standard premature cutoff were tracked over a median of about twelve years.

One miscarriage showed no link after full adjustment, yet two miscarriages raised the hazard and three or more raised it further, with cardiovascular deaths prominent. Simply ever having miscarried was not significant once lifestyle counted. An unhealthy lifestyle amplified the risk in women with repeated losses. The pattern marks recurrent miscarriage as a signal for long-term health surveillance, with lifestyle a modifiable lever.
pmc-13572535:
Siv Therese Bogevik Bjørkedal, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 interview study of young people who used headspace Denmark. Headspace is a civil society service where trained volunteers counsel youth on mental health, outside clinics. Most past research has centred on clinical care, so the civic route was little studied.

Thirteen young people aged 14 to 25 took part in deep interviews about their visits. They called the space safe and welcoming, a place to share thoughts they could not voice elsewhere. Counsellors felt caring and truly keen, more like a trusted friend or family member than a clinician. Rooms felt cozy and home-like, a sharp contrast to clinic settings. The authors argue that volunteer care adds value of its own, not just extra hands for a stretched system.
pmc-13573135:
Nele Krüger, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 chemical method that breaks one of the strongest bonds in organic chemistry at room temperature. Carbon-fluorine bonds resist attack, so joining aryl fluorides to other carbons has needed harsh heat or fierce reagents. The team paired a palladium catalyst with a lithium base to do the job gently.

The catalyst carries a methyl naphthyl frame, and the base forms enolates, reactive carbon partners, in place. Ketone, ester, nitrile, and even amide partners all joined to plain aryl fluorides. Computer models showed why the mild route works: lithium ions grip the fluorine atom, which eases the palladium's entry into the bond. That grip explains a reaction long thought out of reach at such soft conditions. The method widens the stock of building blocks for drug and material synthesis.
pmc-13573435:
Ringga Rahmi Prima, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 case-control study of home conditions and tuberculosis in Padang City, Indonesia. Poor housing has long been tied to TB, yet the fine details of living space were rarely measured. The study homes all shared one trait: a past TB patient had lived there.

From August to December 2024, the team enrolled 105 confirmed cases and two control sets of about a hundred each. Home visits logged room air, house size, and building materials. Small bedroom volume and plaster ceilings went with case status in set comparisons. Outdoor work, frequent coffee shop visits, and more than a year since the prior patient also raised the odds. The authors suggest more bedroom space and screening that stays alert past the first year.
pmc-13574735:
Bina Tariq, with four colleagues, reports on a 2026 study of an AI tool that fixes messy labels on medical scans. Scan files carry DICOM tags for body part, side, and protocol, and sloppy tags block sharing and slow readers. The team tested a shop tool that standardises those tags and asked whether reading times fell after it went live.

Reviewers hand-checked tags on 422 X-ray images and 1,503 CT series, and accuracy ran from the low eighties to full marks by tag type. Reading times for near eleven thousand cases before and ten thousand after were compared. CT reading sped up for belly, whole body, head, and temple bone scans, worth about 270 hours a year. Chest and sinus scans showed no clear change. The authors credit tidier tags for the gains.
pmc-13575035:
Brian I Rini and Benjamin Garmezy discuss a new class of kidney cancer drugs in a 2026 podcast article. Advanced renal cell carcinoma is now treated mainly with immune therapy combinations or immune therapy plus a vessel-blocking drug. Progress has been slow for decades, so fresh options are still needed.

The pair explain bispecific antibodies, single drugs built to hit two targets at once: the PD-(L)1 immune checkpoint and VEGF, a signal that grows blood vessels. Lab work hints that joint targeting may bind more strongly and cut side effects. Several such drugs are in development, named here as PF-08634404, ivonescimab, and BNT327. Early results in other cancers and plans for kidney cancer trials are covered.
pmc-13578735:
Gloria Liou and Louis Tay hunt for visible signs of authenticity in recorded job interviews, in a 2026 study. Feeling genuine at work is praised often, yet what genuine looks like on camera was unclear, and self views may clash with viewer views. Mock interviews were run through automated video tools that count words, tense, and speech traits.

People who rated themselves as genuine used more I words and present tense, and spoke in a looser, less polished style. Raters judged others as genuine on quite different cues: more words overall, faster pace, and plainer speech with fewer adverbs. Short sentences linked to both views. No face or voice cues mattered in the recordings. The split warns firms that an interviewer's gut feel may miss how a candidate sees themselves.
pmc-13585035:
Axel Kramer and Andreas Enz reply to a letter about a hand hygiene guideline in this 2026 response. The exchange centers on surgical gloves: standard double gloving versus indicator gloves, which show a color change when the outer glove is pierced. The writers argue the two systems protect in different ways and should not be judged by the same measure.

A plain double layer works as a stronger barrier, so counting piercings of the inner glove fits it well. Indicator gloves instead earn their keep by spotting a breach early, so the glove can be changed at once. Reviews found they detect holes two to six times more often than same-color pairs. Proof that they cut wound infections, though, is still limited, and the authors ask guideline writers to keep that split in view.
pmc-13585835:
Can Aydogdu and colleagues test a blood test meant to spot bladder cancer spread before surgery in this 2026 study. The test reads tumor DNA floating in the blood, matched to each patient's own tumor. At bladder removal surgery, doctors also take out nearby lymph nodes to check for spread. The step helps staging but adds risk, so a good forecast could spare low-risk patients from it.

Forty patients had the blood test before surgery, and node spread was later found in seven. The test caught most of those cases and, more striking, a negative result was right in the great bulk of cases. Pooling with a past group kept that negative accuracy high. A modeled plan that skipped node removal for negative patients would have missed one case, so the authors call for a larger trial first.
pmc-13587035:
Longji Li and Lifeng Zhang propose a closed-loop digital system for gaming disorder. Gaming disorder, where play escapes a person's control and harms school, work, or social life, is now a recognized diagnosis. Checks today rest on questionnaires and interviews, which freeze a moving problem into a single snapshot taken after the fact. Their review pulls together phone-based tracking, AI risk prediction, and digital therapy into one circle of care.

In the proposed loop, daily signals from behavior, body, mood, and social life feed a model that sorts risk and forecasts its path. When risk climbs, timed micro-interventions land on the person's phone, shaped to their current state. The authors say the loop moves care from one-off testing to constant watching, and from reacting to preventing. Privacy, clear reasoning from the models, and real clinic fit remain open work.
pmc-13588635:
Borja Ibanez and Xavier Rossello reply in 2026 to comments on their analysis of the REBOOT trial, which tested beta-blockers after heart attack in patients whose heart pumping fraction was not reduced. Their reply argues that use of these drugs after myocardial infarction should follow indication, ejection fraction, and current evidence rather than habit.

The authors agree the trial's conclusions apply only to patients like those enrolled. The trials excluded anyone with another reason for beta-blockers. Such reasons include heart failure, reduced ejection fraction, or a need for rate control in atrial fibrillation. REBOOT therefore does not support stopping beta-blockers in all heart attack patients. It challenges only routine use when the recent heart attack is the sole reason, in stable, revascularised patients. The first step in any reduction, they argue, is reassessing why the drug was prescribed, with hypertension needing specific consideration.
pmc-13593235:
Jing Tian leads a team grading, in 2026, how clearly studies report two stomach staging systems used to flag cancer risk. The OLGA and OLGIM schemes grade stomach lining damage from biopsies, yet papers describe their methods unevenly. Three databases plus citation chasing yielded 155 studies that applied at least one scheme. Two reviewers scored each report on biopsy sampling detail and on how grades turned into stages.

Just under half of the studies read as highly interpretable, a similar share landed in the middle, and a small slice scored low. Stage numbers were common, but the steps behind them often went missing. Tian and the team stress that weak reporting, not proven weak method, blocks comparison across studies, and they urge fuller method sections.
pmc-13598135:
Xiaotian Wang and co-authors survey the use of plantar pressure, the pattern of force under the feet, to diagnose and track Parkinson's disease. Gait changes are among the disease's earliest signs, yet clinic diagnosis still leans on subjective rating scales, and their 2026 review covers the full pipeline from pressure-sensing hardware to AI diagnosis.

The sensors capture timing and load detail that directly reflects balance control and disease progression, and neural network models have repeatedly turned those signals into promising diagnostic accuracy in published studies. The authors are frank about the obstacles. Patients bring other conditions that muddy the gait signal. AI decisions need explaining before clinicians will trust them. Ethics questions also trail the data. Their future map points to wearable, always-on monitoring with on-device intelligence, proven in large multi-center studies.
pmc-13600335:
Ömer Polat and three colleagues test whether advice from ChatGPT about preventing blood clots after joint replacement surgery is safe to follow. Preventing venous thromboembolism, clots that form in veins after operations, is a debated area where even experts differ. The team took 33 questions built from four major guideline sources and put each to the chatbot twice, gathering 66 answers for scoring by two orthopedic surgeons.

One standard scale rated 62.1 percent of answers as good quality. A purpose-built clinical scale was stricter: only 45.45 percent counted as clinically adequate, and none reached excellent. Ratings from the two surgeons agreed strongly with each other on every scale. The same answer could look well built yet fall short on clinical detail, which explains the gap between scales. Polat's group concludes that chatbot answers on clot prevention are structured well but not reliable enough to guide care on their own.
pmc-13600635:
Džan Horozić leads an eleven-author team asking whether ultrasound strain measures reveal coronary disease severity after a heart attack warning event. Their 2026 study enrolled 112 patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome whose hearts still pumped normally, with no visible wall-motion damage. Using speckle-tracking ultrasound, the team measured three signs of subtle muscle dysfunction against angiogram results scored by SYNTAX.

Significant narrowing of at least 90 percent in a major artery was present in 70 patients. Global longitudinal strain, how much heart muscle shortens, was the strongest single predictor of severe narrowing and overall disease burden. Two other measures, early systolic lengthening and postsystolic shortening, added some signal. Combining all three gave the best test performance, though not clearly better than strain alone. The authors propose strain analysis as a non-invasive way to sort these patients by risk early.
pmc-13614735:
Manu Saini and colleagues review in 2026 how stem cells and tissue engineering are changing oculoplastic surgery, the repair of eyelids, eye sockets, and nearby structures. Stem cells can grow into replacement tissue and release signals that help wounds heal. The review covers fat-derived stem cells, lab-reprogrammed stem cells, and mesenchymal stem cells from marrow and other tissues.

Engineers combine these cells with soft scaffolds and growth factors to build stand-ins for eyelid skin, the stiff plate inside the lid, the eye's surface lining, and tear glands. Current uses include restoring lost volume around the eye, rebuilding lids, and fitting empty eye sockets. Benefits over grafts include less harm at the donor site. Work is moving toward tear glands grown in the lab and lids that can move, though hard problems remain.
pmc-13615035:
Hasan Jamil and colleagues forecast in 2026 whether Japan can hit its national target of 60 percent screening for colorectal cancer by 2028. Screening rates for people aged 40 to 69 came from a national living-conditions survey covering all 47 prefectures from 2013 to 2022. Statistical models projected each region forward, counting a prefecture as likely to succeed only if its chance of reaching the target passed 80 percent.

Nationwide coverage is projected to reach just 51.9 percent by 2028, falling 8.1 points short. Forty of 47 prefectures had under a 20 percent chance of making it, and only Yamagata cleared the bar for the whole population. Men out-screened women in 41 prefectures. The authors warn that without stronger local pushes, regional and sex gaps will sink the national goal.
pmc-13615235:
Darin T. Okuda leads a team testing in 2026 a commercial blood test that measures many proteins. It may tell a true multiple sclerosis relapse from a pseudo-flare. A pseudo-flare is a worsening of old symptoms without new immune attack. Telling them apart decides whether a patient needs steroids or a change of treatment. The study looked back at patients at one university clinic who had both the blood test and an MRI scan before any steroid treatment.

One group had fresh symptoms that raised fear of a relapse, while a second group came for routine checks, some on approved disease drugs and some not. Matching protein results against scan findings showed how far the blood test agrees with the picture inside the brain. A reliable blood check could spare patients extra scans and speed the right call during a scare.
pmc-13617935:
Hui-Mei Liang and eleven colleagues trace how astragaloside IV, a saponin from the herb Astragalus membranaceus, fights fatty liver disease in mice and liver cells. The disease, now called metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, builds fat in the liver alongside obesity and insulin problems, and few drug options exist. The team fed mice a high-fat diet and loaded liver cells with lipids to model the condition.

The compound cut liver fat by suppressing SREBP-1c, a master switch for making new fat. It did so epigenetically: it lowered an enzyme, GCN5, that loosens DNA packaging, reducing chemical marks at the switch's promoter and weakening a partner protein's drive on it. Forcing GCN5 back up erased the compound's benefits, confirming the pathway. The authors highlight an angle for natural product treatment, in which one molecule rewires the liver's fat-making program at the level of gene regulation.
pmc-13618335:
Sobhi M. Gomha and seven colleagues synthesize two new series of quinazoline-linked thiazolopyrimidine compounds as candidate blockers of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase, the enzyme the virus needs to copy itself. They used choline hydroxide, a benign catalyst, for the green synthesis. The compounds were tested against the enzyme in the laboratory, modeled into its active site by docking software, and screened in the computer for drug-like properties.

One compound, labeled 11e, inhibited the enzyme most strongly, at about one point three micromolar concentration. Docking scores, however, correlated only weakly with measured potency, so the authors treat the modeling as qualitative guidance about binding poses rather than a predictor of strength. Computer safety and absorption predictions looked generally favorable for oral use. They present 11e as a preliminary lead for further development of reverse transcriptase inhibitors, a class under constant pressure from viral mutation.
pmc-13618935:
Quynh Ai Lam and four colleagues test whether two inflammation gene variants track with type 2 diabetes in Kinh Vietnamese adults, a population where such evidence is scarce. Their case-control study at Cho Ray Hospital in Ho Chi Minh City recruited one hundred ninety-six patients and one hundred ninety-six non-diabetic controls between February and August 2025. They genotyped variants in the IL16 and IL1B cytokine genes, adjusting for body measures and family history.

Both variants differed between groups. The G allele of the IL16 variant and its TG genotype came with nominally lower odds of diabetes across several genetic models. The CC genotype of the IL1B variant came with nominally higher odds under a recessive model.
