The authors stress the word nominal: none of the associations survived the corrected significance threshold for multiple testing. They present the findings as hypothesis-level signals requiring replication.
pmc-13620335:
Yuxuan Zhang and three colleagues tested a gene-activity marker, METTL7B, as a warning signal in sepsis, the life-threatening body-wide response to infection. Current markers predict who will die only modestly well. Their prospective study measured the marker in blood from ninety-three sepsis patients and twenty-two intensive care patients without sepsis, alongside standard scores and markers.

Sepsis patients carried much higher marker levels than controls, and non-survivors carried the highest of all. Patients whose organ-failure scores worsened over the first week had started with higher levels too. Alone, the marker predicted twenty-eight-day death better than two common blood markers. Combined with the organ score and another standard marker, accuracy rose further. Regression analysis tied the marker to severity independently. The authors call it a promising companion marker that larger multicenter studies should validate.
pmc-13622335:
Zhu and co-authors wrote a 2026 commentary on aqueous halogen batteries, which store energy in water based cells using bromine or iodine. Such batteries are cheap and safe for grid storage, but dissolved halogen compounds drift across the cell. That shuttle effect corrodes the other electrode and drains performance fast.

Zhu highlights a study by Wu and colleagues that fights the drift at two levels at once. Charged sites inside porous carbon hold the roaming compounds in the cathode bulk through electric attraction. An added salt gathers at the surface during discharge and forms a moving barrier that catches and reuses them. Zhu presents this bulk and interface pairing as a shift from passive trapping toward active control by the electric field.
pmc-13623135:
Yinxia Liang and a large team explore links between HIV testing habits and sexual behaviour among men who have sex with men in southern China. Regular testing is a cornerstone of prevention, and the group tracked use of PrEP and PEP, medicines that prevent infection before or after exposure. Data came from a trial in Guangxi run between 2021 and 2023, with visits every three months for a year.

The analysis covered 327 men, and about three quarters tested less often than every three months. Self-testing did not clearly raise testing rates. Men in the middle testing group reported more partners of several kinds, a pattern the authors treat cautiously. The clearer story ran the other way: more frequent testing went hand in hand with higher use of preventive medicines, rising several-fold in the highest testing group. The authors conclude that testing visits remain a doorway into prevention care.
pmc-13624035:
Vladimir Galdino Sabino leads a tissue engineering study testing whether gentle laser light helps stem cells from children's shed baby teeth grow on a fibrous scaffold. The scaffold, spun from a biodegradable plastic, mimics the mesh that holds cells in the body. Light treatment, called photobiomodulation, is known to nudge cell activity, and the team tried two doses.

Cells were seeded on the scaffold and either left alone or treated with a red diode laser at the start and again two days later. The scaffold held up well under material tests, and cells stayed alive and spread across it in all groups. The higher light dose produced the strongest results: metabolic activity ran above the untreated group at two and three days. Microscope images showed broader living coverage with no rise in dead cells. The authors present the pairing as early support for light-assisted dental tissue repair.
pmc-13628435:
Md Tazvir Amin and colleagues validated phone-collected parental survival histories for measuring adult deaths in Bangladesh. Bangladesh leans on surveys for adult mortality, and phone surveys are cheaper and deployable when travel stalls. Their 2021 mobile survey in the Matlab surveillance area matched 2,231 respondents' parental reports against surveillance records.

Parent names matched in about 91 percent of fathers and 95 percent of mothers, and life-or-death reports agreed over 99 percent. Half of parental ages fell within five years below to three years above surveillance ages, and only about 4 percent of deaths landed wrongly around an eight-year window. Death rates matched almost exactly. Amin and colleagues back phone histories for resource-poor mortality tracking.
pmc-13628535:
Michael Quest and seven colleagues probed how a bicyclic four-silicon ring compound, a heavy silicon cousin of the carbon ring cyclobutadiene, reacts with ammonia, water, and alcohols. Published in 2026, the work tests whether this strained ring can split nitrogen-hydrogen and oxygen-hydrogen bonds, a basic step in much of chemistry.

Ammonia and water each added across the ring to give saturated products bearing the expected new groups. Methanol produced a mixture that included an eight-cornered silicon cluster, ethanol gave a related single product, and phenol yielded a simpler addition compound. Computer calculations helped explain why each partner behaved differently. The results extend the known reaction playground of these unusual silicon rings.
pmc-13630835:
Sohrab Rezvani writes, in a 2026 theoretical article, about perezhivanie, a Vygotskian concept for the lived, emotional process through which a person makes sense of experience and is changed by it. Scholars of teaching and identity use the term heavily, Rezvani notes, yet its meaning stays foggy because Vygotsky never fixed a definition.

To sharpen one strand of the concept, struggle, he brings in Bakhtin's theory of artistic creation, reading personality change through literary situations he calls the absurd, the picaresque, and ressentiment. He then turns the combined lens on his own autoethnographic material, tracing his path toward becoming an environmental scholar-activist. The article is offered as a step toward making the concept a workable scientific tool.
pmc-13631235:
Yunhao Yuan and five colleagues test whether large language models can spot worsening depression from phone data. Phones leave a passive trail of movement, sleep, and usage patterns. Such digital phenotyping collects that trail nonstop. The stream is messy and mixed in format, though. That strains standard prediction models. The study appeared in 2026.

The team worked with patients in major depressive episodes. They compared two ways of using the models. One prompts them with a few examples. The other fine-tunes them on the data. Both beat classic baselines at spotting changes in depression severity. Two fine-tuning styles performed much alike overall. One was stronger on single features. The other was stronger on combined inputs. The authors back the approach with caution. They call for clinical checking and ethical safeguards.
pmc-13633335:
Wu and colleagues studied in 2026 why a radioactive therapy aimed at cancer-associated fibroblasts works unevenly. These fibroblasts are support cells inside tumours that express a protein called FAP, the therapy's target. The team examined human pancreatic cancer tissue and built lab models mixing tumour cells and fibroblasts in flat layers and in 3D balls.

In flat cultures the therapy barely harmed cells, but in 3D balls it caused dose-dependent DNA damage and slowed growth. Mixed balls of tumour and fibroblasts took more uniform damage than layered ones. Yet fibroblasts also shielded tumour cells, linked to their release of IL-6 and TGF-β signals. The authors describe a dual role: fibroblasts help irradiate tumours by crossfire, but also soak up drug and send protective signals.
pmc-13635135:
Lu Li, Junbao Wen, and Liming Jia published this 2026 reference genome for a pest moth of subtropical and tropical Asia. Serrodes campana feeds on soapberry trees and damages orchards, yet it had no genome resources. The team combined several sequencing methods, including long-read DNA, chromosome contact data, and gene activity samples. Their assembly arranges nearly all of the DNA into thirty-one chromosome-scale pieces.

Quality checks recovered nearly every expected insect gene, marking the assembly as highly complete. The genome holds just over sixteen thousand protein-coding genes, and nearly all could be given a functional label. About a third of the DNA consists of repeated elements. The authors offer the assembly and its annotations as a foundation for studying how this moth uses its hosts, resists control measures, and evolved alongside related species.
pmc-13639735:
Xuting Zhang and twelve colleagues report building laboratory-grown coronary artery models for studying Kawasaki disease, a childhood illness that inflames blood vessels and can damage the heart's arteries. No good lab platform has existed for recreating how a child's coronary artery behaves in this disease.

The team printed hollow hydrogel fibers and lined them with human coronary smooth muscle and vessel-lining cells. The constructs responded to inflammatory signals, and adding serum from Kawasaki patients created a disease-like state. Two drugs, atorvastatin and an inflammasome blocker called MCC950, calmed the inflammation. The platform could speed the search for targeted treatments.
pmc-13640435:
Sarah H Saxton and fifteen colleagues describe a 2026 method for growing adult human liver cells briefly as organoids before transplanting them into engineered tissue. Bioengineered livers could ease the donor shortage, but adult liver cells usually survive poorly after placement.

The team cultured cells from eight donors aged nineteen to forty-nine, and the organoids kept mature liver shape, gene patterns, and drug-processing ability. Once transplanted, the primed cells settled in up to twenty-five times better than earlier cell preparations. The authors say a short organoid stage could make lab-grown liver tissue far more practical.
pmc-13645735:
Jiaxin Pu and fourteen colleagues map tiny deposits called hard drusen across the outer retina in a Chinese patient group, in a 2026 study from Zhongshan Ophthalmic Center. The deposits show up as bright dots on a dye-based eye scan and may relate to age-related macular degeneration. The team reviewed five years of scans covering 1,562 normal eyes. A machine learning tool counted deposits across nine retinal zones.

Age fifty stood out as a turning point, after which deposits rose in every zone. The zones toward the nose gathered deposits earlier and more heavily than zones toward the temple. One upper central zone tracked with macular deposits and with later progression to the wet form of macular degeneration. The authors suggest that checking the outer retina during these scans could help monitor patients at risk, once forward-looking studies confirm the link.
pmc-13646035:
Colin R Tang-Whitmore and eight colleagues follow thirty-six infants with critical congenital heart disease at one children's hospital, in a 2026 study, to see how feeding relates to growth. These babies face feeding problems and shifting energy needs, and poor growth is tied to worse outcomes. Weekly measures of weight, length, and head size were modeled against weekly protein and calorie intake. Care ran in a cardiac intensive care unit from January 2020 to August 2023.

Higher energy and protein intake went with better expected gains across all three growth measures. Babies who met the daily calorie goal showed a clear gain in length growth. Meeting the protein goal alone showed no separate link with the growth scores. The authors stress that steady nutrition provision matters for these fragile infants, even when illness makes feeding hard to deliver.
pmc-13646135:
Chunli Yang and three colleagues report a rare skin infection caused by the fungus Microascus trigonosporus in a sixty-seven-year-old woman who had never had a transplant. This fungus usually threatens the lungs of transplant patients, and skin cases worldwide are extremely rare. Her redness and pustules spread for two months and ignored a steroid cream. Scrapings, a skin biopsy, fungal culture, and gene sequencing were used to pin down the cause.

Microscopy showed abundant fungal threads, culture grew the organism, and sequencing confirmed the species. Two antifungal drugs given in sequence cleared the lesions fully, with no side effects and no return over a year of follow-up. The authors say the case widens the known range of this fungus beyond transplant hosts. They also credit fast gene-based identification for ending a long diagnostic delay in chronic skin disease.
pmc-13646835:
Ju Hyun Oh and twenty-one colleagues, writing on behalf of a registry investigator group, report the first nationwide registry of rare interstitial lung diseases in South Korea, published in 2026. These lung-scarring diseases are uncommon, varied, and hard to diagnose. Twenty centers enrolled 304 patients between September 2023 and December 2024. Six diseases were covered, from lymphangioleiomyomatosis to pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, with details on symptoms, treatment, and outcomes.

Two diseases made up just over half the registry, while the fibrotic disease PPFE was rarest and deadliest, killing about a quarter of its patients during follow-up. Collapsed lung was common at diagnosis in Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, and cancer appeared in a quarter of those patients over time. Treatments differed sharply by disease, from steroids to whole-lung washing. The authors say the registry proves these diseases need separate diagnostic and treatment playbooks, not one shared approach.
pmc-13648335:
Madeline Martinez and four colleagues map whole-brain activation in mice after drugs that stimulate either the mu opioid receptor or the related NOP receptor. Mu opioids relieve pain but also cause breathing suppression, constipation, and addiction risk, so comparing a different receptor may point toward safer pain relief.

Using reporter mice whose active neurons become permanently tagged, plus tissue clearing and light-sheet microscopy, the team compared single and repeated morphine dosing with an NOP agonist. Morphine raised activation broadly, more strongly in males, while dependence lowered activity in several regions yet widened co-activation networks. The NOP drug produced a far weaker profile, and the authors offer the model for future targeted studies.
pmc-13651535:
Jonas Djossou and eleven co-authors convert plain amino acids straight into vicinal diamines, prized two-nitrogen building blocks for medicines, through a radical shortcut. The classical swap of an acid group for an aminomethyl group takes many steps and harsh reducing agents, which destroy sensitive groups on complex molecules.

Light-driven catalysis knocks carbon dioxide off the amino acid, leaving a radical beside the nitrogen. That radical is caught by a fleeting formimine partner generated in the same pot, an aminomethyl equivalent too unstable to bottle. The one-step process tolerates groups that hydride reductions cannot, and the two nitrogens in the product wear different protective clothing, so each can be changed on its own afterward. Running the reaction in continuous flow multiplied productivity per volume several hundredfold while improving safety. The authors showcase streamlined access to fragments of drug molecules and propose radical disconnection as a general blueprint.
pmc-13651835:
Alexander Muacevic and seven colleagues test whether living rurally shortens survival with rare malignant bone tumors of the spine and pelvis, cancers whose care concentrates in metropolitan centers. Earlier looks at the question mixed tumor types narrowly, held few rural patients, or skipped adjustments, and none weighed geography directly against the poverty that travels with it.

A national registry cohort from 2000 to 2023 held 3,631 patients with four tumor types, about a tenth of them rural. Rural patients clustered heavily in low-income counties. After adjustment, rural residence itself carried no independent survival penalty for either overall or cancer-specific survival. County income, by contrast, showed a clean staircase: each higher income band lived longer than the poorest counties. Surgery and other treatment factors also mattered. The authors conclude that money, more than miles, is the survival divide to close in this population.
pmc-2740835:
Lemey, Rambaut, Drummond, and co-authors describe how Bayesian methods brought geography into virus family trees. Where viruses live and move shapes both local persistence and epidemic spread. Scientists often read that movement through genetic histories, since viral genes record past travel.

Older inference mostly ignored place or handled it crudely. The authors show how a Bayesian approach can reconstruct dispersal and migration directly from sequences plus locations. That advance let researchers trace outbreaks across regions with measured confidence, a method now central to tracking new epidemics.  Virus hunters now use the same approach during fast-moving outbreak investigations.
pmc-4489235:
Xia, Sinelnikov, Han, and their colleagues released MetaboAnalyst version three in 2015. MetaboAnalyst is a web server for metabolomic data, the study of small molecules in cells and fluids. It supports analysis, visualization, and interpretation in one place.

The server handles a wide range of complex statistics and produces high quality graphics. That combination matters because metabolomics data are large and hard to read raw. Users can move from uploaded data to clear plots and pathway views without coding. Version three made the tool more meaningful for studies of disease markers, nutrition, and drug effects.
pmc-4800035:
James, Sydes, Clarke, and their co-authors reported survival results from the STAMPEDE trial in 2016. For decades, going back to the 1940s, long-term hormone therapy was the standard care when prostate cancer had spread. STAMPEDE tested whether adding other treatments at the start would help men live longer.

The trial used an adaptive multiarm, multistage platform design and recruited men with high-risk or spreading disease. Arms added docetaxel chemotherapy, zoledronic acid, or both to hormone therapy. Platform designs test several questions in one trial, saving years over separate studies. STAMPEDE's results changed first-line care for advanced prostate cancer in many countries.
pmc-5428335:
Nishita, Park, Nishio, and their team reported in 2017 on Ror2 signaling and tumor invasion. Signaling through the Ror2 receptor promotes the formation of invadopodia, small feet that cancer cells use to invade tissue. The authors searched for new targets of this signaling in tumors whose cells have no primary cilium.

They identify a transport protein, IFT20, as a new target in this pathway. IFT20 mediates the ability of Ror2 signaling to shape the Golgi apparatus and its transport work, which in turn supports invasiveness. Blocking such a link could slow the spread of cancer cells into surrounding tissue. The study connects a known invasion signal to the cell's internal shipping system.
pmc-5829835:
Christopher Taylor, Jeneita Bell, Matthew Breiding, and coauthors reported United States data on traumatic brain injury in 2017. Head injuries can cause death and lasting disability. They arise from crashes, falls, and assaults among other causes.

Using national records, the report counts emergency visits, hospital stays, and deaths linked to brain injury in two study years. It compares rates across age groups and causes. Falls stand out in older adults, while crashes weigh heavily on younger people. Public health teams use such counts to aim prevention work, from road safety to fall checks at home.
pmc-6299935:
Steven Ge, Eui Son, and Run Yao introduced iDEP, a web app for RNA sequencing data, in 2018. RNA sequencing profiles gene activity, but the analysis can be slow and hard for bench biologists. Coding skill is often the barrier, not the biology.

iDEP lets users upload gene-level counts and explore them in a browser. It clusters samples, finds genes that differ between groups, and maps them to pathways. Interactive plots help users sanity-check each step. By removing setup pain, the tool lets small labs test ideas quickly before committing to a full custom analysis.
pmc-6815535:
Lian-Jiu Su, Jia-Hao Zhang, Hernando Gomez, and coauthors reviewed lipid peroxidation across cell death types in 2019. Reactive oxygen species can attack the fats in cell membranes. That attack spreads as a chain reaction through the membrane.

The resulting damage helps drive apoptosis, autophagy-linked death, and ferroptosis. Iron feeds the process in ferroptosis, which sets it apart. The authors compare how each death type uses or suffers this chemistry. Antioxidant defenses that break the chain are a shared drug interest across all three areas. Blocking the chain reaction is discussed as a shared strategy across several diseases of aging.
pmc-7164635:
Renhong Yan, Yuanyuan Zhang, Yaning Li, and coauthors solved how SARS-CoV-2 binds human ACE2 in 2020. Viral entry starts when the spike protein latches onto the ACE2 receptor. The team captured the full-length receptor with the spike's binding piece attached.

The structure shows the grip in atomic detail and how it differs from the earlier SARS virus. A tighter, well-fitted interface helps explain efficient human infection. The picture guided antibody and vaccine design aimed at that exact contact surface. It remains one of the most cited structural papers of the pandemic.
poe-unparalleled-adventure-hans-pfaall-1:
Edgar Allan Poe wrote of Hans Pfaall in 1835. The tale is set as a found text from Rotterdam in Holland. Pfaall is a poor bellows mender sunk in debt to harsh men. He builds a vast balloon and gear to breathe in thin air.

He rides the balloon to the Moon in a trip of weeks. The tale revels in gear lists, air math, and the look of Earth from high up. A note from the Moon, sent down in a small craft, ends the tale. The work is a key first tale of the trip to space.
quetelet-treatise-on-man-1835:
Adolphe Quetelet's Treatise on Man is dated 1835 in this entry, from his French work of that year, in English dress of 1842. Quetelet, a Belgian astronomer turned statistician, applied the methods of the observatory to human society. He called the result social physics.

Quetelet showed that births, marriages, crimes, and suicides follow steady patterns year after year, as if society obeyed laws like nature. His famous average man summed up a whole people in one figure. Critics feared his numbers erased free will. The book founded social statistics. It still stands behind every modern claim that human conduct can be counted and foretold.
r-abrahami-eleazaris-uraltes-chymisches-: R. Abrahami Eleazaris uraltes chymisches Werck, 1735. The ancient chemical work. This book preserves that work. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
revelations-cabalistiques-d-une-medecine: A French title page of 1735, dated M.DCCXXXV and much garbled, opens this medical work. Its title promises cabalistic revelations of a universal medicine drawn from wine. Added parts give a way to extract the salt of dew, and a dissertation on sepulchral lamps. It was printed at Amiens by the king's printer, rue de Beau-Puits, at the sign of the Bible d'Or. Its author is named as a doctor of Amiens, but his name is not legible, and no page beyond the title is shown.
seven-witches-witchcrafts-strange-1635:
Seven witches said to work against great persons stand at the center of a 1635 pamphlet, Witchcrafts, Strange and Wonderfull. The print belongs to the Caroline age, when Charles the First held the throne. Beside the case, it offers a guide to finding witchcraft out.

The guide lists signs, acts, and tests by which the guilty might be known. Court news and how-to counsel thus share one small book. Readers of 1635 were taught not just what had been done, but how to watch their own towns. The pamphlet is both a trial record and a manual of alarm.
smith-doctrine-covenants-1835:
Kirtland, Ohio printed the first Doctrine and Covenants in 1835, the young church's book of revelations. Joseph Smith and his counsellors, Oliver Cowdery, Sidney Rigdon, and Frederick G. Williams, stood behind the edition. It gathered the revelations Smith had received, the commandments guiding the Latter Day Saints.

Bound with the revelations stand the Lectures on Faith, seven talks on doctrine later dropped from the book. That pairing makes the 1835 edition precious: later printings changed the contents. As the founding doctrinal text of the movement, this first form shows Mormon scripture before it settled into its standard shape.
social-security-act-1935:
Franklin Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act in 1935, amid deep depression. The New Deal law creates old-age pensions for American workers. Jobless insurance and aid to the needy stand in its other titles.

The act founds what later ages call the American welfare state. Old age, the law pledges, need not mean poverty and fear. Workers and bosses pay in, and the retired draw their checks. Critics then and since have fought over its costs and reach. No New Deal law has touched more lives for so long since 1935. Its monthly checks remain the floor under old age in America.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5035:
Warren Harding gives two yearly addresses, dated December 6, 1921, and December 8, 1922, parted by three stars. The first counts it a glad privilege to come to Congress with the republic at peace with all the nations of the world. More, no near threat of war hangs over the country, and signs grow that the peace so deeply prized will last.

For about ten years, Harding says, the nation has dwelt amid threats of war or in war itself. The aftermath, with its tangled state, has added to the weights of rule in ways none but those who bear them can weigh. The task is the harder since so much of the world shares the tangle. No lasting settling can be made without heed to America's sure tie to world affairs in finance and trade, he argues.
swan-speculum-mundi-1635:
John Swan, an English minister, published Speculum Mundi in 1635. The Latin title means a mirror of the world. Swan set out to survey all creation in order, as an act of both learning and devotion, for readers who wanted the world explained in one book.

Beasts, stars, waters, and wonders pass in review through its chapters. Among them sits the famous tale of the Edam mermaid of 1403. Dutch fishermen, Swan reports, caught her and kept her for years. Such stories stand beside plain teaching without apology. The book shows a pious, curious mind taking in the whole of creation at once.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: The front matter present for this number of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is headed Vol. 1, No. 30, June 3, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only that front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a premium offer for golf sticks. Any one of the sticks shown is sent, express paid, for two new subscribers. A picture lists them: putter, brassie spoon, brassie niblick, driver, cleek, mashie, and iron putter.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
Don Quixote, by Miguel de Cervantes, reaches Volume 2, Part 35 here, in John Ormsby's translation. Chapter fifty-eight tells how adventures came crowding on Don Quixote in such numbers that they gave one another no breathing-time. Free of the castle, the knight feels at ease in open country and in fresh spirits for chivalry.

Turning to Sancho, he praises freedom as one of the most precious gifts heaven has given men. No treasures buried in the earth or hidden in the sea, he says, can compare with it. Cervantes gives the defeated road a noble speech, then lets fresh adventures press in before the knight can rest on it.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
A supplementary number of the Mirror, No. 399, opens its Spirit of the Annuals for 1830 with a kaleidoscopic survey of the gift books. The annuals are called elegant trifles, the very jewellery of art and literature, air-plants whose light flowers entwine with our best affections. The survey begins with The Gem, nearly the youngling of the flock. Its engraving of Verona, by W. J. Cooke, comes from a drawing among the relics of the late Mr. Bonington.

Mrs. Maria Callcott's sketch describes Verona's ancient towers and the Maffei Palace, marks of the Gothic capital of northern Italy. Nature shares the city's charm: the broad, rapid Adige nearly surrounds it. Hills toward the Tyrol soften into vineyards, fields, and gardens among villas and cypress groves as they approach. Readers take a Grand Tour in miniature, gift-book sized, before the other annuals are opened.

Ampthill House, seat of Lord Holland, fills the opening of volume 17, No. 491, dated May 28, 1831. The engraving was copied from a series of select views of Bedfordshire. Letterpress by the Rev. I. D. Parry, author of a history of Woburn, accompanies the picture.

Built of good stone in 1694 by the first Lord Ashburnham, the house stands below a hilltop with a wide view over the vale of Bedford. It has a long, well-windowed front and two deep projecting wings. A lime alley hides behind it, sheltered by trees. Inside, a small collection of paintings, mostly portraits, is noted, along with a large picture once painted on a wall at Houghton House.
tob-0035:
For about two decades the Central Intelligence Agency backed a strange experiment: could trained viewers describe distant places by mind alone? Files from that effort, run under names ending with the Stargate Project, were later declassified. Protocols, session records, and official reviews survive in the paperwork.

Remote viewers sat in offices and reported images of bases, hostages, and hidden sites. The agency's own reviewers weighed hits against misses and judged the results too weak for real spying. The files remain gripping as Cold War history: careful men in gray offices filing reports on psychics. Espionage has no odder chapter.
tob-13335:
Evelyn Underhill published Mysticism in 1911, a study of the nature and growth of man's spiritual awareness. She wrote as a scholar who also practiced the life she described. The large book at once became the standard English work on its subject.

Underhill traces the mystic way through awakening, purification, illumination, the dark night, and union, drawing on saints and writers from many ages. She quotes widely and treats mysticism as a real, testable side of human life. Her book brought the mystics to modern general readers and founded the modern study of the subject in English.
tob-14435:
The Sentences of Sextus gather 451 short sayings on how to live, credited to a sage named Sextus. Pagans and Christians of the ancient world both prized the set. A copy turned up at Nag Hammadi, and church writers quoted it for centuries.

The sayings urge control of the tongue, freedom from passion, care for the soul, and a life made like God's. Many lines run to a single sharp sentence a reader can carry all day. Origen cited the collection with respect. It stands as proof that moral wisdom in the ancient world crossed the lines between faiths.
tob-4135:
A. E. Waite published The Doctrine and Literature of the Kabalah in 1902, the first full English study of Jewish mysticism's teachings and books. The Sefer Yetzirah, the Book of Formation, and the Zohar, the Book of Splendor, receive long treatment. Later Kabbalists and their schools fill out the survey.

Waite reads the tradition as a secret doctrine of the soul's return to God, a view colored by his own mystic hopes. Scholars now correct him often, but for decades his book was the doorway. Verified from the 1919 edition, it shows Victorian occult scholarship at its most serious and industrious.
tob-4235:
William Smith edited the Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities, and the revised edition of 1870 became the Victorian classicist's constant companion. Article by article, the dictionary covers law, war, religion, dress, coinage, and daily life in the ancient world. Smith marshaled a team of scholars to write it.

A student with a question about a Roman court, a Greek ship, or a festival calendar found the answer here, with sources cited. Illustrations of tools, arms, and buildings crowd the pages. Verified from the 1919 edition, the dictionary served schools and universities for a century, and antiquarians still pull it down.
un-ga-res-35: Five states knocked on the UN's door in 1946 and got no answer from the Security Council. Albania, Mongolia, Transjordan, Ireland, and Portugal had all applied, and the Council had made no recommendation on any of them. Resolution 35, passed on 19 November 1946, sends the five bids back. The Council is told to judge each one on its own merits, by the test of the Charter.
un-ga-res-a-69-35:
Zones free of nuclear arms now cover the southern half of the earth, and Resolution A/69/35, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, marks their reach. The text recalls the rules of the 1978 disarmament session on such zones. It backs the 1999 guide lines on how zones should be set up, by free deal among the states of a region.

Four pacts are named: Tlatelolco for Latin America, Rarotonga for the South Pacific, Bangkok for Southeast Asia, and Pelindaba for Africa, with the Antarctic Treaty beside them. All the southern zones, the text notes with pleasure, are now in force. One hundred fifteen states stand as parties to such pacts. Joint work among them, through shared meetings, is urged on.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 35 was adopted on 19 November 1946, at the forty-ninth plenary meeting. It took up five stalled membership bids. Albania, the Mongolian People's Republic, the Hashemite Kingdom of Transjordan, Ireland, and Portugal had all applied. But the Security Council had sent the Assembly no recommendation on any of them. Membership stands open to peace-loving states able and willing to meet the Charter's terms. Recalling that, the Assembly urged the Council to weigh each bid again on its own merits.

General Assembly resolution 69/35 (2014) celebrates the nuclear-weapon-free southern hemisphere. It welcomes the contribution of the Antarctic Treaty and the treaties of Tlatelolco, Rarotonga, Bangkok, and Pelindaba. It notes that all southern-hemisphere nuclear-weapon-free zones are now in force. They cover 115 states parties and signatories. The Assembly calls for adherence to the zones' protocols by the states concerned. It calls for withdrawal of reservations by nuclear-weapon states. It calls for closer cooperation among the zones. It reaffirms freedom of the high seas and rights of passage.
un-sc-res-1035: Bearing number 1035, this resolution of the Security Council is dated 1995 in the catalog. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1335: Holding number 1335 in the Council series, this resolution carries a 1999 date in the library catalog. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-135:
In May 1960, a planned summit of the leaders of France, the Soviet Union, Britain, and the United States fell apart, and public hopes for easing the Cold War fell with it. Resolution 135, adopted on 27 May 1960 by nine votes to none, speaks to that moment of disappointment and rising tension.

The Council warns that the arms race adds to the danger. It recommends that the governments concerned settle their disputes by talks or other peaceful means, as the Charter provides. It appeals to all member governments to avoid the use or threat of force, and to respect each other's sovereignty, land, and political independence.
un-sc-res-1435:
Israeli troops had surrounded the Palestinian leader's compound in Ramallah in September 2002. On 23 September 2002 the Security Council demanded an end to the siege measures. It repeated its call for a complete halt to violence. Terror attacks, provocation, and destruction all had to stop. The Council condemned bombings against civilians in Israel days earlier. It also condemned an attack in a Palestinian school.

Israel had to stop destroying Palestinian civilian and security buildings. Its forces had to pull back fast to the positions held before September 2000. The Palestinian Authority had to bring those behind terror acts to justice. The vote was fourteen to none. The United States abstained.
un-sc-res-1535:
The Counter-Terrorism Committee was rebuilt with a professional arm on 26 March 2004. Resolution 1373 (2001) had set every state's duties after the September 2001 attacks. The committee of Council members had checked state reports for two years. Its report on revitalization, S/2004/124, proposed a stronger structure. States were reminded that counter-terrorism steps must respect human rights, refugee, and humanitarian law.

The Council endorsed the revitalization report. The renewed committee would pair a plenary of Council states with a bureau. A new Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate, CTED, headed by an executive director, would do the expert work. The director had to file an organizational plan within thirty days of taking office. The plan would go to the Council for its blessing. The committee would keep reporting to the Council at regular times. CTED became the standing expert staff of the Council's counter-terrorism watch.
un-sc-res-1635:
MONUC was extended through Congo's election year on 28 October 2005. The Pretoria transition deal still framed the country's path. Elections were the base for lasting peace, the Council stressed. Militias and foreign armed groups in the east kept fighting and threatened the polls. Rights abuses by those groups were deplored.

The Council extended MONUC's mandate until 30 September 2006. The temporary rise in strength granted that September would stay part of the mission until that date at the latest, and its short-term character was stressed. Transitional bodies and all Congolese parties were called to keep the elections free, fair, and on time. The unity government had to press security sector reform and the disarmament of fighters. Donors were urged to keep funding the process as a matter of urgency. MONUC, within its means, was asked to support the electoral work and protect civilians under threat.
un-sc-res-1735:
Sanctions on Al-Qaida and the Taliban are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1735, adopted on 22 December 2006. Attacks in Afghanistan were rising, and the groups were spreading their message online. The sanctions list had grown for seven years, yet states applied it unevenly. Fairer listing steps had become a pressing demand.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council restates the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo on everyone on the list. States proposing new names must now file a detailed statement of case. Listed people must be told why they were named and how to seek removal. The committee gains clearer rules for taking names off. Freeze rules are spelled out to reach money of every kind, even funds behind web services.
un-sc-res-1835:
Iran's nuclear file returned to the Council in Resolution 1835, adopted in September 2008. Earlier rounds had already placed sanctions on Tehran over uranium enrichment. This text restated those demands and pressed Iran to answer inspectors' questions about possible military work.

The members call again for Iran to suspend enrichment and to cooperate fully with the International Atomic Energy Agency. No new sanctions were added, which itself signaled division among the major powers. For readers, the resolution is a snapshot of a standoff hardening: the demands stay fixed while the pressure stalls.
un-sc-res-1935:
Resolution 1935 brought Darfur under a formal Council decision, adopted on 30 July 2010. Security had worsened again that year. Rebel attacks, air strikes by the government, and tribal fighting all rose. Peacekeepers faced ambushes, and one helicopter pilot had been seized. Some armed groups still refused to join peace talks.

The Council extends the African Union-United Nations force, called UNAMID, for twelve months to 31 July 2011. Guarding civilians across Darfur comes first in every use of its strength. Safe and open aid access ranks second. The mission must draft a full strategy to reach those aims. All sides are told to stop fighting and to stop attacking civilians, aid staff, and peacekeepers at once.
un-sc-res-235: The record catalogued as Resolution 235, dated 1967, preserves one formal decision of the United Nations Security Council. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-2735:
Resolution 2735, adopted in June 2024, put the Security Council behind a ceasefire plan for the war in Gaza. The plan, announced by the United States, set out stages meant to end the fighting that began in October 2023. The Council welcomed the proposal and urged both sides to accept it.

The stages in the text move from a first halt in fighting and hostage releases to a permanent end of hostilities and Gaza's reconstruction. It also rejects any change to Gaza's territory. The resolution matters as the Council's clearest shared call to close that war, after months of divided votes.
un-sc-res-335: Two German states were recommended for United Nations membership by the Security Council on 22 June 1973. The Council had taken up the applications of the German Democratic Republic and the Federal Republic of Germany one by one. It recommended to the General Assembly that the German Democratic Republic be admitted. It recommended in the same terms that the Federal Republic of Germany be admitted. The recommendations opened the way for both states to take seats that autumn, a marker of the Cold War division being managed rather than settled.
un-sc-res-35: The Council spoke on Committee work through Resolution 35, adopted on 3 October 1947 by nine votes to none, with two abstentions. A Committee of Three had been formed under an earlier text that year. The Council asks the Secretary-General to call the committee together and arrange how its work is organized. It also asks the three members to take up their duties with the utmost speed. The short text settles only the machinery, leaving the substance to the committee itself.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1035 was adopted unanimously on 21 December 1995. It follows up the General Framework Agreement for Peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina and resolution 1031, which authorized the multinational implementation force IFOR. Acting on the Secretary-General's report of 13 December 1995, the Council approves his proposals for the United Nations part in carrying out the Peace Agreement.

The Council establishes a United Nations civilian police force, the International Police Task Force (IPTF), for one year. The year runs from the transfer of authority from the United Nations Protection Force to IFOR. A United Nations civilian office is established together with it. The Task Force takes the police tasks set out in Annex 11 of the Peace Agreement. It works under the Secretary-General's authority, with coordination by the High Representative. It is to be reported on at least every three months.

For the Prevlaka peninsula, the disputed coastal strip between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, calm on the ground still did not settle who owned the land. United Nations observers, UNMOP, watched that the zone stayed demilitarized. This text of 12 January 2001 decides how long they would stay.

The observers were authorized to keep working until 15 July 2001. The Council welcomed the open crossing points in the zone, which let civilians and trade pass safely in both directions. It still flagged breaches of the demilitarization rules and limits on the observers' freedom of movement, and it urged both sides to resume talks toward a negotiated settlement.

Days after a four-power summit in Paris collapsed, this text of 27 May 1960 speaks to a frightened world. Hopes for a meeting of the leaders of France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States had just failed. Public worry about rising tension and the arms race runs through every line.

Governments are urged to settle their disputes by talks and other peaceful means under the Charter. All states are asked to avoid force or threats and to respect each other's borders and independence. The four powers are pressed to keep working on full disarmament under world control, an end to nuclear tests, and talks against surprise attack.

Israeli tanks surrounded Yasser Arafat's headquarters in Ramallah in September 2002. The siege followed suicide bombings inside Israel on 18 and 19 September. Troops had also re-entered other Palestinian cities. Resolution 1435 was adopted on 23 September 2002. Fourteen members voted yes. The United States abstained.

The Council demanded an immediate end to the measures around Ramallah. Destruction of Palestinian offices and services had to stop. Israeli forces were told to withdraw quickly to positions held before September 2000. Terror attacks on civilians were condemned on all sides. The Palestinian Authority had to bring attackers to justice. Support flowed to the Quartet's peace efforts.

Resolution 1535, adopted unanimously on 26 March 2004, builds a professional staff for the Council's counter-terrorism watchdog. The Counter-Terrorism Committee, created after the September 2001 attacks, reviewed how states carried out their duties to suppress terror financing and deny safe haven. Member states were praised for cooperating with it, and reminded that counter-terrorism measures must still respect human rights, refugee, and humanitarian law.

The Council approved the committee's revitalization plan and created its Executive Directorate, CTED, staffed by experts who would visit countries, assess gaps, and arrange technical help. The directorate was set up as a special political mission for an initial period ending in December 2007, subject to review. Later resolutions kept extending it.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo's move toward elections is the focus of Resolution 1635, adopted on 28 October 2005. The UN Organization Mission there, MONUC, backed a transition set out in a 2002 peace deal. Militias and foreign armed groups still fought in the east, abused civilians, and threatened the planned vote. Illegal mining and the arms trade helped feed the conflict.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MONUC until 30 September 2006. It allows 300 more troops so an infantry battalion can deploy in Katanga for extra safety during the election period. It marks that rise as temporary. It calls on Congolese leaders to hold free, fair, and calm elections on the agreed timetable. It also calls on them to merge the armed forces and national police into one service with proper pay and supplies.

The Al-Qaida and Taliban sanctions machinery is tightened in Resolution 1735, adopted on 22 December 2006. The 1267 Committee's Consolidated List was growing, states were listing names with uneven evidence, and listed people often learned of it late.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council confirms the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo on listed Al-Qaida, Taliban, and associated persons and entities. It stresses that the freeze reaches economic resources of every kind, including internet hosting services. States proposing listings must file a detailed statement of case on a standard cover sheet, marking what can be made public. The Secretariat must notify the states concerned within two weeks of a listing, with the public case summary and delisting procedures. The Committee must keep developing delisting guidelines, weighing mistaken identity, death, or severed association. The window for objecting to basic-expense exemptions grows from 48 hours to three working days.

Iran's nuclear programme is taken up again on 27 September 2008, without new sanctions being added. The atomic energy agency's September report described continued non-compliance. The six negotiating powers had restated their two-track approach: talks and incentives on one side, pressure on the other, and that framework is backed again.

Earlier positions are reaffirmed: the presidential statement of March 2006 and the four Iran resolutions that followed it. Commitment to an early negotiated solution is restated, and continuing efforts toward one are welcomed. Iran is called on to comply fully and without delay with its duties under those resolutions and the agency's requirements, above all suspending enrichment work. The matter stays under review.

Darfur's hybrid mission is extended with civilian protection as its first priority in Resolution 1935, adopted on 30 July 2010. Security in Darfur was deteriorating. There were ceasefire violations, rebel attacks, government aerial bombardment, and inter-tribal fighting. Attacks on humanitarian workers and peacekeepers restricted aid access. UNAMID was nearing full deployment, and Sudan and Chad had normalized relations in January 2010 with a joint border force.

The Council extends the African Union-United Nations Hybrid Operation in Darfur, UNAMID, for twelve months to 31 July 2011. UNAMID must give priority to protecting civilians across Darfur and to safe, timely, unhindered humanitarian access. It must develop a comprehensive strategy for both and support the AU-UN political process and the Joint Chief Mediator. The Council strongly condemns attacks on UNAMID, demands Sudan remove obstacles to its movement and comply with the Status of Forces Agreement, and requires ninety-day progress reports against benchmarks.

During the Six-Day War, Israel and Syria each announced that they accepted the Council's demand for a cease-fire. Resolution 235, adopted unanimously on 9 June 1967, followed two resolutions passed earlier the same week. The Council confirmed those calls for an immediate cease-fire and an end to all military action. It demanded that hostilities stop at once. The Secretary-General was told to contact both governments immediately, arrange full compliance, and report back within two hours. That deadline shows how fast events were moving that day.

A three-phase cease-fire plan for the war in Gaza won the Council's backing on 10 June 2024. Egypt, Qatar, and the United States had been mediating between Israel and Hamas. A new proposal had been announced on 31 May 2024. Resolution 2735 deals with that proposal.

The Council welcomed the plan and noted that Israel had accepted it. Hamas was called on to accept it too, and both sides were urged to carry it out in full. The first phase would bring a complete cease-fire and the release of hostages. Women, the elderly, and the wounded were named in particular. The second phase would end the fighting for good, free the remaining hostages, and pull Israeli forces out of Gaza. The third phase would start a major rebuilding plan for Gaza, lasting several years.

Two German states enter the United Nations in a single text, Resolution 335, adopted on 22 June 1973. The Council considered the applications separately: one from the German Democratic Republic in the east, another from the Federal Republic of Germany in the west. Their applications arrived days apart in June, after the two states had signed a treaty regulating relations between them.

The Council recommends that the General Assembly admit the German Democratic Republic, and then, in a parallel line, that it admit the Federal Republic of Germany. The paired recommendation was a landmark of Cold War diplomacy, accepting divided Germany into the UN as two states. Both took their seats that September.

Early Council business often ran through small committees. Resolution 35, adopted on 3 October 1947, concerns one such group, a committee of three member states. Poland and the Soviet Union abstained in the vote. The committee itself had been created days earlier by Resolution 31.

The text gives the Secretary-General a practical task. He must call the three members together. He must also arrange how their work is organized. The committee, for its part, is told to move fast. It should begin exercising its functions with the utmost dispatch. The resolution is two sentences long, a glimpse of the Council's working habits in 1947.

Armenia emerged from the Soviet Union's collapse as an independent republic. It applied for a UN seat within weeks of the old union's end. Resolution 735, adopted without a vote on 29 January 1992, considered that application. The meeting was the Council's 3041st.

Members recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of Armenia. The Assembly did so in March 1992. Armenia joined alongside a rush of former Soviet republics. Each arrival redrew the UN's map of Eurasia. For Armenia, membership confirmed its sovereignty in law. It also gave the small Caucasus state a voice while war with Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh was intensifying.
